title: The kindness of strangers: I was a ball of stress taking my four children on an international flight – then a passenger tucked a blanket around my sleeping son | Parents and parenting | The Guardian
description: Walking on to the plane with the kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, ‘Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!’
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: Walking on to the plane with the kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, ‘Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!’
Content: ‘My husband travelled ahead to organise a place for us to live. I followed him seven weeks later with our four children.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian designView image in fullscreen‘My husband travelled ahead to organise a place for us to live. I followed him seven weeks later with our four children.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian designKindness of strangersParents and parentingThe kindness of strangers: I was a ball of stress taking my four children on an international flight – then a passenger tucked a blanket around my sleeping sonWalking on to the plane with the kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, ‘Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!’Read more inthe kindness of strangers seriesAnonymous, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwon’t lie – I was having nightmares before the trip. When my family immigrated to Australia from Europe, my husband travelled ahead to organise a place for us to live. I followed him seven weeks later with our four children, all aged under seven. I was aball of stress for weeks in the lead-up.Walking on to the plane with four kids in tow, I could almost hear people think, “Oh my God, I don’t want to be seated next to them!” And I completely understand.The kindness of strangers: On a busy motorway, my child vomited in the car. I was overwhelmed – then a man came with a bucket of waterRead moreI had booked a window row and a seat in the middle row, thinking that I could put all the kids in the window row and then myself in the middle, where I could keep an eye on them. But when we got into the plane, the flight attendant told me that for security reasons we couldn’t do it that way. We had to rejig, my five-year-old son taking the middle-row seat alone, for what was to be a nearly 24-hour flight broken up into two legs.There was a man seated next to my son. He didn’t display any of the annoyance he must be feeling about being seated next to a small child – a very kind act in itself, and one that brought me great relief. But his kindness didn’t end there.At some point during the flight, after the cabin lights dimmed, the other three kids and I dozed off. When I woke up, I looked over to see my five-year-old had fallen asleep as well. The man next to him was pulling his blanket up and gently tucking him in. It was an unguarded moment of care and compassion.I don’t think the man had any idea I saw him do that. We arrived safely and I never saw him again. But it was such a generous thing to do that, 20 years later, the memory remains magical.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: It’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mounts
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: It’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mounts
Content: ‘Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible.’Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible.’Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpAnalysisAs White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrailsJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonIt’s not clear that financial interests are driving White House policy, but they run parallel even as resistance mountsSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareDonald Trump’s sons, through a series ofAI-linked defense and technology ventures, have picked up a $620m Pentagon loan, a Marine Corps robotics contract and an undisclosed air force drone deal in the past year. His longtime friend Michael Dell won a Pentagon contract worth nearly $9bn. And this week, as public support for artificial intelligence sinks to some of the lowest levels ever recorded, the president went to bat for the industry.“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he posted on Truth Social Monday. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers.” It was the first of many aggressively pro-AI posts he would make this week.Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel.The administration frames its resistance chiefly as a matter of competitiveness. Trump and officials including David Sacks, who co-chairs his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, have repeatedly argued that new rules could slow US AI development when the country is racing China for dominance of the technology. Sackssaid at a Politico summiton Wednesday that recent warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI about the technology’s risks amounted to political theater, manufactured by advocacy groups and the press, and said existing laws were largely sufficient.30:27But many concerns are coming from inside the industry itself. In early September,Jacob Coxon– a researcher who spent three years working on the foundational training of AI models at both OpenAI and Anthropic – resigned and published a stark warning.“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said colleagues privately believe the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Anthropic’s head of AI safety, Mrinank Sharma,separately resignedthe same week, writing that “the world is in peril.”Those warnings coincided with a concrete demonstration of AI-enabled risk. A California cybersecurity firmdisclosed this monththat it had used artificial intelligence to build a self-spreading worm capable of hijacking WeChat accounts through a single unanswered call, and then automatically spreading through the victim’s contact list. The firm estimated the technology could compromise more than a billion devices within hours.Tencent,the Chinese tech giant that owns WeChat,patched the vulnerability before it was deployed and said no accounts were affected, but the firm noted that building the exploit, work it said would once have taken a larger team months, took roughly 10 days with AI assistance. Around the same time, JD Vance, speakingon a Christian podcast, described certain uses of AI as carrying “really, really weird spiritual dark energy” and said there are “things about the world” that leave him “not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us”.Polling shows how far out of step Trump’s posture is with the public, particularly once AI’s costs become tangible. A poll released on Wednesday foundjust 11% of Americanssupport an AI datacenter being built in their own community, while 65% oppose one – including 52% of Republicans – and 57% say Trump has handled the issue of AI poorly, up seven points since March. The same day, the Housevoted 417-3to require datacenters to bear the costs of the electricity-grid upgrades their operations demand, underscoring how concerns about AI’s infrastructure costs have moved from polling into Congress.If the federal government did enact regulations that ultimately damaged AI profits, it’s possible some members of the Trump family would feel the pain.Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trumpjoined the investment firm Dominari Holdingslast year and helpedlaunch American Data Centers Inc, an AI infrastructure venture in which Dominari holds a minority stake. The deal came weeks after their father unveiledan expected $20bndatacenter pledge from Emirati billionaire Hussain Sajwani, and$500 bnin planned private sector AI investment, alongside an executive order unwinding Biden-era AI safeguards.Since then, the brothers have moved from infrastructure into defense contracting, most notably through Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth magnet startup whose products are used in AI datacenters, drones and defense systems. Three months before the Pentagonannounced its $620m loanto Vulcan in December – the largest the defense department’s office of strategic capital has ever issued – 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Trump Jr is a partner, quietly took a stake in the company. AProPublica investigationfound the loan request came not from Vulcan or the Pentagon but from Peter Navarro, a senior White House adviser and close friend of Trump Jr’s, and that Pentagon staff were told to move at an “unusually rapid pace”.“The call came from the White House: We have to get this done,” one person involved in the deal told the outlet.Trump Jr’s spokesman, the Pentagon and Vulcan have all said he played no role in the deal and that the company received no political favoritism. Eric Trump, separately, serves as chief strategy adviser to Foundation Future Industries, the robotics startupbehind the $24m Marine Corps contract; senator Elizabeth Warrencalled that award“corruption in plain sight”. A third venture, the drone maker Powerus backed by both brothers and having signed anew agreement with Pakistan’s army, also holdsa $90m air force contract, and has separately pitched its technology to Gulf states amid Iran’s striking of US bases across the region. Drones are widely expected to increasingly utilize AI technology in the coming years.AWashington Post analysis in Julyfound 15 companies tied to the brothers’ investment funds have generated at least $3.2bn in direct federal business since they got involved, but SpaceX and Anduril,the latter an AI-powered defense technology firm behindLatticeaccount for 97% of that figure, and 10 of the 15 companies already had government business before the Trump sons invested.Excluding SpaceX and Anduril, the remaining 13 companies had received $103m in direct federal funding and nearly $1.8bn in long-term commitments after the brothers’ investments.The pattern extends beyond Trump’s family to some of his closest technology allies. Sacks’s influence over Trump’s regulatory decisions has been substantial: in May,he reportedly persuaded the presidentin a last-minute call to scrap a planned executive order that would have subjected AI models to extended government review, overriding the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who had spent months negotiating the stronger version.His own financial position has drawn scrutiny inside the administration as a result. Sacks’s venture firm holds stakes in SpaceX and a range of AI startups, along with earlier investments in Meta, Palantir and Airbnb; federal ethics rules required him to divest only some of those holdings while he served as the White House’s AI and crypto czar, a post he left in March. Some administration officials have privately looked into whether Sacks could personally benefit from blocking new AI rules, the Wall Street Journal reported.The outlet reported that Musk pushed in the same direction, joining Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang last month in personally lobbying Trump against a proposed industry-funded AI oversight body, helping shelve the plan. Dell, a member of Trump’s science and technology advisory council and a longtime friend and donor to the president, saw his companywin the nearly $9bn Pentagon contractin May, prompting ethics watchdogs to question whether his advisory role created an unaddressed conflict.The technology industry is not uniformly aligned behind Trump.Federal filings on OpenSecretsshow the broader communications and electronics sector still sends roughly two-thirds of its political money to Democratic candidates and committees this cycle. Trump’s support among industry figures has come instead from a narrower group: OpenAI’sSam Altmanand Greg Brockman have given tens of millions of dollars to a pro-Trump super Pac and Trump’s inaugural committee, though have also donated to Democrats in the past.The Pentagon’s own account of its safeguards makes no distinction between a routine contractor and a company whose investors include the president’s son, which is a gap Democratic lawmakers asked the Pentagon’sinspector general to investigatelast month.Next week, Trump isset to hostthe leaders of the country’s leading AI companies at the White House, a meeting arranged with the House speaker, Mike Johnson, that will coincide with a visit from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.In the meantime, the investments continue.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)analysisShareReuse this content

title: Singer Becky Hill looks back: ‘Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s’ | Becky Hill | The Guardian
description: The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndrome
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndrome
Content: FlashbackBecky HillSinger Becky Hill looks back: ‘Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s’The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndromeHarriet GibsoneSun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBecky Hill in a sleeveless lilac dress and with a comical smile in 2001 and 2026, aged seven and 32, respectivelyBecky Hill in 2001 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen. Styling: Andie Redman. Hair and makeup: Wendy Turner. Archive photograph: courtesy of Becky HillBorn in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, in 1994 and raised in Bewdley,Becky Hillis a singer and songwriter. She began making music at 14, performing in a band called Shaking Trees, before reaching the semifinals on the first series of The Voice UK. She has since had two top 10 albums and collaborated with David Guetta, Chase and Status, Joel Corry and Rudimental, and won the Brit award for best dance act in 2022 and 2023. Her latest album, Rebecca, is out on 13 November.This was taken for a kids’modellingagency,which we later discovered was a scam. Every stage of the process – getting pictures taken, sending them to the agency, getting them back – cost us more money. We’d wire over £100 and get nothing in return. Our family wasn’t rich, so Mum didn’t tell Dad what we were up to – he probably doesn’t even know about it to this day. As for my modelling ambitions, I never pursued it further. I was cute until the age of seven, then started to go on the turn.Meera Syal looks back: ‘South Asians weren’t seen as funny. We sold you fags or served you curry’Read moreI was a happy, chatty child, but my home life was quite dysfunctional. My parents were on their second marriages, I was their first baby together, and they had five children between the two of them – some lived with us, some didn’t. There was a lot of moving about – a lot of arguing, too, but I always, always felt loved. Everyone had their own taste in music: Mum listened to cassette tapes of Foreigner, Eric Clapton and the Eagles; my sister gave me her computer full of all her downloaded music; and my brother liked Eminem, Blink-182, Slipknot and drum’n’bass.I was always a mummy’s girl,and she and I would go to acting, singing and dancing classes together. She wanted me to find something I was passionate about, as I was bullied at school. I kept my singing a secret mostly, but when I was 11 there was a talent show at school and I performed JoJo’s Leave (Get Out) in front of all the parents. I’ll never forget the feeling of singing that song and realising that everyone’s jaws were on the floor. I could see other parents turning around in their chairs and asking my mum and dad: “Did you know she could do this?”On the car journey home, there was a conversation about my future. Dad asked Mum: “Do we send her to a stage school where her talent can be nurtured?” Mum knew we didn’t have the money or live in the right place. She said: “But if music is meant for her, music will find her,” which I thought was beautiful.Luckily, I found some good support in Bewdley – from my music teacher and Andy Brown, a guy who was dating a friend’s mum. He had management experience and took me under his wing – buying me a guitar and paying for singing lessons and studio time. It was a rare taste of what it was like to be nurtured without expectation.My teenage years were typically fraught – I got my braces off by the time I was 13, so at least my teeth were fixed, but I started smoking weed and was temporarily a bit of an angry kid. Discovering drum’n’bass was a real escape – when I was at a rave, I had music to focus on rather than the way I looked or felt. I remember going to [the London club] Fabric for the first time at 18, walking down the stairs and thinking, “I’m home.”double quotation markIt’s hard to be gentle on yourself in this industry – but I’ve regained the kindness that kid had in abundanceI was 17 when I entered The Voice. I was working two bar jobs and was depressed. I didn’t feel that I had much going for me, but I knew I wanted to get out of Bewdley. University wasn’t an option as I didn’t like hanging around with strangers, but The Voice ticked every box. The high pressure of the live competition each week didn’t bother me as I was so happy to be living in my own flat in London and grateful for this huge, strange experience. I didn’t win, but I came out with all the contacts I needed to start my career.Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s. It was a decade of establishing myself as an artist, shaking off the stigma of coming from a TV show, as well as a lot of personal turbulence. In the same year, I got dropped by my label and raped by a friend. I was 21 and remember sitting in a writing session and telling these three men I was working with about the sexual assault that had just happened – trying to externalise some of the intensity of what I was feeling. A few hours later, I was being pulled into a meeting with my management team to be told I had no label.Around this time, I also met the man who would become my husband – we broke up a few years later, then got back together again. I started having success on featured tracks, but I felt like it wasn’t my success – it was the producer’s. I was always fighting to be heard and seen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter I signed my second record andpublishing deal,I was finally able to take care of my parents. They were going through a lot of stress, and my mum’s parents had just died and she was struggling, so I said: “I’ll pay you not to work any more.” I bought them a house – which they have just paid me back for, even though I told them not to – and I’ve put some money into their pensions.My brother’s family were living in a hovel, so I bought them a house, too. I was still renting my flat at the time and wasn’t on the property ladder, but it was important to me that my family was stable before I was. My brother even works with me now. He was in the Marines from the age of 16 and got shot in the head, but is now my security guy. He comes with me everywhere.So far, I’m loving my 30s,but the landscape has changed for music, and I am probably not having the same level of success that I had in my 20s. At the start of my career, my ambition was to write songs that other people liked, whereas now I am writing songs about what I really want to say – the pressures of the job and of society. So I’m at peace if this new album isn’t as big as the others, because I’m proud of what I’ve made.I’ve been in therapy since I was 22, and have done a decade of working on my internal voice – the impostor syndrome that still creeps in and is so hard to escape when you work in music. It’s hard to be gentle on yourself when you work in an industry that is so fickle and unpredictable. Even at the start of this year, I was panicking that my job was about to end and that I was going to have to work in McDonald’s or try to get a new qualification. I’ve always thought I would like to become an electrician, actually, but I know that I’d be electrocuted within the first five minutes.Really, I can’t do anything else apart from what I’m doing now. So I am glad I am still here, and glad that I’m full of a new sense of kindness – something I lost in my 20s, and something that kid in the photo had an abundance of.Explore more on these topicsBecky HillFlashbackPop and rockDance musicDrum'n'bassFamilyPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Caitlin Moran: social media went from utopia to hellhole in a decade – if you want to feel hopeful again, get offline  | Social media | The Guardian
description: Fourteen years ago, Twitter was the fastest, funniest game on the web. Now I’ve been driven out by so-called ‘online activists’. The only answer is to unplug and try this instead
Author: Caitlin Moran
Headline: Fourteen years ago, Twitter was the fastest, funniest game on the web. Now I’ve been driven out by so-called ‘online activists’. The only answer is to unplug and try this instead
Content: Caitlin Moran, photographed earlier this month.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCaitlin Moran, photographed earlier this month.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianSocial mediaCaitlin Moran: social media went from utopia to hellhole in a decade – if you want to feel hopeful again, get offlineFourteen years ago, Twitter was the fastest, funniest game on the web. Now I’ve been driven out by so-called ‘online activists’. The only answer is to unplug and try this insteadCaitlin MoranSun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLet me take you back to December 2012 …God, I love social media! I cannot believe my exquisite luck – to exist in a time when it was invented! Bliss it is in this dawn to be @live! If you’ve not been on Twitter yet –pleasejoin! It’s kind of like a cross between your best ever pub, and the bit on Live & Kickingwhere celebrities like Duran Duran were doing the phone-in, and you could ring in and talk to them.Literally!Because Duran Duranare on Twitter!Well, Simon Le Bon is. AndSpandau Ballet, too! Well, Gary Kemp. And they’rereallyfunny. During the royal wedding with Kate and William, when all the lesser royals were herded on to some shitty coaches, Kemp was horrified.“Spandau wouldneverhave got into a coach!” he posted sniffily.“Yeah – limosall the wayfor Duran,” Simon replied, with palpable distaste.For a certain kind of person – by which I mean someone raised on Smash Hits magazine – the idea of Spandau Ballet and Duran Duran doing live, bitchy commentary on a royal wedding, on a new communication devicein your pocket?This is all our dreams come true.But it’s not just Camp Old New Romantics Tweeting During a Royal Wedding, though. It’s also acommunity.Everyone’s soniceon there. Everyone is theirbestselves. Last year, there was a mother in Welwyn Garden City whose child had lost its teddy bear. She was, understandably, desperate to get it back – begging everyone to keep an eye out for it on the streets.Obviously, everyone reposted her tweet, and it went super-viral. Then the deputy prime minister, John Prescott, got involved. He wrote a littlepoemabout the bear! And thenthatwent viral! Because everyonereallywanted to find that bear! And, by the end of the day, the bearwasfound – and it was like a breaking news event, but with actualgoodnews. Everyone went bananas!For a certain kind of person – by which I mean someone who wishes our newspapers and news bulletins contained more good news – it’s like a dream come true. Online, every day has a moment where it feels like It’s a Wonderful Life.But the thing is – the fun and the community of Twitteraren’t even the best bit.No! Because the killer thing is: it’s kind of like therevolutionon there. Seriously. For the first time ever, people can communicate with each other, across the world – unmediated by newspapers or TV. Weallhave the power to broadcast, and be heard, now. And do you know who’s basically taken over Twitter in the UK?The women.They’re on there, every night, reviewing the state of feminism through the day’s media – and being Chris Morris-level amusing about how ridiculously male-dominated everything is. And, gradually, they’ve got so pissed off about it, it’s turned into action.double quotation markAt the time I thought, we all have our hands on the levers of power, now Twitter is here. This is the future! This is true equality! We can all be activists nowFor instance, this year, after the Todayprogramme had two days in a row with, madly, all-male panels talking about female issues – first teenage girls and contraception, then breast cancer tests – Caroline Criado-Perez, who wasn’t a journalist, or a media person, but just someone with a job in the pharmaceutical industry, complained to the BBC – and was told it was because the Todayprogramme could not find a female expert in time. She then spent the next month on Twitter, asking for female experts to volunteer to be on a list, titled it The Women’s Room, and sent it to the BBC.And now – they use it! She has been the change she wants to see! She saw a problem, crowdsourced a solution – and fixed it! She has altered female representation, overnight, on the biggest broadcasting platform in the world – just by being able to coordinate a campaign on this new-fangled social media thing!And this will, clearly, be the first ofmanycampaigns like this. This is howeverythingwill change now. Weallhave our hands on the levers of power, now that Twitter is here. This is the future! This is true equality! We canallbe activists now! And at the same time as hanging out with Duran Duran, and Spandau Ballet!We are, clearly, about to enter the most equal, humane, progressive, amusing andadorableera of humanity the world has ever known. Twitter is going to solveeverything.Huzzah!September 2026Well. It’s beenquitethe 14 years. Like they say on social media – or what’s left of it, now it’s mutated beyond all recognition from what it was in 2012 –thatescalated quickly.In 2012, I truly believed social media – andparticularlyTwitter: back then, the fastest, funniest game on the internet – was the greatest force for progressive change the world had seen. I spent hours every day on it – keeping up with the news, signing petitions, mucking around, making a whole new bunch of friends who are still my primary social circle, and, quite frequently, laughing more than I had before or since.double quotation markBack then, the worst thing we knew about Russell Brand was that he had chosen to write something called My Booky WookObviously, part of my love for it was that I was, to use the parlance of the time, totally winning the internet: I had 800k followers and, in 2014, my Twitter feed was added to the list of English A-level set texts, as an example of “modern digital communication and contemporary rhetoric”. Let’s gloss over the fact that this was alongside the Twitter feed of Russell Brand. After all, back then, the worst thing we knew about him was that he had chosen to write something called My Booky Wook.Of course, it was all exciting and new, then. No one knew what it would turn into. But it was, we can see now, a gigantic, unprecedented experiment: not just one in “digital communication and rhetoric” but also in the behaviour of crowds; in exercises of power; in what “the democratisation of communication”reallymeans – especially when it’s incredibly easy for hostile foreign governments to covertly infiltrate, and sabotage, it.It was also an experiment in witch-hunts, and shitposting. In bullying, purity-spirals, public shaming, cancellations and algorithmic radicalisation. In what happens when there’s a form of mass communication in which the majority of the context has been stripped out; escalating rhetoric is financially rewarded; bad faith becomes rampant; and no one has made eye contact with the majority of people they have been talking to.And some of the findings of this experiment are, finally, in: public health services and governments now have so much evidence of its deleterious effects on both mental health and social cohesion, they are banning our children from using it. There are whole subjects – trans rights, DEI, vaccines, Gaza – once seemingly settled, or marginal, but on which social media has now all but obliterated a calm centre-ground. And families, and whole social groups, have imploded – after online skirmishes became unsolvable, and each side slowly migrated to utterly different, algorithm-dictated “realities.”As I look through the list of the people I was chatting to on Twitter in 2012 – people who went to early Twitter meetups; people who were part of my everyday conversation in this imaginary pub/club in the ether – the attrition rate is startlingly high. I would say that fully one-third of them have been fundamentally changed by social media. Like some modern-day version of the rhyme about Henry VIII’s wives – “Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived” – the tally reads: “Cancelled, radicalised, now offline; cancelled, radicalised, survived.”Caroline Criado-Perez? Who, in 2012, looked as if she was changing the face of feminism with a brilliant, amateur, smart, one-woman online campaign? Six months after her success with The Women’s Room, she had received so many rape and death threats online – more than 50per hour –that she could not eat or sleep, lost a stone in weight and felt utterly driven to despair.double quotation markAs anyone who has been subject to mass abuse on social media will tell you, the rape and death threats are, genuinely, not the worst thing that can happen to youWhen MP Stella Creasy tried to highlight Criado-Perez’s problem she, too, received a bombardment of rape and death threats – as did any other woman trying to help. Including me: 2013 was the first time on social media I was told someone wanted to kill me, or rape my children, or find my house and burn it down. And it was not, by a very long chalk, the last.But as anyone who has been subject to mass abuse on social media will tell you, the rape and death threats are, genuinely, not the worst thing that can happen to you online. No – the worst part of being engaged in “activism” online, even in its most mild, polite and humorous form, is what you might term “your own side” turning against you.A mild skirmish with someone you thought like-minded – a classic case of the vanity of small differences – gradually snowballing, thanks to the algorithm, into a pile-on of thousands, until you don’t know whose “side” you’re on any more.Until – seemingly now ostracised by your own community – you’re faced with a stark choice. Carry on batting for “your” side, even though they have denounced you as wrong, toxic and problematic? Or – rejected – go over to “the other side”, who welcome outcasts, and potential new converts, with open arms?If you want to see the most famous instance of this, look at the man who eventually bought Twitter – Elon Musk. In 2012, he was the goofy, Democrat-funding stoner guy – a real life Tony Stark – who was going to save the world with his electric cars. A couple of leftwing backlashes later, and Musk – stung and rejected – had begun a classic journey to “the other side” that saw him first radicalisedby his own algorithm,and then overseeing a darkly re-badged X being flooded with child pornography, “libtard tears” and actual Nazis. It all feels a long way away from John Prescott writing poems about teddy bears.This is why, in 2026, my primary piece of advice to someone who wants to make the world a better place is: don’t become an online activist. In fact – seriously – don’t be online at all.Three years ago, and while in the midst of my menopause, my lifelong, well-concealed anxiety disorder became so out of control I attempted to buy a remote farmhouse in Wales. In many ways, I still think this was a sensible decision: after all, the billionaire tech-bros are buying apocalypse bunkers in Hawaii, New Zealand and remote parts of Argentina. They obviously know something we don’t know. They clearly believe that civilisation will fall, and soon. Follow the money!Unfortunately, six weeks after putting in my offer, and while tits-deep in planning a life of total self-sufficiency – Goats! Wells! An iron-making forge, so I could be in control of my own supply of eg: rakes! – I realised just how much money you actually have to have to follow the money. The surveyor’s estimated renovations bills prompted my mortgage company to withdraw their offer, and the whole deal collapsed.If civilisation was to fall, it became clear, I would have to do it in my old house, in my old life. And if I was to ever get a handle on my rampaging anxiety, I would have to work out just what it was about modern life that was causing it in the first place.This is a peerlessly anxious age, we are constantly informed. The last 15 years or so have seemed so fast, chaotic, polarised and without precedent, we are all frazzled and reeling. The cry of gen X and boomers is: “When will things calm down? When will things benormalagain?”On hearing this, I have noticed – with no little sorrow – that millennials and gen Z and alpha will reply, curiously, “What do you mean – ‘normal’? What would we get backto?” For they, obviously, have no memory of a time before …all this.Before all conversations were about how things are getting worse; before the news of things getting worse pinged, 24/7, in your pocket. Before “responding” to the news, online, became some kind of social duty, but one that could, very easily, if you said the wrong thing, ruin your life.Trying to remember what “before” was like – and why it definitely felt better than what we have now – I drew up a list of ways to improve my life. Some seemed quite random, and all of them were either cheap, or free, but they all made it on to the list because they were things that, I hoped, would help me do two things.View image in fullscreenMakeup and hair: Dani Richardson using Nars and Hair by Sam McKnight. Floor lamp (main image): Ikea Årstid.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianThe first – fall back in love with humanity again. To truly believe – as I once had – that most people are, by and large, good. And then second? To be hopeful again. Hopeful about making the futurebetter.Of the things I tried, I can tell you which ones were a roaring success. Getting a dog. Buying a litter-picker, and regularly acting like a middle-aged Pac-Man, gobbling up the empty vape and vodka bottles of the neighbourhood and depositing them in a big bin bag. Donating blood. Rewilding the garden: “eco grief” is real, but so is “eco relief” when a new pond, and a stretch of unmown grass, sees your previously lifeless garden explode with dragonflies, goldfinches, frogs, and – on what was one of the best days of my life – a peregrine falcon, washing its wings in my homemade waterfall.I was also unexpectedly affected by accidentally losing my headphones, and starting to “rawdog” on public transport. It’s far easier to believe the doom-laden pronouncements of Donald Trump and JD Vance – that London is a seething cauldron of hatred, on the verge of sharia law – if you never leave the house without pumping an “emergency” news podcast through your Bose. It’s far harder when you sit on the bus with what I began to call “naked ears”,actually listeningto what people are saying in London in 2026. Turns out, they’re not seething with plans to begin vigilante mobs at all. They’re just on their phones, talking to their mums (“Press the button at the bottom. Thebottom!You’ve got the camera on reverse!”), or planning whether to have chicken, or sausages, for tea. They’re singing to the baby across the aisle, or giggling about some boy they fancy. If you are feeling paranoid, or dolorous, about your fellow man, I can heartily recommend goingsansheadphones for a spell. It really drops your anxiety rates.However. Without doubt, the biggest change in my life has been changing my attitude to social media. As a middle-aged, feminist lefty on Twitter, I had genuinely bought into the idea that social media was the water-cooler/town square of our times, and that we all had something bordering ondutyto be on it. In this, I was helped by a common online trope – being peevishly reminded, by others, to do so.“Your silence on this topic has been notable.” “I am disappointed you have not used your platform to centre this subject.” Or – the big trebuchet of prompts – “Your silence is violence.” Each person saying this was utterly convinced of the righteousness of their cause, of course – but possibly unaware of just howmanyother people werealsoconvinced by the righteousness oftheircause – and how, ultimately, impossible and mad it would be foreveryoneto speak out abouteveryone’scauses, every day.Additionally, I had started to notice a definite, recurring event: people whose conversation had previously roamed over multiple subjects, and in multiple tones, gradually becoming fixated on just one, single cause. Usually, this was defined by the cause – or, more specifically, the Tweet – which had gone mega-viral. Suddenly faced with a deluge of new followers, Tweeting “My hero!” or “You speak for all of us!” the poster would start posting more and more on this subject – until, one day, it finally became theonlything they posted about. I started referring to this phenomenon as “The Omnicause”: the moment where someone’s online life becomes defined by a single subject.One acquaintance – “A” – took on the Omnicause of homelessness. What happened next was the classic Omnicause domino-effect: viral Tweet; new followers; “You’re my hero!”; escalation; until, finally, febrile, manic obsession. By Christmas Day – just six months after their big, viral Tweet – A was posting videos at 4am, sobbing about how terrible they felt about all the “hate” they were getting from “traitors” whose “silence is violence”, and screaming about government inaction – “These politicians arevermin!They should hang from lamp-posts!” – while their children slept, upstairs, in their parent’s lovely house.As I knew a bit about A, I had a deeper contextual understanding of their Omnicause: a bad childhood, a failing marriage, ongoing mental health problems. To me, it seemed obvious what was fuelling the greater part of this – and, to be honest, so many other – Omnicauses: it was a proxy fury/sorrow about theirownlife. But of course, not one that could ever be admitted, on modern-day social media – where there is alwayssomeone,no matter how bitter your own sorrows, ready to shout “Check your privilege!”, “Stop whining!” or “Think how lucky you are, compared with those in Sudan!”Over the years, I’ve observed just how many of those ostensibly passionate about a cause are, in fact, subtweeting just a single person – a wife; a friend who has turned against them; an alienated social group. And they are often so distressed by their online experience that they don’t realise how, if we are being honest, there is a terrible form of narcissism, which they are blind to, in their posts.I have lost count of people who say they are having a “genuine mental health crisis” about, say, Gaza, or Ukraine. I wonder how distasteful someone actuallyinGaza, or Ukraine, would find these posts: someone in Leytonstone or Brighton claiming to be “broken” by a foreign war in which peopleare actually being bombed.Or – worse – people allowing their “passion” for a subject to becomesointense they are willing to watch whole friendship groups and families divide over the issue and implode. Even to the point – at the most extreme end – of violent marches, and bricks through shop windows.double quotation markHow does a 21st-century person make conversations about the 22nd century flip to the presumption it will be better than this one – and not, as we currently presume, so much worse?Surely, the first response to anybrutal conflict, thousands of miles away, is to do whatever it takesnotto import that conflict back into your own, fortunately peaceful country? You don’t spreadthe kind of ideological contamination that has set another country on fire. You just offer up your most profound and humble thanks you were born in a country currently experiencing far better luck – and then?And then.For whatdoyou do if you really dowant to make the world a better place? How doesa 21st-century person make conversations about the 22nd-century flip to the presumption it will be betterthan this one – and not, as we currently presume, so much worse?Well, first of all – as I said before –get off the internet.Or at least ration itwaydown. If you want to do online activism – if you are on a platform you still, perhaps bafflingly, believecanbe used to spread news, information and ideas for a better world – then, 20 minutes a day, tops, seems optimal. Enough to put something useful, and good, out there – but not long enough to get caught up in snark, and fights, or get co-opted into factional wars in which at least a third of the participants will–and we can now observe this to be true – eventually burn out, radicalise, or go, to use the technical term, “completely crackers”.And secondly? Well, the old Al-Anon saying is popular for a reason: you can only keep your side of the road clean. No one can actually change the world – like Zara’s infamous “death trousers”, it’s both controversial, and far too long. But we can change ourdays.We can changeourlives – just enough to change those of others.Pick litter. Donate blood. Volunteer. Fund a local community centre. Mentor. Flower-bomb wastelands. Clear a river. Raise funds for overseas aid. Talk to someone lonely. Babysit for an exhausted friend. Join an organisation you believe in. Turn up and show solidarity with a local mosque, synagogue or abortion clinic. Read a proper history book on a subject you’ve only read tweets about.Then read another one– as there’s nothing more dangerous than someone who’s only read one book on a subject. Seriously – if I have to explain what “from the river to the sea”actuallymeans to another ardent 21-year-old, I will genuinely lose my mind.Stop listening to emergency podcasts; stop doomscrolling; go for a walk andtalkto people; buy your local newspaper – and, finally, stop believing that we are living “through one of the most difficult, anxious and chaotic times in human history”. Sure, it’s not a golden age – housing, the NHS, the climate crisis, inequality and the rise of intolerance nix that – but, if you’re British, you mustkeep hold of a solid historical perspective: there are no bombs in our skies. There is no plague stalking our streets. We are not living through a Depression so bleak children are abandoned outside churches.For the truth is, the worldis,still, largely, as it was, “back then”, when things were “normal”: a big old mixed-grill of awful thingsandwonderful things; steps backandsteps forward. In reality, there are only two big things that have changed. The first is climate change – something which, as every expert will wearily explain, we already have the solutions to tackle - but still lack enough bracing top-level panic to implement. And this leads to the second, and arguably biggest, change in our times: how we are being told about the world. Who is telling us about the world – and why. You only need to see footage of well-funded bot-farms – thousands of phones and laptops, blankly using AI to argue with real, angry, despairing, crying people – to realise something deeply disruptive is happening here.And if you take your headphones off, put your phone down, and turn all those newly freed-up hours into actuallydoingsomething – however small – then maybe you, like me, will realise that you’ve now passed through Peak Despair. And have, yes, started to become, well,hopefulagain.The writer’s fee has been donated to charity.How to Be Hopeful by Caitlin Moran is published by Ebury at £22. title: Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Nigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and change, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Nigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and change, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianOpinionLabourDon’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happenJohn HarrisNigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and changeSun 20 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareDespite the energised startAndy Burnhamhas made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both theMetropolitan policeandparliament’s standards commissionermay worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and arereportedly already being spenton 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “national emergency” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’sfirst budgetis not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far beenstrangely reluctant to address. But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which areactually going down– and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words wereonce utteredby that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look –look– like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spentwilling on unrest, and where quasi-paramilitariesmenace our ports. Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshireholda referendumon leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it | Andy BurnhamRead moreAs much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quoteJuly’s bulletinfrom the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month,YouGov reportedthat 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime ministerannounced £1bn of investmentin a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only bookIn Place of Fear: in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionEconomic policyImmigration and asylumAndy BurnhamReform UKBudget 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Our children may be surprised by what’s in our will – should we tell them now? | Family | The Guardian
description: You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plans
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plans
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyOur children may be surprised by what’s in our will – should we tell them now?You don’t have to reveal the contents, but I’ve seen families torn apart by unexpected inheritance plansAnnalisa BarbieriSun 20 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 10.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife and I have three children and several grandchildren.Our willmay contain some surprises forthem.Is it better to revealits contents while we are still alive, orlet our beneficiaries discover them when we die?We gave our children considerable financial help, enabling them to buy their first homes. We have also madesizeablecontributions to our grandchildren’s education funds.Our thinking is that our descendants willneedmore assistance when they are young:for their education, setting up home, starting a family. And we want to give them the gift of knowing that my wife and I loved them enough to helpwith these challenges, and thatthe bequests came from us, not through the generosity of their parents.My wife’s jewellery goes only to our granddaughters, and the mothers of our grandsons could feel aggrieved that their sons have been passed over. However, we don’t consider the jewellery to have any financial value, as it should never be exchanged for cash.The financial value of our estate is to be divided one-third to each of the next three generations, with each third divided equally between the members of that generation.We have also stipulated that no generation’s members will receive more than their parent.If we tell our children the contents of the will now, they may think we are asking for their opinions, which we emphatically are not. Making this clear may result in illfeeling. On the other hand, if they discover the will’s provisions only when we die, there may be room for misunderstanding, again resultingin illfeeling.We have explained our thinking in a document that accompanies the will.I wonder if others have wrestled with these questions and arrived at satisfactory conclusions?What riches you have with all these children and grandchildren!I am assuming you live in England and Wales, where you can leave your estate to whomever you want.I went to lawyer and wills specialist Gary Rycroft, who advised that “there is no legal requirement to tell anyone, including your children, what’s in your will. It is your money, your property and, ultimately, your decision. A will is not decided by a family committee.”That said, Rycroft and I both advocate discussing things ahead of time. “I’m a fan of transparency,” said Rycroft. “No one likes surprises in wills, especially if the surprise is getting less than expected. And while the will is clear about who gets what, families can be left very unclear about why.”double quotation markRemember, an inheritance is not just about what you leave behind – it’s also how you will be rememberedSo, yes, we think you should explain ahead of time. I have seen families torn asunder by unexpected wills. Also, who knows what might happen between now and when the will becomes active. What if you have an argument with a family member and they think the will is retribution (even if it was clearly dated before the row)? Also, remember that it is likely that either you or your wife will die first, so if you decide to talk about it beforehand, it’s best done together.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA childhood sexual abuse allegation has rocked our family – what can we do about it? | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreRycroft said to make sure the extra document you mention is a “more formal ‘memorandum of wishes’. The will is still the legally operative document and the memorandum does not rewrite or trump it. Its value is in explaining the decisions.” This stands even if you have a meeting to explain, as people tend to forget what was said or recall only what they want to.“Remember,” counselled Rycroft, “an inheritance is not just about what you leave behind. It’s also about how a person will be remembered.”And don’t forget that anyone you leave things to who is over 18 can vary their inheritance, within a time limit, with a deed of variation and change who gets their share. A reminder that, after death, we cannot control those we leave behind.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.Explore more on these topicsFamilyAsk Annalisa BarbierifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato | Russia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
Content: Polish and Romanian soldiers in the Suwałki Gap – an 80km stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolish and Romanian soldiers in the Suwałki Gap – an 80km stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesRussiaEuropean spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoExclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-opsShaun Walkerin Prague and RigaSun 20 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk,told parliamentthat intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat fromRussia.View image in fullscreenThe Russian president, Vladimir Putin, alongside Adm Viktor Liina, the commander of Russia’s Pacific fleet.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine.Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missilesin the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion ofNatoterritory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources inUkraineand warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.View image in fullscreenMichal Koudelka, the director of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service (BIS).Photograph: CTK/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whethera surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month– during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe CIA director, John Ratcliffe, who made a surprise trip to Moscow last month.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersHowever, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, whenUS officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invadeand the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMoscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as acampaign of sabotageagainst targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition,veered into Polish airspace a year ago.Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.View image in fullscreenA Russian Shahed drone on display in Kyiv.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APIn recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president,Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’scampaign of sabotage in Europeis likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authoritieshave attributed to Russian intelligence.“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.View image in fullscreenA Ukrainian soldier fires at an incoming jet-powered Shahed drone during a Russian aerial attack on Kyiv in August.Photograph: Libkos/Getty ImagesMežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropeVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyyCzechiaLatvianewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
Content: Smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday.Photograph: ReutersUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaignTensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebelsPatrick Wintourin New YorkSun 20 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGovernments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence afterIranclaimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.Map indicating territory under de facto Houthi authority as of 11 SeptemberIran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.The outburst of sabre-rattling appears to have been prompted byattacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.The US largely regards theHouthisas a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies whenhe spurned a call by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthissuddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coastoverlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.In an attempt to keep the US out of its war withSaudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that they would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, a commitment that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News: “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.France will summon Iran’s ambassador ⁠after Iranian ⁠authorities closed a French-language centre affiliated with ​its ‌embassy ‌in Tehran, the ‌foreign ministry said on Sunday.The Iranian judiciary accused the centre of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe French foreign ministry said: “This new attack on the French cultural presence in Iran … is unjustifiable and unacceptable.”Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators.Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning that “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance.He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisYemenSaudi ArabiaIranUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Specialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and Wales | Rape and sexual assault | The Guardian
description: Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward
Content: Plans for courts hearing rape cases include private entrances, facilities for recording evidence in advance and ways to observe sentencing remotely.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenPlans for courts hearing rape cases include private entrances, facilities for recording evidence in advance and ways to observe sentencing remotely.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersRape and sexual assaultSpecialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and WalesFunding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forwardBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpecialist courtrooms prioritising cases of rape and other serious sex
