offences are to be introduced acrossEnglandand Wales, with campaigners welcoming the move as potentially transformative.The changes, designed to encourage more survivors to come forward, will include the provision of private entrances and waiting rooms, and facilities equipped for recording evidence in advance and observing sentencing remotely.Announcing the move,Andy Burnhamsaid victims of rape and serious sexual offences had felt let down by the justice system for too long, adding that prosecution rates for rape remained “shamefully low”, with many victims waiting years for justice.“These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough,” the prime minister said.“So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place.”A multimillion-pound cash injection is intended to make sure every crown court in England andWaleshas at least one room set up specifically to hear rape and serious sexual offence cases within two years.Rape and serious sexual offence cases will also be prioritised in courts more widely, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) announced. Such trials will be given a fixed date, as opposed to being placed on floating lists where they can be moved at short notice and delayed by months.Among those welcoming the announcement was Labour’s Charlotte Nichols, who told the House of Commons this yearshe was raped after an event she attended as an MPand waited 1,088 days for her case to get to court.View image in fullscreenLabour MP Charlotte Nichols, centre, waived her anonymity to tell parliament about her rape and subsequent experience with the courts.Photograph: Parliament LiveNichols said: “Today marks a hugely important milestone, helping to improve the experience of victims and survivors of sexual violence in the court system who are all too often retraumatised by seeking justice.“I’m proud that substantive, meaningful change has come from waiving my anonymity to speak about my own experiences, and am hugely grateful to the prime minister and lord chancellor for taking forward these measures, as I know the difference they would have made for me and so many of the survivors I have worked with in recent years.”The MoJ cited Nichols’ “immense strength and bravery” in its announcement.While welcoming the announcement, there was a warning by the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, that the crown court backlog of rape and sexual offence cases was now “significantly worse” than when she first called for specialist courts in 2021.She said: “Tens of thousands more victims are now waiting for their cases to reach trial, and specialist courts alone will not be enough to tackle the scale of the delays or deliver the swift justice victims deserve. Indeed, court delays could prevent many rape victims from accessing the specialist courtrooms that are being set up to support them.”Further changes announced include new trauma-informed training for court staff and a pilot scheme giving victims of sex offences a single point of contact to ensure their needs are met during the court process.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeparate from the funding for courtrooms, there will also be £43m to support survivors through the national rape and sexual abuse support fund for the next two years, including through counselling, therapy, outreach and group activities.The new measures also include the creation of a rape justice taskforce, drawing figures from across the criminal justice system to tackle the rising rate of postponed rape trials and confront the myths that cause victims to withdraw from cases.The Conservatives’ shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said tackling delays in rape trials was long overdue, but that the courts backlog had been “used” by theLabouras justification for controversial plans to significantly restrict the right to jury trials.“If resources can be found to accelerate rape trials, why are they persisting in their attack on this ancient right to jury trials?” he said.In 2022, an announcement by Boris Johnson’s government of three specialist courtrooms to prosecute rape cases wasdismissed by legal blogger the Secret Barrister as a “gimmick”that did not address the chronic underfunding of the justice system.Changes in the new provisions include many of the reforms that campaigners and charities have been calling for over many years.“Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice,” said Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.“We’re particularly pleased to see measures that will improve trial efficiency and ensure survivors are better able to participate in, and observe, proceedings.”Explore more on these topicsRape and sexual assaultCrimeViolence against women and girlsUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Adults with severe mental illness die 15 to 20 years earlier from diseases such as cancer | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Stark health inequalities in terms of deaths before age of 75, NHS data reveals
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Exclusive: Stark health inequalities in terms of deaths before age of 75, NHS data reveals
Content: Adults with severe mental illness are 3.8 times more likely to die from cardiovascular disease before 75 and 2.3 times as likely from cancer, the study found.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APView image in fullscreenAdults with severe mental illness are 3.8 times more likely to die from cardiovascular disease before 75 and 2.3 times as likely from cancer, the study found.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APMental healthAdults with severe mental illness die 15 to 20 years earlier from diseases such as cancerExclusive: Stark health inequalities in terms of deaths before age of 75, NHS data revealsAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdults with severe mental illness are nearly five times more likely than their peers to die from serious physical diseases before the age of 75, according to research.The analysis ofNHS databy theRethink Mental Illness charity revealsthat people with severe mental health problems die 15-20 years earlier than the wider adult population, largely due to preventable physical conditions.Rethink’s calculations show that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die before the age of 75 than the general population.For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated.Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18 to 74 year olds with severe mental health problems inEnglandduring this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.The report identifies a number of factors driving this excess mortality, including poverty, poor housing, higher rates of smoking, weight gain from medication, physical inactivity, and fragmented care. But the authors conclude that “diagnostic overshadowing” – where physical symptoms are wrongly attributed to mental illness – means potential illnesses are not always properly investigated and treated.The findings come before the government’s independent review of mental health, autism and ADHD, which is expected to be published this week and recommend amore holistic approachto supporting patients with these conditions.Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink, said: “It is a scandal that people living with severe mental health problems are so much more likely than the rest of the population to die from often preventable physical health conditions.“Given that many are in frequent contact with health services throughout their lives, it is clear that opportunities to identify and treat physical health problems are being missed.“These early deaths are not inevitable. The new cross-government mental health strategy … must prioritise physical health checks, improve access to mental-health informed interventions and bolster peer support, if it wants to reduce these terrible health inequalities.”Responding to the findings, Prof Subodh Dave, the president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said: “Having a severe mental illness shouldn’t be an early death sentence. This stark inequality is unacceptable. People with severe mental illness deserve the same opportunity to live long, healthy lives as everyone else. We know that evidence-based solutions to close this gap exist – from smoking cessation to routine physical health checks.But what is lacking is concerted action to prevent these premature deaths.”A Department ofHealthand Social Care spokesperson said: “People living with severe mental illness face stark health inequalities, and too many continue to experience poorer physical health outcomes.“This government is taking immediate action to transform services for people with severe mental illness. We’re developing a new modern service framework to look at what action is needed to help people live healthier and longer lives through high-quality care, opening 100 new community mental health centres, and our mental health strategy will go further, outlining how we plan to build a more integrated system that responds earlier and reduces waiting times for support.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Canada, you can call or text theSuicide Crisis Helplineon 988. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMental healthLife expectancyNHSHealthEnglandCancerHeart diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position
Content: Charles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCharles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSweden‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and homeCharles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration positionLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported fromSweden.Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country afterBrexitcame to an end.An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has in effect been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since BrexitRead more“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow those suddenly left homeless can get help.“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has alreadydeported 458 British peopleafter rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.View image in fullscreenCharles is distraught after landing at Heathrow.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe situation persistsdespite promises from opposition partiesnow on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” – in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.View image in fullscreenA bag containing a toothbrush, toothpaste and earplugs that was given to Charles in the Swedish detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA bright yellow envelope was also handed to him by the captain before disembarking, which he opens for the first time.Inside is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. Another says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case. They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said. “They said we think that if we don’t detain you, you will abscond from Sweden because you are not cooperating.“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.”He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no. He asked if he could drive back to Britain “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said: ‘No, the decision has been made.’”View image in fullscreenA document envelope issued by the Swedish police authority.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBefore Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.The campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued toa 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.View image in fullscreenCharles looking for help at Heathrow.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was alsoordered to leave after 25 yearswhile another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, wasdeported in January.The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position hadinfected decision-making relating to Britonsthere before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”View image in fullscreenCharles leaves Heathrow airport, heading into an uncertain future.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianJane Golding, the chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says. “This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.She points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. “Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropean UnionMigrationEuropeBrexitHeathrow airportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beach | Greece | The Guardian
description: Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
Content: The altercation happened at Vouliagmeni beach, about 12 miles south of Athens, on Sunday morning.Photograph: Geopix/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe altercation happened at Vouliagmeni beach, about 12 miles south of Athens, on Sunday morning.Photograph: Geopix/AlamyGreeceMan, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beachRow at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungersHelena Smithin AthensSun 20 Sep 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man after a brawl over a sunlounger at a beach on the Athenian riviera.The man had arrived at the popular bathing spot of Vouliagmeni before 10am on Sunday hoping to secure a sunbed, but he soon began arguing with a fellow bather – described by authorities as a “76-year-old man unknown to him” – when it became clear loungers were in short supply.The row quickly degenerated into a scuffle as others reportedly joined in. The victim, who was with his wife, is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest during the fight.“It seems that people who were with [the assailant] also participated,” ERT, the country’s state broadcaster, reported.“The 82-year-old was seriously injured, and needed to be transferred by ambulance to Asklepieion hospital in Voula.“Despite the efforts of doctors, at about 11am the elderly man succumbed to his wounds.”A postmortem was immediately ordered.Police arrested the 76-year-old and, initially, a 21-year-old woman who was with him. The beach resort’s manager was also detained for questioning.“The incident is under investigation,” said a source, describing the fight as unprecedented. “InGreecedisagreement is expressed vocally, with a lot of screaming and shouting, not in fistfights like this – especially between two elderly men. I think that’s why it is so shocking.”Like other parts ofEurope, Greece is undergoing a severe cost of living crisis that has heightened tensions and put strain on social relations. An increase in domestic violence and other disputes has been partly blamed on the pressures of everyday life.In recent years, there has been growing anger over private rental outfits hogging prime coastal areas with exorbitantly priced sunloungers in Greece, where the sea has an important place in national identity.Authorities said “all those” involved in the incident would appear before a magistrate.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeOlder peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections | Germany | The Guardian
description: Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin
Content: ‘Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,’ Merz said after the results.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,’ Merz said after the results.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAGermanyFriedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state electionsFar-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in BerlinDeborah Colein BerlinSun 20 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s embattled chancellor,Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just 4.9%, below ⁠the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament and indicating they may be excluded altogether. It would be the CDU’s worst-ever state score, which Merz called a “disaster”.The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendlyAlternative für Deutschland(AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with 38.3%, more than doubling its previous score, according to projections on ARD public television.In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.The deeply unpopular Merz has beenfighting for his political survivalafter a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch afterSaxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routedthe CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s co-chair, Tino Chrupalla, react as he hears the first results of the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election in Schwerin.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersA jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Polandhead into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGermany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support forUkraineand carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival,Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.View image in fullscreenElif Eralp (centre), the candidate for Die Linke in Berlin, reacts to the projected results of the state election.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockMerz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with onlyone in 10 Germanssaying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked inthe former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Victoria Starmer models clothes at London fashion week show | London fashion week | The Guardian
description: Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Wife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of Sisyphus
Content: Victoria Starmer, a known fan of Edeline Lee’s clothes, takes part in her fashion show at Haverstock school.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenVictoria Starmer, a known fan of Edeline Lee’s clothes, takes part in her fashion show at Haverstock school.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPALondon fashion weekVictoria Starmer models clothes at London fashion week showWife of former PM takes part in designer Edeline Lee’s show inspired by the Greek myth of SisyphusHannah Al-OthmanSun 20 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictoria Starmer has taken part in aLondon fashion weekshow, in one of her first public appearances since her husband, Keir Starmer, stepped down as prime minister.Lady Starmer appeared at Sunday’s Edeline Lee show. The London-based, Canadian British designer’s clothes are a favourite of the Princess of Wales, and have also been worn by celebrities including singer Taylor Swift and actor and screenwriter Phoebe Waller-Bridge.Lee’s spring/summer 2027 show took place in the unusual setting of a north London school sports hall. Starmer wore a bright turquoise knitted midi dress with a high neckline, pleated detailing and short, sculptural sleeves, paired with white block-heeled shoes, with her hair worn in loose waves.Rather than preparations for the show taking place backstage in the usual way, in Lee’s unique show, models were fitted and adjusted in full view of the audience, dancers rehearsed beside the catwalk, while a drone followed proceedings from the high ceiling of the gymnasium.Starmer was photographed having her makeup done beside the catwalk, against a backdrop of a football net, with makeup and hair products spread out over a table in front of her. Ballerinas stretched beside the catwalk and synchronised swimming-inspired dancers performed in bright red costumes as part of the show, in the school in Chalk Farm.View image in fullscreenLady Starmer has her hair done during preparations for the show at Haverstock school in Chalk Farm, north London.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAThe collection was based on the Greek myth of Sisyphus, in which a man is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down again each time he reaches the top.“There’s a general feeling right now of relentlessness, a sisyphean cycle,” Lee said. “I was already thinking about the ballet – dance is incredibly transporting, but the work behind it is so intense, the way dancers train for years, the endless repetition, for one ecstatic moment of performance, and then they’re back in the studio.“I wanted to acknowledge the rigour and hard work behind that moment – much like the skill and artistry required of my team to present beautiful clothes.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS fashion CEO resigns after physically restraining animal rights activistsRead moreThroughout Keir Starmer’s time in office, Lady Starmer kept a low public profile, but her “political chic” and “modern British” sense of style was often admired. She has favoured contemporary British brands, including ME+EM, Needle & Thread, and Edeline Lee, whose main creative design studio is based in east London.At London fashion week’s spring/summer shows in 2024, when her husband was prime minister, Lady Starmer took a front-row seat at Edeline Lee’s show, which took place at Millbank Tower, a former campaign HQ of Labour and the Conservatives, where Reform UK’s central office is now based.She wore a borrowed £615 cream pussy-bow blouse with a navy polka dot print and matching £715 wide-leg trousers.View image in fullscreenLady Starmer attends the Edeline Lee London fashion week show in 2024.Photograph: Ben Perry/Rex/ShutterstockIt came amid a row over free clothes for Lady Starmer, with Keir Starmer facing an investigation at the time over apossible breach of parliamentary rulesaround gifts.He had failed to declare thatsome of his wife’s designer clotheshad been bought for her by his biggest personal donor, Lord Alli. The Sunday Times reported that the Labour peer had paid for a personal shopper, clothes and alterations before and after Starmer became prime minister.Explore more on these topicsLondon fashion weekKeir StarmerFashion weeksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy
Content: Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpAnalysisAndy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictablePippa CrerarPolitical editorPM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economySun 20 Sep 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareNo international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink hismidterm dreams.When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle onNatoand Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.Starmer’s“keep calm and carry on”strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in Junesignalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the morecombative approachof Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trumpsuggested Burnham was “extremely liberal”(not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that hemight not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and thathe would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shownwith the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about theUK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trumptold world leaders their countries were “going to hell”over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weaponsRead moreWith Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamUS politicsNatoanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Feeling ‘forced out’ by Badenoch? Lib Dems conference welcomes young Tory defectors | Liberal Democrat conference | The Guardian
description: Self-described moderates say Ed Davey’s party offers them a home as Conservatives shift further right
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Self-described moderates say Ed Davey’s party offers them a home as Conservatives shift further right
Content: Cody Butler, the 21-year-old former chair of the One Nation Conservative Network at the Lib Dems conference in Brighton on Sunday.Photograph: Alexandra Topping/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCody Butler, the 21-year-old former chair of the One Nation Conservative Network at the Lib Dems conference in Brighton on Sunday.Photograph: Alexandra Topping/The GuardianLiberal Democrat conferenceFeeling ‘forced out’ by Badenoch? Lib Dems conference welcomes young Tory defectorsSelf-described moderates say Ed Davey’s party offers them a home as Conservatives shift further rightAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClimbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree.But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago,he joined the Lib Dems.“There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.”Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party.Butler has been joined by Josh Bancroft, a former Tory councillor on Cannock Chase council, who left the party to join the Lib Dems earlier this month. “Moderates like me have been forced out of the big tent over the past few years,” he said. “My politics haven’t changed, but the party has.”The 26-year-old said moderates looking for the exit have grown in number since Badenoch embarked ona purge of the Conservative parliamentary party.In July, the Tory leader warned that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former ministerGavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member,Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing againfor the party.View image in fullscreenEd Davey taking part in a Q&A session with the journalist Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems conference on Sunday.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA“TheConservativeshave taken leaps to the right and left me and millions of voters behind,” Bancroft added. “The Liberal Democrats can be and should be their new political home.”Bancroft and Butler have been welcomed with open arms into the Liberal ranks, with one MP joking that Badenoch had become the Lib Dems’ most effective recruiter. During a Q&A on the first full day of the conference, party leaderEd Daveyrepeatedly mentioned Badenoch, referencing her decision to freeze out members and MPs who support net zero policies.“Unlike Kemi Badenoch, who thinks there wasn’t a problem with this summer’s heatwaves, we actually realise you have to take action on climate change and we’re leading that debate,” he said.Despite being stuck at about 11% in national polling, many Liberal Democrat activists and MPs in Brighton are talking with atypical swagger about cementing the foundations of the so-called orange wall. They point to the 72 seats they won in the last election, making them the largest third party in British politics for over a century. And ofthe 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024, 20 were taken by the Conservatives.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen asked if reaching 100 seats by taking those targets was the aim, Davey insisted there was “no ceiling” to the Liberal Democrats’ ambitions. “If we have great local councillors, great local candidates and great local campaigners, we can beat Reform, the Tories, Labour, Green, the SNP, anyone. We can win anywhere where there’s a multiparty fight.”On Sunday, Davey explicitly ruled out any future pact with the Tories. But when asked about an arrangement with Labour, he said maximising the number of Lib Dem MPs would give his party a stronger hand in any future negotiations. “That means you have to box really smartly,” he said.While that prospect may have some pure-blood Tories running for the hills, it could lure others into the Liberal Democrat ranks, argued Butler.“It used to be that if you wanted power you could only join the Conservatives or Labour, but that reality doesn’t exist any more in a five-party system,” he said. “My message to other One Nation Conservatives is: you can be true to what you believe, and if you back the Liberal Democrats, you’re actually backing the future kingmakers of government. They will write the budget. The Conservatives won’t.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal Democrat conferenceLiberal DemocratsConservativesKemi BadenochEd DaveynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I feel betrayed’: inside Ed Sheeran’s controversial return to the stage | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Some fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of Palestine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Some fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of Palestine
Content: Pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrate outside Ed Sheeran's concert venue in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersView image in fullscreenPro-Palestinian protesters demonstrate outside Ed Sheeran's concert venue in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersEd Sheeran‘I feel betrayed’: inside Ed Sheeran’s controversial return to the stageSome fans were hesitant to turn the page after Sheeran’s tour resumed in Philadelphia after the removal of Macklemore, who spoke out in support of PalestineWill Groff in PhiladelphiaSun 20 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“This is not usually how I would open the show,”Ed Sheerantold the crowdat Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night, a humble preamble to a three-plus-minute speech addressing the greatestcontroversyof his career. Shaky-voiced and stealing glances at the monitor at his feet, he looked every bit the chastened superstar.‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture warRead more“I have tried in my careernot to be a political commentatorof any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division, about humanity, not politics, but this is a humanitarian issue and I cannothide how I feelabout it any more,” Sheeran said. He described the Hamas-led attack at the Nova music festival in Israel on 7 October 2023 as “horrific”, and expressed heartbreak over civilian deaths in Gaza and the West Bank, describing the situation as “catastrophic and unjustified and disproportionate”.He ended his speech with an appeal for “love, hope and unity”.“Everyone here can stand by people that they don’t agree with on everything, but they can always agree on singing these songs,” he declared shortly before launching into Castle on the Hill, a rousing anthem about growing up in rural England. The guitar jangled, fireworks lit into the sky and pastoral scenes filled a giant screen behind the pop star as fans sang along. There was an overwhelming sense, between Sheeran and his ecstatic audience, of wanting to turn the page.Cindy Lucente, a 73-year-old retiree who attended the show with her daughter and granddaughter, described the speech as “eloquent” and said that she was impressed by Sheeran’s mettle.“People kept telling me I should probably get rid of my ticket because he’s going to cancel,” she said. “But I knew he wouldn’t.”View image in fullscreenHillary Steinberg outside Lincoln Financial Field.Photograph: Will GroffThe night marked Sheeran’s return to the stage after the rapper Macklemore wasremoved from the touraftercontroversyerupted over his remarks during a performance at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on 5 September. In a statement shared to Instagram last Tuesday, Sheeran said that hefaced pressure from venue owners– includingRobert Kraft, the billionaire who owns Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots – to excise Macklemore from the lineup, but that his removal “was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine”. The statement was met with widespread condemnation, with detractors accusing Sheeran of cowing to corporate interests and putting profit over freedom of expression.“I feel betrayed about how he handled this,” said Hillary Steinberg, a 34-year-old sociology PhD who was among the pro-Palestine protesters gathered outside the NRG metro station, a group that reached about 100 at one stage. “It has sort of soured how I think about him as an artist.”After getting her ticket refunded earlier in the week, Steinberg decided to come to the stadium and try convincing others to do the same. She wore a black and white keffiyeh and held a sign that read: “If you leave now you will have more spine thanEd Sheeran.” By the end of the night, she said that she and her boyfriend had convinced “at least five” other people to get refunds.Despite reported safety concerns and fears of an outright cancellation, the mood at Lincoln Financial Field was light and at times triumphant. The singer repeatedly invoked the controversy but spoke in broad terms and with an air of self-deprecation. He did not mentionKraftorMacklemoreby name.“I hope you enjoyed the opening acts – I heard they were great,” Sheeran joked early in the show, waving off concerns about having to carry the event alone. Per its moniker, the Loop tour mostly features Sheeran performing solo and utilizing a looping pedal to create his own soundscapes.View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran addresses Macklemore controversy at his Loop tour show in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Ed Sheeran/Instagram/ReutersOne of the night’s many standing ovations came after Sheeran brought out a group of musicians, led by the fiddler Alicia Enstrom, to back him on a number of songs including the lilting Galway Girl. The Irish folk band Beoga, which had played behind Sheeran during this section on earlier stops, was among the acts whodropped out in solidaritywith Macklemore. They were joined by the Danish band Lukas Graham, the Irish singer Aaron Rowe, and Finneas – brother and collaborator to Billie Eilish and a musician in his own right – who was slated to join Sheeran for a South American leg later this year.Sheeran made it clear that Enstrom and the others were to be Beoga’s replacement.“They said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought that I was a certain type of person,” Sheeran said to rapturous cheers from the audience.Melody Fillier, a 49-year-old who works in the pharmaceuticals industry, was among those who applauded the new backing band.View image in fullscreenA pro-Palestinian demonstrator waves a flag during a protest before the Ed Sheeran concert.Photograph: Allie Ippolito/AP“They had balls,” she said. “The other ones didn’t.”Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was | Jason OkundayeRead moreThe other conspicuous change was the absence of a retractable bridge and smaller “B-stage”, which had positioned the singer much closer to the crowd during intimate sections of earlier shows. Sheeran explained that he didn’t want to risk having things thrown at him.“I took the B-stage out because I was afraid what might happen if I stood in the middle, and I will admit that,” he said, grinning sheepishly.Throughout the night, Sheeran returned again and again to themes of political harmony. The pop star appeared less defiant than humbled, repeatedly describing the concert as the greatest of his career. It seems unlikely that his words, which mostly served to justify the actions of the preceding week, will satisfy his critics. But in the city of brotherly love, where the stadium appeared mostly full even as the concert stretched past the three-hour mark, fans of the singer seemed more than satisfied.“I didn’t come here for politics,” said Tim Matkosky, a 59-year-old entrepreneur who was among those who stayed to the bitter end, up on their feet and dancing as the bassline thumped and fire plumes filled the air. “I came here to get away from politics.”Explore more on these topicsEd SheeranPalestinePop and rockIsrael-Gaza warPhiladelphiaMacklemorePennsylvaniafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Kane and Mulberry make swaggering joint comeback at London fashion week | London fashion week | The Guardian
description: Appointment of Kane as creative director signals the return of serious style ambition for former It-bag brand
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Appointment of Kane as creative director signals the return of serious style ambition for former It-bag brand
Content: This was punchy, full-throttle fashion, accessorised with money-making bags and shoes.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThis was punchy, full-throttle fashion, accessorised with money-making bags and shoes.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesLondon fashion weekChristopher Kane and Mulberry make swaggering joint comeback at London fashion weekAppointment of Kane as creative director signals the return of serious style ambition for former It-bag brandJess Cartner-MorleySun 20 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith spicy leather mini-dresses and shoes with miniature axes for heels, two beloved British names made a swaggering joint comeback atLondon fashion week.Fifteen years ago,Christopher Kaneand Mulberry were two of the biggest shows on the line-up. Kane was the brilliant young designer who could find fashion in the most unlikely places: rubberised lace minis were inspired by “Princess Margaret on acid”; while illustrations from the 1972 classic The Joy of Sex appeared on slinky slip dresses. Mulberry was London’s home-grown It-bag brand: anyone who was anyone had a Bayswater or an Alexa.The pandemic hit independent designers hard, and Kane placed his brand in administration in 2023. Mulberry hit the ropes after price hikes misfired, fighting off a takeover bid as profits plunged. But a new chief executive and a renewed focus on Britishness and craft is fuelling a revival at Mulberry, with sales up 23% in the first quarter of this year. Theappointment of Kane as creative directorsignals the return of serious style ambition at Mulberry, and gives a new platform for Kane’s talent.View image in fullscreenThere were leather sheath dresses and elegantly spare leather car coats, as well as heeled loafers featuring Mulberry’s signature postman’s lock.Composite: Getty imagesOn paper, it is an unlikely match.Mulberryis rooted in its Somerset factories and makes understated practical bags; Kane has a flair for bad-girl party dresses learned on the streets of Glasgow where he grew up.Where they meet is leather. There were leather sheath dresses and elegantly spare leather car coats, as well as heeled loafers featuring Mulberry’s signature postman’s lock. Kane builds each collection around one visual motif – Frankenstein, gorillas, the reproductive organs of plants – and for this collection, took the castellated leather flaps of Mulberry’s Bayswater bags and turned them into notched hems and necklines. This was punchy, full-throttle fashion, accessorised with money-making bags and shoes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSimone Rocha on the runway on Sunday.Photograph: Shutterstock“Town, city, country” was Kane’s name for the show. Colours were inspired by “the bleak, post-industrial Scotland where I grew up – grey concrete, and coalminer orange”. Soft plaid checks added a rustic touch. “I want Mulberry to be about a Britishness that’s not London-centric,” he said backstage.This London fashion week has renewed confidence and a packed schedule of shows. Simone Rocha said that a story about an unknown Caravaggio discovered in a Dublin drawing room set her thinking about “beautiful things in unobvious places”, which in turn led to her knockout dresses, intricate silk roses trailing from hems or half-hidden under tulle. Erdem found a muse in Barbette, an avant-garde trapeze artist in 1920s Paris whose act ended with the revelation that “she” was a Texas-born man. Leotard-tight dresses were veiled in spiders’ webs of crystals, or worn with high-collared circus master coats.Edeline Lee dressed artists from the Royal Ballet in her dance-inspired pieces – neatly waisted, full-skirted dresses and practice-studio slouchy knits – for a catwalk in a north London school sports hall. Emilia Wickstead describes herself as “an old-school girl. I love classic shapes, vintage references. I have jazz music playing. But I’m always trying to make things a little foreign, a little forbidden, too.” She is “outgrowing the space” at the London boutique that usually doubles as a tiny catwalk, so this season she filmed a show and held screenings, enabling a set design of interwoven pastel rooms “that we couldn’t have done here physically, and don’t have the budget for”. American artist Lee Krasner inspired silk dresses, painted with daisies and overlaid with an apron of fine tweed sprouting colourful threads like flecks of paint, and striped artists’ shirts.Explore more on these topicsLondon fashion weekChristopher KaneMulberryFashion weeksnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Split Up review – this soapy divorce drama is loads of lavish, nonsensical fun | Television | The Guardian
description: Sanjeev Bhaskar plays a patriarch handing over the family firm in a spinoff of The Split. It’s full-on sudsy fun right from the off
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Sanjeev Bhaskar plays a patriarch handing over the family firm in a spinoff of The Split. It’s full-on sudsy fun right from the off
Content: ‘Nicely drawn tensions’ … The Split Up.Photograph: BBC/Sister PicturesView image in fullscreen‘Nicely drawn tensions’ … The Split Up.Photograph: BBC/Sister PicturesTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Split Up review – this soapy divorce drama is loads of lavish, nonsensical funSanjeev Bhaskar plays a patriarch handing over the family firm in a spinoff of The Split. It’s full-on sudsy fun right from the offLucy ManganSun 20 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdo like a soap that doesn’t hang about. That works itself up to a creamy lather and invites you to shut the bathroom door against real life and dive into a hot bath with it immediately for a much-needed break.The Split Up delivers full-on sudsy fun from the start. From the team behindThe Split, it’s another glossy tale of a family-run family law firm specialising in the never-too-complicated divorce cases of any high net worth individuals in their vicinity. This time, it’s written by Ursula Rani Sarma instead of Abi Morgan, the family is British South Asian and the location is Manchester not London, but beyond that it’s very much business as usual. A case of the week functions as the still eye of the ever-growing storm composed of the love lives, personal concerns and professional ambitions of the interrelated lawyers and their friends, colleagues and enemies – who are often, of course, one and the same thing. Mild glamour meets much plot; viewer happiness ensues.The new clan, the Kishans, comprises recently widowed patriarch Dhruv (Sanjeev Bhaskar), who is preparing to hand over the firm he has spent decades building from scratch to his charismatic, highly competent daughter, Aria (Ritu Arya), who is as driven and ambitious as he was at that age. But Dhruv is older now, and driven and ambitious youth does not seem quite the unassailable asset it once was. Caution and consolidation perhaps have their place, too. He ponders this quietly. Aria is too busy laying plans, busting divorce balls and dealing with her portion of B-plots to notice immediately.The main complication to Aria’s narrative is her dad’s unilateral decision to add financial specialist Luke (Dimitri Leonidas) to the firm. Of all the forensic accountants in all the world … Luke is the one Aria had a one-night stand with at a conference a couple of years ago. His re-entry into her world delights her not, and would delight her boyfriend, Neal (Danny Ashok) – who was also her boyfriend at the time – even less. Aria and Luke had better keep their former association hidden and their relationship going forward strictly professional. That’s a very good plan. Like most good plans, it fails on first contact with the extremely hot enemy.In the mix we also have Aria’s sister, Maya (Aysha Kala), who is a lawyer. Perhaps wisely, she took herself out of the melee a while back and just pops in now and again to lend a hand, in between raising a handful of kids and enjoying a strong and happy marriage, despite the long hours and late nights her husband (Tom Forbes) is putting in at his demanding job. Viewers hope that this is a sign of his unflagging commitment to providing for his family, but viewers have been here before.Rounding out the family is little brother Kav (Arian Nik). He is gay, which is fine by Dhruv, but he is also requiring multiple goes at passing his law exams, which is not. Journalist-influencer Ashok (Mawaan Rizwan) is keen to take his mind off things. Though he is also keen to glean gossip about the firm’s celebrity clients. Viewers hope no personal-professional lines are crossed. But viewers have been here before.View image in fullscreen‘Multiplying personal dramas’ … Arian Nik as Kav and Mawaan Rizwan as Ashok in The Split Up.Photograph: Ben Blackall/Sister Pictures/BBCAmid the familial and genital shenanigans (and they are not one and the same – this is not exactly a family show, except that it’s a show about a family, but it’s not THAT unfamilyish a show), the Kishans do occasionally muster some billable hours. In the first episode, these are mostly invoiced to Tash and Alex (Jane Horrocks and Lenny Henry, respectively), hosts of a wildly popular podcast about making marriage work, called Marriage Works, until one of them was caught in flagrante with a younger woman. Twist – it was Tash! The lady half of the couple! She doesn’t want a divorce, she wants an open marriage. Aria wants Alex to protect his assets. Alex wants Tash to be happy. Aria wants to eyeroll, hard, but Alex is an old friend of her father and she resists. In episode two, the guest star is Jameela Jamil, as another internetty type about to be screwed over by whatever the Modern is for “absolute bounder” until Aria rescues her too.But ultimately, the cases of the week are very slight, forgettable things, clearly of little interest to anyone involved and the site of most of the weak spots in the script (“Our friendship is our legacy, that’s the real loss here”). It’s the multiplying personal dramas and the nicely drawn tensions and tendernesses between the Kishans – who are all depicted with wit and warmth – that will keep us coming back. It is great fun: lavish nonsense with just enough truth in it to stop it becoming utterly preposterous. Come on in, the water’s lovely.The Split Up is available on BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDramaSanjeev BhaskarreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Pizza dough and TV prison dramas: how Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe survived jail in Iran | Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe | The Guardian
description: Former charity worker tells Big Brue festival in Somerset of the strange comforts that helped her during imprisonment
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Former charity worker tells Big Brue festival in Somerset of the strange comforts that helped her during imprisonment
Content: Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe speaking at the Big Brue festival.Photograph: Max Milligan photosView image in fullscreenNazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe speaking at the Big Brue festival.Photograph: Max Milligan photosNazanin Zaghari-RatcliffePizza dough and TV prison dramas: how Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe survived jail in IranFormer charity worker tells Big Brue festival in Somerset of the strange comforts that helped her during imprisonmentHelena HortonSun 20 Sep 2026 03.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a TV show about women confined to prison in the US, butNazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffefound watching Orange is the New Black with her fellow inmates a strange comfort after smuggling episodes into her Iranian jail cell, downloaded on to an illegal USB stick.The British-Iranian former charity worker was detained in 2016 for more than five years and kept in thenotorious Evin prisonin Tehran.She told an audience at theBig Brue festivalin Bruton, Somerset, that she thought she would never be released, so did not mind risking her freedom by sneaking in contraband.This included USB sticks preloaded with Netflix shows. She said: “We watched Breaking Bad, Prison Break andOrange is the New Black. It was very unusual, but it kind of connected us to the life we had before. Orange is the New Black is a whole different kind of genre of somebody who’s in prison.”Zaghari-Ratcliffe also danced with her fellow prisoners to contraband Zumba videos and cooked pizza for them in an oven she managed to cobble together money for and have sent to the prison. “I was the queen of the pizza dough in prison,” she said.She also discussed how she got permission to use the prison sewing machine, whichhelped her pass the timeas she sewed clothes for her young daughter and her friends, the other prisoners.This newfound artistic hobby spawned a collaboration with London’s Imperial War Museum and the fabric department of Liberty, creating three new prints that explored her experience as a prisoner.Iranian actor Laleh Marzban faces severe threats after Venice film festival speechRead moreThe riskiest item of contraband she snuck into prison was a Swiss Army knife. She said: “I realised, they don’t care what I do. I’m just a political hostage. So I can basically do anything in prison. I can be naughty. I can smuggle things, and once I smuggled this massive whopping Swiss knife.”She placed it in her shoe, but said: “It was so chunky, I just couldn’t walk. Having a knife in prison is a real crime. But I felt if they had found it, they would have given me what sentence? I was already in prison, and they couldn’t have done anything else to me.”Zaghari-Ratcliffe wasreleased in March 2022after the then Conservative government paid back a multimillion debt the UK owed to Iran. The Iranian regime had accused her of spying – a charge she denied and for which no evidence was ever produced.It became increasingly clear she was being held as a state hostage to try to force the UK to pay back its debt arising from a military deal struck with the deposed Shah ofIran.Though she is still traumatised by her time in prison and is visiting a therapist, Zaghari-Ratcliffe said she had continued to find solace in sewing.“When themilitary attack on Iranhappened at the end of February, for five days, I didn’t do anything. I just couldn’t do anything. The only thing that I could do was sit at my sewing machine and sew,” she said.“I thought, I don’t even know where my parents are. There was an internet blackout for a good two months, and I just couldn’t control the world around me, but I could control my own world. Sewing was the only thing that could calm me down. So yes, still, that’s still my refuge.”Explore more on these topicsNazanin Zaghari-RatcliffeIranOrange is the New BlackfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I suck at breaks’: a day in the life of an aerial cellist | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Cellista, an aerialist who regularly performs upside down with her cello, shares what her life looks like training for the stage
Author: Jaya Saxena
Headline: Cellista, an aerialist who regularly performs upside down with her cello, shares what her life looks like training for the stage
Content: Cellista: ‘You’re tempted to default to being nice because it feels easier in the moment.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Terence O'DonnellView image in fullscreenCellista: ‘You’re tempted to default to being nice because it feels easier in the moment.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Terence O'DonnellA day in the lifeWell actually‘I suck at breaks’: a day in the life of an aerial cellistCellista, an aerialist who regularly performs upside down with her cello, shares what her life looks like training for the stageJaya SaxenaSun 20 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMastering the cello is hard enough, butCellistaalso regularly performs upside down. She’s based in Las Vegas, but the aerialist spoke to us while traveling in Germany, and told us about what her life looks like training and writing for the stage.What time did you wake up?I woke up at 7.10am and beat my alarm clock, which was set for 8.01am. I felt triumphant. The feeling lasted until 11am and then I was back to my usual self.Did you eat breakfast?I fast. I really dislike eating in the morning and never have much of an appetite when I wake up. Although, technically I cheat because I have a nice big cup of coffee with ample milk and sugar.What did you do before work?I start every day by reading and journaling over coffee. I’ve been reading Nabokov’s love letters to his wife, Véra. He’s one of my favorite writers, but I now suspect from his letters that he was a neurotic love-bomber.After reading, I write. I’m currently writing a book to accompany my aerial theater piece, Mémoire. It interlaces my writing, old journal entries, a film I direct and aerial cello into one stage poem or one-woman show.What did work look like for you today?I began the process of submitting the album that accompanies Mémoire for Grammy consideration. I also had to follow up with a client about their very overdue payments. It felt weirdly emotional for me. It’s the freelancer life: you feel guilty asking for what you’re worth, or requesting what is due to you, and you’re tempted to default to being nice because it feels easier in the moment.Do you take breaks?I suck at breaks. I know that rest is better for my body and mind. But my mind just chatters away, and it feels incredibly difficult to take enough time off from training.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCellistaPhotograph: Terence O’DonnellWho was your favorite person you spoke to today?I got to chat with my dad. He was aprofessor of philosophyfor 42 years at the University of Denver and I was sharing my experience visiting Nietzsche’s house in Naumburg. We talked about Nietzsche’s breakdown in Turin when he tried to shield a horse from being beaten by its owner and became inconsolable at the horse’s suffering. Nietzsche never recovered; it was the onset of the neurosyphilis that would kill him.What did you do for dinner?Since I’m in Bayreuth for the Wagner Fest, I got to eat schäufele, which is roast pork shoulder with crispy yummy skin. It came with a potato dumpling the size of the moon, and cabbage.When did you go to sleep? Do you have a routine you follow?I try my best to sleep by midnight. Every single night, I watch old episodes of The X-Files, but nothing after season seven because that is when it gets intolerable. I usually have a cup of cocoa and three Voortman Vanilla Wafers while I watch. By the time Scully utters her last exasperated “Mulder!!!!”,I pass out.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyA day in the lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘As a Catholic monk, I was celibate. But sex with Orla feels so natural’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Rory left the monastery after feeling lonely; with Orla, herself a Catholic, he’s been making up for lost time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rory left the monastery after feeling lonely; with Orla, herself a Catholic, he’s been making up for lost time
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘As a Catholic monk, I was celibate. But sex with Orla feels so natural’Rory left the monastery after feeling lonely; with Orla, herself a Catholic, he’s been making up for lost timeHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told to Olivia LadanyiSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrla, 25double quotation markWe had sex after a week. I remember thinking afterwards wow, everything has changedOn our first date, last October, I asked Rory how conservative he was and he said: “I have premarital sex, but I’d rather die than eat meat on a Friday.” I’d been single for almost three years and wondered if I’d ever meet someone who understood both sides of me: Catholic but liberal. When we told each other we were bisexual, I felt a huge sense of relief.He introduced me to his friends straight away and we had sex after a week. I remember lying in bed afterwards and thinking wow, everything has just changed.I usually struggle to feel present during sex, but I can lose myself with Rory. I orgasmed from oral sex for the first time with him – I’d never felt comfortable enough before. In past relationships, I’d use sex to gain affection and attention or I’d withdraw it to say: please show me you still love me.Sex was a way to prove I was enough, and so the focus was always on the other person’s pleasure. But with Rory I feel safe, and I don’t use sex as a bargaining chip. If I can’t come, it’s not a big deal.double quotation markRory was celibate for three years, so he’s proven he can go without it – there’s never any pressureWhile training to become a Catholic monk, Rory was celibate for three years, so he’s proven he can go without sex – there’s never any pressure. We have it three or four times a week, sometimes twice on a Saturday morning. That’s my favourite time, when we can take it slow.In Catholicism, premarital sex is considered a mortal sin, so you’re not supposed to take communion. At mass, when everyone goes up to receive communion and we stay sitting, sometimes I worry about being judged. Rory wonders whether sex will feel less exciting when we’re married.The sex we have is fairly standard, but emotionally it feels new. Had he continued his training, Rory would have become a priest this year. Knowing how different our lives could have been – that we could so easily never have been together – makes what we have feel even more meaningful.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreRory, 31double quotation markI thought I’d never get married; I’m a bisexual ex-monk – too weirdI converted to Catholicism at 22 and then decided to train to become a monk, joining a monastery just after my 24th birthday.At the monastery, I found celibacy surprisingly easy, despite having a high sex drive. I left because I was lonely. People think the physical side of celibacy is the difficult part, but for me it was the thought that I’d never be able to have a deep emotional connection with a partner. When I left the monastery, I thought I’d never get married; I’m a bisexual ex-monk – too weird.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is how we do it: ‘My ex wouldn’t even kiss me during sex. Marcus is happy to take his time’Read moreThe first time I saw Orla, she was smoking a cigar. We were at a Catholic society party, and a man was telling her that he didn’t think Catholic women should smoke. She told him to fuck off. She was fun, confident and clearly knew herself, which I found attractive because I’m quite reserved. I liked that she wasn’t a stereotypical good Catholic – there was something different about her and it excited me.double quotation markAll the sex I’ve had has been naughty in some wayI’ve always struggled talking about my bisexuality with partners and it contributed to my last relationship breaking down.
