But with Orla, I could be open and vulnerable about it. I feel comfortable with my sexuality for the first time.The church’s teaching on sexuality is quite strict. I’m attracted to people I shouldn’t be – all the sex I’ve had has been naughty in some way. On the other hand, it feels very natural that Orla and I have sex. It’s a physical expression of our love.Although the sex we have isn’t very exciting, and sometimes I worry my preferences are too vanilla for Orla, it is passionate and emotional, and that intensity makes it special. We have an ongoing fantasy where Orla is a princess in a tower waiting for me to rescue her. Sex is one of the ways I make her feel safe and reassure her that she’s beautiful – simply telling her rarely works.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Donald Trump addresses the 80th United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York, 23 September 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump addresses the 80th United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York, 23 September 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOpinionUnited NationsIn a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it?Steve BloomfieldAs the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lackingSun 20 Sep 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTShareIf all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of theUnited Nationsheadquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry hasaccused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out byDonald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gatherfor the annual summit.The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rosein last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.Ten years ago,the election of António Guterresof Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of theSouth Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump with António Guterres at the 80th United Nations general assembly in New York, September 2025.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersEarlier this year, he announced the US’s withdrawal from 31 UN organisations, including the bodies responsible for dealing with climate change and women’s health, while in July his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the administration’s desire to “dismantle” the international criminal court “brick by brick”. The abrupt closure of the US’s aid and development programme, USAID,led to deaths around the world.Most controversially, the establishment of Trump’s Board of Peace sparked fears that it could be used to supplant the UN itself. The UN meanwhile is in the grip of a financial crisis, with Guterres warning during the summer thatit faced “imminent financial collapse”due to unpaid dues, much of it owed by the US.And yet, despite everything, the UN is still standing – and still matters. It is only the UN, through its Framework Convention on Climate Change, that manages to focus international attention on the greatest crisis the world is facing. Despite dramatic cuts in funding, there are still 11 peacekeeping missions staffed by more than 50,000 personnel in some of the most dangerous parts of the world. The UN’s office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs remains the best hope for negotiating access to deliver aid in war zones, including Sudan.This year the general assembly passed two landmark resolutions: one recognising the transatlantic slave trade as a crime, another to adopt a new world map that correctly recognises Africa’s size.We don’t know what the candidates think of these decisions, nor do we know where they stand on the war in Ukraine or what their stance is on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Despite the election’s importance – and despite the relatively recent transparency of “vision statements” and hustings – the candidates’ campaigns have been overwhelmingly cautious.Part of the reason, of course, is that someone standing on an ambitious platform would stand no chance of getting the job.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUN experts believe there is a chance that the two current frontrunners, Guyana’s former foreign ministerCarolyn Rodrigues-Birkettand Costa Rica’s ex vice-presidentRebeca Grynspan, might become good secretary-generals. But no one is blown away by the choice on offer.For Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband, both of whom will be in New Yorkthis weekat the UN general assembly, there is a choice to be made. The UK is yet to express a preference, indeed the UK team at the UN is said to be unimpressed with all the candidates. So far, it’s understood, they have not voted in favour of anyone in the first three straw polls. The UK and France are both hoping another candidate will emerge.Whether they will be any better is an open question. The New York Postreported in Julythat Trump wanted Fifa president Gianni Infantino to get the job. There is next to no chance that would happen, but European diplomats fear a Trump-backed dark horse – possibly one without a diplomatic background – may emerge in the coming weeks. This is, after all, the man who has outsourced his nation’s diplomacy to his son-in-law and a real estate investor. So far, Trump has said nothing in public, although that may change on Tuesday when he gives his speech at the general assembly. Or a social media post spat out at two in the morning could upend the race entirely.The chances of the “Permanent Five” failing to agree on a name remain slim, but plans are already being drawn up in case the worst happens. Guterres may be asked to stay on, while another possibility is that a collection of senior UN officials is asked to serve in administrative roles until a candidate is found. Either way, it would leave the UN rudderless at a time it needs to be anything but.No one is getting this job without Trump’s say so. But once the new general secretary is in office, the US president will have less sway on their actions. They will potentially serve for 10 years, eight of which will be without Trump in the White House.But even without Trump, this will be an almost impossible job. The UN’s financial crisis is not going away. Severe cuts are coming. There will be no easy return to the 1990s and early 2000s, when the UN was at the heart of world events. A new leader will need to reinvent multilateralism in a world where it’s going out of favour.Depending on the choice they make, we could look back at this decision as the moment that the crumbling international rules-based order began to be rebuilt – or when it slid irretrievably into irrelevance.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prizeExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionHuman rightsHumanitarian responseDonald TrumpInternational lawcommentShareReuse this content

title: AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threat | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by tech firms is a worry
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by tech firms is a worry
Content: There is ample evidence that AI urgently needs regulating.Photograph: Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThere is ample evidence that AI urgently needs regulating.Photograph: Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/ShutterstockEconomics viewpointAI (artificial intelligence)AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threatHeather StewartScale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by tech firms is a worrySun 20 Sep 2026 06.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWarnings about powerful and uncontrolled AI have dominated the headlines this past week. But even amid theomens of apocalypse, it is still worth asking if the entire AI-industrial complex is sailing towards a financial iceberg.It will hardly be our most pressing concern if the bots are poised to take over the world, but a collapse of the AI bubble would have repercussions far beyond the US.AI bosseshave united in recent daysto warn us the immensely powerful product they have sunk billions into creating may or may not destroy the human race.Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents growRead moreSome are also calling for limits on how rapidly the technologies should be allowed to progress, and how they can be used.There is ample evidence that AI urgently needs regulating – from the ability of Meta’s pervert glasses (sorry, smart glasses) tofilm us without consentto the lack of adequate safeguards that allowed swarms of chatbotsto go on a hacking spree.Some of the suggestions currently being mooted, including independent analysis of AI models, seem important improvements on the ungoverned status quo.But we should also be alert to the risk that a small number of intricately linked megafirms that have racked up multibillion-dollar debts are hoping the state will throw a regulatory moat around them.Perhaps a government-backed AI “pause” could prevent cheaper Chinese options from encroaching on Silicon Valley’s market dominance, for example.Away from the risk that their product might obliterate human life, there are more old-fashioned reasons for tech bosses to be fearful – including the fundamental one of whether the economics of their businesses work.The first worry is the sheer scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by the hyperscalers building them – Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle – $132bn (£99bn) this year aloneon one estimate.In a world of fragile bond markets with yields on 10-year US treasuries, a global benchmark for borrowing costs,hovering at about 5%, the size of these debt piles could be one potential trigger for a market rethink.View image in fullscreenThe scale of debt issuance being used to fund the hectic pace of the datacentre rollout by the hyperscalers has been estimated at $132bn.Photograph: Aleksei Gorodenkov/AlamyThat is especially true given the second reason for concern: the fact that the “unit economics” of AI continue to be questionable and aren’t moving in the right direction.As a recent Bloomberg reportput it: “The price of AI is collapsing, while the cost of building it is not.” It pointed out that OpenAI has repeatedly cut its fees to hang on to customers, for example.An index by theresearch company Silicon Datathat aims to track how much customers are paying for a million tokens – the units of data processed by large language models – shows it more than halving since June, to less than $1.Yet at the same time, frenzied demand for the real-world components of datacentres – semiconductors, for example – is keeping costs elevated.The maths only works, it seems, on the assumption of epic revenue growth. Anthropicapparently told investorsrecently that its “adjusted operating income” was positive – the only problem being that this measure effectively excludes many of its costs.As thedigital rights campaigner Cory Doctorow puts it: “These companies are claiming that they are so cool that their profitability can only be measured using a novel, secret form of mathematics.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome aspects of this edifice may seem familiar to veterans of the global financial crisis: masters of the universe, with a business model that is so clever mere mortals can’t be expected to understand it, all propped up with ample dollops of leverage.Afrankly terrifying recentresearch note from the financial analyst Groundbreaker made this analogy clear, by unearthing a third reason to worry – just totting up debt underrepresents the financial promises underpinning the boom.It sets out the $1.5tn “compute commencement wall” faced by the AI labs over the next couple of years, drawing a comparison with the moment when cut-price “teaser” mortgage rates began to run out in 2007 and 2008.When those rates ended, flipping low income homeowners on to much higher rates, borrowers began defaulting in their droves, lighting the touchpaper on what became the global financial crisis.According to Groundbreaker’s analysis, in many cases datacentres are being built and kitted out on “take or pay” contracts, with not a dollar due until a deadline is hit (often two to three years), and they hum into life.In the interim, the hyperscaler building the datacentre books the value of the contract as expected future revenue, and shareholders cheer. Meanwhile, the buyer, (a frontier lab such as OpenAI or Anthropic) doesn’t yet have to account for the costs it will have to pay, once it starts using it.The analysis suggests the abrupt jump in costs, as contracts mature and datacentres come online, could be an eye-watering $700bn next year and more than $800bn in 2027.That could all be just fine if revenue continues to rocket. Or perhaps not so much, if AI’s end users aren’t prepared to pay enough to cover the costs – perhaps because cheaper options arise.This isn’t, technically, debt – but the impact, if obligations can’t be met in full, would shake the foundations of the entire edifice.Given the spate of recent revelations about revolting bots, the focus on AI safety and the risks to humanity may well be justified, and should be tackled.But that should not prevent us from fretting about the delicate, interlinked financial structures that underpin the AI boom, and the risks for us all if they crumble.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Economics viewpointTechnology sectorDatacentresChatbotsGoogleAmazonMicrosoftcommentShareReuse this content

title: My mum has died - and every decision I make about her belongings feels wrong | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Until now I’d never realised how much work is involved in sorting out a parent’s affairs, and how much heartbreak, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Until now I’d never realised how much work is involved in sorting out a parent’s affairs, and how much heartbreak, writes Polly Hudson
Content: Polly’s mum, Val, with Polly as a newborn.Photograph: courtesy of Polly HudsonView image in fullscreenPolly’s mum, Val, with Polly as a newborn.Photograph: courtesy of Polly HudsonOpinionBereavementMy mum has died - and every decision I make about her belongings feels wrongPolly HudsonUntil now I’d never realised how much work is involved in sorting out a parent’s affairs, and how much heartbreakSun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTShareIn all the talk of thefive stages of grief,I don’t recall one of them being spending hours on hold to energy suppliers. Perhaps I misunderstood, though, and that’s entirely what they’re about. This call won’t take long (denial); aargh, are they ever going to answer? (anger); if I hang on for five minutes more, they’ll definitely pick up (bargaining); they are never, ever going to pick up (depression); and I live on hold now – this is my life (acceptance).You hear the term “sadmin” bandied about, you understand there’s paperwork to do after somebody dies – but until it’s you who has to do it, you don’t realise how much, what it entails or how encompassing it is. My mum’s death has basically become my full-time job. The hours are terrible, the pay is worse and the promotion prospects sobering, to say the least.Received wisdom is that you should ask your parents lots of questions while they’re still around. For me, this feels increasingly true. There’s so much I now wish I’d asked my mum – namely who her mobile phone provider was and the number of her milkman. I don’t know where the water meter in my own house is, let alone anyone else’s, so it would have been handy if that had come up, too.When my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about griefRead moreI’m lucky my mother died after the introduction ofTell Us Once, the one-stop shop for notifying government departments and council services. But so far my experience is: tell them once, tell everyone else 47 times and prepare yourself for a variety of responses in reaction to the news.I’vepreviously coveredthe odd sentences people insert in the gap after “I’m calling to let you know that my mum has died,” a sentence that drives home reality sledgehammer-style whenever you hear yourself say it. In fairness, many call centre employees have been empathic and kind. However, this week, one responded: “That’s not a problem,” and I was too stunned to reply with any of the killer sick burns I’ve since thought of.The DVLA staff, whom I’ve spoken to thrice and counting, did not react. On the last call, I’m afraid I snapped a bit – third time unlucky – and suggested that acknowledging what I’d said in a manner that was vaguely human was perhaps a tactic they could try in future. I was told that this was not policy: they were trained to stay silent. I wonder whether this is true, or just quick thinking.On top of the sadmin, there’s thestuff. A whole homeful of it. Deciding what to keep and what to donate or – eek – chuck is a battle with nostalgia and sentimentality.double quotation markWe don’t need a tea cosy we’ll never use, a collection we didn’t collect. The connection is baked into our bonesMy house is full, but what am I supposed to do with the plates I ate off as a child? The table we sat around every Christmas? My mum’s diary, the old-fashioned, paper variety, full of appointments, meetings and get-togethers it turns out she’ll never attend, in handwriting as familiar as my own? A photo of my parents with nine of their friends, only two of whom are still alive? Here, they’re in their 40s or 50s, on holiday somewhere, laughing and mucking around, looking pretty similar to me and my frie … nope, let’s steer well clear of that, thanks.Becoming an orphan attempts to force you to face your own mortality, when I would rather pack it away and give it to a charity shop. But as I sit with this picture in my hands for too long, which I’d do even if I didn’t have such a lengthy to-do list, I have to accept that, if I take it home, I’m merely ensuring my son will have to decide what to do with it when his turn comes. The circle of sadmin.Every decision feels incorrect. Keeping this kind of photo is silly, but throwing away evidence of anniversary parties, minibreaks, school uniforms, long-departed pets, Wednesdays, is worse. These pictures are proof of life. But I don’t need proof: I was there, living it. I remember it well. And, realistically, I’m not going to frame them all, hang them on my walls, turn my house into a shrine to the past. They’ll gather dust in a drawer, letting me off my guilt on a technicality.Is there a right way to do this? It seems extremely important not to get it wrong.When my dad died, in 2012, I kept everything he had ever touched – and many things just in case he might have. There was an offcut of string he’d wound up in a precise, careful way that was so unmistakably him that I found it impossible to discard, or even use when I randomly needed a bit of string exactly that length, which would actually have pleased him immensely.Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before | Gaby HinsliffRead moreA while afterwards, I read a bedtime story to my friend’s son. It was a book calledThe Invisible String, which helps children process grief by reminding them they’re always linked with those they love. It was so on the nose, including the title, the parallels too obvious to ignore.These bonds go well beyond the tangible. We don’t need a tea cosy we’ll never use, a collection we didn’t collect, a painting we wouldn’t have chosen ourselves. The connection is baked into our bones. It would remain even if we didn’t have a single worldly possession. It carries on, regardless.Gradually, over the years that followed, I managed to do without many of the superfluous items of my dad’s that I’d clung on to. I do wear his watch, even though it stopped working years ago (it’s right twice a day). And I still have the neat little knot of string. Hey, nobody’s perfect.What if my attitude to my mum’s belongings is all wrong? What if it isn’t a case of now or never? Not getting rid of an object immediately doesn’t mean I’m keeping it for ever; it could be that the lesson here is to give myself a bit of grace. Maybe sometimes it takes a little longer to let go.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Hungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating together | Shadi Khan Saif | The Guardian
description: Mealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade stories
Author: Shadi Khan Saif
Headline: Mealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade stories
Content: ‘Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itReligionHungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating togetherShadi Khan SaifMealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade storiesMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTShareWhen I was growing up in a Muslim household, food was rarely just food. As the youngest child, my job was to bring out a large water jug with a matching basin pot and soap to help the family wash their hands. Mum would distribute freshly baked breads to everyone to have with the soup or curry. Dad would have me sit next to him as he presided over the gathering – asking questions, giving directions all the while passing food and utensils around. My older brother would take turns helping everyone wash their hands.There was even a small ritual around something as ordinary as a piece of bread. If it fell on the ground anywhere in the house or was even seen on the ground outside, we would pick it up, clean it, kiss it respectfully and place it somewhere clean and safe.Foodwas not to be treated carelessly.And sending a guest away without offering them a meal is unthinkable – almost a sin.As a child, I didn’t think of any of this as “spirituality”. It was simply what you did. Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.Only later, after leaving Afghanistan and building a life in Australia, did I begin to understand what those ordinary habits carried with them: gratitude, hospitality and a sense that food was something to be celebrated – and shared.Islamis hardly alone in this.Make yourselves at home: the meaning of hospitality in a divided worldRead moreInJudaism, the Shabbat meal brings families together around food, prayer, conversation and ritual. Christianity has the shared meal at the centre of one of its most powerful religious symbols, while the Gospels repeatedly depict Jesus eating with others, including people considered outsiders.Across Hindu traditions, food is associated with gratitude, hospitality and community. In Sikhism, thetradition oflangarmakes the social meaning of eating together particularly explicit. People sit together and share a free meal regardless of wealth, status or social position. Everyone is fed. Just as importantly, everyone eats together.The traditions are different, of course. But across them runs a familiar idea: food can bring people together in ways that go well beyond satisfying hunger.During a fieldwork assignment, a group of strangers and I were thrust together for an orientation meeting over lunch.Nerves stopped everyone from taking the first bite. So our team leader smiled and said: “Buon appetito.” I replied with the Afghan equivalent: “Ishteha-e-khoob” – enjoy your meal.Halfway through eating, our team leader suddenly apologised for his habit of eating quickly. He explained that he had grown up as the youngest of nine children in a poor Italian family, where you learned early to eat before the food ran out.Others began opening up and telling their own stories about food.For some, family meals were about far more than what was on the plate. They created a pause in the day when parents and children sat together, listened to one another and traded stories. In an era before smartphones, and when many families turned the television off at dinner, the table was the centre of family life.I left that lunch thinking about how much can be contained in something as simple as sitting down to eat.These days, more often than not, I find myself eating lunch on the go – in my car, on a Teams meeting or while scrolling on my phone. Once, amid community engagement work and endless spreadsheets and trackers, I forgot that I had left my lunchbox in the car.That’s modern life, I suppose.Food is easily reduced to fuel: something we need to get through the day before moving on to the next task. We don’t always have the time to wait for others to join us. We don’t always ask whether someone has eaten. And yet we seem to spend an extraordinary amount of time looking at photographs of food online.Perhaps there is something slightly strange about that. We have never had so many pictures of beautifully presented meals yet so little time to sit down and enjoy our food with the people we love.Buon appetito. Ishteha-e-khoob!Explore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itIslamFoodFamilyJudaismSikhismHinduismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Star Trek is turning 60 – and the vision it promised feels more distant than ever | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the future
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the future
Content: ‘Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be bad now, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be bad now, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionStar TrekStar Trek is turning 60 – and the vision it promised feels more distant than everDave SchillingThe US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the futureSun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTShareWho among us doesn’t dream of space in their youth?OK, maybe some of us. Like the ones with lives. While you were out playing hopscotch with little Jimmy and Susie, I was locked in my room mainlining episodes of Star Trek or theweird, sanitized version of Aliensthat aired on broadcast TV. Fantastical science-fiction adventure seemed to offer more than playground games and actual human connection. Spaceships over relationships.Star Trek, celebrating its 60th anniversary this month, offered a utopian vision of the future. Highly competent scientists traveling the galaxy solving moral and ethical quandaries with grace and intelligence. It was a vision of Earth that had overcome greed and selfishness to pursue a more peaceful world Kirk and Spock. Picard and Data. These were characters that were ethical, witty and heroic. Better that than little Jimmy burning ants with a magnifying glass.The Alien franchise, on the other hand, was the complete opposite. In the second film, Aliens, which coincidentally is turning 40 this year, the characters are mostly brain-dead killing-machine soldiers and venal corporate stooges. This one sounds a bit more familiar, doesn’t it? The entire known universe is controlled by a diabolical company whose only aim is profit at the expense of the average person. Both Star Trek and the Alien films offered the requisite thrills and whiz-bang action to titillate a young boy like myself back in the 1990s, but they were also diametrically opposed visions of what the world might look like when I became an adult. Would it be along the lines of alush beige carpet and colorful pajamasor asoaking wet murder machine covered in KY Jellygrinding the working class into the ground? It took a few decades, but I think I found my answer.US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in spaceRead moreThe US air force announced on Monday that it haddeployed weapons into space, thumbing its nose at the unwritten rule that space is for peace, not for war. The US rationale is,well, everyone else is doing it!Officials point to the increased militarization of space, including a 2024 Biden administration report claiming Russia wasdeveloping the capability to detonate nuclear weapons in spaceto disable or destroy orbiting satellites, which are crucial pieces of global infrastructure.The air force secretary, Troy Meink,referred to the deploymentas “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action”. He wouldn’t say what they were, what they could actually do, or even what they look like. Which is always so comforting when futuristic space guns are involved. Is it a giant laser beam? Missiles? A claw that can grab satellites out of the sky? A large hammer? A Trump-shaped robot gollum that could swallow the International Space Station with the ease and gusto of the real person chowing down on a Big Mac? My imagination, stoked by years of sci-fi television, is running rampant. At the very least, I hope it has a series of blinking lights all over it. And an off-switch.Back in the 1980s, when Star Trek was at its creative peak, the idea of weaponizing space was considered such a joke that President Reagan struggled to amass a consensus around hisStrategic Defense Initiative(derisively nicknamed “Star Wars”), which would have created a US orbiting missile deterrent. But now, Donald Trump is making fantasy space battles a key element of his rapidly deteriorating legacy. The US space force, his absurd brainchild,presented new uniformsthat look like they wereleftover from a Paul Verhoeven movie. If one wants to conquer a lifeless galaxy full of dirt, rocks and little else, one must be wearing the shiniest black boots possible. Also a hat.The space force uniforms are certainly lightyears away from the ones on Star Trek, where everyone wears bright colors that immediately make the viewer think they’ve accidentally stumbled onto a rather unique discotheque. The Star Trek creator, Gene Roddenberry, made sure that the phaser weapons depicted on the show had a non-lethal stun setting. I think if anyone proposed a non-lethal weapon for the US space force, they’d be A) fired immediately and B) called woke to their face (and on Fox News in front of millions of people).Looking back six decades at the world Star Trek was born in, there was optimism in the world, mixed in with the chaos of political assassinations, riots, a war in Vietnam, and the ever-present threat of nuclear annihilation. The idea of going to space and landing Apollo 11 on the Moon was inspiring to a world that needed more cheering up thanEd Sheeran trying to find an opening act for his tour. Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be badnow, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.Countless modern scientific achievements – cellphones, tablets, the internet, medical advancements – can be attributed to Star Trek beaming ideas of benevolent futurism into homes around the globe for 60 years. But did society actually learn anything from Star Trek? The Federation and the Klingons made peace in the film Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, but could their real-world analogues – the United States and Russia – be any further apart? Of course, if you know anything about the future-history depicted on Star Trek, you know utopia doesn’t occur until after a global nuclear holocaust, in case you want to be even more depressed today.Star Trek’s impact is immense, especially for a TV show that only lasted for three years and often deployed styrofoam rocks, wobbly models, and dodgy rubber aliens in its design. That impact is a testament to the writing, acting, and film technique that grabbed millions of people and changed their lives. But I’ve never been more pessimistic about humanity achieving the beautiful dream of Gene Roddenberry. With every fascist-looking spacesuit or space laser, I feel like we’re progressing backwards, step by step. Given the proliferation of pandemics, climate change, species extinction, and contaminated food supplies, I’m more apt to wake up expecting to have anHR Giger-inspired genetic abominationgnawing at my face. At least my years staring at my TV screen alone prepared me for what’s to come.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsStar TrekOpinionUS militaryUS televisionTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: From Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers? | Rebecca Rideal | The Guardian
description: Another true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’, says historian and author Rebecca Rideal
Author: Rebecca Rideal
Headline: Another true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’, says historian and author Rebecca Rideal
Content: Ella Beatty as Lizzie Borden in the new Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenElla Beatty as Lizzie Borden in the new Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixOpinionTV crime dramaFrom Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers?Rebecca RidealAnother true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.41 EDTShareOn 20 June 1893, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a packed courtroom waited with bated breath for the jury to return its verdict following a gruelling double-murder trial. Against a backdrop of intense media interest, they had heard the prosecution argue that the accused had hacked to death their own parents with a hatchet, had burned their clothing to hide evidence of blood, and had done so out of hatred. The question the jury was asked to answer was simple – was Lizzie Andrew Borden guilty of murdering her father and stepmother? Jurors took just one hour to reach a decision: not guilty.Yet, almost as soon as the trial came to an end, the mythmaking around Borden began – from fevered speculation about her motives and theinfamous nursery rhymeto the many film and TV retellings of the story. The latest incarnation, Netflix’sMonster: The Lizzie Borden Story, opens with an axe-wielding Borden committing the murders, and frames the crimes around a fictionalised queer romance between her and the family’s housemaid, Bridget Sullivan.Why, after 130 years, are we still enthralled by the Borden murders? Part of the answer, I think, speaks to a wider obsession with female killers (or alleged female killers in Borden’s case) and the way in which society ties itself in knots to try to explain, excuse or justify violent women. Statistically, globally and historically, homicide is a largely male crime – in terms of both perpetrators and victims. Female killers are rare: they representedjust 7%of convicted homicide suspects in England and Wales between 2019 and 2022. It is precisely this rarity that sees homicides with female perpetrators (or alleged perpetrators) disproportionately sensationalised, mythologised and forced into recognisable tropes – the femme fatale, the wrongfully accused, the passive victim or the monstrosity.That is not to say there isn’t some truth in each of these ideas.But very often a female perpetrator of a violent crime will also trigger or become the face of wider societal debates about crime, punishment, justice and womanhood. History is littered with examples.The execution of Marie Manning in 1849, alongside her husband, for the murder of her lover, Patrick O’Connor, was followed by tens of thousands of Londoners, includingCharles Dickens, and spawned close to 2.5m broadsheet sales. The shock of seeing a woman hanged triggered a nationwide debate about the ethics of public executions (they were abolished in Britain less than 20 years later). So notorious did Manning become that Madame Tussauds created a wax model of her, dressed in the black satin dress the killer supposedly wore at her execution.The statue remained in its chamber of horrors until 1971.View image in fullscreenCharlize Theron as the serial killer Aileen Wuornos in the 2003 film Monster.Photograph: Newmarket Films/AllstarSimilarly, the trial of the chocolate poisoner, Christiana Edmunds, forced Victorian society to confront the idea that a single middle-class woman could intentionally cause indiscriminate harm. When an attempted plea of insanity failed and she was found guilty of the murder of Sidney Barker and attempted murder of Mrs Beard, she was sentenced to death. But the home secretary stepped in, asked for her to be reassessed and granted her a reprieve. She spent the rest of her days at Broadmoor psychiatric hospital.As the historianJill Newton Ainsley attests, “Declaring her insane and therefore not responsible for her actions provided a bizarre and unprecedented crime with a relatively simple explanation.” This reluctance to acknowledge women’s agency when it comes to violent crime plays out in statistics too. Newton Ainsley has shown that between 1832 and 1901 women were twice as likely as men to be granted an acquittal on the grounds of insanity – even when charged with similar crimes.For very different reasons, the acquittal of Beatrice Pace in 1928 captured public attention. She had been accused of murdering her abusive husband by arsenic poisoning, only to become the poster girl for wronged women. Upon her acquittal, newspapers reported emotional scenes where “women clasped one another by the hands and some cried”. Hundreds of women later wrote to her expressing their well wishes for her future. A few decades later, in 1955, after shooting her abusive lover, David Blakely, five times with a revolver, there was no such sympathy for Ruth Ellis at her trial. She was found guilty of murder, but her subsequent execution shone a spotlight on theethics of capital punishment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLindsay Clancy’s case is a Rorschach test | Moira DoneganRead morePerhaps the most chilling manifestation of female violence in the 20th century comes in the person of the child killer Myra Hindley. Despite conducting the crimes alongside Ian Brady, the criminologistMark Pettigrew has notedthat the press coverage of Hindley, with the infamous mugshot, far exceeded that of Brady. Additionally, her unsuccessful parole attempts opened a wider debate about whether “life” should mean life. More recently, the case of the convicted murderer Lucy Letby has become deeply political with regard to whistleblowing, medical care and the role of expert witnesses.When it comes to this latest iteration of the Lizzie Borden story, the Netflix show appears to make a connection between Borden and 20th-century serial killer Aileen Wuornos, who received her own Hollywood treatment in a filmstarring Charlize Theron, also called Monster. This seems designed to, as the publicity materials state, tap into a “legacy of female rage” and provide an “exploration of why women kill”. From the opening episode, the show takes a highly sexualised and graphic approach to the story of the killings.Was Borden guilty? We may never know. What we do know is that there were four people in the Borden household on the morning of 4 August 1892: Andrew Borden, Abby Borden, Lizzie Borden and Bridget Sullivan. By lunchtime, Andrew and Abby were hacked to death; Abby’s body was abandoned face-down on a bedroom floor and Andrew’s lay on a blood-drenched sofa. The brutal reality is that this was a horrific crime – whether a result of “female rage” or not.Rebecca Rideal is a historian and the author of1666: Plague, War and Hellfire. She co-hosts the historical true-crime podcast seriesBuried Evidence, and writes on history, true crime and cultureDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is
Content: ‘This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many professional fields against the companies that develop these systems.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many professional fields against the companies that develop these systems.’Photograph: AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see thatEditorialOpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really isSun 20 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareOn 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “existential crisis” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAImisused human work.The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”.View image in fullscreenTristan Buckmaster.Photograph: The Washington Post/GettyThis lack ofattribution and compensationfor the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use theirmodels’ maths prowess as an advertisement. But they rely on mathematicians to check their –often sloppy and baffling– work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment.Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as theycommit their namestoopen lettersdenouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been anuanced discussionof how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities.Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematicianNestor Guillenwrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionMathematicsComputingeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the last instalment of the Seven Up! series: growing up in public | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The compelling documentary series is drawing to a close. But following people from childhood raises difficult ethical questions
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The compelling documentary series is drawing to a close. But following people from childhood raises difficult ethical questions
Content: Bruce Balden, one of the Seven Up! children.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBruce Balden, one of the Seven Up! children.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockOpinionTelevisionThe Guardian view on the last instalment of the Seven Up! series: growing up in publicEditorialThe compelling documentary series is drawing to a close. But following people from childhood raises difficult ethical questionsSun 20 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareIn 1963, a television crew documented the lives of 14 children.Michael Apted, then a young researcher, saw Seven Up! as an opportunity to expose the British class system, juxtaposing public schoolboys with counterparts from children’s homes and council estates. Seven years later, Apted returned to direct an update – then went back again, and again. For the most part, his subjects followed the socioeconomic paths one might have predicted. But what emerged over the decades was much more piercing and poignant than initially envisaged. It turned out – as its participants have noted – that the programme was as much about life itself as class.The final instalment,70 Up, currently being shown in two parts on ITV, is extraordinarily moving. We know that the children we see in the original footage will struggle with divorce, bereavement, depression, homelessness, redundancy and ill-health. Two of the original participants, and Apted himself, have died;Nick Hitchon, the boy from a Yorkshire farm who became an expert in nuclear fusion, gave a final interview days before his death. Yet these closing episodes, directed by Asif Kapadia, also capture deep joys such as parenthood, and the satisfaction of the self-knowledge they have earned. There are no simple arcs of redemption or tragedy, but something more muddled and nuanced.View image in fullscreenMichael Apted.Photograph: Photoshot Holdings Ltd/Rex/ShutterstockTo watch these lives unspool is a remarkable privilege. Yet it is not always a comfortable one, nor one which could easily be repeated. The loss of innocence that 70 Up captures is not only that of its youthful subjects, but of the society around them. Apted’s questions could be blunt, verging on cruel. But the seven-year intervals mean that while the series captured lives, it did not expose them as brutally as the relentlessness of today’s reality television and social media schedules, and the endless replay of clips and memes, would. No subject now could expect anonymity between the instalments. Most would want to shape their own narrative. At least one would surely establish their own supplements line, or become a streamer.More children than ever are served up for the public gaze, directly by their families as well as the TV and film industries: at the same time, the viewer is increasingly aware of the toll that such attention has previously taken on children in the spotlight, from youthful Hollywood stars to those monetised from babyhood by their parents. Horrifyingfamily influencer scandalsunderline the questions about who is benefiting and who is watching, in an age where the UK’s National Crime Agency haswarned parentsagainst putting their children’s images on public display online because of concerns over AI-generated images of sexual abuse.Even in the best-case scenario, it is hard to know whether parents, as well as children, can truly understand what exposure to the public eye will mean not only in the moment, but later in life. Fictional versions are not immune to the challenges. Richard Linklater filmed scenes every year to construct hismoving film Boyhood, which captures a childhood from five to 18 – but the director’s daughter Lorelei, who played the protagonist’s sister, wanted to opt out as a teenager.Apted’s subjects pushed back at the director’s biases as they grew and in some cases quit the programme – though all but one returned, and several speak fondly about what it has meant to them. Viewers will be grateful. But it is harder to justify the greater toll of growing up in public these days.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionOpinionITV plcTelevision industryMichael AptededitorialsShareReuse this content

title: Our understanding of the slave trade is still evolving | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to William Pettigrew’s article about the lasting significance of the slave trade to Britain’s politics, economy, institutions and culture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to William Pettigrew’s article about the lasting significance of the slave trade to Britain’s politics, economy, institutions and culture
Content: Illustration, titled The Mode of Flogging Slaves, published in The West Indies As They Are, by the Reverend Richard Bickell, 1825.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenIllustration, titled The Mode of Flogging Slaves, published in The West Indies As They Are, by the Reverend Richard Bickell, 1825.Photograph: AlamySlaveryLettersOur understanding of the slave trade is still evolvingReaders respond to William Pettigrew’s article about the lasting significance of the slave trade to Britain’s politics, economy, institutions and cultureSun 20 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWilliam Pettigrew’s book, Britain’s Slave Traders: A Forgotten History, adds a further dimension and depth to our understanding of how entrenched and significant Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade was. The landmark University College London’sLegacies of British Slaveryproject previously documented the “compensation” payments to 46,000 persons who, at the time of its abolition in 1834, had a financial interest in slave ownership – the £20m paid out is generally reckoned to beworth around £17bnat 2019 prices, or 40% of total government expenditure in 1834 – a vast national debt that was only fully amortised in 2015.The earlier study thus highlighted the extensive involvement of sections of the British public in profiting from slavery, and the further financial benefit from “compensation”. The recent study tracks back into the prior history from the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade through the 18th century, and shows how its tentacles throughout that time reached out deep into the economy and society. The economic impact over this whole period should not be underestimated. As Pettigrew observes (Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation, 14 September), the slave trade provided some of the seed funding for the Industrial Revolution. The flow of income back from the Caribbean sugar plantations provided capital surpluses to fund new industries, through an expanded banking system, not to mention personal wealth. Defending these assets in turn stimulated the growth of the British navy, and its eventual control of the seas.Until American independence in 1776, the colonists relying on enslaved people for their cotton and coffee plantations were British settlers, paying taxes to the British exchequer. In the 19th century, “compensation” payouts fed into investments in the new railways; into banking; and into the funding of stately homes and the arts. Taken together, it could therefore be reasonably argued it was the slave trade that made Britain the cradle of the Industrial Revolution.Chris HendryEmeritus professor, City, University of LondonWilliam Pettigrew is right that slavery was not a footnote to British history. His account powerfully demonstrates how the slave trade was entangled with the state, finance, politics and culture. But there is a further question: what about class? Pettigrew speaks of “Britain” and says “we are all – in some way – connected to it”. Yet Britain was never a single social actor. The slave owner, merchant and investor had a fundamentally different relationship to slavery from the growing cotton-mill proletariat whose labour helped turn slave-grown cotton into commodities.The danger is that “we are all connected” obscures the asymmetry of accumulation between those who owned capital and accumulated wealth from the system, and those who possessed only their labour and received wages. The question is not simply how slavery shaped Britain, but how its wealth entered an expanding capitalist economy – and was distributed through profoundly unequal class relations.David EatonSunderlandThe Guardian’s excellent presentation of the findings of the Register of British Slave Traders (What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?, 14 September) highlighted what has been long known. It is also timely if it persuades anyone to question the thinking that underlies the philosophy shared by most western leaders that “western democracy” shines out in a challenging world, representing the best of humanity.Historians know that this is based on contradictions. The world’s first known democracy, the dazzling civilisation of ancient Athens, was based both on slavery and on a thoroughly undemocratic empire, the Delian League.Slaveryhas been practised across history by all types of government from despotic monarchies to republics and democracies. Put this alongside the fact that the democratic rights we now enjoy had to be extracted, sometimes by force, from the ruling class, and we might have a more humble evaluation of the place of our civilisation in the world. As Gandhi famously said when asked what he thought of western civilisation, “It would be a good idea”.Dr Peter PurtonSouthall, LondonAs slavery was abolished, poor laws were enacted across England. A distinction began to be established between those deemed to be worthy of charity and those who were not. The workhouse consolidated the form and substance of these differences. Distinctions established then persist today in ideas about the undeserving and deserving poor, scroungers and strivers, immigrant and indigenous labour.Rod EarleGuildford, SurreyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Double cleansing benefits the beauty industry, not consumers  | Skincare | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers reflect on an article which explored whether we should be cleaning ourselves twice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers reflect on an article which explored whether we should be cleaning ourselves twice
Content: ‘My skin is perfectly healthy and I don’t smell anything other than naturally human.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘My skin is perfectly healthy and I don’t smell anything other than naturally human.’Photograph: GettySkincareLettersDouble cleansing benefits the beauty industry, not consumersReaders reflect on an article which explored whether we should be cleaning ourselves twiceSun 20 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareWith reference to your article about the merits, or not, of double cleansing (Double cleansing: should we really be cleaning ourselves twice in each shower?, 15 September), I wish to report that I shower once a week, while in between times wash daily with soap, flannel and a bowl of water (which then flushes the loo). I do this because I am deeply concerned at our misuse of the planet’s resources. We currently use fresh water at a faster rate globally than it can be replenished. Here in the UK, it ispredictedthat by 2055 we will have a 5bn litre a day shortfall for public water supplies – with a further 1bn litre a day deficit for the wider economy. My skin is perfectly healthy and I don’t smell anything other than naturally human.Judith RussenbergerLondonAll right, so I am a man, and I suspect that this piece is aimed at women, but do we really need all this? It is now nearly 10 years that I have not used any body wash or hair shampoo. My showers last no more than two or three minutes: any more is a waste of hot water. The run-off from these “cleansers” is not environmentally friendly.I do not smell of anything except lightly of myself. My skin at the age of 89 is quite healthy as I do not take out any of its natural oils. On the negative side, however, I undertake a wet shave every day with a proprietary shaving cream.Alan CrawChesterfield, DerbyshireDouble cleansing? No benefit to you, but loads more money for the manufacturers of beauty products.Dr Lynda MorganLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Letter: Cheryl Hall obituary | Mark James | The Guardian
description: Mark James writes: She deployed her acting skills to make her points forcibly on a NOC (no overall control) council run by Labour and the Liberal Democrat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mark James writes: She deployed her acting skills to make her points forcibly on a NOC (no overall control) council run by Labour and the Liberal Democrat
Content: Cheryl Hall in the early 1980s.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCheryl Hall in the early 1980s.Photograph: ShutterstockLocal governmentLettersLetter: Cheryl Hall obituaryMark JamesSun 20 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTShareThe actorCheryl Hallcertainly made an impression as a Kent county councillor when I served with her as a Labour member. After her first win for the party in Ramsgate South in 1993, she held the seat in 1997, while on the same day standing unsuccessfully as the Labour parliamentary candidate for Canterbury.She deployed her acting skills to make her points forcibly on a NOC (no overall control) council run by Labour and the Liberal Democrats, specialising in the arts and culture. Indeed, her approach to debate was no holds barred for an old-fashioned council that had probably long needed a shake-up.The 1980s had been pretty barren for Labour inKent, I recall as a parliamentary candidate myself, but Cheryl’s fearlessness and infectious enthusiasm made her a force of nature.Explore more on these topicsLocal governmentTelevisionKentlettersShareReuse this content

title: It’s not just young people who need jobs | Unemployment | The Guardian
description: Letter: There should be provision for people who find themselves out of work when they approach state pension age, writes Peter Wade
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: There should be provision for people who find themselves out of work when they approach state pension age, writes Peter Wade
Content: ‘Our current social security and pensions system has roots in the reforms of the early 20th century.’Photograph: Roger Bamber/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Our current social security and pensions system has roots in the reforms of the early 20th century.’Photograph: Roger Bamber/AlamyUnemploymentLettersIt’s not just young people who need jobsThere should be provision for people who find themselves out of work when they approach state pension age, writesPeter WadeSun 20 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareI am now in my 61st year, haven’t worked for more than two years and have stopped applying for jobs (‘I feel invisible’: over-50s reveal harsh realities of trying to get a job, 17 September). The bulk of my career was as an advice worker, specialising in debt, housing and energy advice.Some years ago I worked with a client in her late 50s who had been a hospital cleaner. She had expected to retire earlier, but the changes to women’s state pension age meant that she faced several more years before retirement. She could no longer do the physical work of cleaning, yet starting a new career while managing her physical health seemed a daunting prospect. At the time I was looking at this situation from the other side of the desk. Now my perspective is rather different.There quite rightly needs to be an emphasis on young people who are out of work, but I have felt for some time that there also needs to be an alternative route for people who find themselves out of work when they are approaching state pension age. Our current social security and pensions system has roots in the reforms of the early 20th century, developed through theBeveridge report of 1942and the postwar reforms of the Attlee government.Since then, the system has been adapted and tweaked many times. But perhaps we have reached the point where tweaking isn’t enough. What we need is Beveridge for the 21st century.Peter WadeLeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Carrick disputes Cunha’s claim that Manchester United lacked energy in Fulham draw | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick has said his Manchester United side ‘kept pushing’ and rejected Matheus Cunha’s claim that Fulham ‘put in more energy’
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Michael Carrick has said his Manchester United side ‘kept pushing’ and rejected Matheus Cunha’s claim that Fulham ‘put in more energy’
Content: Michael Carrick said he is ‘not despondent and down because we’re showing some good signs’.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick said he is ‘not despondent and down because we’re showing some good signs’.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersManchester UnitedCarrick disputes Cunha’s claim that Manchester United lacked energy in Fulham drawMichael Carrick insists team ‘kept pushing’ for levellerMatheus Cunha: ‘Fulham put in more energy than us’David Hytnerat Craven CottageSun 20 Sep 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick rejected the suggestion that hisManchester Unitedplayers lacked physical fitness after they snatched a last-gasp 1-1 draw at Fulham on Sunday. The statistics showed the home side ran a collective 6.6km more than United, whose goalscorer in the 89th minute – Matheus Cunha – was critical of his team’s efforts.United were poor after the restart at 0-0, leading up to a disastrous Lisandro Martínez own goal in the 63rd minute, with Cunha saying they had to give more. “In the beginning of the second half,Fulhamput in more energy than us and we cannot accept this,” Cunha said.Manchester United’s engine room runs out of puff as fans begin to voice frustration | Jacob SteinbergRead moreThe draw was not the result Carrick or United wanted after a week during which they lost the derby against Manchester City and exited the Carabao Cup against Brighton; both matches were at Old Trafford. Carrick will take it under the circum­stances and he tried to ­highlight the positives which he said took in the never-say-die spirit of his ­players. They fought until the end and were rewarded when ­Cunha’s shot from distance took a heavy deflection off the ­Fulham defender David ­Affengruber to wrongfoot Bernd Leno.Carrick said he did not agree with Cunha’s comment about the collective energy levels. “I don’t, ­particularly,” the manager said. “The way we finished the game … it didn’t look like that for me. I was quite happy with the way we finished the game. We kept pushing. I don’t think that’s an issue, no.“The response [to the own goal] was really pleasing … the way we went about trying to get back into the game. [We] kept the ideas, kept the patience, kept the real purpose to it. We finished on a positive, which is a small step for us … without ­getting carried away it’s a good step. We came to take three points but at least we’ve taken something to build on ­moving forward.“It has been pretty fine ­margins [so far this season] that have flipped it [the wrong way]. I know we can do better, we need to do better at certain things. But I’m not despondent and down because we’re showing some good signs.”A section of the United support booed Carrick’s decision to ­withdraw Kobbie Mainoo in the 80th minute; the manager sent on Mason Mount in his place. “There’s always going to be ­certain reactions when you’re ­making changes,” Carrick said. “I ­understand. We’re chasing the game and ­everyone’s a little bit emotional. I don’t take any negatives or offence to it.”Carrick was asked whether he felt a certain deflation among the fans, who have been expecting a big season from United. “It’s still a big season ahead,” he said. “It’s a long season and you’re going to have spells through it. That’s part of the journey.“I’m not playing it down. We wanted more points. I’m not saying everything’s great. I understand the frustration. But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club. The players didn’t have that on the pitch today and that’s what will carry us through the season.”The Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, was unhappy with the officials and he claimed they did not want United to lose after what had ­happened in the City game last ­Sunday when Erling Haaland’s ­winner was allowed to stand despite his teammate, Enzo Fernández, being in an offside position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideNeville says United 'absolutely pathetic'ShowGary Neville branded Manchester United’s early second-half display against Fulham as the worst he had seen in more than 45 years. Reflecting on United’s lethargic, error-strewn start to the half, the Sky co-commentator called the period “absolutely pathetic”, saying: “I’ve watched Manchester United since the age of five and that’s the worst 15 minutes I’ve ever seen. I’ve never seen such a lack of effort. What must Michael Carrick be thinking?”Guardian sportWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Arbeloa highlighted what he said was a soft free-kick in Harry ­Maguire’s favour on halfway, which came 35 seconds before Cunha’s equaliser. Maguire felt the contact from the ­Fulham substitute, César Palacios.“All the fouls for them,” Arbeloa said to Sky Sports straight after the game. “You can see before they scored, the foul against Maguire … he’s a guy who is 100 kilos. Every decision was for them. And I knew. I knew after the game against Manchester City that they [would not] let Manchester United lose here.”Arbeloa rowed back on his comments in his main press conference but still said he was “not really happy”. The referee, Peter Bankes, gave Fulham the benefit of the doubt in the 86th minute when a Martínez shot hit Calvin Bassey’s hand inside the area. Bassey did put his hand up but it remained close to his body.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickFulhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maresca dismisses title talk as ‘too early’ after Manchester City take over at the top | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The manager said after the frantic home victory against Sunderland: ‘I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but I expected a very difficult game’
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The manager said after the frantic home victory against Sunderland: ‘I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but I expected a very difficult game’
Content: Enzo Maresca said Manchester City ‘need to avoid conceding goals’ like the three they did against Sunderland.Photograph: Roger Evans/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca said Manchester City ‘need to avoid conceding goals’ like the three they did against Sunderland.Photograph: Roger Evans/Action Plus/ShutterstockManchester CityMaresca dismisses title talk as ‘too early’ after Manchester City take over at the top‘I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but expected a difficult game’Semenyo scored twice in 5-3 victory against SunderlandJamie Jacksonat the Etihad StadiumSun 20 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca dismissed ­Manchester City pulling ahead in the title race afterSunday’s 5-3 win over Sunderland, with the manager stating it is “too early” in the season.The frantic victory at the Etihad Stadium gave City 15 points from their opening five league matches, three more than Arsenal after the championslost at Brightonon Saturday. Maresca was asked about his team being top before the three-week international break.Semenyo helps chaotic Manchester City beat Sunderland despite Brobbey hat-trickRead more“It’s much better to win games,” he said. “In this moment, it’s better to have three points more than less, no doubt. But at the same time, we know that it’s quite early. The international break is good. We can review what we have done and what we can do better, and at the same time, we can relax a little more.”Of the victory againstSunderland, Maresca said: “I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but I expected a very difficult game – I knew how good they are, off the ball, very aggressive. I knew it was a difficult game but happy because we found a way to win the game.“We scored five. We could have scored probably more goals. So that means that we create enough, but at the same time we need to avoid conceding goals like today. We had four clean sheets in a row and today we conceded three goals.”City twice took the lead in the first half after goals from Enzo Fernández and Rayan Cherki, yet each time Sunderland found equalisers from Brian Brobbey, before Antoine Semenyo’s 43rd-minute strike gave the home team a 3-2 half-time lead.After the break the winger’s second made it 4-2 before Brobbey completed his hat-trick to make it 4-3 on 59 minutes. While Erling Haaland’s late strike completed the scoring Brobbey became the first player to score three and be on the losing side in the Premier League since Roque Santa Cruz in Blackburn’s 5-3 loss at Wigan in December 2007.At 3-2 Elliot Anderson appeared to handle in his area but was not penalised and City subsequently launched the attack that created Semenyo’s second.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRégis Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager, said: “It was hard to see that as not a handball. It is what it is and we have to accept the decision. It’s hard to comment. It’s a defeat, but we are proud of the level of the squad. It is really tight at this level against one of the best teams in Europe. A half chance gets punished, and it’s probably the lesson of the day.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaSunderlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elvira’s fairytale crumbles at the last to hand Spaun PGA Championship title | European Tour | The Guardian
description: Manuel Elvira endured a nightmare final hole at Wentworth to see victory at the PGA Championship slip through his fingers and hand the trophy to JJ Spain
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Manuel Elvira endured a nightmare final hole at Wentworth to see victory at the PGA Championship slip through his fingers and hand the trophy to JJ Spain
Content: Manuel Elvira is unable to hide his disappointment as he lets victory slip away on the final hole.Photograph: Colorsport/Daniel Bearham/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenManuel Elvira is unable to hide his disappointment as he lets victory slip away on the final hole.Photograph: Colorsport/Daniel Bearham/ShutterstockEuropean TourElvira’s fairytale crumbles at the last to hand Spaun PGA Championship titleWorld No 294 lets victory slip in agonising fashionJJ Spaun triumphs by two shots at WentworthEwan Murrayat WentworthSun 20 Sep 2026 14.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe will come to JJ Spaun and Jeremy Clarkson later. Only those without an ounce of compassion in their body could feel no sympathy for Manuel Elvira. The Spaniard, without a professional win to his name, stood on the 18th fairway at Wentworth’s West Course with one of golf’s most extraordinary stories in his grasp. Having just eagled the 71st hole and found the short grass on the friendly par five, the 30-year-old who began tournament week as the world’s 294th ranked player knew a birdie would seal the PGA Championship title. A par would force Spaun into a playoff.What happened next was a form of sporting torture rather than the realisation of a fairytale. Elvira pulled his layup into a bunker, flew the green, fluffed a chip into another sand trap and missed a bogey putt from 4ft. He did exceptionally well not to burst into tears. The disastrous 18th meant Elvira finished in a four-way tie for second place. Even Spaun, a winner on his Wentworth debut, had to be bashful at the manner of success.Jon Rahm shoots 78-77 and slumps off in last place at PGA ChampionshipRead more“It is devastating that I hit the wrong shot on the layup and left myself the toughest shot in the fairway bunker,” Elvira said. “I wasn’t able to pull it off. I have played some of the best golf probably of my life.”Beware the jilted golfer. Spaun arrived in England carrying a grudge at being overlooked for next weekend’s Presidents Cup where the US will take on an international team at Medinah. His omission was odd even before this victory.Rory McIlroy, during post-tournament media duties, had assumed Spaun was part of Brandt Snedeker’s team. Americans have now won three of the last six editions of the DP World Tour’s flagship event.“I played with a huge chip on my shoulder,” said Spaun. “I definitely had something to prove this week but everything happens for a reason.” Spaun was already a major champion. This win means it is seriously difficult to believe Spaun will be ignored again when the US take on Europe in Ireland at next year’s Ryder Cup. His game can travel.View image in fullscreenJJ Spaun lifts the trophy on his Wentworth debut.Photograph: Colorsport/Daniel Bearham/ShutterstockSpaun and his family have become regular visitors to the Cotswolds after developing a fondness for the television show Clarkson’s Farm. To add to a wacky closing scene in Surrey, Spaun’s wife was waving a Clarkson mask around as the champion was confirmed. “I’ve kind of blossomed into this player I never thought I could be,” Spaun said. “To take my game across the world – more specifically here in England, a place that’s dear to my family’s heart – the stars kind of aligned for me to come out on top.”Spaun’s fourth round of 67 included four birdies in the final five holes. Seventeen under par proved sufficient to take the trophy by two strokes. Those alongside Elvira were McIlroy, Aaron Rai and Adam Scott.McIlroy’s weekend involved missed opportunity.
