Lots of people come and chat, they talk about plants, it gives them a social thing.”He hopes to get funding for a community hub and coffee shop. “On the platform there is a very ancient station house, to the back of that there was an area which was neglected and used as a community rubbish dump. We have turned that into a garden. Now, we hope we can open a coffee shop on the site.”View image in fullscreenThe volunteer gardeners at the back of the old Alresford station house.Photograph: Oliver DixonIn Cardross, the gardeners have become fast friends. Connolly said: “We garden together and there is always laughing and joking and there is often more joking than working! We go out socialising together now as well. It is a very social thing.”Wildlife has returned to Alresford station, according to Belgrave. “We have noticed incredible amounts of wildlife, bees particularly. Honeybees, solitary bees, butterflies. That has changed a lot, we have seen the return of hedgehogs, we have slowworms.”The gardeners hope their example will encourage others to get involved.Belgrave said: “There are lots of stations which aren’t in the scheme, so if people do get involved it would be really good. It would be nice to see more stations planted up.”Explore more on these topicsGardensRail transportBritain in BloomWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agency | Liberal Democrats | The Guardian
description: Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for
Content: Ed Davey interviewed by Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems’ Brighton conference. The party plans an Online Crime Agency to tackle offences from child sexual abuse material and deepfake AI porn to drug and weapons trafficking.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEd Davey interviewed by Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems’ Brighton conference. The party plans an Online Crime Agency to tackle offences from child sexual abuse material and deepfake AI porn to drug and weapons trafficking.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PALiberal DemocratsLib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agencyProposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands forPeter WalkerandAlexandra ToppingSun 20 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheLiberal Democratssay they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for.The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled.Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape.Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71.The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which wasformed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens.His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England.One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEd Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference beginsRead more“If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south.Party figures see the conference as a chance to set out a more coherent and striking policy platform, including on the economy and immigration.But there is worry among some MPs that the problem is wider. “We already have quite a lot of policies, if people look at them,” one said. “It’s less about what you get if you vote Lib Dem than why you should – about what we represent. And people don’t really know that.”One longtime party activist said: “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election. It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsLiberal Democrat conferenceTechnology policyFuel dutyEd DaveyPetrol pricesTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta launches legal challenge against UK media regulator over Online Safety Act | Ofcom | The Guardian
description: Action against Ofcom comes as social media companies are being accused of using courts to slow down implementation
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Action against Ofcom comes as social media companies are being accused of using courts to slow down implementation
Content: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. A spokesperson said the company was ‘challenging specific aspects of implementation’.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenMeta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. A spokesperson said the company was ‘challenging specific aspects of implementation’.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOfcomMeta launches legal challenge against UK media regulator over Online Safety ActAction against Ofcom comes as social media companies are being accused of using courts to slow down implementationBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta has launched a fresh legal challenge against Britain’s media regulator in the latest of a slew of actions by social media companies who are accused of using the courts to slow down implementation of the Online Safety Act.Lawyers for the parent company of Facebook served notice during the week in an appeal against placing WhatsApp andInstagram, which are also owned by Meta, in a category that subjects them to additional duties.Those additional responsibilities include greater transparency, more user controls, measures to protect users from fraudulent advertising and increased recording of illegal content.The move comes against the backdrop of hostility on the part of US tech corporations, and Donald Trump’s White House, over the fees and fines regimeOfcomis enforcing under landmark digital safety legislation.Meta launched a legal challenge in London in May, claiming that Ofcom’s methodology for calculating the charges was flawed and should not be based on a company’s global revenue.Breaches of theOnline Safety Actcan be punished by fines of up to 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue (QWR) or £18m – whichever is higher. Ofcom is funding the operating costs of carrying out its online safety work by drawing on a proportion of that revenue.Other legal action is being taken by TikTok and X over how much information the companies need to give Ofcom to carry out its job of monitoring their services.A senior director at the regulator told a committee in the House of Lords on Tuesday that Ofcom was “operating in a highly litigious environment”, including facing two actions by Meta and others from “a raft of services” bringing judicial reviews against the body for trying to collect data.“We absolutely are looking to drive change in the best way we can,” Oliver Griffiths, the Ofcom group director for online safety, told peers hearing evidence about the Online Safety Act. “We have all come to work to make this happen, but, if we run unnecessary risks, we are going to get absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms.”Speaking about the latest legal challenge, a spokesperson for Meta said: “Like many others in the industry, including TikTok, Roblox, X and Quora, we are challenging specific aspects of implementation.“These are not challenges to the law itself, but how Ofcom has interpreted it. This is a normal feature of any new regulatory regime being bedded in and ensures questions of process, scope and implementation get settled so the law is applied proportionately, accurately and consistently.”Lisa Nandy, the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, vowed last week to keep introducing legislation to govern the internet. “I think we’re going to have to start getting used to the idea, actually, that government is going to be far quicker, far more interventionist, and I think I’m going to have to see the law updated regularly because tech is changing so fast that we’ve got to be able to respond,” she told the Sky News Electoral Dysfunction podcast.Explore more on these topicsOfcomMetaInternet safetyTechnology policySocial mediaMedia lawInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The fears begin to fall away’: why Britain’s mosques are opening their doors to public | Communities | The Guardian
description: As attacks on Muslim places of worship rise, this weekend more than 100 mosques offered conversation, food and friendship to challenge prejudice
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: As attacks on Muslim places of worship rise, this weekend more than 100 mosques offered conversation, food and friendship to challenge prejudice
Content: Judith Prinsley, Bibi Khan and Kazi Abdul Kadir take part in a Visit My Mosque event at the London Islamic Cultural Society in Haringey.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJudith Prinsley, Bibi Khan and Kazi Abdul Kadir take part in a Visit My Mosque event at the London Islamic Cultural Society in Haringey.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianCommunities‘The fears begin to fall away’: why Britain’s mosques are opening their doors to publicAs attacks on Muslim places of worship rise, more than 100 mosques this weekend have offered conversation, food and friendship to challenge prejudiceSammy GecsoylerandAamna MohdinSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt one mosque in north London, a woman shouted at worshippers that more of their children should be killed, as children had been in Gaza. On another occasion, gas pipes were ripped from the building and reconfigured so leaking gas built up inside it.These are among a series of incidents the London Islamic Cultural Society has faced in the past three years. But rather than retreat behind closed doors, the mosque has opened them wider. It is one of more than 100 across the UK, including in London, Birmingham, Sheffield, Manchester, Glasgow, Southend and Cardiff, that have invited in members of the public this weekend to learn more aboutIslamand British Muslims.As part of Visit My Mosque, they have offered tea, cultural food, talks, multi-faith activities and art exhibitions as well as workshop discussions with members. The event, hosted by the Muslim Council of Britain, is now in its 11th year and organisers say it has taken on added importance amid rising anti-Muslim hatred.Dr Wajid Akhter, the secretary general of the Muslim Council of Britain, said: “In the current climate, far too many people are getting their information about British Muslims and their neighbours from an algorithm and foreign-funded billionaires fuelling toxic hate towards faith communities, both online and on our streets in Britain.”Sufia Alam, the head of the Maryam Centre at the East London mosque and the London Muslim Centre, said their mosque was taking part to show that friendship and solidarity were stronger than hate. “We cannot allow hatred to define the relationship between Muslims and their neighbours,” Alam said.View image in fullscreenSufia Alam outside the East London mosque.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian“At a time whenIslamophobiais becoming more visible and more normalised in parts of our public discourse, initiatives like this matter deeply. When people walk through the doors of a mosque, meet Muslim families, volunteers and worshippers, and simply have a conversation, many of the stereotypes and fears begin to fall away.”The event comes amid heightened concerns about the safety of Muslim places of worship. One mosque is attacked in Britain every five days,according to the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred. Attacks included acts of intimidation, violence, property damage, harassment, anti-Muslim hate speech, online abuse and vandalism.At Cheadle mosque in Greater Manchester, Farooq Rafiq described the Visit My Mosque day as an “invitation to experience a space and faith that are often misunderstood”, adding: “We have seen over the past year this manifest in the rise of Islamophobia.”Mohammed Kozbar, the chair of Finsbury Park mosque, said the best way to respond to rising anti-Muslim hatred was with “openness, dialogue and solidarity”.View image in fullscreenA roundtable discussion at the London Islamic Cultural Society as part of the Visit My Mosque weekend.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianAt the London Islamic Cultural Society on Saturday afternoon, people of all faiths walked in as it opened its doors. The north London mosque is run by Bibi Khan, the first woman to become president of a mosque in the UK.“In this day and age, we see things in the media that don’t reflect what’s going on in our community. It’s so important for us to reach out and to be able to communicate exactly what’s happening with us in terms of our faith, the people we serve, what do we do and what we believe in,” said Khan.There was a heavy police presence, with officers greeting people attending the open day. About two dozen people sat down for a roundtable discussion, speaking about their association with the mosque or, for those who didn not practise Islam, why they wanted to learn more.Among those in attendance was Judith Prinsley, the deputy for Muswell Hill United synagogue who also serves as the vice-chair of the security, resilience, and cohesion division for the Deputies of British Jews. Khan and Prinsley, who are both part of the Haringey Multi-Faith Forum, have a close bond.Anti-Muslim and antisemitic incidents have risen sharply in the UK since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel and Israel’s war in Gaza. Haringey, where the London Islamic Cultural Society is located, has large Muslim and Jewish communities.Khan said: “In Haringey, especially with brothers and sisters from the Jewish community, it’s really important that we understand each other and stick together, even where there are times when we don’t agree with each other.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s really important that we understand each other and stick together’ … Bibi Khan (left) and Judith Prinsley.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianPrinsley said there had been antisemitic graffiti near her synagogue and that some worshippers were scared to attend. She said she was “shocked” by the gas pipe incident and how little attention it had received outside the Muslim community: “I thought, how come we hadn’t been made aware of it? Why wasn’t it on the television?”For Khan, social media is a big concern in terms of escalating incidents. She mentioned a false conspiracy theory, spread online, that “Albanians” were supplying mosques in the UK with guns. “Think about it. Somebody comes outside demonstrating and they’re going to automatically carry a weapon because they think we’ve got one,” she said.Explore more on these topicsCommunitiesIslamophobiaAntisemitismIslamReligionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hacked | RNLI | The Guardian
description: Data raid comes amid targeting of lifeboat charity by far-right agitators who object to migrant boat rescues
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Data raid comes amid targeting of lifeboat charity by far-right agitators who object to migrant boat rescues
Content: A company the RNLI uses for  customer relations was targeted, the charity revealed.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA company the RNLI uses for  customer relations was targeted, the charity revealed.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockRNLIRNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hackedData raid comes amid targeting of lifeboat charity by far-right agitators who object to migrant boat rescuesHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 08.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupporters of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution have been warned that their personal information may have been stolen by hackers amid targeting of the charity by far-right agitators.In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned members that their “name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI” could have been breached in the raid on a company it uses for customer relationship management.The Telegraph,which first reported the story, said the RNLI told its supporters that Beacon CRM advised the RNLI to “assume that data held within its systems was taken” in a cyber-attack that affected about 1,500 charities in late July.The letter added there was no evidence to date that there had been misuse, sharing or publication of members’ personal data. But news of the breach comes after targeting of the RNLI by people who object to the charity going to the aid of people trying to reach the UK on small boats.On Thursday, it emerged that a lifeboat station in Portsmouth, close to where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing, had beenforced to temporarily shut.On Sunday 6 September, activists tried to blockade the road leading to a landing spot where two RNLI crewshelped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekersto Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station. Police officers were injured in clashes.In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, includingat the RNLI headquartersin nearby Poole, where a museum telling the story of the RNLIclosed temporarily.Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page and RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing the charity’s branded clothing if they felt it could put them at risk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRNLI steps up security after abuse by far-right agitators over small boat rescuesRead moreThe RNLI vice-president, Sir Robin Knox-Johnston, condemned the intimidation aimed at staff and volunteers, including “online and physical abuse”, as “frankly quite disgraceful”. Far-right protesters had called for people to stop donating to the charity, but it reported that it had subsequently experienced a“significant” boostto its fundraising.It has stressed that only 1.2% of its rescue work last year – 109 callouts out of 9,058 – was to small boats in the Channel.A report on the hack published by Beacon CRM earlier this month said there was no evidence that it was a targeted attack on Beacon or any specific customer, and that the cyber-attacker had contacted it “only to indicate they would be deleting any data they have exfiltrated and no copy would be retained, sold or shared”.A spokesperson for the RNLI said: “Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.“At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused.”Explore more on these topicsRNLICybercrimeHackingCharitiesImmigration and asylumMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice award | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festival
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: The queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festival
Content: Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo.Photograph: Leonardo Ramirez/Eyepix Group/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJavier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo.Photograph: Leonardo Ramirez/Eyepix Group/ShutterstockToronto film festival 2026La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice awardThe queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festivalBenjamin LeeSun 20 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish queer drama La Bola Negra has won this year’s people’s choice award at theToronto film festival.The film, which takes place in 1932, 1937 and 2017, focuses on the lives of interconnected gay men. It premiered at this year’s Cannes film festival with the Guardian’s Peter Bradshawcalling it“handsomely produced, lovingly detailed and confidently constructed” in a four-star review.After a competitive bidding war after its premiere in May,Netflixpicked up the rights and the film will be released later this year.In a prepared statement, directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi said that connecting with Toronto audiences in this way was “the greatest gift we could receive”.The Black Ball review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly toldRead moreIt marks the first foreign language winner of the awardsince 2011’sLebanese drama Where Do We Go Now?The award has come to be used as a predictor of Oscar success with past best picture winners such as Green Book, 12 Years a Slave, Nomadland, Slumdog Millionaire and The King’s Speech all picking it up.Last year’s winnerwas Chloé Zhao’s Shakespeare dramaHamnet, which was nominated for eight Oscars,winning onefor best actress Jessie Buckley.The Sylvester Stallone biopicI Play Rockyand disability activism dramaBeing Heumannwere named this year’s runners-up.For the second year, the international people’s choice award was also handed out, with British 80s-set Aids dramaElsinorenamed as the 2026 winner. Last year’s was given to Park Chan-wook’s darkly comedic thrillerNo Other Choice.The Toronto winners come after May el-Toukhy’s suspense dramaWoman Unknownwonthe Golden Lion awardat the Venice film festival. At Cannes back in May, Cristian Mungiu’s family dramaFjordwonthe Palme d’Or.Explore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026Toronto film festivalFestivalsDrama filmsWorld cinemaPeriod and historical filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary general | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Former president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Former president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest
Content: Bachelet is a former high commissioner for human rights at the UN.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersView image in fullscreenBachelet is a former high commissioner for human rights at the UN.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersUnited NationsMichelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary generalFormer president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contestReuters in GenevaSun 20 Sep 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending an attempt ​that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”Costa Rican diplomat emerges as strong contender to be first female head of UNRead moreThe two-time Chilean ​president and former ‌UN human ‌rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and ‌international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeedAntónio Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term as secretary general on ‌31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.Her ​withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll putCosta ⁠Rica’s Rebeca Grynspanin the lead.The UN security ​council ​will formally recommend ​a single candidate to the 193-member general ​assembly for election. ‌The assembly’s ​approval ​has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsMichelle BacheletChileAntónio GuterresAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK startup snares $20m to recreate gigs with ‘hyper-realistic’ digital avatars | Music industry | The Guardian
description: Unit1 hopes to offer lower cost version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venue
Author: Alex Lawson
Headline: Unit1 hopes to offer lower cost version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venue
Content: Scottish musician KT Tunstall filmed a pilot for Unit1 in a London studio.Photograph: Unit1View image in fullscreenScottish musician KT Tunstall filmed a pilot for Unit1 in a London studio.Photograph: Unit1Music industryUK startup snares $20m to recreate gigs with ‘hyper-realistic’ digital avatarsUnit1 hopes to offer lower cost version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venueAlex LawsonSun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former chief executive of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s entertainment group has obtained a near-£15m investment for his UK music tech startup that hopes to recreate classic concerts by manifesting musicians as digital avatars.Unit1 was set up last year by Barney Wragg, an entertainment executive who ran Lord Lloyd-Webber’s Cats-to-Evita empire for five years from late 2011. It has secured the $20m in funding from a group of investors, including tech backer Balderton Capital through its partner Daniel Waterhouse, who made early investments in Spotify.The company hopes to stage concerts fronted by the “hyper realistic” digital avatars of living artists who are no longer touring and by recreating existing performances from dead musicians. In the latter case, it will develop the avatars through a mixture of archive footage and hiring actors and musicians who either look or play like the departed star, before blending the footage together.View image in fullscreenBarney Wragg, the founder of Unit1, ran Andrew Lloyd Webber’s empire for five years.Photograph: Unit1Unit1 has tested the technology with Scottish singer-songwriter and musicianKT Tunstall, who worked with Wragg during a stint at the music company EMI. In the pilot, Tunstall wasfilmed in a London studioby motion capture cameras as she recreated a two-decade-old performance on Later… with Jools Holland, using the avatar to update her features to the way she looks now.The music industry has long flirted with the idea of creating avatars of its biggest stars, such as the 2012hologram projectionof the late rapper Tupac Shakur alongside Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre at Coachella festival.Abba Voyage review: jaw-dropping avatar act that’s destined to be copiedRead moreThe concept found mainstream success with the 2022 launch of Abba Voyage, a lucrative virtual concert with avatars of the Swedish pop group, which runs in a purpose-built venue in east London.Unit1 hopes to offer a lower cost to produce version of the Abba Voyage experience, by providing artists, venues, their rights holders and promoters with a route to digital shows without needing a dedicated space. The setup also means a show could in theory tour in several countries simultaneously.The business will invest the fresh funds into research and development, as well as securing intellectual property and licensing deals with artists and their estates.View image in fullscreenUnit1 hopes to stage shows with real musicians playing alongside digital avatars of musicians such as KT Tunstall.Photograph: Unit1Unit1’s aim is to stage shows with real musicians playing live instruments on stage alongside digital performers. The audience will view a high-definition LED screen, which is combined with extra lights, sound and props to give them the illusion they are watching a fully human performance.Ozzy Osbourne, Black Sabbath frontman and icon of British heavy metal, dies aged 76Read more“For the audience member in the room it is seamless between the digital and the physical room, immersing them,” Wragg told the Guardian. “It’s a teleportation of an audience member to a time and place.”However, some fans have expressed unease about dead musicians being digitally resurrected. Earlier this year, a plan to create a lifesize AI-powered avatar of the late Black Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbournewas criticisedas being disrespectful and in poor taste by some fans.View image in fullscreenFans of the late Ozzy Osbourne, pictured on a mural near Aston Villa’s football ground, did not approve of plans to resurrect the musician in digital form.Photograph: Nigel French/PAWragg said that, in most cases, the startup was “dealing with family members of estates to create something which is well documented and understood – extremely well-known concerts or live recordings. We are mindful that you do not want to be distasteful.”He was tight-lipped on which classic concerts Unit1 could recreate. He has previously said he wished he could have seen various well-known performances, including Queen at Live Aid, the Beatles’ performances at the Cavern Club and Jimi Hendrix at Woodstock.Balderton – which has also backed music rights firm Kobalt and fintech Revolut – was joined in the funding round by its existing investors, including the venture capital firm Mercuri and Paul McGuinness, the Irish music executive who managed U2 from the late 1970s until 2013.Explore more on these topicsMusic industryDigital music and audioKT TunstallAI (artificial intelligence)Andrew Lloyd WebbernewsShareReuse this content

title: China’s stranglehold on rare earths must be ended, says hopeful supplier to EU | Critical minerals | The Guardian
description: Rafael Moreno, whose company has opened demo plant in Brazil, says market is ‘nervous’ as Trump-Xi summit looms
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Rafael Moreno, whose company has opened demo plant in Brazil, says market is ‘nervous’ as Trump-Xi summit looms
Content: Jozef Síkela, European commissioner for international partnerships (left) with Moreno at the rare earths site in Brazil in June.Photograph: ViridisView image in fullscreenJozef Síkela, European commissioner for international partnerships (left) with Moreno at the rare earths site in Brazil in June.Photograph: ViridisCritical mineralsChina’s stranglehold on rare earths must be ended, says hopeful supplier to EURafael Moreno, whose company has opened demo plant in Brazil, says market is ‘nervous’ as Trump-Xi summit loomsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of a mining company hoping to supply the EU with rare earths in two years’ time has said it is “paramount” to end China’s stranglehold on the supply of the raw materials used in everything from cars to wind turbines and military jets.As Donald Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet on Thursday in their second summit of the year, Rafael Moreno said it was also “imperative” that they do a deal for Beijing to ease up, once again, on its threat to ban exports of rare earths.“The market is nervous,” said Moreno, the managing director of the Australia-listed Viridis Mining and Minerals, which has assets inBrazil, Australia and Canada.China first brought in controls on rare earth exports in April 2025, hitting the auto industries in the EU, UK, US and Japan hard.After a summit last October with Trump in South Korea, Xiagreed to suspendthe introductionof even stricter global restrictions, but only for 12 months.Industry leaders had hoped Trump would have sealed a deal to extend the suspension atthe two leaders’ last summit in Maybut the question remains hanging over next week’s summit.“It cannot not be extended if they are to continue to have these presidents’ meetings regularly,” said Kurt Tong, a managing partner of the Asia Group, a Washington strategic advisory and public policy firm.But he said a suspension deal could be delayed until November, when Trump is expected to travel to China again to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) governmental forum of 21 countries.Viridis is already attracting attention in Brussels, where diversification of supply chains away from China is a top priority of Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president.It has opened a demonstration plant to scrape the surface of its mine in Minas Gerais, Brazil, and produce a crumbly powder, which will then be further separated, potentially in France, to isolate the rare earths.View image in fullscreenPowder containing rare earths scraped from earth’s surface in BrazilPhotograph: ViridisThe EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, will travel to Beijing for his own summit with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, on 8 October to try to avoid a trade war.The EU is deeply concerned about what Šefčovič has said is the “unsustainable” deficit with China, now running at €1bn a day, with the scale of exports of electric vehicles, cars and renewable energy machinery as well as components deep in supply chains causing alarm.While Šefčovič heads up the urgent trade mission, senior EU politicians and officials are scrambling to find alternative supplies of critical raw materials and rare earths.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut their challenge is long-term, as China controls between 80% and 90% of the world’s raw materials and processed end products, giving it powerful leverage over global manufacturing. The Chinese exchange rate is also driving down the cost of imports from China.Eurometal, a trade group representing buyers of steel products,protests that Brussels does not fully appreciate the pressuresindustries are under, saying component buyers or original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) are under pressure each day to opt for Chinese goods, which can sometimes be 30% cheaper than domestic alternatives.The EU’s international partnership commissioner, the Czech politician Jozef Síkela, visited Viridis’s Colossus demonstrating plant this year in Brazil to hear how the company hopes to win 5% of the rare earths market, with production starting at the end of 2028.Moreno said: “It is natural for a company or OEM to want to buy the cheapest product, but then, you know, the impact of them not supporting a domestic supply chain means that the domestic supply chain just never gets off the ground.”He is working with the French chemical company Solvay to process the rare earths. “We are looking forward to keep moving forward with our strategic partnership with Solvay to start to supply all the OEMs, car manufacturers, you know, wind turbine manufacturers like Siemens Gamesa, for example, all that sort of stuff here in Europe,” he said.“What we’ve started to design and build now, is around 5% of the world’s rare earths market share in terms of those precious magnets. So that’s that’s where we’re starting. So this is not a small project, as you can imagine.”Explore more on these topicsCritical mineralsChinaInternational tradeMiningEuropean UnionBrazilnewsShareReuse this content

title: US environment agency let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Environmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal rule
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Environmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal rule
Content: Soybean plants on the left show signs of being affected by Dicamba (stunted growth, curled up leaves, low bean yield.) Soybean plants on the right were planted later in the season and stand taller, on 9 August 2017.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoybean plants on the left show signs of being affected by Dicamba (stunted growth, curled up leaves, low bean yield.) Soybean plants on the right were planted later in the season and stand taller, on 9 August 2017.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesTrump administrationUS environment agency let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents showEnvironmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal ruleTom PerkinsSun 20 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EPA allowedpesticidegiant Bayer topickfrom a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, newly released internal agency documents show.The documents provide an unusually clear look into the process of developing pesticide regulations, which is typically done out of public view. It shows in detail how the EPA asked Bayer which regulations it wanted, received a response from Bayer, then put Bayer’s choices into aproposedfederal rule.Dicamba is drift prone and kills vegetation and crops for miles around fields where it is sprayed, and is linked to liver cancer and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Courts havetwiceordered it off the market because of its drift problems, but the EPA has re-approved it.US ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to fight climate crisisRead moreThe EPA solicited Bayer’s input on the level of restrictions to limit dicamba volatility and runoff, ranging from more protective to less protective, records released in ongoing litigation over the substance show. The EPA concluded one presentation with a slide entitled “Registrant response needed” which posed the question “Which mitigation option to go forward with?”Bayer chose the least protective for one regulation, and the middle of three levels of protection for another regulation. It also got one other change it requested into the rule.Pesticide regulations are typically a negotiation between industry and the EPA, but the exchange that the documents reveal is “crossing a line”, said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center for Biological Diversity, which is litigating on the issue.“The EPA is allowing Bayer to choose its preferred measures to limit dicamba’s damage as if it was ordering up a late-night dinner à la carte from Chili’s,” Donley said. “It becomes troublesome when the EPA allows them to regulate themselves by choosing the mitigations.”The Center for Biological Diversity and the Center forFoodSafety brought the lawsuit. The documents come as the EPA has faced criticism for stacking its leadership with industry veterans. The top four toxics office positions at the EPA are held by former chemical industry leaders, including Kyle Kunkler, a former pesticide industry lobbyist who is now a deputy assistant administrator and oversees the pesticides program.Despite repeated assurances from the EPA that it has put effective protections in place, dicamba drift hasdamagedmillions of acres of farmland and caused damage to orchards, vegetable farms, home gardens, native plants, trees and wildlife refuges across the country since its first approval in 2016. Experts havefounddicamba drift damage to be the worst of any herbicide in the history of US agriculture. Still, the current approval provides evenfewer protectionsfrom dicamba drift and damage than past approvals, the lawsuit alleges.In a statement to the Guardian, an EPA spokesperson said: “Make no mistake: this is not a compliance failure; it is the regulatory system working exactly as intended.”“The agency notifies the [pesticide maker] and works with them to identify possible solutions” to risks, the spokesperson wrote. “[Companies] are permitted to submit mitigation ideas that preserve their product’s utility, and EPA also will independently develop its own proposed mitigations. To be explicitly clear: the registrant does not dictate terms.”During a May 2025 EPA meeting with Bayer, the agencygave Bayertwo mitigation choices that would allegedly address dicamba’s high volatility, which is what makes it drift prone. A more restrictive option would have prevented dicamba applications above 85F, and a less restrictive option would allow applications up to 95F, if the acreage treated was reduced.California bans paraquat, highly toxic herbicide outlawed in more than 70 countriesRead moreThe EPA also gave Bayer three options for addressing dicamba runoff, documents show. It then concluded the presentation with a solicitation for Bayer to decide.An EPA manager thenwrote in an emailthat “the next step in the process beyond the [presentation] is getting feedback from the registrants on what mitigation and mitigation implementation option they would like to move forward with”.Separate documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity showed the plan was presented to Nancy Beck, a controversial former lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council who now leads the EPA’s office of chemical safety.The revelations drew condemnation from “make America healthy again” (Maha) advocate Kelly Ryerson, who said: “It is now undeniable that the EPA remains fully captured by a crooked collection of pesticide company players who so enthusiastically ignore the substantial losses of farmers and the federal courts who mandated a halt to dicamba use.”Eight days later, a representative from Bayer emailed the EPA: “After discussion with EPA and reviewing these options carefully, Bayer would like to proceed as described below … ”Bayer chose the less restrictive option for volatility mitigation, which would allow it to be applied at up to 95 degrees as long as the dicamba-treated area would be reduced. Bayer alsowantedanother option that the EPA had not proposed, emails show. It wouldallowfull-field dicamba treatments at higher temperatures if dicamba was not tank mixed.The EPA granted both requests, and Bayer’s preferred option for mitigating run off. These were included in the rules proposed a few months later, documents show.“In return for this egregiousness, I would like the EPA to propose a menu of options to Maha for significantly decreasing our exposure to known carcinogens and endocrine disruptors,” Ryerson added.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS Environmental Protection AgencyHerbicidesBayerFoodUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Turn of the Screw review – Henry James’s classic ghost story with added jump scares | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own cleverness
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own cleverness
Content: Startling moments … Amy Tara in Turn of the Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStartling moments … Amy Tara in Turn of the Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewThe Turn of the Screw review – Henry James’s classic ghost story with added jump scaresArcola theatre, LondonThis slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own clevernessArifa AkbarSun 20 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is Henry James’s canonical ghost story with modern-day jump scares. And, more audaciously, a new framing device by writer-adapter, Morgan Lloyd Malcolm, which explains itself in a final, added, twist.The jump scares do their work, Hattie North’s jagged sound design enacting its shocks, and the production is slick and stylised – but not all the elements pay off.It is the same story, of a governess (Amy Tara) who, wooed by a roguish gentleman (Jim Fish) becomes a tutor to two young charges in a tenure that culminates in tragedy.Lloyd Malcolm’s framing device features an unnamed (imaginary or real?) man interrogating the governess’ version of events: that her two seemingly angelic charges are possessed. His accusatory questioning suggests the age-old contention that the woman is an unreliable narrator and unhinged fantasist but his interruptions are too numerous, hampering the buildup of dread and tension. The chopped up nature of the story (you hear what is coming, travelling back and forth in time sequences) has the same effect.The production sets itself up with great promise. The two children, Flora (Kathleen McAuley Irvine) and Miles (Toby Beynon), appear suddenly out of darkness on Matthew Cassar’s elegantly gothic set of screens. So does housekeeper, Mrs Grose (Katy Slater, not the friend and confidante she is in the novella), as well as the apparitions of dead manservant Quint and former governess Miss Jessel (played by the children).Directed by Nicky Allpress, the action is stylised, with minimal props used. Flora’s eerie doll raises the hairs and the screens are used inventively. But you don’t always know what is going on, which becomes most apparent in the lake scene in which the governess finds herself under water. There are whistles, screams and characters who suddenly appear and disappear. It’s creepy, but too much too soon, leading to inevitable repetition.View image in fullscreenInventive screens … Tara, Toby Beynon and Kathleen McAuley in Turn Of The Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe children look like grownups, in costume, and this draws them closer to the adults (Quint for Miles, and Miss Jessel for Flora) who the governess believes have taken possession of them. It gives them an added edge of sinister knowingness that comes close to menace at times: Flora’s glassy-eyed smiles and Miles’s joshing as he queasily puts his head under the governess’s skirts. But his innocence is particularly eclipsed by Beynon’s physicality: he looks like Quint from the off, so it is harder to believe in him as the 10-year-old.There are some startling visual moments: the screens do a fine job of bringing on characters as if out of nowhere. The final twist, looping back to the beginning, half explains the puzzle of the governess’s interrogation (Who is the man? What does he want to prove? Which timeframe is she in?) and the idea of women having to eternally defend their version of events. But the production is hampered by its own cleverness, the elliptic storytelling a distraction from the clarity and intrigue of this story’s psychological questions around fear, sexual desire and moral corruption.AtArcola theatre, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreHenry JamesArcola theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Resident Evil movies? I’ve never seen one’: Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchise | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans
Content: Scare in the community … Austin Abrams (left) and Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil.Photograph: Dusan MartincekView image in fullscreenScare in the community … Austin Abrams (left) and Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil.Photograph: Dusan MartincekHorror filmsInterview‘Resident Evil movies? I’ve never seen one’: Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchiseEllen E JonesRaised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fansSun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenBarbarian, Zach Cregger’s debut film as a solo writer-director, came out in 2022, it was a big success, creating a buzz among horror connoisseurs, garnering good reviews, and grossing $46m. Then his second film,Weapons, came out in 2025 and did even better. Mounting industry buzz around the project crystallised into a fierce bidding war; Jordan Peele was reportedly desperate to produce and, incensed by his failure to secure the rights, allegedly fired his managers. The rumours went viral, resulting in a wave of incredible PR that saw the film wildly outperform box office expectations and win an Academy Award (forAmy Madigan’s blunt-fringed, bonsai-pruning best supporting actress turn as instantly classic villain Aunt Gladys).Even if Cregger had not had a box-office smash that crossed over into awards contention, there would still be an atmosphere of hushed expectation around his next move. Both Barbarianand Weapons addressed hot-button issues – sexual assault and school shootings, respectively – while resisting easy interpretation. Both, too, started out seemingly heading in one narrative direction, before thrillingly careening off elsewhere. Thus, with just two features, Cregger had established a reputation for totally terrifying, utterly unpredictable and – most importantly – genuinely original movies.Yet the real shocker from this nascent horror auteur is still to come. For his third film, Cregger has taken inspiration from existing intellectual property – or IP, those two little letters bound to strike fear into the heart of even the most stoic cineaste. Zach Cregger has made aResident Evilmovie.View image in fullscreenMotivated cellar … Barbarian.Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy“Look, I could make a different movie now if I wanted to,” he says, when I put to him the obvious question: why? He is talking to me via video call, from a warmly furnished but ominously low-lit room, wearing a crumpled navy T-shirt, and sounding much less defensive than his words might suggest. “I understand how people could be like: ‘Why IP?’ But to me, that’s just such a secondary concern because the IP is not the point. The point is the story. The point is, it’s an original movie, even though it is Resident Evil.” He sighs. “And now I can’t wait for everyone on the internet to be like, ‘He admitted it!’”Cregger is referring to the stick he’s been getting online from more obsessive gamers ever since thefirst teaser trailer launched in April. “I feel like there’s been so many people taking what I say about this exact thing out of context and saying: ‘He just wanted to make the movie that he wanted to make, and then slap Resident Evil on it, so he could get a bigger budget.’ Which is not the case. It was conceived to be a Resident Evil story. And when you watch the movie, you’ll know that’s the case, because it’s undeniable.”But what is “a Resident Evilstory”? For those who are unfamiliar, the franchise began as a Japanese survival horror game released for PlayStation in 1996. It was then adapted into a live-action film series – Cregger’s film will be the eighth instalment – beginning in 2002, with the Paul WS Anderson-directed Resident Evil,starring model turned actor Milla Jovovich as a woman battling a zombie contagion let loose on Raccoon City by the shadowy Umbrella Corporation. The film series, like the game, has been hugely profitable – that’s why they keep making ’em – and could at one point boast (at nearly $1.2bn and counting) of being the all-time highest-grossing horror film series, until being overtaken by the Conjuring Universe and the Alien series.View image in fullscreenStrange bedfellow … Amy Madigan in Weapons.Photograph: AlamyYet from the perspective of those aforementioned cineastes – and also more casual movie lovers – Resident Evil’s reputation is distinctly mid. On reviews aggregate site Rotten Tomatoes, the highest-rated film from the franchise is 2016’s Resident Evil: The Final Chapter, which scores an ignominious 39% “splat”. So while Cregger was – and is – a big fan of the games, the films? Not so much. When I ask what the relationship is of his film to the rest of the series – a sequel? Prequel? Universe-expanding retro-reboot? – he shrugs and says, somewhat proudly: “I couldn’t really say. I’ve never seen one.”Still, as Cregger appreciates, video game adaptations are tricky for a reason: they are expected to serve the play-experienced aficionadosandthe clueless noobs. Cregger’s big idea for bridging this gap is to create a moviegoing experience that feels like a 90-minute session on the PlayStation, even for those audience members who may never have previously heard of Resident Evil. Narratively, this means following a single character, medical courier Bryan (Austin Abrams), as he attempts to deliver a cooler containing a transplant organ from hospital A in the flatlands to hospital B in the remote mountains near Raccoon City, Colorado, where – unbeknown to Bryan – a zombie outbreak is now under way. As in the game, Bryan regularly switches environment, progressing from snowy road to deserted farmhouse to sewage tunnel. In each new place, he must find the resources to survive. Shooting the film in a rural part of Czechia was, therefore, an appropriately gruelling experience for Cregger. “It was dark. It was cold. It was unrelenting,” he says. “I had pneumonia for the first half of the movie, and a horrible bacterial infection for the back half … It sucked.”View image in fullscreenFight or fright … Zach Cregger.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/Dusan MartincekIt may have sucked, but it worked. Judging by the 30-minute preview made available to press, Cregger’s film is exhilarating and immersive. He utilised the over-the-shoulder camera angles now synonymous with third-person shooters to mimic gameplay, and Bryan’s dialogue is mostly a soliloquy of disjointed profanities. “That’s how I talk to myself when I’m sitting on the couch playing Resident Evil,” says Cregger.“I mean, I basically only say ‘fuck’ and run away from things.”Is Bryan based on Cregger himself, then? “One hundred per cent,” he says. “Everything about him is me, my anxieties and my personality.” This helps explain why Bryan has a verisimilitude that isn’t always present among the plot-serving panickers and simplistic scream queens of horror. “It’s fun to have a character who is a real character and convincing in the scenario, but also behaving the way that I think most people who play Resident Evil would behave,” says Cregger. “He’s more suited to be on the couch playing Resident Evil than surviving Resident Evil,and that’s why he’s the perfect person to put into this scenario.”Cregger grew up, as video game-playing everymen tend to do, in “a typical, middle-class, suburban neighbourhood”. He was one of four boys raised by a stay-at-home mother, and a father who worked “in mortgages and foreclosures” – a job description that instantly conjures the boarded-up houses of Barbarian’s Brightmoor, Detroit setting. Cregger’s mother was always “very, very involved in the church”, and when his parents divorced, she got a job there too, meaning the brothers attended services four or five times a week. The young Cregger still found time to ride around on his bike, watch movies and play video games, of course. It was “kind of like that classic 80s American upbringing”. Which is to say, for the most part Spielbergian, but with the potential for abject Lynchian horror.As a teenager, Cregger began playing in punk bands, which gave him his first experience of “catching the big fish”, a transcendental meditation technique pioneered by David Lynch, which has become foundational to his creative process. “I remember I would write these songs and I’d be like: ‘There’s no way this is mine. This just feels like this is from somewhere else, and I’ve just been lucky enough to hook it.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe grass is always greener … Brian Sacca and Cregger in Wrecked.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThen, in college, Cregger formed his comedy troupe, The Whitest Kids U’Know (“I’ve always hated the name,” he says), which achieved success on the cable TV channels Fuse and IFC, before essentially disbanding in 2022 after the accidental death of founder member, and Cregger’s close friend, Trevor Moore. (Their final project, the film Mars, was eventually released in 2024.) It was in the midst of this bereavement that Cregger wrote the screenplays for Weapons, Resident Evil and his planned next project, a sci-fi film called The Flood, in quick succession. Of The Flood, he says: “It may be the script I’m the most proud of, because it has its own strange anatomy that just fits. I’m very excited to start.”A background in comedy – Cregger also starred in the TV shows Guys With Kids and Wrecked – is common to many of horror cinema’s most exciting new talents. To Cregger, the connection is clear: “That muscle group that you work out in comedy, where your brain is constantly trying to think, ‘What’s the surprise? How can I inject an interruption into what we’re expecting?’ That’s the same muscle group you need for a scare. So all of my time spent in comedy was going to the gym for horror as well.”And just as every good standup learns to distinguish different shades of audience laughter, so a horror film-maker hopes to elicit a whole spectrum of scares, from slight startles to full-on existential dread. “My favourite kind is anything that gets me with stillness or a bizarre image,” Cregger says, citing as an example a scene from Curry Barker’sObsession. “Her, running around, holding the flowers in front of her face? I was like, this is fucked!” And, to clarify: “That’s agoodfeeling!”Cregger is often grouped with online-adjacent horror auteurs such as Barker, Kane Parsons (the maker ofBackrooms) and Jane Schoenbrun (the writer and director ofTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma). But at 45, his inspirations bypass online “creepypasta” in favour of more enigmatic, classically rooted and traditionally cinematic influences. Barbarian, for one, was directly inspired by a self-help book, Gavin de Becker’s The Gift of Fear, published in 1997.Resident Evil at 30: how Capcom’s horror opus has survived and thrivedRead more“I have a lot of hippy ideas about creativity,” he says. “I just love the idea of being a conduit for the art, and that these objects of art exist with or without you [as an individual artist]. I understand how somebody could be like: ‘Dude, what are you talking about?’ Fine. I don’t care. I like choosing to exist in that reality where I have the ability to go into my subconscious, cast a wide net and see what I can snag. And if the universe or whatever is smiling on me, I’ll get something that will really make me happy, and that I’ll get to spend a year and a half of my life bringing it to the surface.”Back here on dry land, however, Hollywood’s current horror boom is mostly attributed to some more straightforward, bang-for-buck economics. The genre can reliably serve up sensation for a sensation-seeking generation, without relying on big budgets, big-name talent or even – sometimes – pre-existing IP. But what horror filmsdorely on – franchise fare or otherwise – is a film-maker skilled at accessing the audience’s most primal, subconscious terrors. Yes, Cregger has made a Resident Evil movie, and, more’s the surprise, it might actually be really good.Resident Evil is in cinemas now.Explore more on these topicsHorror filmsResident EvilfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We broke the rules:’ why chef Ferran Adrià is the subject of new TV drama | Ferran Adria | The Guardian
description: Six-part drama Gènesi tells the story of Adrià’s Catalan restaurant El Bulli from the day he arrived as a kitchen hand
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Six-part drama Gènesi tells the story of Adrià’s Catalan restaurant El Bulli from the day he arrived as a kitchen hand
Content: A scene from Gènesi, the TV dramatisation of the history of El Bulli.Photograph: 3CatView image in fullscreenA scene from Gènesi, the TV dramatisation of the history of El Bulli.Photograph: 3CatFerran Adria‘We broke the rules:’ why chef Ferran Adrià is the subject of new TV dramaSix-part drama Gènesi tells the story of Adrià’s Catalan restaurant El Bulli from the day he arrived as a kitchen handStephen Burgenin BarcelonaSun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRevered and reviled, during the 28 years he presided over El Bulli, a small restaurant in a remote corner of Catalonia,Ferran Adrià changed cooking for ever.Now he is the subject of Gènesi (Genesis), a six-part TV drama screening on Catalan television with a worldwide release later in the year that recounts the story of El Bulli from the day he arrived there in 1983 as a kitchen hand with no background at all in haute cuisine.“No one knew what to call what we were doing, and if something doesn’t have a name they don’t know how to talk about it,” Adrià told the Guardian. “Journalists called it molecular cuisine. I preferred the term ‘techno-emotional’.”Adrià quickly rose to become head chef. He was relatively inexperienced – before starting as a line chef at El Bulli, he had worked as a dishwasher in a hotel and then as a cook during military service. But despite this, he says he never experienced impostor syndrome.“In 1995, it was unthinkable that a chef who wasn’t French would be on the front pages,” he says. “Then I was on the cover of Time, which described me as one of the 100 most influential people in the world. But we weren’t interested in being famous.”View image in fullscreenMiquel Fernández as Adrià in Gènesi, the TV dramatisation of the history of El Bulli.Photograph: 3CatWhile much of Gènesi, which was partly funded by the Catalan government, has the look of a travel promotion, both El Bulli’s kitchen and 70 of the 1,846 original dishes it produced are lovingly recreated, including the famous moment when Adrià makes atortilla de patataswith crisps.Some cooking scenes are oddly frantic, given that Adrià was not a shouty chef à la Gordon Ramsay, nor even slightly in the rock’n’roll mode of Anthony Bourdain. His kitchen was a place of calm, nothing like the TV series The Bear in which the chefs work in a state of perpetual nervous collapse.Business really took off in 1996 when Joël Robuchon, the doyen of French cuisine, called Adrià “the best chef on the planet”. After that, El Bulli would regularly receive over a million requests for its 8,000 available seatings each season.Its foams, liquid nitrogen and molecular madness were key to its image in the cultural sphere, but for those fortunate enough to obtain a reservation and able to afford a menu that never quite covered its costs, eating in El Bulli was an unforgettable experience. Each dish was a surprise, the meal an entertainment and a show, but with food that was utterly original and exquisite.View image in fullscreenA scene from Gènesi.Photograph: 3CatSituated at the end of a windy road on the Costa Brava and with almost as many chefs as diners, the restaurant was never profitable, and although it could have charged what it liked, Adrià says it was never supposed to succeed as a business.“Avant garde cuisine is true to itself or it doesn’t work,” he says. Heavily in debt, El Bulli closed in 2011. “When I say the most important thing is to conceptualise, I mean what matters isn’t creating dishes but to explore the limits of innovation of both the produce and the diners. We never valued produce in terms of what it cost; a lentil was worth the same as caviar.”The essence of Mediterranean cuisine is to let the produce speak for itself, so subjecting it to a series of esoteric techniques was also a departure.“I don’t really see a contradiction,” says Jordi Artal, chef at the Michelin-starred Cinc Sentits in Barcelona. “The important thing for me is whether the technique is being used for its own sake, or in the service of improving the ingredient.“Ferran and El Bulli developed a whole new vocabulary of techniques and ways of looking at ingredients. You could change a texture, temperature or form without losing the identity of the product.“He demonstrated that cooking could be a creative discipline, that a chef could question things and develop his own language, to rethink what perhaps previously was just accepted as ‘the way’.“This gave all of us who followed the confidence to look beyond classical models and ask what our own cuisine could become.”View image in fullscreenFerran Adrià.Photograph: Robin Townsend/EPAAdrià says that before El Bulli, French cuisine dominated the world, but insists his approach was never a rebellion against the French.“I am who I am thanks to France, but that doesn’t mean French cuisine can’t be questioned. If all we do is reproduce canonical recipes, we’re just robots.”Much of El Bulli’s legacy lies in the many chefs who have used the experience and cachet of working there to open restaurants of their own. Among them is Oriol Castro who, with two fellow El Bulli alumni, runs Disfrutar in Barcelona, voted best restaurant in the world in 2024.Castro says one of the most important things was that El Bulli shared its techniques and recipes with the rest of the world.View image in fullscreenMiquel Fernández as Adrià in GènesiPhotograph: 3Cat“It was very exciting to work in a kitchen where we were breaking all the rules, trying to do something different. And there was a great atmosphere; it was like a family, really. It was magical.”Adrià says “the most important thing about El Bulli is that it empowered everyone. It was a bit like Obama’s slogan, ‘Yes, we can.’” He adds: “El Bulli was always a controversial restaurant and still is, 15 years after it closed.”Explore more on these topicsFerran AdriaFoodCataloniaTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the Alps | Agatha Christie | The Guardian
description: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?
Content: Agatha Christie skiingPhotograph: © The Christie Archive TrustView image in fullscreenAgatha Christie skiingPhotograph: © The Christie Archive TrustAgatha ChristieI was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the AlpsHer last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?Lucy FoleySun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world ofAgatha Christiewas through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side.Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now …As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else?View image in fullscreenGeraldine McEwan (right) as Miss Marple, with Greta Scacchi.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. Perhaps because I’d started with Orient Express, a glamorous setting was a foundational part of the Christie experience for me, especially after I’d watched the 70s film with Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman and Sean Connery sweeping down the platform trailing smoke and old-school Hollywood style. Poirot gets most of the fun, far-flung locations: the French Riviera, Egypt, the Greek islands and the Dolomites, to name a few.To a younger reader, Miss Marple’s world initially felt quite small in comparison. It was only when I reread the books as an adult that I understood the genius of the character, and came to appreciate how clever and radical Christie had been in making an elderly spinster her master sleuth – occupying a space somewhere between that of a detective and a bystander. She had taken one of the “left behind” women – a figure typically both pitied and scorned by society for not having been able to find a partner after the first world war – and shown her running rings around the other characters, using her invisibility as a kind of superpower. And in creating Miss Marple, she had broken one of the oaths made by the Detection Club (of which Christie was a member) not to use “Feminine Intuition” as a means of solving the crime. So much in the Miss Marple books relies on her intuition: there are physical clues, yes, but it is her understanding of human nature, an understanding that is coded as specifically and peculiarly “female”, that really wins the day.I came to appreciate Miss Marple’s lack of ego, her sense of humour: she is always in on the joke, always understands and plays up to the image others have of her. I enjoyed her sudden and surprising touches of darkness. I also loved that, while the Poirot books can feel quite timeless, the Marple books form a fascinating portrait of social change in Britain across the decades: the evolving landscape of the English village as documented between the 1930s setting of The Murder at the Vicarage and the 1950s period of The Mirror Crack’d from Side to Side (in which a new housing estate has been built), the postwar unease about not knowing one’s neighbours in A Murder Is Announced and the swinging 60s raciness of At Bertram’s Hotel.All of which I came to appreciate anew when planning my own novel. I knew that Miss Marple herself was the key to it all, the element I had to get absolutely right. She had to be Christie’s Miss Marple in all her complexity and brilliance. The other vital factor was the perfection of Christie’s plotting: the element that had kept me up into the small hours as a preteen, trying to use all the tools provided to guess whodunnit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PRBut in other areas I knew that I had to break new ground. I didn’t want this book to be an exercise in ventriloquism – there was only one Agatha Christie, and to try to ape her exactly would be an exercise doomed to failure. It also wouldn’t be any fun, creatively. From the outset I realised that this would be a book inconversationwith the original books, and indeed with other Agatha Christie books, but one that delivers new elements, and in doing so has its own raison d’être.When I learned in my research that Death on the Nile was originally meant to be a Miss Marple novel, I found my jumping-off point: here was my way into the project. A way of including my own love of cinematic locations, and indeed what I had loved about those glamorous Poirot novels, in a new Miss Marple adventure. I would take her on holiday – high in the Swiss Alps, to the Grand Alpine Hotel, with its glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes. I realised, too, that using multiple first-person point-of-view narrators would be a fun way of replicating something Christie does so beautifully: telling us a great deal about her characters by showing how they react to Marple, how they by turns underestimate, admire or fear her.Finally, I wanted my book to be in conversation with our own times. This wasn’t about shoe-horning in themes, but drawing out parallels between then and now. In doing so I wanted to interrogate modern society’s fear of ageing and the invisibility of old age that has hardly changed since Christie’s time. I wanted to highlight the prevalence of certain toxic male egos at the heart of culture and politics: figures who have attempted, at times, to rewrite history to further their own ends or disappear past misdeeds. All, apparently, with a total lack of consequence.Which brings me to another thing I love about Christie’s writing: the grim satisfaction of seeing the past catching up with the wicked. The meting out of just deserts. It may not be happening out there in the real world at the moment, but rest assured, it happens here.Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley is published by HarperCollins. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAgatha ChristieFictionCrime fictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Not I review – a mouth steals the show in Rufus Norris’s strange and deeply moving take on Beckett | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Soprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flair
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Soprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flair
Content: Lips that really move … Booth’s mouth in Not I.Photograph: University of ReadingView image in fullscreenLips that really move … Booth’s mouth in Not I.Photograph: University of ReadingTheatreReviewNot I review – a mouth steals the show in Rufus Norris’s strange and deeply moving take on BeckettMinghella theatre, ReadingSoprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flairArifa AkbarSun 20 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a long preamble to Samuel Beckett’s short play, performed in darkness by an unstoppably animated mouth. First, Luciano Berio’s experimental Sequenza III, performed by soprano Claire Booth, which becomes a musical companion piece to Beckett in retrospect for its stuttering repetitions, gasps and throat-clearings. Then a trio of short films about the Irish playwright’s relationship to Folkstone (where he got married in 1961). It is a three-part programme, part of the 2026 Beckett Biennale, culminating in the drama.None of the buildup is required.
