The mouth, also played by Booth, is still arresting in its speed and urgency, reaching for a truth that rests just beyond its rapid articulations, even as syntax breaks down.Under the direction of Rufus Norris, the setup is academic, the theatre part of Reading University’s campus, but the production has nothing dusty or donnish about it. It is impressively delivered by Booth, who captures the racing brain, the split interior self and the speed of desperation to replay a life that seems to be flashing before a woman’s eyes – or rather, her mouth – from her birth to this moment in a field, among the cowslips at the age of 70, which might be the moment of death. You glean, from the repetitions and verbal hiccups, that it has been hard, loveless and undermining, yet there is an insistence on speaking it aloud.View image in fullscreenClaire Booth and Rufus Norris.Photograph: University of ReadingBooth brings added musicality, singing words, adding operatic cadence. These flecks make you feel as if this woman, what’s left of her, could be a darker version of Winnie, the occasionally singing woman of Happy Days, not up to her waist or neck in earth now but reduced to just her mouth. And still speaking to herself, before the earth covers her completely, into silence.Pin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame finds fresh absurdity in ArgentinaRead moreLike many of Beckett’s characters, this mouth seems to be asserting its survival through sounds and words. She doesn’t stop talking, the play simply tunes out her voice. Her vulnerability amid the vast, pitch-black emptiness that swallows her up, startles you and wrings your heart. When the single spotlight fades to black, it almost brings tears to your eyes. A strangely, deeply moving 15 minutes.Until20 September.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSamuel BeckettreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time review – a fun and inventive sensory assault | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Alex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Alex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging
Content: Puzzled by human interactions … Alex Keenan with Joe McFadden in The Curious Incident of the Dog in The Night-Time.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenPuzzled by human interactions … Alex Keenan with Joe McFadden in The Curious Incident of the Dog in The Night-Time.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewThe Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time review – a fun and inventive sensory assaultBirmingham RepAlex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new stagingMark FisherSun 20 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most alarming moment in Mark Haddon’s young adult novel is when Christopher Boone, a 15-year-old on the autism spectrum, flees his Swindon home for London. After a perilous train journey, he arrives at Paddington station and is overwhelmed. The book’s text becomes a barrage of fonts and type sizes to express the information overload: announcements, shop signs and adverts all shouting for his attention.That sense of cacophony, a sensory assault of products, people and places, characterises Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging of theSimon Stephens adaptationfor Birmingham Rep and Melting Pot. Eleanor Bull’s bare stage, an outsize studio in white, alternates between clean geometric lines, such as the row of pastel-coloured houses that form a picture-book street, and more detailed high-definition projections.Hayley Egan’s excellent video design lays out everyday objects – wrench, tampon, wooden spoon – for careful study as if in a Dorling Kindersley illustrated hardback. It makes the familiar seem strange and demanding. The busy percussive score by Giles Thomas only offers more to process, while a multitasking ensemble drift in and out, surreal and playful, police officers one minute, tumblers the next. There is much to take in, much to make sense of.View image in fullscreen‘A clever theatrical representation of Haddon’s literary idea’ … Alex Keenan’s Chris is greeted by giant yellow balls at Paddington station.Photograph: Johan PerssonAt the vulnerable centre, a gender-swapped Chris (Alex Keenan) gets to Paddington and is plunged into a storm of bouncing balls – all yellow, her hated colour, all bearing advertising slogans and all trying to knock her off course. It is a clever theatrical representation of Haddon’s literary idea: Chris v an unfathomable world. To make it on to a tube train, she has to master a skipping rope, as if navigating the city were like making it through an adventure playground.Elbows high, head tilted, Keenan captures Chris’s combination of bewilderment and cheeriness. She is puzzled by human interactions, certain in her love of maths and science. In a high-energy professional debut, she charms with her enthusiasm enough to carry us through the distressing times when Chris turns inwards or lashes out as facts and emotions become too much to process.Fun and inventive, Bennett’s staging has the dreamlike quality of something created before our eyes. Sex, death and infidelity are handled with matter-of-fact sensitivity as we cheer Chris for triumphing in the face of adversity.Touringuntil 28 May.Explore more on these topicsTheatreMark HaddonBirmingham RepreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephanie Cole obituary | Television | The Guardian
description: Stage and screen actor admired for her television roles in Waiting for God, Tenko and Doc Martin
Author: Toby Hadoke
Headline: Stage and screen actor admired for her television roles in Waiting for God, Tenko and Doc Martin
Content: Cole, left, as Diana Trent with Graham Crowden as Tom Ballard in the BBC’s retirement home sitcom   Waiting For God, 1994.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyView image in fullscreenCole, left, as Diana Trent with Graham Crowden as Tom Ballard in the BBC’s retirement home sitcom   Waiting For God, 1994.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyTelevisionObituaryStephanie Cole obituaryStage and screen actor admired for her television roles in Waiting for God, Tenko and Doc MartinToby HadokeSun 20 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStephanie Cole, who has died aged 84, was a skilful actor with a powerful voice. She was also an exemplar of the strong, no-nonsense characters that she played with layers of vulnerability, humour and kindness.She made her television debut in a 1968 episode of Z Cars and maintained a solid screen career before coming to prominence as a leading member of a strong female ensemble in theBBCseries Tenko (1981-84, and Tenko Reunion, 1985), as the stoic Dr Beatrice Mason, doing her best to maintain the health of her fellow internees in a Japanese prison camp during the second world war.Convincingly realised and well-drawn, Tenko offered three-dimensional characters and tackled morally complex storylines – regularly achieving more than 14 million viewers.View image in fullscreenStephanie Cole in Bath, 2014.Photograph: Mike Lawn/ShutterstockThereafter she was rarely off our screens, particularly popular as irascible senior citizens inTV comedy, despite being 48 when cast as the most enduring of these – the acerbic Diana Trent in the retirement home sitcom Waiting for God (1990-94). The role won her a 1992 British Comedy award for best TV comedy actress.She was born in Solihull, Warwickshire, the daughter of June (nee Sheldon), an art student, and, Stephanie believed, Leslie Cole, an RAF airman, wartime lovers who split before she was born. She later learned that she was in fact the progeny of an affair between June and a man called Charles Wilson, whom she encountered only briefly in adult life (although she became close to her half-sister, his daughter).Stephanie soon moved with her mother and great-aunt Peg to Croyde, north Devon, and she was sent as a weekly boarder to a local school aged five, where she fell in love with literature, poetry and theatre: she discovered that she had a gift for different voices and accents.View image in fullscreenStephanie Cole, fourth right, with other members of the cast of Tenko.Photograph: Moviestore CollectionWhen June remarried, Stephanie moved with her to Bitton, Gloucestershire, but she did not enjoy her time at Clifton high school for girls, inBristoland, after throwing a Latin book at a teacher who had scoffed at her acting aspirations, she was told she would not be welcome back after completing her O-levels.She subsequently got a secretarial qualification from the College of Commerce in Bristol before enrolling at theBristol Old Vicdrama school: among her first roles there – aged 17 – was Madame Arcati in Blithe Spirit, an early indication of her tendency to be cast older than she was (she later played the role professionally at the Savoy theatre at the more sensible age of 63).Upon graduation she joined the Old Vic as an acting assistant stage manager before repertory theatre beckoned in Lincoln, Canterbury, Hornchurch and Salisbury (where, among many roles in her six-year tenure, she played the Nurse in Romeo and Juliet, and Martha in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?).Continually told that her career would take off when she was older, and beset with depression, she quit the profession in 1972 and worked briefly as a bookbinder and drama teacher before being invited to star in Tina at the Orange Tree theatre, Richmond (1975). She appeared in Noises Off (Savoy theatre, 1982) Steel Magnolias (Lyric theatre, 1989), Kay Mellor’s A Passionate Woman, directed byNed Sherrin(Comedy theatre, 1994), The Shell Seekers (national tour 2003) and as Mrs Higgins in Pygmalion (Chichester, 2010).View image in fullscreenStephanie Cole as Joan Norton in Doc Martin, 2009.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockIt was TV, though, that made her a household name. Concurrent with Tenko she showed her aptitude for comedy in Roy Clarke’s Open All Hours (1982, 1985) as the gloomy “Black Widow” Delphine Featherstone, reprising the role in the 2013-19 revival Still Open All Hours. She was good value inDavid Nobbs’s social function comedy A Bit of a Do (1989) as the gossipy, and often inebriated, Betty. She was an addled matriarch in Keeping Mum (1997-98), and a potty-mouthed aunt opposite Greg Davies in Man Down (2014-17).In 2011 she joinedCoronation Streetas Sylvia Goodwin, crotchety mother of the amiable Roy Cropper (David Neilson). Continuing that programme’s fine tradition of amusing and formidable northern women, Sylvia garnered Cole a British Soap award for best comedy performance in 2012.Her other notable television roles included Muriel, a widow with a can-do attitude, in Soldiering On, one of Alan Bennett’s acclaimed Talking Heads monologues (1988), Dame Lettie Colston in the BBC’s excellent adaptation of Muriel Spark’s Memento Mori (1992) and Martin Clunes’s aunt Joan in ITV’s popular series Doc Martin (2004-09). Her apparent on-air suicide in the groundbreaking, meta and liveInside No 9 episode Dead Line(2018) was unforgettable event television, and more recently she was in Gentleman Jack (2019-22).She also made her mark on radio, featuring in two BBC Radio 4 comedies: from 2005 to 2021 she played the ostensibly sweet but trouble-making Olive, a creative writing student of Christopher Douglas’s misanthropic writer in Ed Reardon’s Week, and was Carolyn Knapp-Shappey, former owner of the world’s smallest airline – crewed by Roger Allam and Benedict Cumberbatch – in John Finnemore’s much-lovedCabin Pressure(2008-14).Her autobiography, A Passionate Life, was published in 1998 and she was appointed OBE in 2005.Her 1973 marriage to the writer and stage combat teacher Henry Marshall ended in 1988, and in 1998 she married the actor Peter Birrell after meeting him at a reunion event decades after they had last seen each other as colleagues at Bristol. Peter died in 2004 and she is survived by her daughter, Emma, from her first marriage.Patricia Stephanie Cole, actor, born 5 October 1941; died 18 September 2026Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBBCTV comedyBristolTheatreCoronation StreetBristol Old VicobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Ms Rachel, the controversial queen of toddler TV: ‘My goal isn’t to be the most liked. It’s to help kids and speak the truth’ | Educational TV | The Guardian
description: Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics
Content: Ms Rachel: ‘All my experiences have led me to knowing that we should take care of each other.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMs Rachel: ‘All my experiences have led me to knowing that we should take care of each other.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianEducational TVInterviewMs Rachel, the controversial queen of toddler TV: ‘My goal isn’t to be the most liked. It’s to help kids and speak the truth’Sophie McBainHer catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politicsSun 20 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheYouTubestar Ms Rachel, toddler whisperer extraordinaire, spots me before I clock her, and even from a distance and without her trademark pink T-shirt and denim dungarees, she is instantly recognisable by her wave, which is accompanied by an enthusiastic bounce. I half expect her to say, “Hi, friends”, as she does at the start of many of her videos. Instead she bounds over, wearing a classic off-duty mum uniform – Sesame Street sweatshirt, grey leggings, baseball cap that reads “Mama” – and removes her oversized sunglasses. She’s very sorry, she says, rubbing her eyes, that she is so tired – but her manner remains unfailingly, characteristically peppy.It is only seven years since Rachel Accurso, who used to be a preschool music teacher, uploaded her first video to YouTube, a counting song for preschoolers calledBubble, Bubble Pop!. She and her husband, Aron Accurso, who worked as a music director on Broadway, made the video because their one-year-old son had a speech delay and there seemed to be a dearth of quality videos online that could help toddlers learn to speak.Nowadays, theMs Rachel YouTube channelhas more than 21 million followers, and since she signed with Netflix in 2025, the series has been streamed more than 69m times, becoming the highest-ranked new kids’ TV show. You can buy Ms Rachel dolls, rattles, talking toy phones, books and pyjamas. The couple are releasing their first album this month.Ms Rachel, who is 43 and has a 17-month-old daughter, Susannah, as well as her eight-year-old son, Thomas, has also amassed a huge following on Instagram (5.5 million) and TikTok (11 million), where the mums of her superfans congregate, and where she cuts a more controversial figure, having become a vocal opponent of the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, and a campaigner on other humanitarian issues, such as family immigration detention centres in the US and the war in Sudan. She champions LGBTQ rights, posts about the case for slavery reparations and free universal childcare, and is emerging as a hero of the American left. This month, when the rapper Macklemore pledged $1m to organisations supporting Palestine,Ms Rachel said she would match the donationand said every “wealthy white celebrity” should do the same. Earlier this year she was on the inauguration committee for Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s charismatic leftwing mayor. She has publicly endorsed other insurgent progressives, such as Abdul El-Sayed, who recentlywon the Democratic Senate primaryin Michigan – making her a whole lot more political than any children’s presenter needs to be.We are meeting in a park close to her in-laws’ home in Colorado, where she filmed during the pandemic, which is when Ms Rachel videos began taking off in a very big way. Her preschool fanbase are, of course, unaware of any of her politics, and they cannot get enough of her. Her videos use song and play to teach first words, early phonics and other essentials like potty training. One has been viewed over 2bn times, considerably more than the average Taylor Swift music video. Even the first clip she ever made has now been viewed 21m times. “That’s funny, because it’s not that good!” she jokes: she and Aron filmed it in their New York apartment with her phone balanced on a stack of books.View image in fullscreen‘When your child is having fun, you’re having fun.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianThere’s often something mysterious about internet fame: in a crowded field of self-taught content creators, what distinguishes the star? Accurso sometimes cannot believe the twist her family’s life has taken. “If 10 years ago someone said, ‘You’re in Rolling Stone’, we’d be like, ‘For what?’ And if they said, ‘For The Wheels on the Bus and the Caterpillar song’, we’d be like, ‘What?! How did that happen?!’” she says.But, though unpredictable, the couple’s success is hardly random. Accurso points out that they identified a niche, an untapped demand for educational content for toddlers, and that their videos were co-created with their early audience, who told them what they liked and what they wanted more of. “It almost feels like this live thing you’re creating with parents,” she says.Then there’s the fact that if you set out to identify the perfect couple to make hit toddler TV, you would struggle to improve on Rachel and Aron Accurso. Consider their professional and academic backgrounds: she has two master’s degrees – in music education and early childhood education – and early learning professionals attest to the science behind her approach. In an era of screen-time shaming, the Accursos create shows that parents don’t feel guilty about letting their young kids watch.And then there is Accurso’s personality, her wide-eyed warmth and wholesomeness. She seems to be the rare person who truly loves hanging out with kids – who is genuinelydelightedto play not only with her own, or her friends’ children, but with any five-year-old.double quotation markIt’s good to criticise governments for violating children’s rights. It’s something that everyone should be doingShe and her husband – who also just seems so freakingnice– have complementary personalities, she says. She’s always bursting with ideas; he knows how to winnow them down and organise a timeline. They call each other “instant oatmeal” and “slow-cook oatmeal” because, “I just want things fast and he takes his time,” she says. And this is “crazy”, she tells me, but once, long after they had established these nicknames, they were both making breakfast and she looked over and saw that he was stirring slow-cook porridge while she was making instant! They are ridiculously cute.So why get involved in politics? Accurso says she was advised to keep quiet on political issues, and she fielded arguments that “didn’tfeelright”, such as, “If you don’t say anything about anything controversial, you’ll help more kids, because more people will watch.” She has faced pushback from conservative parents over her support for LGBTQ rights, and for using they/them pronouns when introducing the musician Jules Hoffman, who is non-binary, but this has been eclipsed by the response to her criticism of the Israeli government.Accurso says she witnessed footage from Gaza and spoke to families there, and cannot understand why anyone who has done the same would not feel moved to do all they can to stop the violence. “It’s good to criticise governments for violating children’s rights. It’s something that everyone should be doing. Because we’re the grownups of this world and we’re meant to keep children safe. And the fact that we are not is horrific,” she says.View image in fullscreenWith her husband and creative partner, Aron Accurso, at an awards ceremony last year.Photograph: Stephanie Augello/Variety/Getty ImagesFrom a pure business perspective, the advice about staying silent may have been right. When she began speaking out about the humanitarian toll on Gaza, the backlash, which included accusations of antisemitism, took her by surprise. “I was confused and devastated that people said because you care about children who are starving, and whose food is being blocked, you don’t care about these [Jewish] kids,” she says. “I was like, oh my gosh, I have a deep love for, a deep care for, all children.” She has posted messages of sympathy for Jewish victims, and has collaborated with groups such as Parents Circle, which works with Israeli and Palestinian families who have lost loved ones, and yet the public response to her work is as messy and heated as you’d expect: the pro-Israel group StopAntisemitism nominated her for antisemite of the year in 2025, although many other Jewish organisations have rallied in her defence. She says she has grown accustomed to the maelstrom. “I had this moment when I was praying to God, like how do I handle people hating me? And I feel like I got the message that our goal in life isn’t to be the most liked or the most loved,” she tells me. “It’s that you’re meant to help kids, and stand with kids, and speak the truth about things.”Because of her outspokenness on Gaza, some Jewish parents have switched allegiance to Ms Sara, a kids’ YouTuber who even looks a lot like Ms Rachel – with the same long brunette hair and knotted headband – and who teaches Jewish culture and songs. “I think she’s wonderful!” Accurso says, when I mention her. “I’m never like, ‘Don’t watch this person – watch me’, at all.”One of her more hardline public stances is her refusal to work with people who have not publicly spoken out in defence of civilians in Gaza. “I’m going to work with people who aren’t in a privileged position, because that’s not fair to them if they could lose the ability to put food on the table. But people whoareprivileged who don’t say anything? Yeah, I’m not interested in working with them. Because I feel like maybe if we all said something, the genocide would stop,” she explains.double quotation markWe didn’t know that toddler TV could be big businessNot everyone will agree with this analysis; where some hear compassion, others will diagnose political naivety. “Why are we starving kids when there’s enough food in the world? Why are kids in Sudan starving? Why are kids in the Congo facing sexual violence? They’re kids. I don’t understand. And why do we dehumanise other people when I just feel like every person is different in beautiful ways but also so similar? How could we not want to help everyone?” she asks at one point. Sometimes she says she feels as if she’s living in a “fake, surreal world” because she does not understand how we can tolerate so much unfairness and unchecked suffering. She thinks all elected politicians should be forced to meet children like Rahaf, a three-year-old Gazan amputee she invited on the Ms Rachel show, so they understand the stakes. So is she naive, or is politics too unfeeling?“I just have a really good moral compass,” she tells me at one point. Which may be why, for all the controversy, she says she is often approached and thanked by strangers on the street, and she enjoys a lot of breathless, all-caps online support. “Ms Rachel for president,” her supporters sometimes write underneath her posts. When the Democratic candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the Maine Senate race after being accused of sexual assault, Accurso – who is from Maine – was spoken of as the dream candidate for Democrats there. “That’s hilarious,” she says. She has no interest in entering politics. But, she adds, sounding unusually tentative because “maybe everyone will be upset”, she hopes to one day become a Christian minister. One thing you need to know about Ms Rachel is that she’s the kind of person who prays every day for the people who hate her.Accurso says she was “born spiritual”. She was raised in small-town Maine by a single mum, who dropped out of university when Accurso’s elder sister was born, but later retrained as a social worker and was often juggling multiple jobs. Her mother remains her lodestar, and she named her daughter – born via surrogate in 2025 – after her. It was “rough at times”, growing up with little money, and Accurso felt rejected by her father and used to wonder why he didn’t seem to want her. That said, her mother surrounded her with “so much unconditional love”. She watched her mum shovel snow and build a treehouse and fix the plumbing by herself, and it expanded her own ambitions. It also shaped her politics. “All my experiences have led me to knowing we should take care of each other,” she says.Accurso was an anxious child, who by seven or eight was showing signs of OCD, flicking her light switch on and off to ward off trouble. She felt things deeply. Her mother has kept a note of how, at three, when she heard her neighbour was killing ants she exclaimed, “Don’t kill ants! Let them be free and feel the world!” When her mother could not take her to church because she had a new weekend job at Pizza Hut, Accurso, though only nine, went by herself. She didn’t join the children’s Sunday school but sat through the sermon for adults, praying and trying to “figure things out”.View image in fullscreen‘Space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianAs a young adult she considered joining the seminary, but while working at a school for children with disabilities she felt “led” in a new direction. She formed a close bond with a child with cerebral palsy who was nonverbal, and her supervisor told her she had a “rare talent” for connecting with kids. Galvanised, she went into teaching, and later enrolled for a master’s at New York University, where she wrote a thesis on how to use songwriting to empower children going through hardship. She joined the Unitarian church when she moved to the city – it had a preschool attached and she figured she might get work there. The first time she went, someone offered to introduce her to “the best musician in the world”, and Aron Accurso ambled over.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAron, who loved her smile, offered to walk her out, asked for her number, and made her wait a torturous three days before inviting her on a date, where she ate shrimp for the first time and thought, as they talked about music, that he might be her future husband. On their third date, she asked him if he liked Mr Rogers, the gentle, cardigan-wearing children’s TV presenter, and – what do you know? – he loves him, too. The couple married in 2016. “I feel like our souls are totally meant to be together,” she says.Rachel and Aron had always enjoyed being “silly” together, and at first their Ms Rachel videos felt like “play”, but during the pandemic, when Accurso was teaching on Zoom, and Aron was stuck at home because theatres were closed, and parents were wondering how on earth to entertain their children through long lockdown days, things started taking off. Accurso soon received offers from executives hoping to buy the company. She would sit through meetings hosted by a “bunch of men” with ideas for how to commercialise the project and, although she was suspicious of their lack of interest in the educational side of her work, it was Aron who kept reminding her that she didn’t need their expertise. “Forever, I thought I was going to be replaced as the host,” she says. “Once we had millions and millions of views I thought, oh, maybe a real TV place will get a real actor and see that this was a good concept.” For years she felt as if she was just some “35-year-old mom”, a stand-in for the real, professional Ms Rachel. “We didn’t know that toddler TV could be big business,” she says.The Accursos say their wealth is nowhere near the figures circulating online – I saw $50m – and most of their profits are put back into the company. Still, the couple must have more money than they ever imagined – enough that, on top of their recent $1m donation to Palestinian charities, the Accursos donated $1m to the World Food Programme in 2025. “My spirit doesn’t want to ever …” she says, struggling to express herself. “Well, I don’t have any fancy things, I could say that.” Oh, come off it, I say, but a bit more politely: what’s the fanciest thing you’ve bought yourself? “I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun, little fidget toys and stuff,” she replies. She has a cupboard filled with gifts in her house, so that any child who visits can pick out something for themself. That doesn’t count, I say. Have you ever bought yourself an expensive handbag? She only has one handbag, she says, because she has ADHD and has learned that if she has more than one, she loses important stuff. What about a fancy car? Nope. House? “I think space in New York is hard to come by and space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.”“Oh no!” Accurso suddenly exclaims, when we have been speaking for almost 90 minutes, and Aron is due to join us in the park. She is supposed to be talking about her album and she has been going off on all these tangents! Aron arrives a few minutes later, blond and very blue-eyed in a blue button-down shirt and smart linen trousers – they have taken a very different approach to dressing for this interview, she jokes with him as he approaches.The forthcoming album, I’m So Happy, is Aron’s passion project. The couple had received business advice that they should scrape their most popular songs from YouTube and get the thing out as soon as possible – but Aron wanted to devote “extra care” to the album. He ended up collaborating with 19 singers and 42 instrumentalists, and worked with Michael Starobin, who has orchestrated several Disney films. “I really believe that kids respond to it, and kids deserve that kind of rich, beautiful music,” Aron says. Among the 23 tracks are classic nursery rhymes, like The Wheels on the Bus, and songs written by the Accursos themselves, including Caterpillar, a surprisingly affecting tune Aron wrote while trying to get their son to sleep. Whenever they play the song for their children, everyone starts weeping, and I must confess that when I listened ahead of the interview I grew teary, too. “Every day you’re growing bigger, you once were a little guy, but caterpillar, caterpillar, soon you’re going to fly,” it goes. (OK, I know. But, trust me, try listening to it.)View image in fullscreen‘I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianThe musical flourishes are a boon for parents, who will inevitably hear these songs on infinite loop – more than any human should ever have to listen to anything, I say, experiencing a sudden intrusive memory of My First Album by Peppa Pig. “When your child is having fun, you’re having fun,” Accurso replies, because that is the kind of pure-hearted person she is. But then she does mention this one annoying song that Thomas really latched on to when he was two … before requesting this detail be removed from public record because she doesn’t want to be mean.An album also has the advantage of allowing children to enjoy Ms Rachel without looking at a screen, I suggest. That’s true, Accurso says, but she does think we’re too hard on parents (and on ourselves) about screen time. “There’s a lot of judgment and shaming of parents, and I think if you understood what most parents are going through, that wouldn’t be there,” she says. She is not exactly a neutral party to the screen-time debate – toddler screen time is how she pays the bills – but she points out, quite fairly, that sometimes we all need our kids to veg out in front of the TV so that we can get stuff done. It can also be a useful tool for children with additional needs. It was a “gamechanger” for her son, who was too busy charging around to listen to Accurso as she followed after him, instructing him to “say Mama”; but when she was on a screen teaching him how to articulate his first words, he focused.So, what are her screen-time rules, I ask. “Rules?!” she exclaims, sounding confused. “Just kidding!” Although her daughter loves singing with them both, sometimes the only thing that will calm her down on planes is watching Ms Rachel on TV. That morning, Accurso let her watch Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood, a cartoon inspired by Mr Rogers, so that Susie would stop trying to do dangerous stuff while Accurso was getting Thomas ready for summer camp. Susie is “such a sweet baby, but she has a hitting problem”, Accurso says, and this morning’s episode was about feeling mad. Susie has made progress, of sorts. Now, after she has hit someone, she says, “I’m mad.”Accurso seems more relaxed – and goofier – with Aron present. At one point she slumps over the table, and he asks if she’s OK. “Just looking at a spider! Keep going!” she says. “You focus, and I’ll be the ADHD person.” Ms Rachel’s political profile must have taken a toll on the whole family. They have had security problems that they don’t want to go into. “We’re learning how to deal with that,” is all Aron says. When I ask if he ever wished for Accurso to stop talking about controversial issues, he replies that her compassion and empathy are “genuine” and are “something I fell in love with and admire about Rachel”. There was no question of stopping her, because if she didn’t stand up for her values, she wouldn’t be Rachel, he adds. “Aww, thank you, Aron,” she coos, reaching for his hand, “that is so sweet.”Accurso still suffers from anxiety and OCD, struggling with intrusive thoughts, but her health is well managed with medication and therapy. It helps that she is learning that the internet is “not real life”, and that she doesn’t need to listen to the online vitriol. This morning, she received an email warning her of some new online nastiness about her, and she decided to simply not look.Learn With Ms Rachel review – undoubtedly the TV event of the year for millions of usRead moreI noticed when I scrolled through her Instagram and trawled through the comments that I started to feel anxious myself, imagining the extraordinary pressure she is under. The pressure comes not only from the hatred but from the adulation, the weight of expectations, the requests for help. I read a message from someone who said they had designed a headstone in her likeness for their one-year-old who had died unexpectedly, and could they show her a picture?Then there is the immense responsibility that comes from having such a large platform. In January 2026, screenshots circulated showing that she had liked the comment “Free America from the Jews”, under a post she had shared that read “Free Palestine, Free Sudan, Free Congo, Free Iran”. Rachel issued a tearful apology, explaining that she had clicked “like” accidentally when she was trying to delete the remark. She shared a screenshot of the private conversation she had with a follower who drew attention to her like, which supported her version of events: “Ya I believe I deleted that earlier right when I saw it! I hate antisemitism,” she wrote.“After that I got a turtle puppet,” she says, momentarily confusing me – does she mean some kind of automatic moderation software? Before I can ask an embarrassingly stupid question, she clarifies that she literally means a turtle toy. She and Susie were playing with it, “and I was like, I need to slow down like this turtle because I can’t afford to make a mistake like that again”.She tries, as much as any supercelebrity can, to keep her focus on her family. She and Aron had always assumed they would have kids right away, but they struggled with fertility for years. Thomas, Ms Rachel’s first muse, has overcome his early speech struggles. He likes to deliver lectures to his parents that he closes with a professional, “Any questions?” Susie is currently Christmas-obsessed – Accurso recently found herself Googling short-sleeved Santa costumes, until it struck her that that isn’t a thing – and is “so cute and aggressive”. Having a toddler in the house again is, of course, providing inspiration for the show. They need to do something new about boo-boos, Accurso says, and another bathtime song and, yes, definitely, something about how it’s not OK to hit.Ms Rachel’s album,I’m So Happy, is out on 25 September.Explore more on these topicsEducational TVEarly years educationTelevisionYouTubeNetflixSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dominic West backs ‘top shagger’ Byron in poetry battle with Bob Geldof | Dominic West | The Guardian
description: Actor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festival
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Actor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festival
Content: Dominic West (right) and Bob Geldof at the Big Brue festival event.Photograph: Max Milligan photosView image in fullscreenDominic West (right) and Bob Geldof at the Big Brue festival event.Photograph: Max Milligan photosDominic WestDominic West backs ‘top shagger’ Byron in poetry battle with Bob GeldofActor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festivalHelena HortonSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDominic West has said Lord Byron is his favourite poet because he was a “top shagger” and said he was not concerned the rise of AI might snuff out poetry.The actor was taking part in a “poetry battle” at the Big Brue festival in Somerset, against rock starBob Geldof, who said he preferred the Irish poet WB Yeats to the excesses of Byron.West said of Byron, who was one of the great Romantic poets: “Byron was shagging everything. Byron was the proto-rock star. He was a top shagger.”He also said he was unconcerned that AI might stop humans from writing poetry, and added that today’s rappers are the new poets.“Someone described to me the last thing that AI is going to take over is standup comedy,” West said, “but it’ll definitely be poetry because no machine could ever get to someone’s soul like these guys can, and I think that’s one thing that’s safe from AI.”He added: “Poetry is still being written. Rappers are people writing amazing poetry every day.”Byron, famed for poems such as She Walks in Beauty and the unfinished epic Don Juan, went into self-enforced exile because of mounting financial debts, as well as rumours that he was sleeping with his half-sister, and accusations of homosexual behaviour which was illegal at the time.West, who is best known for his roles in The Wire and The Affair, added: “There was all sorts of reasons for his exile and being cancelled, and so I, you know, but actually he’s a towering figure.“He unfortunately towers above Yeats. I mean, Yeats is an incredible poet and a wonderful man; you wouldn’t possibly hesitate to call him a legend. You’d certainly hesitate to call him a man who enjoyed sex.”The actor then recited She Walks in Beauty, and said: “Byron wrote this one after an all-night party, as he was getting undressed, drunk, about a woman he’d just seen.”Geldof, former lead singer of the Boomtown Rats, acknowledged that his literary hero, Yeats, was not a “shagger”.He said: “He only got shagged when he was, I think, 31 by Olivia Shakespear, and he was very practical about the whole thing. But it drove a vast energy into his poetry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYeats, the Irish poet who wrote such famed poems as The Second Coming, was one of the giants of 20th-century literature. He is known for his lyricism and his writing on Irish political struggles, including the 1916 Easter Rising, an armed rebellion by Irish Republicans against English rule.Geldof said that Yeats is the greatest poet the world has ever seen, adding: “Yeats is to us [Irish people] what Shakespeare is to the English.“He didn’t just set about writing the most beautiful lyric love poetry ever, but some of the most impassioned contemporary poetry. A lot of which you know has gone out to the world and is constantly recited in newspaper headlines.“He set up the first Irish ballet school. He set up the first Irish National Theatre. He revived the Irish language.”Explore more on these topicsDominic WestGeorge Gordon ByronPoetryBob GeldofWB YeatsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A Reform politician and an NHS worker had different takes on Nigel Farage, but could they agree on renewable energy or tax policies?
Author: Erica Buist
Headline: A Reform politician and an NHS worker had different takes on Nigel Farage, but could they agree on renewable energy or tax policies?
Content: Chris (on left) and Alex. All photographs: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChris (on left) and Alex. All photographs: Sarah Lee/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree’A Reform politician and an NHS worker had different takes on Nigel Farage, but could they agree on renewable energy or tax policies?Erica BuistSun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenChris, 42, LondonOccupationElectrical supervisor of the maintenance team at an NHS hospitalVoting recordLabourAmuse boucheHe used to play and referee mid-level community rugby until he got “too old and unfit”View image in fullscreenAlex, 42, LondonOccupationLondon Assembly memberVoting recordConservative for most of his life, then during the pandemic he moved to Reform (in a move his still-Tory husband characterised as “throwing a strop”) because he didn’t agree with lockdown, masks or banning social gatherings of more than six peopleAmuse boucheHe has two Brittany dogs, and one won a class at CruftsFor startersAlexI didn’t know what to expect, though part of my job is talking to people with different views. Chris was really friendly.ChrisWe got on well. Alex is a really nice, personable guy, and it’s quite hard to question somebody belligerently when they’re so easy to talk to.AlexI had calamari to start, which was lovely. For the main course, I had fettuccine with lamb ragu and a glass of montepulciano, and for dessert I had my go-to: tiramisu. It was great.ChrisI had the calamari to start, with a minty tartare dip. Then I had a spicy pepperoni pizza, a couple of bottles of beer, and for dessert a really nice lemon tart.Dining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’Read moreThe big beefAlexHe suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree, but it’s a perfectly understandable position. Nigel Farage clearly believes (and I support him) that ultimately his constituents should be the judge – and they gave him a resounding vote of confidence.ChrisIf constituents could be the judge, then why would there be another byelection later if he’s found to have breached parliament’s rules? In Clacton, you’d only need about 8,000 people to sign a petition to recall him, which seems likely because almost 10,000 people voted for a man with a bin on his head.AlexIt was a lot easier canvassing for Reform in Clacton than in the local elections earlier this year in London. I got more abuse during that campaign than I had had in 27 years of politics.ChrisI said, imagine how it is now for a canvasser who isn’t a middle-aged, white, Anglo-Saxon male. If you’re a woman, or from an ethnic minority, or if you’ve got a disability, you’re probably going to get a lot more abuse.Sharing plateAlexHurtling towards an artificial target of net zero is counterproductive. We’re doing self-inflicted damage to the economy for what’s largely virtue signalling, in my view, because of the 1% of emissions we’re responsible for. Fundamentally, we need to keep the lights on and food on the table. I support more efficient use of our own natural resources, including oil and gas.ChrisI’m in favour of investing in renewable energy; he’s more in favour of bringing energy costs down by extracting more fossil fuels. I said we can do that, but it’s going to make global warming worse. At our NHS hospital, we’re pretty much at maximum electrical capacity, and if we were to install loads of extra air-conditioning units, as people think we should, that would overload our electrical system.View image in fullscreenFor aftersAlexAndy Burnham is not willing to make tough decisions on things like welfare spending. My view would be that we need to look very seriously at things like Pip [personal independence payment] and foreign-born residents being able to claim universal credit.ChrisHe was all for shrinking the state a bit, but he didn’t really go into much detail on how he would do that. I think we should try to raise revenue in other ways, such as bringing capital gains tax in line with income tax, going after big corporations because they’re not paying proper tax, and reforming other taxes like VAT and council tax, because I believe those are regressive taxes that hit the people in the lowest income brackets the hardest.TakeawaysAlexI think that just by having an interest in politics you’ve got more in common with someone else, even if they’re taking a contrary view. Even though we disagreed, we had that shared interest.ChrisWe swapped numbers. He was nice, personable and easy to get on with. I imagine he’ll stand as an MP in the next general election, so I’ll probably text him around then and see how he’s doing.Additional reporting: Kitty DrakeAlex and Chris ate atCitro, London N6.Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant review | Turkish food and drink | The Guardian
description: Our main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Our main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean
Content: Kid, London W1: ‘A rhapsody of browns.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKid, London W1: ‘A rhapsody of browns.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsTurkish food and drinkReviewKid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant reviewOur main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely cleanGrace DentSun 20 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this month, a kind-of Turkishocakbaşıopened on a corner in London’s Soho. The brains behindKidare chef Sertaç Dirik and restaurateur David Carter, and I say “kind-of” because, yes, while it has a Turkish-influenced menu –sucukwith grilled peach,pide,börek, hummus,içli köftewith aged beef – and the whiff of live fire, nothing either of them does is ever remotely straightforward, hence the buzz around their new place.Carter foundedSmokestaka decade ago in Shoreditch, a wild, Americana-tinged barbecue joint where, somehow, he made brisket in buns and peach cobbler old fashioneds London’s hottest ticket. Five years later, he openedManteca, also in Shoreditch, a reimagining of the Italian trattoria for the 2020s, followed byOma, his Greek-influenced Michelin-starred venture in Borough, and its little sister Agora, and all of them remain dependable places where you get serious bang for your buck. All of those influences – American smoke, Italian flair and Greek boldness – are present and correct at Kid. Dirik’s story, meanwhile, has about it elements of TV’sThe Bear: a Copenhagen-trained chef cajoled home to bolster the family business and going on to create the hugely lovedMangal 2in Dalston. What Dirik and Carter have in common, aside from reputation, is a love of setting fire to stuff, in a culinary sense rather than in aProdigy’s Twisted Firestartersense. Kid’s Galata mackerel is testament to this: it’s almost completely blackened and has an incredible hit of smoke in its flesh.View image in fullscreenKid’s menu is familiarly Turkish but with clever tweaks, as in the likes ofsucukwith grilled peach puree.Kid’s website says it’s on Frith Street, but the entrance is actually on Bateman Street, thanks to an aggressively discreet front door that will have you wandering around the glass-fronted corner like some confused visitor at Sea Life, pressing their nose against the tank looking for jellyfish and turtles. Here, however, there are diners beyond that glass, and you may cry when you see them inside sipping theirgemlikmartinis (black olive, black pepper, white vermouth, frozen gin). Warning: do not accidentally wander into Regulation, a boutique emporium of a very different persuasion just 10 metres away and where a very different type of lubrication is on offer. And of stuffing, for that matter. I shall leave the parallels there.Kid, as its name suggests, favours the use of kid goat, which will either delight or unsettle the British diner, because as a nation we still quibble about goat meat but for some reason raise no such objection to lamb. They have much in common taste-wise, and Kid’s signature dish – a £65 kid with fig leaf and freekeh for two – comes in an earthenware pot looking very much like a plump lamb shank just waiting for all that flesh to be pulled through the cooked grains beneath. The dish arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean, as did the pickles alongside: fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance.View image in fullscreen‘Undoubtedly the star of this show’: Kid’s Galata mackerel.The room is a rhapsody of browns, with an industrial feel and wilfully uncosy, a design movement that I’m calling “sumptuous sackcloth and ashes”, and there’s a long counter that focuses on a central grill. We visited on day four, and the place was already packed with Smokestak cultists, Mangal 2 zealots and assorted food writers, all of them gazing at the fire and tearing at blistered, kaymak-slicked grilled pide, as well as seededramazanpide as fluffy as a Turkish morning after too many rakis.We began with courgette flowers, which at £7 each will make some people reach for the smelling salts. But these are not those flaccid petals draped over unseasoned ricotta with which Brits habitually offend the French. Here, the batter is intensely crisp, the goat’s cheese insides rich, with atom honey to cut through: it’s a crunchy, sticky, oozing delight. A round of bluefin tunaezme, a fine, fresh tartare in the Turkish style, comes on what can only be described as a poppadom-like cracker – fried, decadent and completely naughty.View image in fullscreenKid’s mastic ice-cream topped with mint oil ‘tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment’.The mackerel, however, is when you understand the point of all this live-fire hoopla. A huge butterflied fish with blackened skin comes crisp from the grill, its flesh all soft and meaty, and stuffed with a carrot-based slaw cooked in what tastes like rich, deep shellfish liquor. It’s the undoubted star of this show.We end with mountain tea rice pudding infused withsideritis, a wild Anatolian herb that’s warm and vaguely honeyed, and finished with a crunchy, brulee top; it’s also one of the finest desserts I’ve eaten all year. Don’t skimp on the mint oil-topped mastic ice-cream, either: it tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment.A very long lunch closed with shots of Turkish coffee that even Carter admitted tastes “slightly muddy”. That coffee sent me blinking into the daylight and I was still wired six hours later. Much as Kid did itself: distinctive, delicious and thoroughly making its mark.Kid53-55 Frith Street, London W1 (no phone). Open Mon-Sat, lunch noon-3pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £45 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsTurkish food and drinkGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodRestaurantsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect apfelschmarrn – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect apfelschmarrn.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect apfelschmarrn.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.How to cook the perfect ...FoodHow to make the perfect apfelschmarrn – recipeThis fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our residentperfektionistinflips through a selection of the best recipesFelicity CloakeSun 20 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchmarrn, orschmarren,Anja Dunkwrites, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation,pancake, a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and abatter pudding. Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports inher book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings, it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, includingkaiserschmarren(studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.View image in fullscreenAlfons Schuhbeck’sapfelschmarrnuses twice as much flour as other recipes. All thumbnail images by Felicity Cloake.The batterAll the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important.Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipein The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who senthis recipe to the New York Times in 1980in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes fromDunkand theDiscover SüdTirol website, which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft andHinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book, for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.The flavouringsAs Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargenkirschwasser, all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.View image in fullscreenErnest R Schulz’s apfelschmarrn employs similar quantities of milk and flour.The fruitBoth Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).View image in fullscreenAnja Dunk’s apfelschmarrn is ‘filling, simple and comforting’.The methodTraditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.View image in fullscreenDiscover SudTirol’s apfelschmarrn is more egg-heavy than most.The toppingA cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). We also like Dunk’s crunchy flaked almonds, but both are entirely optional. As with the nutmeg, chopped hazelnuts, pecans or walnuts would make a fine substitute for those not concerned with authenticity, and even those who are should know that this can be served with any sort of fruit compote, and is particularly good with plums.Perfect apfelschmarrnPrep10 minCook15 minServes2-4, depending on appetite40g butter90g flour½ tsp salt3 eggs75ml milk75ml cream(single, whipping or double), or 50ml extra milkFinely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemon(optional)1 tbsp caster sugar1 dessert apple25g raisins, or currants or sultanas (optional)1 tbsp icing sugar½ tsp ground cinnamon(optional)Flaked almonds, to finish (optional)Melt the butter in a medium ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat, leave to brown to a pale golden colour, then take off the heat – reheating will continue the browning process. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.View image in fullscreenPut the flour and salt in a large bowl. Separate the eggs, then put the whites in a large glass or metal bowl and the yolks in a smaller bowl.Beat the milk and cream, if using, into the egg yolks, then whisk into the flour to make a smooth batter. Stir in the lemon zest.Beat the egg whites until foamy, then add the caster sugar and whisk to soft, creamy peaks that hold their shape but flop over at the top. Fold a little of the egg-white mix into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest.View image in fullscreenCut the apple into thin wedges, and remove and discard the core. Pour two tablespoons of the melted butter into a bowl, put the pan back on a medium heat and, once sizzling, pour in the batter. Arrange the apple slices and raisins, if using, on top, then leave to cook to a rich golden brown underneath. Carefully flip over the pancake (don’t worry if it breaks), then put in the hot oven for five minutes.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMeanwhile, mix the icing sugar with the cinnamon, if using. Use two forks to break the pancake into bite-size pieces. Tip out on to a plate or work surface and put the pan back on a medium-high heat with the reserved melted butter. Add the almonds, if using, and lightly toast, then top with the pieces of pancake and sprinkle with most of the sugar. Toss over the heat to coat, then divide between plates. Sprinkle with the remaining sugar and serve hot.View image in fullscreenSchmarren, schmarrn – however you spell it, please share your wisdom on this homely Germanic mountain favourite. Or do you prefer to enjoy it in the sophisticated coffee houses of Vienna? Sweet or savoury? Fruity or plain? Baked or fried? All tips appreciated!Explore more on these topicsFoodHow to cook the perfect ...BakingCakeDessertMain courseFruitGerman food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Kimchi tuna and beetroot halloumi: 10 easy, delicious lunch bowls to make for work – as suggested by chefs | Food | The Guardian
description: A ‘packed lunch revival’ is under way among office workers who want to eat more healthily. From bread salads to rice bowls, food experts offer their ideas
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: A ‘packed lunch revival’ is under way among office workers who want to eat more healthily. From bread salads to rice bowls, food experts offer their ideas
Content: ‘The perfect lunch bowl is all about getting a good mix of flavours and textures.’Photograph: vaaseenaa/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘The perfect lunch bowl is all about getting a good mix of flavours and textures.’Photograph: vaaseenaa/Getty Images/iStockphotoFoodKimchi tuna and beetroot halloumi: 10 easy, delicious lunch bowls to make for work – as suggested by chefsA ‘packed lunch revival’ is under way among office workers who want to eat more healthily. From bread salads to rice bowls, food experts offer their ideasLeah HarperSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearlyhalf of office workers are making packed lunches more regularlythan they were a year ago, thanks to the rising cost of buying food on the go, according to new research. Does this mean employees will be lunching on soggy sandwiches and ultra-processed snacks? Apparently not.The survey, by online supermarket Ocado, found the “packed lunch revival” was, in part, driven by a rise in the number of people opting for more nutritious “lunch bowl” options, often inspired by ideas shared on social media. With this in mind, we asked food writers and chefs how to make the perfect lunch bowl – something to brighten up your break, and keep you feeling satiated until you clock off.Kimchi tuna crunch bowlMy go-to lunch bowl follows a formula: grains or pulses, something fermented, an easy protein and something fresh and punchy. I often cook a whole packet of quinoa, then freeze it in large ice-cube trays so I can defrost a portion whenever I need it. Otherwise, I’ll use a jar of lentils or beans. Then, I’ll add kraut or kimchi for acidity and crunch, followed by a tin of good-quality fish – I love Ortiz’s tuna in olive oil – or a couple of jammy eggs. A handful of chopped fresh herbs or some pink pickled onions finishes it off.Rachel Khoo, chef, broadcaster and author of several books includingThe Smallest Restaurant in ParisView image in fullscreenA go-to lunch … a kimchi tuna rice salad.Photograph: vaaseenaa/Getty Images/iStockphotoForgotten-courgette bowlI love turning a forgotten courgette into a satisfying Turkish-inspired lunch bowl. Soften an onion in olive oil with tomato salça [a rich paste], then add any leftover peppers and tomatoes you have. Add diced courgette, followed by green lentils and vegetable stock, and simmer until tender. Once cooled, finish with lemon juice, pul biber [aleppo pepper] and olive oil. Spoon over leftover rice, bulgur or grains and top with a dollop of yoghurt and chopped dill or mint. It’s easy, nourishing, filling and full of flavour.Akacan Ağır, head chef atLokal, LondonPanzanellaMy favourite lunch bowl is panzanella [a bread salad]. Bread is brilliant here because it absorbs all the dressing and juices, so you can throw it together in the morning and by lunchtime everything has properly melded. It doesn’t have to be the classic tomato version either: I love roasted beetroot, green beans or courgettes, plenty of herbs, then something substantial, such as cheese, eggs or pulses, with a nice sharp dressing. One of my favourite combos is puy lentils, roasted squash, leftover bread and pink pickled onions. It’s colourful, satisfying, travels brilliantly and, crucially, gets better as it sits.Rachel Morgan, owner ofTwelve Triangles, EdinburghMiso grain bowl with chilli-crusted salmonFor me, the perfect lunch bowl is full of protein, fibre, good fats and plant variety but, most importantly, it tastes great. I’d start with our miso grain, which includes emmer wheat, pearl barley and marrowfat peas, mixed with lettuce (a combination of red oakleaf, corn salad, cos and sweet gem) for freshness and crunch. Then I add sauerkraut, chicken crackling and shredded carrots with grape mustard for some zest. I dress it with zhoug [a chilli sauce] and tahini for a bit of spiciness, and top with smoked paprika olives and chilli-crusted salmon.Christian West, founder ofPick Your Own, LondonMung bean glass noodle bowlYou can get lovely sesame paste from Asian supermarkets, which I mix with fish sauce or soy sauce, honey and some bird’s eye chillies. I keep the dressing separate from the noodles until I’m about to eat it, as otherwise it can become claggy. I tend to add edamame beans, beansprouts, tons of finely sliced carrots, cucumber (which I de-seed, so it doesn’t make everything too soggy) and raw courgette. For protein, I’d go for smoked mackerel – or shredded poached chicken, which can be a bit more sociable! Top with crispy shallots or peanuts.Julie Lin, cookbook author and chef atTacos Lah, EdinburghSoy chicken rice bowlFor me, the perfect lunch bowl is all about getting a good mix of flavours and textures. I’d start with steamed rice, add some roasted or grilled protein – maybe chicken marinated in soy sauce and Shaoxing wine – then pile on seasonal vegetables. I’d finish it with a punchy ginger and spring onion dressing with soy and rice vinegar. You’ve got something comforting, but also fresh and light. I’d suggest keeping the components separate while travelling, then quickly putting it all together when you’re ready to eat.Fai Choi, research and development chef – UK, atHakkasanView image in fullscreenRoast pulses until crisp for extra texture.Photograph: OksanaKiian/Getty Images/iStockphotoChilli-salt tofu rice bowlI’m a big believer that the rice needs to taste good on its own, so season it properly rather than treating it as something that’s just there to fill the bowl. My go-to is seasoned rice, avocado, miso mayo, mung beans, pickled ginger and furikake [a Japanese condiment with dried seaweed], then chilli-salt tofu on top. My slightly underrated hero is the pickled ginger. It cuts through all the richer flavours and gives the whole thing a bit of a kick. And don’t be shy with the furikake.Miles Kirby, co-founder and executive head chef atCaravan Restaurants, London and ManchesterCoronation chickpea bowlFor me, feeling satiated after lunch is so important because otherwise I end up having an afternoon crash. I like to do a chickpea riff on coronation chicken with a half yoghurt, half mayo dressing, mixed with finely chopped shallots cooked in mild curry powder. I also add mango chutney or apricot jam for the sweetness. It goes well with sliced grapes and wild rice, and I love to top it with Indian snacks or crispy onions for added indulgence. I mix it all together – it doesn’t look very pretty, but I want every mouthful to have every element of the dish.Amelia Christie-Miller, founderBold Bean CoPrawn noodle bowlAt the start of the week, I’ll usually batch cook some prawns because they’re so versatile and I can create a few dishes out of them without getting bored. For a lunch bowl, I love to pair them with cold soba noodles and a sesame or peanut dressing, topped with something pickled, such as red onion, and something fresh and crunchy, such as cucumber. Finish with crispy chilli oil and a packet of crispy seaweed and you’ve got the best meal deal going – it’s been my go-to for surviving the heat over the summer.Lawrence Burrows, food to go development chefThe Sea, The Sea, LondonBeetroot halloumi bowlI always start with the base: I like a beetroot puree stirred through quinoa. Then add a pulse, such as butter beans or kidney beans. Keep them soft for something comforting, or roast them until crisp for extra texture. Add your vegetables according to the season: fresh, raw salads work beautifully in warmer months, while autumn is perfect for a tray of roasted vegetables. For extra protein, add something with a bit of character, such as salty halloumi. The joy is that it is completely adaptable. Mix and match with what’s in season, what you enjoy and what you already have in the fridge.Bettina Campolucci Bordi, wellness chef, author and educatorTell us: what’s in your packed lunch?Read moreExplore more on these topicsFoodVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attack | Scams | The Guardian
description: Scam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs such as miсrosoft.com
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Scam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs such as miсrosoft.com
Content: Many scams have near-identical URLs but a closer look reveals a cyrillic letter, which offers a world of difference between legit and scam.Photograph: Kirill Ivanov/AlamyView image in fullscreenMany scams have near-identical URLs but a closer look reveals a cyrillic letter, which offers a world of difference between legit and scam.Photograph: Kirill Ivanov/AlamyScam watchScamsReαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attackScam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs like miсrosoft.comHilary OsborneSun 20 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve read the email carefully and it looks legitimate. The link it asks you to click on has none of the usual red flags: there are no weird numbers or extra parts to the URL. You feel safe to proceed.But if you had looked slightly closer you may have noticed something slightly wrong with one of the characters. Just as in the headline of this piece where instead of “a” we used the Cyrillic “α”.Fraudsters can use letters from different alphabets to create URLs and email addresses that look almost identical to the real thing, but in reality send anyone who clicks on them to a spoof website or inbox. From there they can harvest personal details to use in their scams.There are other letters and symbols that are easily switched. Last year tech experts spotted fraudsters usingthe Japanese hiragana character んto look like a / in an address designed to look as though it was on Booking.com’s website.Jake Moore, global security adviser at cybersecurity company ESET, says the fraudsters “love Microsoft” as a company identity to spoof. “A fake site might use the Cyrillic “с” instead of the Latin “c” (miсrosoft v microsoft),” he says.View image in fullscreenMost phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAMoore says this type of fraud – known as a homoglyph attack – is becoming increasingly popular. A homoglyph is a character that looks very similar, or even identical, to another one.“Most phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments. Attachments can easily be scanned and caught by security software if malicious,” he says.“Therefore, criminals need to design their websites where the links look genuine and casually request people to click on them without thinking.”Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, says homoglyph attacks “are really more of a psychological trick than a technical one”, because the fraudsters are typically trying to panic you into responding quickly, rather than taking time to check things out.“The goal is to create a sense of panic so you don’t look too closely at the URL. They’re betting that when we’re in a rush, our brains see what we expect to see,” Briedis says.double quotation markIt just goes to show that the split-second decision you make when clicking a link is often the most vulnerable part of the whole security chain.”What it looks likeThe real thing. Until you look closely.You will receive an email or text message suggesting you need to click on a URL or email to sort something out.View image in fullscreenIf you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.Photograph: Sergey Tolmachev/AlamySome fonts make substitutions almost impossible to detect. In an email address given in comic sans , for example, the Cyrillic a does not look at all out of place.“We’ve spent years telling people to check the website before trusting it but the problem with this technique is that you can do exactly that and still be fooled as it can look as it should,” says Moore.If it’s a URL, Moore says typically it will lead to a site that encourages you to enter your credentials for the real site, including your username, password and even a one-time passcode.What to doIf you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.“If any text, WhatsApp or email is asking you to log in anywhere, it is vital that you independently visit the genuine website rather than trusting the link in front of you to save a few seconds,” says Moore.And apply the same thinking to email addresses. Type in the address you know to be correct, rather than clicking on a link.Keep your browser updated. It will flag up suspicious websites, and by keeping it updated it will catch the criminals’ latest workarounds.Put in place two-factor authentication, or multifactor authentication (2FA or MFA), which means you have two steps to log into a site.If you find that your details have been compromised, change your passwords immediately. Contact your bank and report the phishing attack to Report Fraud.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchCybercrimeConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I got married in it’: readers on their favourite secondhand fashion finds | Fashion | The Guardian
description: To mark Oxfam’s Second Hand September, here are some of your best thrift discoveries and the stories behind them
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: To mark Oxfam’s Second Hand September, here are some of your best thrift discoveries and the stories behind them
Content: Alicia in her $5 dress that she bought in 1996 and wore on her wedding day.Photograph: Alicia SiegelView image in fullscreenAlicia in her $5 dress that she bought in 1996 and wore on her wedding day.Photograph: Alicia SiegelGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Fashion‘I got married in it’: readers on their favourite secondhand fashion findsTo mark Oxfam’s Second Hand September, here are some of your best thrift discoveries and the stories behind themSun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOxfam’sSecond Hand Septembercampaign encourages people to avoid buying new clothes for 30 days and choose preloved pieces instead. From £28 Prada skirts to £5 wedding dresses, we asked people to share their favourite fashion finds and the stories behind them.‘It arrived crumpled like a tissue’View image in fullscreenNisha in her pink-and-red Prada skirt.Photograph: Nisha DaneilI bought this pink-and-red Prada pleated silk jacquard skirt in 2022 for £28 on eBay and it arrived crumpled like a tissue. But for just under £32, including postage to my then London address, I didn’t complain. It took about three hours and as many rounds with an iron before the worst of the wrinkles were gone and the pleats restored. It’s a classic style but distinctive and unusual, thanks to the colour and pattern.
