Definitely no basic.Nisha Daniel, lawyer,Kolkata, India‘This blue 1960s number called my name from the rails of a shop called Shag’View image in fullscreenDeb Grant at the Brit awards in her secondhand dress.Photograph: Deb GrantHunting for cool vintage clothes is a huge passion of mine, particularly when I’m travelling. I was in Melbourne last summer, and this blue 1960s number called my name from the rails of a shop called Shag. It cost $50 and I was so pleased to have an occasion to wear it when the Brit awards came to Manchester recently. It felt really special to wear something so unique.Deb Grant, DJ and radio presenter on BBC Radio 6, Manchester‘My son was very much into hat-wearing for festivals so I bought it for him’View image in fullscreenGraham bought this hat for his son.Photograph: Graham BerridgeThis hat, which I bought from a BHF [British Heart Foundation] shop in Epsom, cost £2. My son was very much into hat-wearing for festivals and often wore burgundy and red, so I bought it for him. It’s a bit like a newsboy cap, with a small peak. But instead of the usual round top, this is arranged in a series of peaks, a bit like a crown. It’s quite a heavy knit, and very warm on the head. Sadly, a few years later, he gave it to his then girlfriend. When they split up, she kept the hat.Graham Berridge,retired academic, Epsom, Surrey‘A few months later, we got married. I had this dress in my bag, so that’s what I wore’View image in fullscreenAlicia wore a $5 dress on her wedding day.Photograph: Alicia SiegelI bought this dress for $5 in 1996 from an opportunity shop (op shop) in Orange, New South Wales. I met my husband in New Orleans and, a few months later, we got married It worked out, and we have been married for 21 years. I had this dress in my bag, so that’s what I wore. It’s from the 70s, is still in good shape and I absolutely still love it. From a distance it looks pink, but as you get closer you realise it’s swirls of pink dots creating an optical illusion.Alicia, works in politics, Adelaide‘It turned out not only to be sterling silver, but by the Italian designer OP Orlandini’View image in fullscreenRachel’s necklace.Photograph: RachelMy mum found a choker at an op shop in Armadale, Western Australia, when I was a teenager. She was pretty sure it was real silver, and liked the design, so she paid the $5 asked and took it to a jeweller to be cleaned. It turned out not only to be sterling silver but by the Italian designer OP Orlandini. The jeweller was so impressed he didn’t charge her. I wore it for years and now my daughter wears it.Rachel,teaching assistant, Tasmania, Australia‘I was torn between considering it glorious versus ghastly’View image in fullscreenJane: ‘I discovered that the suit is from Altuzarra, a luxury New York brand, and worth at least £2,000 new.’Photograph: Jane TremlettI bought a startlingly orange suit from one of Lewes’ great and varied charity shops, hesitating for a while at the £50 price tag and torn between considering it glorious versus ghastly. I thought it might add a little flair in my special educational needs role in a state secondary school. Subsequently, I discovered that the suit is from Altuzarra, a luxury New York brand, and worth at least £2,000 new. It turns out that even the most grumpy maths teacher loves it, and the kids complain when I dare to turn up in anything different.Jane,secondary school SEN teacher, Lewes, East Sussex‘Eighty years after somebody first made it, it is still being worn rather than sitting in landfill’View image in fullscreenMJ wearing her shearling wrap.Photograph: MJMy 1940s shearling wrap has shoulder pads so big they enter the muddy field several seconds before I do. It was a long while ago that I found this in a charity shop and really cannot believe that I ‘ummed and ahhed’ a bit over the £15 price tag wondering ‘would I really wear it?’ Of course, I would. Mostly, I wear it to walk the dog or it occasionally makes an appearance at a party. Eighty years after somebody first made it, it is still being worn rather than sitting in landfill and doing a considerably better job of keeping me warmer than most things I could buy new.MJ, executive coach and education adviser, Norfolk‘I often wear it around the house as it makes chores so much more enjoyable’View image in fullscreenJosie in her pink dress, bought for £15.Photograph: Josie BrooksI bought this pink dress in a charity shop off Lavender Hill in south London 15 years ago. It was £15, which remains my highest charity shop spend. I’m known for my secondhand successes. It was initially for a friend’s 40th, but I’ve worn it as a zombie bridesmaid and Miss Piggy, and often just around the house as it makes chores so much more enjoyable. The crazy thing is that I went back to the charity shop two years ago when visiting London and they had the same dress in turquoise. Of course I bought it.Josie, works for an assistance dog organisation, Sheffield‘I knew I didn’t want to spend a lot of money on a synthetic dress I would wear only once’View image in fullscreenNicola, wearing her thrifted wedding dress, and her husband on their wedding day.Photograph: Ilaria MarchioneMy best find has to be my wedding dress. It was such a joy to wear. It’s an early 70s cotton Edwardian revival in broderie anglaise with a short train. Having organised a lot of weddings, I knew I didn’t want to spend a lot of money on a synthetic dress I would wear only once. My dress was £175 fromOxfamonline (plus another £100 in alterations and cleaning). Seven years later, I have indeed worn it only once. But I have plans to have it shortened and the train turned into cushion covers so I can continue to enjoy it.Nicola, academic, LondonExplore more on these topicsFashionOxfamCharitiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie | Adventure travel | The Guardian
description: Beautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbers
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Beautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbers
Content: Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa ‘has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order’.Photograph: David Forster/AlamyView image in fullscreenCabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa ‘has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order’.Photograph: David Forster/AlamyAdventure travel10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomieBeautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbersKevin RushbySun 20 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCabaña Verónica, SpainA good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity.€15,reservarefugios.comI skied up to the highest mountain hut in the Swedish Arctic. My reward? A whiteout …Read moreLåktatjåkko, SwedenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Wolfgang Kaehler/AlamyAn absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions.When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such asFridtjof Nansen(there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather.From 515 Swedishkronor(£40),laktatjakko.seGaustatoppen, NorwayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Robert Harding/AlamyLike many other huts belonging to the wonderfulNorwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-schoolfunicular railwayone kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province,Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway.From 1,550 Norwegiankroner(£122),dnt.noChata pod Rysmi, SlovakiaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vladimir Cuvala/AlamyThe Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October.€65,chatapodrysmi.kst.skKredaricaon Triglav, SloveniaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mikadun/ShutterstockThis is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential).€30 half-board,triglavskidom.siLe Refuge deCiottuludi Mori, CorsicaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Florian Neukirchen/AlamyOne of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker.€15,le-gr20.frBreiðuvik, IcelandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gestur Gislason/AlamyThe east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations,Brieðvikis part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association.11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70),ferdaf.isScotland’s mountain bothiesView image in fullscreenElphin Bothy in Sutherland.Photograph: Tom Richardson Scotland/AlamyThe UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them.mountainbothies.org.ukRifugio Nuvolau, ItalyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianThe Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from theBaron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory.€51 B&B,rifugionuvolau.itRifugio Lagazuoi, ItalyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Frank Bienewald/AlamyMany huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido.From €85 with breakfast,rifugiolagazuoi.comExplore more on these topicsAdventure travelEurope holidaysHotelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Water your plants and get an eye mask: 48 life rules every student – and adult – needs to know | Students | The Guardian
description: If you’re a fresher, this may be the first time you’ve ever lived away from home. So how should you socialise, feed yourself and look after your health?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: If you’re a fresher, this may be the first time you’ve ever lived away from home. So how should you socialise, feed yourself and look after your health?
Content: Cheers to the student life.Photograph: Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCheers to the student life.Photograph: Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027StudentsWater your plants and get an eye mask: 48 life rules every student – and adult – needs to knowIf you’re a fresher, this may be the first time you’ve ever lived away from home. So how should you socialise, feed yourself and look after your health?Zoe WilliamsSun 20 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t realise until you leave home just how idiosyncratic every family is, and how many of its customs are tacit, invisible, or maintained by someone else. Now you’re among people who emphatically aren’t related to you. How would you have any idea which of your practices were universal, and which common courtesies your upbringing had totally skipped? How do you even know how to keep your own body and soul together without the behind-the-scenes input of parents, who also have peculiarities of their own? Here’s a starter pack on how to function.FoodThe basicsAnything with blood goes at the bottom of the fridge (although fridge-sharing between vegetarians and meat-eaters should be negotiated first thing).Refrigeration is a game-changing technology but it doesn’t work if you just leave foodnearthe fridge, even for a couple of hours. Likewise, nothing that’s been defrosted should be frozen again.Don’t put a cooked chicken on a board that hasn’t been washed since it had a raw chicken on it. Likewise, without getting overanxious about it, exercise caution around all raw meat. Don’t cross-contaminate utensils (that is, use the same knife on raw chicken and then salad, without washing it).Ice doesn’t go off.Hopefully, you won’t have a dishwasher, as washing-up is a life skill. But if you do, don’t put anything with an electrical plug in it.Don’t use a wet cloth to protect your hands when you take things out of the oven. Use an oven glove.View image in fullscreenYou can’t go wrong with a bolognese.Photograph: Evgeniya Moskova/Getty ImagesThe eating bitYou need the following repertoire:Something quick that has protein in it and is not toast. Suggestion: an omelette.Something that is a full meal, covers protein and vegetables, and can be eaten over several days. Suggestion:bologneseorvegetarian chilli.Something that you can scale up to feed two or four without bankrupting yourself or showing off. Suggestion: pesto pasta, but please always add broccoli right at the end – such a small price to pay to not get scurvy.Something that you can make for others that is comforting and nobody can take against or be allergic to. Suggestion:risotto.Something that you can just pour boiling water over, like a cup of tea, only it’s food. Suggestion: miso soup or soba noodles.The habit formingIt is actually quite hard to integrate fruit and vegetables into your diet if you’re cooking for yourself but don’t want to spend a lot of time on it. They don’t just magic themselves into food. You should keep a stock of things you can mainline raw while you’re doing something else – carrots, apples, tomatoes, cucumbers.Everything is edible with the right chilli sauce: harissa, Tabasco, piripiri, sriracha, or for special occasionsHungarian pistaor crispy prawn chilli oil. Likewise, pickles: lime pickle, gherkins, jalapeños.You will probably be about 40 before you can be trusted to spontaneously grate ginger. Pastes in jars or tubes are a cheap alternative: arrive with one garlic and one ginger.HealthView image in fullscreenMost universities have a student health centre.Photograph: SDI Productions/Getty ImagesDr Imogen Bloor, who recently retired as a full-time GP and clinical lead in London, is the source of this expertise.Before you leave : make sure all your jabs are up to date, principally the new meningitis B vaccine and the five tetanus jabs you should have had during childhood. “Tetanus is incredibly rare, but if you get a wound, you’ll be much less anxious about it,” Bloor says.If you have an existing health condition, make sure you take enough medication with you so you don’t have to register with a new GP in a panic.Do register with a GP at your new address, though. Most universities, particularly campus ones, have a student health centre, which is essentially a GP practice but skewed towards a younger population. It will have ancillary services such as counselling and physio.“In the olden days, everyone had a Reader’s Digest Family Health Guide, and the internet has replaced that,” Bloor says. But the internet isn’t as easy to interpret. “You’re not born with the ability to separate the wheat from the chaff.” TheNHS symptom checkerandpatient.infoare the wheat. “Common things occur commonly – people latch on to likely cause #63. An 18-year-old with a hoarse voice almost certainly hasn’t got laryngeal cancer.”If you were at home and something happened, you would ask a parent. So call a parent.Pharmacists can see and treat a whole range of conditions, from hay fever to urinary tract infections. Calling 111 can be helpful, as they can provide advice and signpost you to appropriate services.Is it freshers’ flu? “As a general principle, if you’ve got mild symptoms and you take paracetamol and fluids and you rest and things seem to improve, that’s a good sign.”Or isn’t it freshers’ flu? “If you have a severe headache which isn’t relieved by simple pain relief, or if you’ve got associated symptoms, like loss of balance or confusion or altered consciousness, or you’re vomiting or you feel too unwell to get out of bed, then it is important to seek medical advice.”double quotation markIf you were at home and something happened, you would ask a parent. So call a parentOther red flags include: rapid onset, so if you feel a lot worse in a short time; a purpuric rash (one that doesn’t fade when you press on it – the classic meningitis symptom). Bloor remembers vividly from her sepsis awareness training “a number of patients who say, ‘I feel like I’m going to die.’ If you feel that ill, it’s more likely that you are really ill.”If you get infected hair follicles or a boil on your butt (perianal abscess), don’t be too embarrassed to go to the doctor; it won’t get better on its own. Bloor has seen a lot of young people who depilate their pubes, and boys their chests, and it’s really easy to get an infection there if you don’t clean and exfoliate properly.You don’t need a GP referral to use a sexual health or family planning clinic – just look up where it is. When you get there, be frank. “You can’t shock a doctor; most doctors have seen most things. It’s human and natural to feel shy or embarrassed but you’ve got to try not to worry about that.”If you think you might be so drunk you have to go to A&E, you’re probably lucid enough that you’ll be fine. But if a friend is so drunk that they’ve lost consciousness, are vomiting uncontrollably, or have banged their head, take them to A&E. “There is a small risk of a subdural haematoma [bleeding around the brain] without knowing.”Diarrhoea only, you’ll most likely be fine within 48 hours. Some stomach bugs can cause blood in your poo, but that’s unusual and you should consult a doctor. Eat bland, dry food and drink flavoured fluids (squash, stock) to replace salts and sugar, not just water. Persistent vomiting is riskier and you shouldn’t eat for 24 hours, stick with the flavoured fluids (little sips but often), but seek medical advice if the vomiting doesn’t settle or you can’t keep any fluids down. Be vigilant with hand hygiene and don’t prepare food for other people until you’re completely better.On injuries – is it broken? “Seek help if it’s very swollen, or painful to weight-bear, and doesn’t settle with ice compression.”Animal bites? “Especially if they’re penetrating rather than just a scratch, you should contact a GP promptly as they usually need prophylactic antibiotics.”Bloor’s most important advice of all, in my opinion: “Speaking both as a doctor and a human being, I would never discourage someone from contacting their GP if they’re worried. Young people are on a journey of learning and understanding self-management, and unless they’ve got someone to sense check against, they won’t know. Stoicism is fine but it can be dangerous.”CleaningView image in fullscreenRead the labels – they mean something.Photograph: Alfonso Soler/Getty ImagesWash dark colours separately from light ones, and whites separately from both – all colours can go in the same dryer, however.Read the labels –they mean something.If in doubt about what temperature to wash at, most modern washing powders do a good enough job on a cold wash (it’s often a snowflake symbol).Hang up your towels to dry (spread out flat) after a shower. Then you can use them more than once.Don’t use other people’s towels – they don’t like it.Wash your bedding every two weeks. Realistically, every month is fine, unless you’re entertaining frequently, in which case, every week.If you leave your washing in the machine too long (say for the entire day), it takes on a weird mouldy smell, and people don’t like that.Never be the person who thinks someone else in the accommodation is going to do their washing-up. It’s such a dick move.If you leave a toilet with any visible sign that you’ve been there, someone will be taking a picture of that and putting it in a WhatsApp group that you’re not in.InteriorsView image in fullscreenPut pictures on your walls – or it will look like a prison cell.Photograph: DragonImages/Getty ImagesWhatever you’ve got to put on your wall, you need seven times as many things. Every prison room you’ve seen on TV, that’s what a university room is like.If you’re going to have plants, water them, otherwise you’ll look like a weirdo.Take an eye mask; there is always something wrong with the curtains.You may take this as your first opportunity to be as messy as you like, and that is your right, but make a little area where you always keep vital things – you are now the only person who has your keys.SocialisingView image in fullscreenHave fun – but it’s a good idea to let people know where you are going and when you’ll be back.Photograph: Peopleimages/Getty ImagesDoes anyone know where you’re going and what time you think you’ll be back? Don’t get too hung up on it, but it’s good if someone has a vague idea.Nobody knows you well enough to have taken against you. So if everyone’s going to a thing and you’re not sure if you’re invited, just say, “Am I allowed to come to this thing?”‘Just be aware of what you’re spending’: budget hints for studentsRead moreYou’re going to meet a lot of people who aren’t like you, haven’t grown up in a nearby street, don’t have the same set of references, don’t have the same associations. Try to accentuate the positives – they haven’t brought their gun with them – and don’t overreact.You might join a lot of clubs and societies trying to find your tribe, and get rapidly disillusioned, because it’s not a very solid basis for commonality, “both thinking you might like Irish dancing”. Or maybe it is! Just don’t panic, is the point.Friendships are very intense in a closed environment – say, if you only socialise with people on your course, or in your halls. It’s easy to lose perspective. Leave a bit of space and time for unconnected others, friends from school, weird library people.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Which leader from history does the world need now?  | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Would a Churchillian figure fit the bill?Photograph: Universal History Archive/UIG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWould a Churchillian figure fit the bill?Photograph: Universal History Archive/UIG/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesLife and styleWhich leader from history does the world need now?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsLast week’s replies:What would be the most useful superpower?Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 16.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s clear that the world as it is – considering the climate crisis, the rise of nationalism, geopolitical tumult, the possibility ofAI killing us all by the end of the decade– could do with some more ethically astute and capable leadership. title: Tell us: what’s in your packed lunch? | Food | The Guardian
description: If you take lunch into work, is a sandwich, salad, soup or something else? We’re looking for the healthiest, best-value ideas
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: If you take lunch into work, is a sandwich, salad, soup or something else? We’re looking for the healthiest, best-value ideas
Content: We would love to hear about people’s healthiest and most affordable packed lunches.Photograph: Olga Navarro/AlamyView image in fullscreenWe would love to hear about people’s healthiest and most affordable packed lunches.Photograph: Olga Navarro/AlamyFoodTell us: what’s in your packed lunch?If you take lunch into work, is a sandwich, salad, soup or something else? We’re looking for the healthiest, best-value ideasGuardian community teamSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore people are bringing packed lunches to work as they try to save money and eat healthily.According to a poll by Ocado, nearly half of UK professionals bring a packed lunch more frequently than they did a year ago, with 69% saying that buying lunch near their office was now too expensive.We would love to hear about people’s healthiest and most affordable packed lunches. Are you a fan of the classic sandwich or do you like to experiment with a lunch bowl or bento box? What’s your go-to easy lunch for work?Share your experienceYou can share your response using this form.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: More than a dozen arrested in connection with 2021 assassination of Haitian president | Haiti | The Guardian
description: Jovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in Haiti
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in Haiti
Content: Haiti's president Jovenel Moïse speaks during a press conference in March 2020.Photograph: Andrés Martínez Casares/ReutersView image in fullscreenHaiti's president Jovenel Moïse speaks during a press conference in March 2020.Photograph: Andrés Martínez Casares/ReutersHaitiMore than a dozen arrested in connection with 2021 assassination of Haitian presidentJovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in HaitiAgence France-PresseSun 20 Sep 2026 16.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, according to US officials.Moïse, 53, was shot dead on 7 July 2021 at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him.“Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on Sunday.The suspects have been taken to Florida to stand trial.In the same post on X, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the southern district of Florida.”“Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing.In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moïse, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad.The men face possible sentences of life in prison.All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moïse’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors.Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil.Five of them have been sentenced to life in prison, including a former Colombian soldier, a former Haitian senator, a Haitian Chilean businessman, a retired Colombian soldier and a Haitian American.Haiti has descended into deeper chaos since Moïse’s killing, and currently has no president.It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on 13 December – if security conditions allow.Gangs control about 80% of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation.A UN-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesperson said earlier this month.Announced by the UN security council last year, the Gang Suppression Force was expected to ramp up between April and October to a planned capacity of 5,500 uniformed personnel and 50 civilian staff.As of July, it comprised fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, Mongolia, Jamaica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Sri Lanka. More recent figures have not been disclosed.Explore more on these topicsHaitiAmericasCaribbeannewsShareReuse this content

title: Michelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary general | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Former president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Former president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest
Content: Bachelet is a former high commissioner for human rights at the UN.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersView image in fullscreenBachelet is a former high commissioner for human rights at the UN.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersUnited NationsMichelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary generalFormer president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contestReuters in GenevaSun 20 Sep 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending an attempt ​that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”Costa Rican diplomat emerges as strong contender to be first female head of UNRead moreThe two-time Chilean ​president and former ‌UN human ‌rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and ‌international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeedAntónio Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term as secretary general on ‌31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.Her ​withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll putCosta ⁠Rica’s Rebeca Grynspanin the lead.The UN security ​council ​will formally recommend ​a single candidate to the 193-member general ​assembly for election. ‌The assembly’s ​approval ​has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsMichelle BacheletChileAntónio GuterresAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development | China | The Guardian
description: Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace
Author: Rebecca Bailey
Headline: Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace
Content: AI is being encouraged across the Chinese economy as a way to promote growth.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAI is being encouraged across the Chinese economy as a way to promote growth.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockChinaAnalysisWhy China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI developmentRebecca BaileyChina correspondentBeijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and paceChina bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioSun 20 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareAbout two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others inChina, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioRead moreBut over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.And last SaturdayAnthropic chief executive Dario Amodeipitched a “worldwidepacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksRead moreThat contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this weekcalled fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.‘If you build something vastly smarter than you, it better be on your side’: can we stop AI from deceiving us? – podcastRead moreAt the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech websiteyangtzeer.com.“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”Explore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAsia PacificAnthropicanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Police allege mother behind Blue Mountains stabbing attack on three children that left one dead | Blue Mountains | The Guardian
description: Bystanders found all four on the side of the road at Valley Heights on Sunday with stabbing injuries
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: Bystanders found all four on the side of the road at Valley Heights on Sunday with stabbing injuries
Content: Three children and a woman were found with stab wounds on a road in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Sunday afternoon.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPView image in fullscreenThree children and a woman were found with stab wounds on a road in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Sunday afternoon.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPBlue MountainsPolice allege mother behind Blue Mountains stabbing attack on three children that left one deadBystanders found all four on the side of the road at Valley Heights on Sunday with stabbing injuriesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastIma Caldwelland AAPSun 20 Sep 2026 19.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 20.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have alleged that a mother was behind a stabbing attack on three young children that left one dead and two others fighting for their lives in hospital.The woman, aged in her 40s, is also in a critical condition.Bystanders were first on the scene after finding the three children and the woman with stab wounds inside a vehicle at Valley Heights in theBlue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Sunday afternoon.One young child died at the scene despite witnesses rushing to help, delivering first aid while waiting for emergency services to arrive.The alleged domestic violence incident came at the end of a horror weekend acrossNew South Wales, after three women were allegedly murdered inside their homes within a 12-hour period on Saturday.Three men charged with domestic violence-related murders after three women killed in separate incidents in NSWRead moreThe police deputy commissioner Peter McKenna described the past two days as devastating.“It’s a horrific and tragic weekend and it’s like one that I don’t remember in my career,” he told Nine’s Today on Monday.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Those three … plus the no-more-tragic situation that we had in the Blue Mountains. Put them all together and it’s unfathomable.”Paramedics treated the mother and children at the scene on Sunday before taking them by road to Westmead hospital and Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.“The two children and their mother are in a critical condition,” McKenna said.“The mother is the suspect in this matter, for domestic related homicide, and that investigation is ongoing.”McKenna told reporters on Monday the woman remained in a critical condition and police had “to wait for the medical side to play out”.“If she recovers from those injuries, certainly our people … will be intent on charging [her] with homicide,” he said.Hours after the incident, NSW police Supt John Nelson said the father of the children had been notified.The father had been at work when he received the call from police, he said.“You can imagine receiving that tragic news,” Nelson told reporters.McKenna said the father was immediately taken to hospital. “He’s supporting these two children that are in a pretty good condition at the moment. He’s assisting us with the investigation,” he said.He said the woman had not previously come to the attention of police and that investigators were not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.The woman was aged in her 40s and the children were all under five. All three had undergone surgery in hospital.Nelson praised the efforts of the “upstanding” members of the public who responded to the tragic scene.“People are just going about a lovely Sunday afternoon, and being confronted with this is traumatic and tragic for anybody,” he said.Responding officers would not be spared the hardship and would have access to available support services.Police said the weapon used and the circumstances surrounding the incident would form part of their investigation.Blue Mountains councillor Darren Rodrigo on Sunday described the news as “absolutely horrendous and tragic”.“Our deepest love and condolences to the immediate family and our prayers with all the children involved,” he said.“A massive thank you to the community members [who] intervened to provide medical assistance and to our first responders for their incredible support and courage during this time.”Separately, McKenna said the weekend had been “tragic and horrific … in relation to domestic violence”, referring to three other alleged homicides in NSW.“We’ve had four incidents, one at Wagga, one at Tenterfield, one at Bondi and … terrible scenes at the Blue Mountains yesterday,” he said. He said police would allege that in all four incidents “knives or edged weapons were used”.“It’s actually very, very confronting,” McKenna told reporters.Support for anyone affected by the subject matter of this report is available at Full Stop Australia (1800 385 578)Explore more on these topicsBlue MountainsAustralian police and policingNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese launches bid for UN security council seat and names former Murdoch aide to top diplomatic post | Anthony Albanese | The Guardian
description: Australia and Finland are vying for a spot on the council, and the PM needs two thirds of member states to back him
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australia and Finland are vying for a spot on the council, and the PM needs two thirds of member states to back him
Content: Prime minister Anthony Albanese said he was optimistic Pacific countries would support Australia’s bid to join the UN security council.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenPrime minister Anthony Albanese said he was optimistic Pacific countries would support Australia’s bid to join the UN security council.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAnthony AlbaneseAlbanese launches bid for UN security council seat and names former Murdoch aide to top diplomatic postAustralia and Finland are vying for a spot on the council, and the PM needs two thirds of member states to back himFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSun 20 Sep 2026 17.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia having a seat at theUnited NationsSecurity Council will be able to help with the cost of living back home, the prime minister insists.Anthony Albanese has launched a formal bid for Australia to serve a two-year term on the UN security council in 2029 and 2030.Albanese also defended former News Corp head of broadcasting Siobhan McKenna as Australia’s next consul general to New York.A vote for the UN council spot won’t be held until mid 2028, but lobbying efforts will intensify during the prime minister’s visit to New York for the UN general assembly.The prime minister said Australia’s role on the council would be able to benefit ordinary citizens.“Engagement with the world matters. It matters because it makes a difference to the cost of living, to inflation, to Australians’ way of life,” he told reporters in New York on Monday, Australian time.“That is why we can’t afford to not be engaged with the world, because it has a direct impact on the quality of life of Australians on a day-to-day basis.As China rises, Australia is increasingly enmeshed in the US war machine. Is the alliance still worth the risk?Read more“We have an opportunity through this potential seat on the UN security council to play a key role in shaping the global issues that really matter to Australians.”Australia has served on the security council five times since the UN was established after the second world war.The most recent stint was in 2013 and 2014, where Australia was able to lead a response to the Russian downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17.View image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese unveiled former News Corp head of broadcasting Siobhan McKenna as Australia’s next consul general to New York.Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty ImagesAlbanese said the role Australia played during that period was evidence of what a spot on the council could achieve.“We do need to stand up to the Middle East conflict. I think there is a role for middle powers to engage, and Australia has done that as we’ve engaged with the war in Ukraine in the coalition of the willing,” he said.Two countries are elected to the security council from the Western Europe and Others group, which includes Australia.So far, only Australia and Finland have put their hands up for a spot on the council, but other countries from the bloc could still launch bids.Even if the two countries run unopposed, Australia would still need support from two-thirds of the 193 UN member states to be successful.Of the 15 members on the security council, China, France, the US, UK and Russia are permanent members, while the remainder serve two-year terms.The prime minister said he was optimistic of getting support from Pacific nations, as well as south-east Asian countries in the Asean pact.Part of the campaign will seek to leverage Australia’s role in the Pacific and action on climate change in the region.The campaign, called “we listen, we partner, we protect”, will also focus on aiming to boost the voices of middle powers and smaller nations in the UN.Action taken by Australia to be the first country in the world to ban people under 16 from using social media will be at the forefront of the campaign, as well as recent efforts to place guardrails on the expanding use of AI.During the press conference, Albanese was asked whether he had sought assurances McKenna wouldn’t “continue to lobby or deal with Mr Murdoch in advancing business interests” but the prime minister did not confirm.“Siobhan McKenna is a professional, and she will do an outstanding job representing Australia and the Australian government here in New York,” he said in response.“And the fact that she has experience in both the private sector and the public sector is a very good thing. I’m someone who supports people being appointed on merit. Siobhan McKenna has been appointed on merit.”McKenna, the chair of Australia Post and former chair of the NBN, will take up the role later in the year.Explore more on these topicsAnthony AlbaneseUnited NationsAustralian foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation-linked company built $56,000 shed on private property of Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man | James Ashby | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: James Ashby also drives new Ford Ranger given to party and is main pilot of plane donated by Gina Rinehart, which he says are not for personal use
Author: Sarah Martin
Headline: Exclusive: James Ashby also drives new Ford Ranger given to party and is main pilot of plane donated by Gina Rinehart, which he says are not for personal use
Content: James Ashby looks on as One Nation leader Pauline Hanson addresses media.Composite: AAP/Guardian designView image in fullscreenJames Ashby looks on as One Nation leader Pauline Hanson addresses media.Composite: AAP/Guardian designThe Populist: Pauline Hanson's divided nationJames AshbyOne Nation-linked company built $56,000 shed on private property of Pauline Hanson’s right-hand manExclusive:James Ashby also drives new Ford Ranger given to party and is main pilot of plane donated by Gina Rinehart, which he says are not for personal useListento episode 2 of The Populist podcastFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah MartinSenior correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePauline Hanson’s right-hand man, James Ashby, is enjoying generous benefits as a result of his role working for One Nation, with documents showing that a company linked to the party built a $56,000 shed on his central Queensland property.Guardian Australia understands that Ashby, formerly Hanson’s chief of staff and now the party’s national director, also drives a new Ford Ranger that was “personally” gifted toOne Nationby Hancock Agriculture’s chief executive, Adam Giles, in April. Hanson said the vehicle would help the party’s campaign efforts and “provides us the presence we need in the lead-up to the next federal election”.Pauline Hanson’s daughter Lee working for a NSW One Nation senator remotely from Tasmania without ministerial approvalRead moreSources say Ashby is earning a lucrative salary in his new high-profile role. He also has regular access to the $2m Cirrus plane gifted to the party by Giles’ employer and Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart.The aircraft is kept at Rockhampton airport, not far from Ashby’s home, and he is its main pilot.The PopulistThe Populist: The favourite son | Episode 2 – podcastSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://audio.guim.co.uk/2026/09/20-27700-THE_POPULIST_E2_FAVOURITE_SON.mp300:00:0001:04:45In a statement to Guardian Australia, Ashby said the car was used “for campaign and branch purposes” while the plane was “not used for personal transportation”.“I have a privately owned vehicle for personal use,” he said.A friend of Ashby’s travelled on the plane with him and Hanson on its maiden flight to Albury in May.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereProperty records show that Ashby bought a “lifestyle property” near Yeppoon inQueenslandin 2025. A development application lodged with the shire of Livingstone lists the One Nation-linked company, Small Batch Brewing Pty Ltd, as the purchaser of a $56,706 shed on the land.Small Batch Brewing is also named as the customer on documentation provided by an independent engineer and included in the council paperwork.The company – jointly owned by Ashby, Hanson and the party’s national treasurer, Alexander Jones – has been described as a craft-brewing venture but Guardian Australia has confirmed that it does not hold a liquor licence to sell alcohol. It also has no excise licence, which is required to manufacture alcohol products in Australia. A different brewing company, Sunshine and Sons, is listed as the manufacturer of One Nation’s branded liquor line.Ashby told Guardian Australia that Small Batch Brewing was “currently a non-trading entity”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The business will go through the necessary licensing application and approval process when the time is right,” he said.It is unclear how the company bought a $56,000 shed.Ashby regularly conducts live television crosses for News24 (formerly Sky News) from the building. Council records show he has received approval to build a house and an in-ground pool on the Yeppoon property.Australian Securities and Investment Commission records show that Small Batch Brewing’s principal place of business is One Nation’s Brisbane headquarters, on an industrial estate at the airport.Ashby’s move into the role of the party’s national director sparked speculation that he was clearing the way to run for One Nation at the next election.In May Hanson asked the Department of Finance for permission to establish a second electorate office in Yeppoon, further fuelling suggestions that Ashby was preparing a tilt at federal parliament.When asked if he would run at the next election, Ashby told the Guardian: “No.”Explore more on these topicsJames AshbyThe Populist: Pauline Hanson's divided nationOne NationPauline HansonAustralian politicsQueenslandBusinessAustralian political donationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections | Germany | The Guardian
description: Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin
Content: ‘Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,’ Merz said after the results.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,’ Merz said after the results.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAGermanyFriedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state electionsFar-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in BerlinDeborah Colein BerlinSun 20 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s embattled chancellor,Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just 4.9%, below ⁠the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament and indicating they may be excluded altogether. It would be the CDU’s worst-ever state score, which Merz called a “disaster”.The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendlyAlternative für Deutschland(AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with 38.3%, more than doubling its previous score, according to projections on ARD public television.In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.The deeply unpopular Merz has beenfighting for his political survivalafter a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch afterSaxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routedthe CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s co-chair, Tino Chrupalla, react as he hears the first results of the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election in Schwerin.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersA jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Polandhead into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGermany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support forUkraineand carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival,Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.View image in fullscreenElif Eralp (centre), the candidate for Die Linke in Berlin, reacts to the projected results of the state election.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockMerz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with onlyone in 10 Germanssaying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked inthe former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Man, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beach | Greece | The Guardian
description: Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
Content: The altercation happened at Vouliagmeni beach, about 12 miles south of Athens, on Sunday morning.Photograph: Geopix/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe altercation happened at Vouliagmeni beach, about 12 miles south of Athens, on Sunday morning.Photograph: Geopix/AlamyGreeceMan, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beachRow at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungersHelena Smithin AthensSun 20 Sep 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man after a brawl over a sunlounger at a beach on the Athenian riviera.The man had arrived at the popular bathing spot of Vouliagmeni before 10am on Sunday hoping to secure a sunbed, but he soon began arguing with a fellow bather – described by authorities as a “76-year-old man unknown to him” – when it became clear loungers were in short supply.The row quickly degenerated into a scuffle as others reportedly joined in. The victim, who was with his wife, is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest during the fight.“It seems that people who were with [the assailant] also participated,” ERT, the country’s state broadcaster, reported.“The 82-year-old was seriously injured, and needed to be transferred by ambulance to Asklepieion hospital in Voula.“Despite the efforts of doctors, at about 11am the elderly man succumbed to his wounds.”A postmortem was immediately ordered.Police arrested the 76-year-old and, initially, a 21-year-old woman who was with him. The beach resort’s manager was also detained for questioning.“The incident is under investigation,” said a source, describing the fight as unprecedented. “InGreecedisagreement is expressed vocally, with a lot of screaming and shouting, not in fistfights like this – especially between two elderly men. I think that’s why it is so shocking.”Like other parts ofEurope, Greece is undergoing a severe cost of living crisis that has heightened tensions and put strain on social relations. An increase in domestic violence and other disputes has been partly blamed on the pressures of everyday life.In recent years, there has been growing anger over private rental outfits hogging prime coastal areas with exorbitantly priced sunloungers in Greece, where the sea has an important place in national identity.Authorities said “all those” involved in the incident would appear before a magistrate.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeOlder peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato | Russia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
Content: Polish and Romanian soldiers in the Suwałki Gap – an 80km stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolish and Romanian soldiers in the Suwałki Gap – an 80km stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesRussiaEuropean spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoExclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-opsShaun Walkerin Prague and RigaSun 20 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk,told parliamentthat intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat fromRussia.View image in fullscreenThe Russian president, Vladimir Putin, alongside Adm Viktor Liina, the commander of Russia’s Pacific fleet.Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine.Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missilesin the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion ofNatoterritory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources inUkraineand warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.View image in fullscreenMichal Koudelka, the director of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service (BIS).Photograph: CTK/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whethera surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month– during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe CIA director, John Ratcliffe, who made a surprise trip to Moscow last month.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersHowever, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, whenUS officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invadeand the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMoscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as acampaign of sabotageagainst targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition,veered into Polish airspace a year ago.Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.View image in fullscreenA Russian Shahed drone on display in Kyiv.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APIn recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president,Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’scampaign of sabotage in Europeis likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authoritieshave attributed to Russian intelligence.“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.View image in fullscreenA Ukrainian soldier fires at an incoming jet-powered Shahed drone during a Russian aerial attack on Kyiv in August.Photograph: Libkos/Getty ImagesMežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropeVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyyCzechiaLatvianewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election | Russia | The Guardian
description: At least three people killed and oil refinery damaged as doubts cast over initial reports of ballistic missile use
Author: Dan Sabbagh
