Headline: At least three people killed and oil refinery damaged as doubts cast over initial reports of ballistic missile use
Content: Smoke rises from an oil refinery in Moscow, Russia on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from an oil refinery in Moscow, Russia on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersRussiaUkraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian electionAt least three people killed and oil refinery damaged as doubts cast over initial reports of ballistic missile useDan Sabbagh,Pjotr Sauerand agenciesSun 20 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 02.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack that involved hundreds of drones.The attack killed at least three people and damaged what Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said was one of Russia’s “key oil industry facilities” on thefinal day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.Zelenskyy said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, initially thought to be a short-range ballistic missile, but which sources said later was a winged drone.Fires at Moscow oil refinery facility after drone attackThe president did not offer any further details, prompting media reports in Ukraine that it was a ballistic missile, only for doubt to be cast on the weapon identification later in the day.Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep insideRussiaand has the range to reach the country’s capital.Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels posted images of what they said was debris from a Flamingo missile found in the Moscow region, though the claims could not be independently verified. Ruslan Leviev, the head of the open-source investigation group Conflict Intelligence Team, said the debris probably came from a Flamingo missile.View image in fullscreenWorkers at Fire Point’s secret factory in Ukraine inspect one of their FP-5 Flamingo missiles last year.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APMoscow’s mayor, Sergey Sobyanin, said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, though these figures are often exaggerated, and Ukraine’s daily drone fire rate estimated a number in the low hundreds.Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election in Russia that is expected to tighten Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.At least three people were killed, including a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man, in separate incidents.A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drone’s origin.Kyiv has stepped up itscampaign of long-range drone strikes against Russiain recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort.Ukrainian ​strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil-refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties were reported and emergency services were on the scene. The refinery had already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening gripRead moreThe Pelican missile was initially thought to be the FP-7 made by Fire Point, Ukraine’s most successful long-range drone and missile maker. But several hours later, as the speculation persisted, other military sources said it was a long-range drone.The company is also developing the longer-range FP-9, which has a range of more than 500 miles, meaning it could be used to target Moscow in the future. A test flight is expected later this autumn.The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s firstparliamentary electionssince Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropeOilVolodymyr ZelenskyyDrones (military)Vladimir PutinnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position
Content: Charles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCharles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSweden‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and homeCharles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration positionLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported fromSweden.Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country afterBrexitcame to an end.An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has in effect been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since BrexitRead more“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow those suddenly left homeless can get help.“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has alreadydeported 458 British peopleafter rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.View image in fullscreenCharles is distraught after landing at Heathrow.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe situation persistsdespite promises from opposition partiesnow on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” – in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.View image in fullscreenA bag containing a toothbrush, toothpaste and earplugs that was given to Charles in the Swedish detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA bright yellow envelope was also handed to him by the captain before disembarking, which he opens for the first time.Inside is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. Another says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case. They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said. “They said we think that if we don’t detain you, you will abscond from Sweden because you are not cooperating.“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.”He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no. He asked if he could drive back to Britain “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said: ‘No, the decision has been made.’”View image in fullscreenA document envelope issued by the Swedish police authority.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBefore Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.The campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued toa 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.View image in fullscreenCharles looking for help at Heathrow.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was alsoordered to leave after 25 yearswhile another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, wasdeported in January.The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position hadinfected decision-making relating to Britonsthere before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”View image in fullscreenCharles leaves Heathrow airport, heading into an uncertain future.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianJane Golding, the chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says. “This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.She points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. “Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropean UnionMigrationEuropeBrexitHeathrow airportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
Content: Smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday.Photograph: ReutersUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaignTensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebelsPatrick Wintourin New YorkSun 20 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGovernments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence afterIranclaimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.Map indicating territory under de facto Houthi authority as of 11 SeptemberIran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.The outburst of sabre-rattling appears to have been prompted byattacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.The US largely regards theHouthisas a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies whenhe spurned a call by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthissuddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coastoverlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.In an attempt to keep the US out of its war withSaudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that they would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, a commitment that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News: “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.France will summon Iran’s ambassador ⁠after Iranian ⁠authorities closed a French-language centre affiliated with ​its ‌embassy ‌in Tehran, the ‌foreign ministry said on Sunday.The Iranian judiciary accused the centre of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe French foreign ministry said: “This new attack on the French cultural presence in Iran … is unjustifiable and unacceptable.”Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators.Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning that “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance.He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisYemenSaudi ArabiaIranUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July
Content: Smoke rises from a fuel storage depot near Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from a fuel storage depot near Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport.Photograph: ReutersSaudi ArabiaThick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capitalAuthorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in JulyDonna Ferguson,Yassin El-Mouddenand agenciesSat 19 Sep 2026 20.21 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’sHouthissaid they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday.The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July.Explosions were heard in Riyadh as firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport.Map showing location of King Khalid airport in Saudi Arabia and wider regionResidents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there were “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index.“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.The Saudi civil defence force sent air raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities. The military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward ​Riyadh.Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflictRead moreThe all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds.A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blamingSaudi Arabiaand vowing a response. The group also said the Saudi air force had conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children.It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen,where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday.The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group.The Houthis recentlyseized control of strategic the Red Sea islandsof Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured theport of Mokha and Perim islandin the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis.The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis.A US state department security alert issued on Saturday for Americans ‌in the Middle East cited Houthi attacks. The state department urged US citizens in the region to “exercise heightened vigilance” and said Americans outside the Middle East “should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region”.Elsewhere in the region, Israel’s military launched airstrikes in several areas of southern Lebanon after it said that two of its soldiers were wounded by a “Hezbollah explosive device”.Associated Press also reported on Saturday that Israeli strikes had killed three men in the Gaza Strip.In Iran, a man accused of spying for Israel was executed in the latest of a recent surge of executions in the country.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaHouthisYemenMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Lib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agency | Liberal Democrats | The Guardian
description: Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for
Content: Ed Davey interviewed by Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems’ Brighton conference. The party plans an Online Crime Agency to tackle offences from child sexual abuse material and deepfake AI porn to drug and weapons trafficking.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEd Davey interviewed by Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems’ Brighton conference. The party plans an Online Crime Agency to tackle offences from child sexual abuse material and deepfake AI porn to drug and weapons trafficking.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PALiberal DemocratsLib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agencyProposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands forPeter WalkerandAlexandra ToppingSun 20 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheLiberal Democratssay they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for.The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled.Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape.Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71.The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which wasformed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens.His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England.One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEd Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference beginsRead more“If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south.Party figures see the conference as a chance to set out a more coherent and striking policy platform, including on the economy and immigration.But there is worry among some MPs that the problem is wider. “We already have quite a lot of policies, if people look at them,” one said. “It’s less about what you get if you vote Lib Dem than why you should – about what we represent. And people don’t really know that.”One longtime party activist said: “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election. It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal DemocratsLiberal Democrat conferenceTechnology policyFuel dutyEd DaveyPetrol pricesTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Specialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and Wales | Rape and sexual assault | The Guardian
description: Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward
Content: Plans for courts hearing rape cases include private entrances, facilities for recording evidence in advance and ways to observe sentencing remotely.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenPlans for courts hearing rape cases include private entrances, facilities for recording evidence in advance and ways to observe sentencing remotely.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersRape and sexual assaultSpecialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and WalesFunding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forwardBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpecialist courtrooms prioritising cases of rape and other serious sex offences are to be introduced acrossEnglandand Wales, with campaigners welcoming the move as potentially transformative.The changes, designed to encourage more survivors to come forward, will include the provision of private entrances and waiting rooms, and facilities equipped for recording evidence in advance and observing sentencing remotely.Announcing the move,Andy Burnhamsaid victims of rape and serious sexual offences had felt let down by the justice system for too long, adding that prosecution rates for rape remained “shamefully low”, with many victims waiting years for justice.“These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough,” the prime minister said.“So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place.”A multimillion-pound cash injection is intended to make sure every crown court in England andWaleshas at least one room set up specifically to hear rape and serious sexual offence cases within two years.Rape and serious sexual offence cases will also be prioritised in courts more widely, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) announced. Such trials will be given a fixed date, as opposed to being placed on floating lists where they can be moved at short notice and delayed by months.Among those welcoming the announcement was Labour’s Charlotte Nichols, who told the House of Commons this yearshe was raped after an event she attended as an MPand waited 1,088 days for her case to get to court.View image in fullscreenLabour MP Charlotte Nichols, centre, waived her anonymity to tell parliament about her rape and subsequent experience with the courts.Photograph: Parliament LiveNichols said: “Today marks a hugely important milestone, helping to improve the experience of victims and survivors of sexual violence in the court system who are all too often retraumatised by seeking justice.“I’m proud that substantive, meaningful change has come from waiving my anonymity to speak about my own experiences, and am hugely grateful to the prime minister and lord chancellor for taking forward these measures, as I know the difference they would have made for me and so many of the survivors I have worked with in recent years.”The MoJ cited Nichols’ “immense strength and bravery” in its announcement.While welcoming the announcement, there was a warning by the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, that the crown court backlog of rape and sexual offence cases was now “significantly worse” than when she first called for specialist courts in 2021.She said: “Tens of thousands more victims are now waiting for their cases to reach trial, and specialist courts alone will not be enough to tackle the scale of the delays or deliver the swift justice victims deserve. Indeed, court delays could prevent many rape victims from accessing the specialist courtrooms that are being set up to support them.”Further changes announced include new trauma-informed training for court staff and a pilot scheme giving victims of sex offences a single point of contact to ensure their needs are met during the court process.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeparate from the funding for courtrooms, there will also be £43m to support survivors through the national rape and sexual abuse support fund for the next two years, including through counselling, therapy, outreach and group activities.The new measures also include the creation of a rape justice taskforce, drawing figures from across the criminal justice system to tackle the rising rate of postponed rape trials and confront the myths that cause victims to withdraw from cases.The Conservatives’ shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said tackling delays in rape trials was long overdue, but that the courts backlog had been “used” by theLabouras justification for controversial plans to significantly restrict the right to jury trials.“If resources can be found to accelerate rape trials, why are they persisting in their attack on this ancient right to jury trials?” he said.In 2022, an announcement by Boris Johnson’s government of three specialist courtrooms to prosecute rape cases wasdismissed by legal blogger the Secret Barrister as a “gimmick”that did not address the chronic underfunding of the justice system.Changes in the new provisions include many of the reforms that campaigners and charities have been calling for over many years.“Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice,” said Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.“We’re particularly pleased to see measures that will improve trial efficiency and ensure survivors are better able to participate in, and observe, proceedings.”Explore more on these topicsRape and sexual assaultCrimeViolence against women and girlsUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN
Content: Bridget Phillipson: ‘People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.’Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson: ‘People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.’Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APBudget 2026UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budgetBridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UNPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentSun 20 Sep 2026 15.36 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNext month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue.Burnham isexpected to meet Trumpearly next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10.As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”.Asked about the comments,Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique.“People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.”She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies,causing significant inflationary pressures, saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget.The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures.She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home.“We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end.“And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything thatAndy Burnhamhas done since becoming prime minister.“I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ in budget as inflation rises to 3.1%Read moreIn a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation.She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco.Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.”With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties.She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister.“It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026Andy BurnhamDonald TrumpBridget PhillipsonUS-Israel war on IranEconomicsUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Deaths of three women in sea at Brighton had no criminal involvement, police say | Brighton | The Guardian
description: Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from Uxbridge were found on 13 May
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from Uxbridge were found on 13 May
Content: L-R: Jane Adetoro, Joseph Jacobson, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters, in an old family photo.Photograph: Sussex PoliceView image in fullscreenL-R: Jane Adetoro, Joseph Jacobson, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters, in an old family photo.Photograph: Sussex PoliceBrightonDeaths of three women in sea at Brighton had no criminal involvement, police sayJane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from Uxbridge were found on 13 MayCharlie MoloneySun 20 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe deaths of three sisters found in the sea offBrightonbeach did not involve any criminality or third-party involvement, police have concluded.The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, from Uxbridge, west London,were foundon 13 May. A postmortem conducted that month confirmed all three women died by drowning.Specialist detectives worked to trace the sisters’ final movements and understand how they came to be in the water that morning, Sussex police said.The investigation found all three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive, the road running along Brighton Beach, at 10.20pm on 12 May, wearing everyday clothing.No evidence was found to suggest they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time and the investigation concluded all three women entered the water near to where their bodies were found, the police spokesperson added.A spokesperson for the force said: “The purpose of the police investigation was to identify any evidence of criminal offending linked to how the sisters came to be in the water or their subsequent deaths.“We can confirm the thorough police investigation has not found any evidence of a crime being committed or involvement by a third party.”Additional details such as the sisters’ specific movements before their deaths and their potential reasons for entering the water will be considered during the East Sussex coroner’s inquest.Ch Supt Adam Hays said his force had been “acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident” and “concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water”.He said: “Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information. We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss.”After the sisters’ deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt unbearable but that he held on to the memories they had shared and “the bond that death can never take away”.In a statement released through Sussex police, Jacobson said: “Jane, Christina and Becky were more than daughters to me: they were my joy, my strength and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love.“Each of you was unique and precious in your own special way. Your smiles brightened dark days, your laughter brought comfort and your presence made life more meaningful. Though your time on Earth was short, the impact you made will remain in our hearts for ever.”A GoFundMe online fundraiser for the women’s funerals has received more than 2,200 donations from members of the public, totalling nearly £46,000.Explore more on these topicsBrightonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy
Content: Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham will meet Donald Trump face-to-face on Tuesday.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpAnalysisAndy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictablePippa CrerarPolitical editorPM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economySun 20 Sep 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareNo international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink hismidterm dreams.When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle onNatoand Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.Starmer’s“keep calm and carry on”strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in Junesignalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the morecombative approachof Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trumpsuggested Burnham was “extremely liberal”(not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that hemight not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and thathe would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shownwith the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about theUK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trumptold world leaders their countries were “going to hell”over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weaponsRead moreWith Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamUS politicsNatoanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ICE agent shoots and wounds man at traffic stop in Austin, Texas, officials say | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Anti-ICE protests break out in push for transparency as unnamed man is in serious but stable condition at hospital
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anti-ICE protests break out in push for transparency as unnamed man is in serious but stable condition at hospital
Content: A car  is damaged at the site where local officials say an ICE officer shot a person earlier in the day in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Shahrzad Rasekh/ReutersView image in fullscreenA car  is damaged at the site where local officials say an ICE officer shot a person earlier in the day in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Shahrzad Rasekh/ReutersICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)ICE agent shoots and wounds man at traffic stop in Austin, Texas, officials sayAnti-ICE protests break out in push for transparency as unnamed man is in serious but stable condition at hospitalAssociated PressSun 20 Sep 2026 19.37 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and wounded a man on Sunday afternoon inTexas’s capital ofAustin, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.The unnamed man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the city’s north side, Austin’s police chief, Lisa Davis, said at a news conference with the mayor and other city officials.The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn’t immediately respond to requests for details.Austin police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Davis told reporters.Kirk Watson, Austin’s Democratic mayor, said he wants the city’s police department to be involved in the investigation so it can provide “clear, third-party eyes” in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.Austin residents have “a right to feel safe in their city”, Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.View image in fullscreenPeople speak during a demonstration where a man was shot in his vehicle by an ICE officer, on 20 September in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/APDavis said she did not yet know the nationality of the person who was shot. The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident, but added that her department’s special investigation unit was at the scene.A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes, local media reported.A large law enforcement presence was at the scene, along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying “Nobody is safe” and on the other side, “ICE Nazi”.Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state.”Greg Casar, a Democratic congressman representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.View image in fullscreenAuthorities deploy ‘non-lethal’ weapons near a demonstration where a man was shot in his vehicle by an ICE officer, on Sunday in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/AP“It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep,” Casar told reporters. “For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here.”The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than50,000 arrestsa month for the first time in its history in July and August.In July, an ICE officerfatally shot52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.Also in July, Johan Sebastián DuránGuerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man, wasshotby an ICE officerin Maine. The officer is an army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood andnever should havebeen given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relativestoldthe Associated Press.The administration’s enforcement effortswerewidelycondemnedlast winter after thekillingsof Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)TexasAustinUS immigrationTrump administrationUS politicsProtest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Trump reportedly to form health funding board that could veto ‘woke’ initiatives | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: President’s latest order expected to bring NIH funding under control of Trump administration to align with agenda
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: President’s latest order expected to bring NIH funding under control of Trump administration to align with agenda
Content: Donald Trump speaks during an event about healthcare in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on 18 September.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks during an event about healthcare in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on 18 September.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APTrump administrationTrump reportedly to form health funding board that could veto ‘woke’ initiativesPresident’s latest order expected to bring NIH funding under control of Trump administration to align with agendaCoral Murphy MarcosSun 20 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s latest executive order is expected to establish a board responsible for approving National Institutes of Health grant funding, marking another attempt by theTrump administrationto censor topics that do not align with the president’s agenda.The executive order, reported by outlets includingthe Washington PostandPolitico, was discussed in a meeting on Friday where senior administration officials accused the NIH of funding “woke” initiatives that went against Trump’s political priorities.Russell Vought, the director of the White House’s office of management and budget (OMB), and other administration officials proposed an executive order that would create an external committee that could veto awards in biomedical research that do not align with Trump’s goals, according to several people who spoke to the Washington Post.The board would include Vought and the NIH director, Jay Bhattacharya, according to Politico, and it would be required to reach unanimous decisions on grant awards. The OMB is the White House agency in charge of implementing the president’s policies in the executive branch.‘Clear retribution’: dismay as key Alzheimer’s study cancelled amid Trump attacks on scienceRead moreEstablishing an external commission to award grants based on the president’s ideological agenda breaks with the agency’s traditional process of evaluating proposals on scientific merit. Bhattacharya hasresistedcuts to federal research spending anddefendedthe NIH’s grant-making process on Friday, while Vought expressed a desire to reshape federal spending.The reported ⁠move comes as the NIH, the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research, faces aclass-action lawsuitby researchers arguing that the Trump administration is hindering and terminating scientific grants to censor opposing views to the president’s ideological agenda. Researchers are accusing the administration of violating the first amendment.“What the First Amendment does not allow is the government’s use of its funding power to target or silence the expression of disfavored viewpoints within the biomedical research community,” reads thelawsuit.Since Trump took office for his second term, billions of dollars in federal grants related to health, nutrition, the environment and disaster relief have beencut or frozen. Research withkeywordsincluding “equity”, “racist”, “gender”, “climate change” and others has been flagged by the administration to hinder funding for scientific research.The Department ofHealthand Human Services, which oversees the NIH, and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS healthcareDonald TrumpUS politicsHealthResearch fundingUS domestic policynewsShareReuse this content

title: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’
Content: María Elvira Salazar speaks during a press conference at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 20 May 2026.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersView image in fullscreenMaría Elvira Salazar speaks during a press conference at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 20 May 2026.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersRepublicansHouse Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcementFlorida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’Ed PilkingtonSun 20 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaría Elvira Salazar, theRepublicancongresswoman who hasaccusedthe president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warningDonald Trumpthat some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”.In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, theFloridarepresentative who is locked in atight racefor re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” hisrelationshipwith Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vauntedambitionto carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history.“I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the southFloridaarea that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said.Asked by Face the Nation whether she were referring toTom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, orStephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who hasspearheadedthe removal of undocumented children, Salazar placed the onus on Trump. “He is the only elected official in the White House. He is the one who has to determine who he listens and who he does not listen to. He is the president.”House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policiesRead moreLast week Salazar became a rare voice ofinternal criticismwithin the Republican party towards Trump when she released a30-second advertpointing out that evenlaw-abidingundocumented immigrants were getting caught up in the aggressive federal sweep. The ad said: “In July, 50% of the50,000 peoplethat were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”Salazar’s warning has been backed up by a slew ofrecentopinionpollsthat show many Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Trump in 2024 are nowturning awayfrom him. They are being repulsed by the rising cost of living and concern about his handling of the economy, as well as by the hardline immigration drive that has led to many hardworking, taxpaying undocumented immigrants being rounded up, detained and deported.In her CBS News interview, Salazar described herself as “a proud Republican”. “I’m first-generation American, and I want to preserve the American values that are entrenched in the [Republican party] and that the Hispanics share”.She is currently facing a tough re-election battle in her Miami-area district against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, despite havingwonin 2024 by 20 points. Trump also won the district by 15 points that year.SalazartoldCBS News that 70% of Americans wanted to see some type of immigration reform. She also pushed back on the administration’s deportation of all undocumented immigrants irrespective of their criminal status.“The average America understands the difference between the narco and the nanny, and the gangster and the gardener.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Saturday, Trump responded to Salazar’s criticisms, saying: “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling about the border. I do.” He added: “Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected.”By breaking her silence on immigration, Salazar has put a spotlight on rising fears within Republican circles that the displeasure of Hispanic voters towards the administration’s policies could cost the party dear in November’smidterm elections. Several House seats in Colorado, Florida, Texas, Nevada and other states could be tipped in the Democrats’ favor as a result.Steve Scalise, the second-most powerful Republican in the US House, acknowledged on ABC News’s This Week that immigration was creating divisions within his party. Asked what he thought of Salazar’s comment that many Hispanic voters feel betrayed, he said: “I don’t necessarily agree with that statement.”He added: “When you look at what María said, obviously we have a lot of disagreements in Congress … Even amongRepublicanswe have disagreements on how to actually get to the secure border that we have.”Explore more on these topicsRepublicansUS politicsFloridaTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)newsShareReuse this content

title: La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice award | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festival
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: The queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festival
Content: Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo.Photograph: Leonardo Ramirez/Eyepix Group/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJavier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo.Photograph: Leonardo Ramirez/Eyepix Group/ShutterstockToronto film festival 2026La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice awardThe queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festivalBenjamin LeeSun 20 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish queer drama La Bola Negra has won this year’s people’s choice award at theToronto film festival.The film, which takes place in 1932, 1937 and 2017, focuses on the lives of interconnected gay men. It premiered at this year’s Cannes film festival with the Guardian’s Peter Bradshawcalling it“handsomely produced, lovingly detailed and confidently constructed” in a four-star review.After a competitive bidding war after its premiere in May,Netflixpicked up the rights and the film will be released later this year.In a prepared statement, directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi said that connecting with Toronto audiences in this way was “the greatest gift we could receive”.The Black Ball review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly toldRead moreIt marks the first foreign language winner of the awardsince 2011’sLebanese drama Where Do We Go Now?The award has come to be used as a predictor of Oscar success with past best picture winners such as Green Book, 12 Years a Slave, Nomadland, Slumdog Millionaire and The King’s Speech all picking it up.Last year’s winnerwas Chloé Zhao’s Shakespeare dramaHamnet, which was nominated for eight Oscars,winning onefor best actress Jessie Buckley.The Sylvester Stallone biopicI Play Rockyand disability activism dramaBeing Heumannwere named this year’s runners-up.For the second year, the international people’s choice award was also handed out, with British 80s-set Aids dramaElsinorenamed as the 2026 winner. Last year’s was given to Park Chan-wook’s darkly comedic thrillerNo Other Choice.The Toronto winners come after May el-Toukhy’s suspense dramaWoman Unknownwonthe Golden Lion awardat the Venice film festival. At Cannes back in May, Cristian Mungiu’s family dramaFjordwonthe Palme d’Or.Explore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026Toronto film festivalFestivalsDrama filmsWorld cinemaPeriod and historical filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LA | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: People are increasingly crossing paths with the wild animals as homes ring the outskirts of forests, sparking a new era of coexistence
Author: Nick Visser
Headline: People are increasingly crossing paths with the wild animals as homes ring the outskirts of forests, sparking a new era of coexistence
Content: As communities on the outskirts of LA grow, bears are being drawn to residents’ pools, chicken coops, fruit trees and trashcans.Photograph: Poolbearlife via InstagramView image in fullscreenAs communities on the outskirts of LA grow, bears are being drawn to residents’ pools, chicken coops, fruit trees and trashcans.Photograph: Poolbearlife via InstagramLos AngelesBear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LAPeople are increasingly crossing paths with the wild animals as homes ring the outskirts of forests, sparking a new era of coexistenceNick VisserSun 20 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery year, as summer draws to a close and fall begins, California’s bears get hungry.Black bears have long roamed the state, hunting for acorns, ants and pine nuts by the bucketload to pack on calories before hibernation. But increasingly, for every berry and root, there’s an even greater temptation: our trash and the detritus of human existence.That dynamic is playing out in perhaps a surprising place:Los Angeles. As communities on the outskirts of the metropolis grow, bears are butting up against humanity, drawn to residents’ pools, their chicken coops, their fruit trees and trashcans.“Black bears are incredibly adaptable, versatile omnivores,” said Wilson Sherman, a PhD student at the University of California, Los Angeles, who studies human-wildlife interaction. “They can eat everything we can eat.”View image in fullscreenVideos show bear cubs with their snouts bubbling in the water, climbing – and falling from – trees.Photograph: Poolbearlife via InstagramHuman-bear interactions have increased since the 1990s, Sherman said, which makes sense as communities expand and the state is now home to some 50,000 to 70,000 black bears. A few hundred of those live in the Angeles national forest, just north of the city and its millions of hungry households.Brian Gordon and his partner moved to the state’s bear capital – Monrovia, California – four years ago. Their house is the last before the Angeles national forest begins, and as they were buying the home, a family of bears wandered through the back garden. It was the start of a new era of coexistence.Family of bears play in swimming poolNow, the pair regularly share their pool with a family of bears and document their exploits on an Instagram account called PoolBearLife. Videos show bear cubs with their snouts bubbling in the water, climbing – and falling from – trees and causing adorable, young bear mayhem.“I only had education up until I bought this house of bears from whatever I saw online. I actually thought people get eaten by bears a lot,” Gordon said. “But after we bought the house, we had bears walking through. That’s really all they’re doing. I realized, OK, I have an unnatural fear of these animals and we’ve kind of adapted to living around them.Experience: we found a bear swimming in our poolRead more“People will say ‘you guys are the bear experts,’” Gordon went on. “No, we’re city boys. We bought a house that happened to have bears.”Gordon and his partner live amongst the bears, but they’re also vocal advocates for doing so safely. Trashcans are kept clean, temptations are removed and, despite the filming, they give the bears their space. Sometimes mistakes are made and a bearfinds a case of beerin the garage.But with consideration, bears don’t even stop to sniff the trash cans and will just pass through the backyard like it’s an extension of the forest nearby, the couple said.In a perfect world, Sherman said, human dominated landscapes that buttress the natural world would take steps to minimize bear contact. That means making neighborhoods as unattractive to bears as possible.“Pet food left outside, koi ponds, fruit trees with a lot of fruit on them, swimming pools, all these things can be attractive to bears,” he said.It’s not that human food tastes better, it’s just much more calorie dense and therefore easier for bears to pack on the pounds. In fact, bears that live or forage near human environments tend to reproduce more often and at higher rates, likely due to the availability of our food.“It takes a lot of work to get the calories from, say, a half eaten pizza in the trash in equivalent calories from acorns and ants,” he said. “It makes sense to get calories from human food.”The other major factor is climate crisis. Warmer summers can alter the availability of natural food and force bears to expand their ranges. Major wildfires like the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires were also linked to a lack in natural food sources, prompting the bears near Los Angeles to search in neighborhoods instead.View image in fullscreenAs September draws to a close, interactions between bears and Angelenos will thin out for the season.Photograph: Poolbearlife via InstagramAlex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, said human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall. September is often a really active month as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation hungry period, known as hyperphagia. 2026 is on track to be a record-setting year when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said.It’s also a time when humans are out in force around Labor Day for the year’s final picnics and camping excursions. Fish and wildlife officials will often get reports of bears creating a nuisance and occasionally damaging fences, getting into sheds and making a mess as they look for calories.“The bear’s just looking for food, doing natural behavior, but it’s creating a situation that’s not ideal,” Heeran said. “A lot of the conflict can be prevented.”Sometimes, however, that conflict can escalate, which can result in a bear being euthanized or relocated. It’s rare and wildlife officials try and prevent situations from escalating to that point, but it happens.Bear drinks from water bowlEarlier this year,the city of Monrovia erupted in furyafter a mother bear known as “Blondie” was euthanized. Officials had determined she had swiped at local residents twice, causing minor injuries. She had two cubs at the time. They are now being raised in captivity until they can hopefully be released back into the wild.Residents rallied for an alternative plan, but that effort ultimately turned into a memorial walk through the city in Blondie’s honor.“The city was not a part of that conversation or decision,” Becky Shevlin, the mayor of the city, which is peppered with monuments to black bears,toldthe Los Angeles Times in March. “We were absolutely devastated, especially when you think about her having the two little cubs.”Sherman said the spread of bear footage on social media, many of it captured by doorbell cameras that have exploded in the last decade, is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, people get to see bears being bears, doing cute things.“Bears are really cute, and a lot of the things they do are really cute … This is a real way to build meaningful empathy for wildlife, and building empathy for wildlife is a powerful motivator for conservation actions,” he said. “There is this risk of … kind of Disney-fying them. Black bears are by nature not particularly aggressive unless they are put in a dangerous or threatening situation, but they can cause damage. It’s best to give them their space.”As September draws to a close, interactions between bears and Angelenos will thin out for the season. But residents of the city will have to contend with their neighbors again come spring, alongside the mountain lions, deer and coyotes that call the city’s outskirts home.“When people move to these foothill neighborhoods, a lot of people are moving in because they think it’s a suburb of LA.
