Rangers dominated the central areas, where Dan Neil and Nicolas Raskin are already forging a formidable partnership and James Penrice merrily stomped all over the place.O’Neill gambled on a back five, on Luke McCowan in a sort of withdrawn winger role, discarded both at half-time, rolled through his substitutions, but the plan never really emerged from the fog. Celtic are basically like the tangled ball of printer cables and headphone wires in the bottom drawer, where you’re never quite sure whether you’re unpicking the knots or making them tighter.Naderi’s goal, bundled in from close range after Kim Min-su’s long-range effort was parried helpfully into his path by Viljami Sinisalo, was simply the most consequential emblem of Rangers’ superiority here. Emmanuel Fernandez got a rough ride early on, Tierney clipped the bar from distance and Ivor Pandur made a fine save from Colby Donovan early in the second half. That was basically it, as far as explicit threat went. Donovan’s header was the only Celtic shot on target.“For a young team, it’s brilliant that they can take the good from this,” said McInnes. “Coming to places like this, it won’t get much more difficult. It’s only three points, but in the context of the season it was important for lots of reasons.” He knows, of course, that Rangers are not the finished article. But right now there is a power vacuum at the top of Scottish football and his improving side may as well be the one to fill it.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticRangersmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We miss her the same every day’: Olivia Cusack on her late footballer sister Maddy | Women's football | The Guardian
description: Olivia Cusack tells Tom Garry of her determination to ensure Maddy’s ‘legacy lives on’ three years after the Sheffield United player’s death
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Olivia Cusack tells Tom Garry of her determination to ensure Maddy’s ‘legacy lives on’ three years after the Sheffield United player’s death
Content: Olivia Cusack (left, with Maddy) and her loved ones are enduring a ‘frustrating and confusing’ wait for answers about the circumstances surrounding her death.Photograph: Olivia CuscakView image in fullscreenOlivia Cusack (left, with Maddy) and her loved ones are enduring a ‘frustrating and confusing’ wait for answers about the circumstances surrounding her death.Photograph: Olivia CuscakWomen's footballInterview‘We miss her the same every day’: Olivia Cusack on her late footballer sister MaddyExclusive interview byTom GarryFamily is determined to ensure her ‘legacy lives on’ three years after the Sheffield United player’s deathSun 20 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlivia Cusack says her sister, the late Maddy Cusack, is on her mind every single day and she is determined to ensure her “legacy lives on” three years after the former England youth international midfielder’s death.Olivia, together with family and friends of Maddy, walked 29 miles from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United’s home, to their family’s home in Horsley, near Derby, on Saturday to raise funds and awareness. Maddy’s loved ones are still enduring a “frustrating and confusing” wait for answers about the circumstances surrounding her death on 20 September 2023.An inquest into the death of the 27-year-old Sheffield United playerwas adjourned again in Julyand has been scheduled to resume on 7 December after fresh evidence came to light. Cusack, a former England under-19 international, was the first player to appear in 100 matches for the Sheffield United women’s team.Olivia says the walk on Saturday, “Bringing Maddy Home”, was motivated by some of the evidence during the inquest. “After the inquest we wanted to bring her home from Bramall Lane, back to our family home,” she says. “Many people know Maddy as the professional football player and the name on the back of her shirt, the number, the colours she wore, the club she was associated with.“But I felt in the inquest it was lost that she was a person, she wasn’t an object that we were discussing. She’s a person, she’s a family member of ours [and] a person that’s sometimes been lost within the chaos surrounding her death really, so that’s the notion behind the walk. To claim her back, bring her home and protect her.”A minute’s applause will be held before kick-off on Sunday at the Women’s Super League 2 fixture between Newcastle and Sheffield United. Discussing that anniversary, Olivia says: “We miss her the same every day, as I will on Sunday. The anniversary is always something that creeps up on us. It’s very emotional and it’s a time where we just reflect, but we do so much throughout the year so she really is at the heart of pretty much every single day. Not a day goes by where we don’t think about her.View image in fullscreenSheffield United and Maddy Cusack’s family paid tribute at Bramall Lane shortly after her death.Photograph: Richard Callis/MB Media/Getty Images“There can be days when you just feel absolutely drained and you know you don’t quite know what the right thing to do is, but I think the way that we just get through it is that we remember who she was as a person. She loved her life, she loved trying new things and just enjoying life’s simple pleasures, we try and embody that on every day, not just the anniversary.“I really do encourage people to, as difficult as it can be sometimes, share the photos, share the memories, bring her up in conversation wherever you can, talk about her, and between all of us, you know her legacy will live on.”The family have already endured eight full days of evidence, after the hearing began belatedly on 29 June, but the discovery of additional documents led the proceedings to be paused until December. The coroner apologised to the family for yet another delay. The case had been set previously to start being heard on 5 January 2026 after additional postponements in 2025.“It’s been really difficult,” Olivia said of the delays. “It’s not something that any of us anticipated to happen. It’s very confusing and it can be very frustrating, the length of time it’s taken, it can be difficult to work that out and to know how you should be feeling and the process of it. However, we know that for the right outcome it has to be taken seriously. They need the time to come together and really get an outcome.View image in fullscreenMaddy Cusack was also remembered during the Premier League match between Sheffield United and Newcastle.Photograph: George Wood/Getty Images“It feels as though she can’t be at peace until it’s finished. And I do feel that’s quite upsetting to think about and to work through. It needs to come to a conclusion.”Olivia said she would “channel Maddy’s energy” during the 29-mile walk on Saturday, when a group of about 15 family and friends travelled in the reverse direction to another fundraising walk in February 2024 from Pride Park to Bramall Lane.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis time they set off from Sheffield at 5.30am. Afundraising pagefor the walk had surpassed £1,100 as of Saturday afternoon. Olivia described that tally as “incredible – £1,000 is just amazing, it’s more than I ever expected” and said: “Particularly with it being Maddy’s anniversary, it’s going to be very much a mental challenge as well as a physical one, so it gives you that extra motivation to make the people who’ve donated proud.”The money is being raised for the Maddy Cusack Foundation, which is helping a range of causes targeting women’s and girls’ football and “letting girls be seen within sport”.“We provided Derby County Community Trust with a series of bursaries for girls and families who struggle with the financial prospects of becoming dedicated to their football. It’s a helping hand for any child that needs that extra sort of funding, taking away the barriers that they might face.”The foundation has also partnered with the Stockport County left wing-back and former Derby, Sheffield United and Nottingham Forest player defender Ben Osborn’s organisation Elite Football Development, which aims to inspire young people through sport and education.“They work with girls and boys but we sponsor the girls’ side of things, which is focused around post-16 study, and allows girls to gain qualifications alongside being able to train and live the life of a professional footballer. We were really keen to get involved in this as Maddy was really passionate about education.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123.In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsWomen's footballinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hayen must worry about his Burnley future but fans’ fears are existential | Burnley | The Guardian
description: Derby’s stoppage-time equaliser leaves Burnley winless at home since last October and financial problems are mounting
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: Derby’s stoppage-time equaliser leaves Burnley winless at home since last October and financial problems are mounting
Content: Burnley head coach Nicky Hayen watches on during the draw with Derby.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PAView image in fullscreenBurnley head coach Nicky Hayen watches on during the draw with Derby.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PABurnleyHayen must worry about his Burnley future but fans’ fears are existentialDerby’s stoppage-time equaliser leaves Burnley winless at home since last October and financial problems are mountingDominic Boothat Turf MoorSun 20 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe greatest moments of Burnley’s history were beamed on to a big screen before kick-off at Turf Moor, accompanied by famous lines of commentary. The final one, the moment promotion was sealed under Scott Parker in April 2025, was soundtracked by: “Burnley are back in the big time.” That feels a long time ago now, with a return to the Premier League a remote prospect.Kanté and Mavropanos rescue late point for West Ham in derby thriller at MillwallRead moreBurnley appeared to have this game against Derby sewn up, leading through Zeki Amdouni’s first-half header, but a stunning stoppage-time strike from the Rams’ substitute Mo Fuseini soured the Turf Moor mood. It means Burnley’s winless home league run could now reach a year, the Clarets last tasting victory at Turf Moor on 18 October 2025. Their last win in any competition in 90 minutes was on 11 February.The draw left Nicky Hayen, the under-fire head coach, under scrutiny, though the majority of fans will direct their anger towards Alan Pace, the chair, given the financial problems and off-field turmoil that plagued the club during a disruptive summer.Hayen vowed to fight for his future and revealed he would talk with Pace, though could give no assurances he will remain in charge for the next game at Watford on 10 October after the extra-long international break. “I can understand the fans are angry after a start like this, it’s not what they want to see from their team or from myself,” he said. “It’s my responsibility. But I’ve always shown resilience and I’m always going to fight. We need this [international] window to change a lot of things.”View image in fullscreenMohammed Fuseini celebrates scoring a late equaliser for Derby.Photograph: Alfie Carling/PPAUK/ShutterstockIn his programme notes before the game, Pace called for fans to “unite and show togetherness”, after they had chanted for his removal during the home defeat by Bristol City a fortnight ago. There was some early encouragement for Hayen’s team as they sought to make inroads against Derby. Although a lack of thrust in the final third was evident at times, Burnley made the breakthrough via Amdouni’s forehead, the forward peeling around the back post to nod home Lucas Pires’s corner.Hayen, who was managing Haverfordwest County in the Welsh Premier four years ago and was not Burnley’s first choice to replace Parker, celebrated. Having been accused of muddled selections in his tenure so far, he had made some brave calls, dropping the club captain, Kyle Walker, and struggling goalkeeper Max Weiss, and recalling Marcus Edwards, who had been jettisoned after featuring in the campaign’s opening two games.Those decisions were nearly vindicated, right up to the moment Fuseini pounced, leaving Hayen to bear the brunt of more fan criticism. “It is really difficult [to take],” he said. “You saw the reaction of the players after the game, sitting on the ground, disappointed. We wanted to give the fans the win, I wanted this for them, I can accept their frustration. I want to give back to the fans, I feel we can give back a lot. You saw we were close, we wanted to do it just before the international break.”Quick GuideLópez fires Wolves to derby win over West BromShowFer López fired Wolves to a 1-0 win against arch rivals West Brom in a bruising Black Country derby on Sunday. Lopez punished a blunder by Albion defender Nat Phillips to score his fifth goal of the season in the second half of the Championship clash at Molineux. It was no more than Wolves deserved after Albion keeper Max O’Leary had kept West Brom in the game during the first half with three outstanding saves. Albion rarely threatened to snatch an equaliser in the first Molineux meeting between the west midlands rivals in five years. After fears of a repeat of the serious crowd trouble that marred their previous showdown at West Brom two years ago, the derby passed off peacefully inside the stadium. Elsewhere in the Championship,Boltontwice came from behind to win 4-3 in a thriller atNorwich.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The break may represent a chance for Hayen, if he remains, to regroup, though for Pace and the board there remain unanswered questions about the £142m of external debt the club owes, as well as the £81m owed by his firm ALK Capital to the club itself after a leveraged buyout in December 2020. Comparisons with the Glazers’ takeover and ownership of Manchester United have been made. James Holroyd’s recent departure, after 15 months as chief executive, feels reflective of the worsening malaise in the boardroom. Holroyd previously worked under the Glazers at United.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite two promotions under the current regime (and three relegations) the Clarets’ financial situation has deteriorated, with some fans now harbouring genuine fears of total extinction if debts are not repaid. Parachute payments may help for a time, but Burnley no longer have the cash reserves they boasted in their debt-free era before Pace and ALK when they enjoyed five successive seasons in the Premier League under Sean Dyche. Such stability now feels a world away and problems are spilling on to the pitch. Money has been spent on transfers, with squad turnover high in recent seasons, but there was particular concern when the £20m made from the sale of Zian Flemming was not reinvested in a new striker, with 39-year-old Jamie Vardy hastily arriving on a free transfer after the transfer window had closed.View image in fullscreenZeki Amdouni sprints off to celebrate his goal for Burnley.Photograph: Alfie Carling/PPAUK/ShutterstockHayen sent on Vardy and loan signing Largie Ramazani to retain a counterattacking threat against Derby late on, as Burnley hung on. But with a slender lead going into stoppage time, their confidence appeared brittle. Goalkeeper Grégoire Coudert had been forced into a couple of late interventions after Ryan Hedges should have equalised for Derby on the hour mark.Then, just when it seemed Burnley’s winless streak would be broken, the rocket from Fuseini snatched two points away, leaving them bottom of theChampionship. “It’s hard to take,” said Hayen. “It’s frustrating.”Explore more on these topicsBurnleyDerby CountyChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andros Townsend avoids injury after bizarre pitch roller incident in Thailand | Soccer | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The former England winger Andros Townsend has joked Stoke away ‘wasn’t so bad after all’ following a bizarre incident in Thailand where he was run over by a pitch roller
Content: Andros Townsend seen shortly after joining Kanchanaburi Power in 2025. He joined PT Prachuap this year.Photograph: Kanchanaburi PowerView image in fullscreenAndros Townsend seen shortly after joining Kanchanaburi Power in 2025. He joined PT Prachuap this year.Photograph: Kanchanaburi PowerSoccerAndros Townsend avoids injury after bizarre pitch roller incident in ThailandFormer England player run over while warming up‘It turns out Stoke away wasn’t so bad,’ says wingerPress AssociationSun 20 Sep 2026 06.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former England winger Andros Townsendhas jokedStoke away “wasn’t so bad after all” following a bizarre incident in Thailand where he was run over by a pitch roller.The former Tottenham and Crystal Palace attacker currently plays in Thai League 1 for PT Prachuap and made headlines on Saturday night when a clip emerged on social media which showed the 35-year-old being taken out before a fixture at Pattani.Townsend was warming up when a member of staff at Pattani appeared to lose control of the pitch roller and it crashed into the 13-cap England international. The left leg of the Prachuap player briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he did feature off the bench late on in the 3-0 win.Regular ITV pundit Townsend later took to Instagram to make light of the incident, referencing one of his recent posts in which he contrasted a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke’s windswept stadium.Townsend said on his Instagram story: “It turns out Stoke away wasn’t so bad after all. Swipe to see why.”Another post described Townsend as ‘The King of Memes in Thai League history’ and he replied “trust me” with four laughing emojis.Explore more on these topicsFootballnewsShareReuse this content

title: McCullum hails Brook’s captaincy as England move top of T20 world rankings | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: McCullum says that Brook has ‘grown as captain and as a person’ as England prepare for their ODI series against Sri Lanka this week
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: McCullum says that Brook has ‘grown as captain and as a person’ as England prepare for their ODI series against Sri Lanka this week
Content: Harry Brook (centre) chats with Brendon McCullum (left) after England completed a 3-0 T20 series clean sweep over Sri Lanka.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenHarry Brook (centre) chats with Brendon McCullum (left) after England completed a 3-0 T20 series clean sweep over Sri Lanka.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAEngland cricket teamMcCullum hails Brook’s captaincy as England move top of T20 world rankingsMcCullum: Brook has ‘grown as captain and person’England begin ODI series against Sri Lanka this weekTanya AldredSun 20 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s white-ball coach, Brendon McCullum, was full of praise for the captain, Harry Brook, after Saturday’seight-wicket victoryover Sri Lanka completed a T20 series whitewash and took the side to No 1 in the world.Brook, player of the T20 series against Sri Lanka, has now won 23 of his 26 completed games as captain. If he is not yet considered a suitable candidate as Test leader, the cap fits nicely in the smash and grab format.‘I can’t wait for the Ashes’: new Test coach Fleming wants England to be No 1Read more“He’s grown not just as captain, but as a person as well,” said McCullum. “He seems very comfortable now as a leader of this side and the guys follow him, they trust him. Obviously his batting’s been on a different planet when it comes to T20 cricket, but I think his ability to do things differently based on what’s required with the conditions, and also against the opposition, has been probably the most impressive element.“Twenty20 is such an inconsistent game, so you can never take your eye off what you’re trying to achieve, but over the last 18 months or so we’ve found a nice level of consistency. We are not the finished article as yet, but the work we’ve done on the environment and the setup, and the depth that we’ve got in our side now is certainly encouraging.”Quick GuideMiddlesex win One-Day Cup to end white-ball waitShowRyan Higgins [pictured] made a fine 100 and then took the key catch to dismiss fellow centurion Nick Kelly as Middlesex beat Leicestershire by 31 runs to win the Metro Bank One-Day Cup final at Trent Bridge.Higgins’ first List A century and a 135-run sixth wicket partnership with Harry Duke (55) had earlier helped turn Middlesex’s innings around from 71 for five to 231 all out. After Leicestershire slipped to 79 for five, Kelly dug in with a determined 103 of his own.Once Kelly had been caught by Higgins at mid-wicket off Tom Helm with nine overs left, Middlesex picked up the final two Leicestershire wickets to secure a first trophy since their 2016 Championship triumph, and first men's white-ball trophy since winning the Twenty20 Cup in 2008.Higgins was out for 100, which came from 114 balls, and included nine fours, at the start of Middlesex’s 49th over, caught by Kelly when trying to go over long-on off Ian Holland. Leicestershire wicketkeeper Ben Cox took five consecutive catches while Holland claimed five for 36 and Rehan Ahmed three for 55.After the Leicestershire captain, Stephen Eskinazi (12), was out at the start of the sixth over, the Foxes continued to lose wickets as Toby Roland-Jones took three for 27 in his 10-over spell. Kelly then steadied the innings alongside Holland to push Leicestershire’s reply on to 110 at the halfway stage.The partnership was finally broken in the 29th over when Holland (15) was stumped off Zafar Gohar. Kelly brought up his century at the start of the 41st over, coming off 103 balls with 10 fours and three sixes before his resistance was finally broken.PA MediaPhotograph: Mike Egerton/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Alongside his relationship with Brook, there is a new guy in town to manage – McCullum’s old buddy and the new Test coach, Stephen ­Fleming, who was also at Old Trafford on Saturday.“Flem and I are great mates,” said McCullum. “He was my captain coming through and the great thing about him is he always made you feel like his equal. Our relationship is brilliant and fundamentally we both just want what is right for English cricket and will do whatever we can across the formats to make cricket as good as we can in the time that we’re here. I think our relationship is a real strength, we talk regularly regardless of these jobs.”View image in fullscreenHarry Brook flicks a shot away en route to his 33-run tally against Sri Lanka on Saturday.Photograph: Roger Evans/Action Plus/ShutterstockAnd he was confident that their relationship would ensure there was no conflict when there is a clash between Test and white-ball commitments. McCullum even drew Fleming into the England huddle before Saturday’s game. “He was a bit reluctant but it’s brilliant to have him around. He’s one of the most successful T20 coaches in the world, so it is quite handy to have him run his eye over the environment.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland begin a three-match ODI series against Sri Lanka on Tuesday. McCullum had warm words about Sonny Baker, whose control and pace has been a revelation. “He bowls 90mph, has a good slower ball, can swing the ball both ways and is an incredible competitor. He has been tested in international cricket and probably didn’t get the instant results he wanted but he’ll be walking a foot taller now and that’s great for all of us whether that’s T20 cricket, one-day cricket, or Test cricket. People like him are rare commodities.”Towards the other end of his England career is Adil Rashid, who will be 40 by the time the next T20 World Cup comes around in 2028.“We hope Rash is around for a long time. He’s a world-class performer but we do have to have plans in place. We have guys we are keeping an eye on consistently, obviously Rehan Ahmed has been around our squad a lot and he’s never let us down, there are lots of other guys out there as well. The one-dayers could be an opportunity to have a look.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamBrendon McCullumHarry BrookCricketSri Lanka cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Luke Littler threatens to boycott Netherlands darts events after booing | Darts | The Guardian
description: Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam
Content: Luke Littler celebrates at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam, where he faced a hostile reception this weekend.Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuke Littler celebrates at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam, where he faced a hostile reception this weekend.Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty ImagesDartsLuke Littler threatens to boycott Netherlands darts events after booingWorld No 1 jeered in Amsterdam defeat to Jonny ClaytonRoss Smith beats Price to win World Series of Darts FinalsPress AssociationSun 20 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. Littler lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals, with Ross Smith going on to win the event.The back-to-back world champion faced a hostile environment during his win against the home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday and it escalated on Saturday night as the referee had to intervene in the last-16 win against Nathan Aspinall.‘It was very hurtful’: darts cult hero Stephen Bunting on death threats, social media – and the new Luke LittlersRead moreLittler has taken a stance against volatile crowds before, refusing to travel to European Tour events in Germany as a result of his treatment from fans there. He is “100%” prepared to do the same in the Netherlands.“With the Germans, I haven’t been for a long time, we will have to see in Dortmund whether it changes or stays the same,” Littler told OnlineDarts. “If the Dutch stay like this, then I’m not going to do any Euro tours over there.”“There’s just no point in me travelling, wasting my time whilst I’m getting booed. I just want to play my darts, obviously sign autographs,” the world No 1 added. “The past two nights, I’ve done nothing, I’ve just walked off stage without thanking anybody. There’s no point thanking everyone when they are booing me.”Despite the bearpit atmosphere, Littler came out on top in a last‑leg decider with Aspinall but was defeated 10-4 by Clayton in their quarter-final on Sunday to end the 19-year-old’s hopes of becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year, having triumphed in the first five.After a competitive start, Clayton levelled at 3-3 with a 136 checkout and he soon took charge of the contest, completing his victory with a checkout of 40 to set up a semi-final tie with fellow Welshman Gerwyn Price.Price went on to beat Clayton 11-7 and followed up with a 10-7 semi-final victory over James Wade to set up a final against Smith, who had claimed a 11-8 win over Gian van Veen in the other final-four tie.Initially little could separate Price and Smith during the final but with the score locked at 5-5, Smith suddenly took control, winning the next six straight legs and finishing with an average of 103.89.Smith’s 11-5 win over Price in the final secured a maiden World Series of Darts Finals crown for the Englishman. Victory also sealed a second major PDC title for “Smudger”, and his first since the European Championship in 2022.His path to the final saw him beat Josh Rock 10-7 in the quarter-finals to set up that meeting with Van Veen, who had recovered from trailing 8-6 to claim a 10-8 win over Dirk van Duijvenbode in the last eight.Explore more on these topicsDartsLuke LittlernewsShareReuse this content

title: Patten and Skupski take Great Britain past Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Final 8 | Davis Cup | The Guardian
description: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won their doubles match in straight sets to put Great Britain into the Final 8 in Bologna in November
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won their doubles match in straight sets to put Great Britain into the Final 8 in Bologna in November
Content: Henry Patten (right) and Neal Skupski celebrate with their captain, Leon Smith (centre), after sealing the 3-0 win.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenHenry Patten (right) and Neal Skupski celebrate with their captain, Leon Smith (centre), after sealing the 3-0 win.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersDavis CupPatten and Skupski take Great Britain past Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Final 8GB pair win doubles match in straight setsFinals to be played in Bologna in NovemberTumaini Carayolat the Copper BoxSun 20 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew people across London enjoyed a more soothing night’s sleep than Leon Smith on Saturday. After an ideal first day for his team in theirDavis Cupqualifier against Ecuador, where his singles players handled business efficiently, the Great Britain captain had the luxury of calling upon one member of each of the two best doubles pairs in the world to close out the tie.In just their second match as partners rather than rivals the world No 1, Henry Patten, and Neal Skupski, the US Open champion a week ago, played their roles to perfection as they convincingly sealed their place in the Davis Cup Final 8 with a clinical 6-3, 6-4 victory against Gonzalo Escobar and Diego Hidalgo, securing for Great Britain an unassailable 3-0 lead. Harry Wendelken, the British No 7, closed out the tie with a 6-2, 6-3 win against Angel Veliz in the dead rubber.GB take command of Ecuador Davis Cup tie on Arthur Fery’s London returnRead moreThe British team will next head to Bologna for the quarter-final knockout stage of the competition, which takes place between 24 and 29 November in the final week of the tennis season, for the first time since 2023. Their success in east London was dictated by wins on Saturday byArthur Fery, the British No 1, and the No 5, Toby Samuel, who overcame tense starts before settling down and easing to victory.“There’s obviously a lot of tennis to be played before [the Davis Cup Finals], but it’s really a great thing to look forward to,” Smith said. “I’m really pleased how each of the players have gone about things in different ways yesterday and today. I think starting today, it’s a real privilege to have Henry and Neil at the top of the game. And just like we talked about in the singles, upsets happen, but they didn’t let it happen. The way they prepare, their quality, their competitiveness. I thought they were excellent.”Smith had warned on Saturday evening that there would probably be few breaks in the doubles match because of the fast indoor conditions inside the Copper Box. It was a source of great pleasure, then, when Patten and Skupski burst into the match with a brilliant opening return game, immediately breaking serve with no fewer than three lob winners, including a particularly sweet backhand from Skupski on break point.The British pair did not face a break point in the match, finally breaking serve at 4-4 in the second set from a brilliant forehand return winner by Skupski. “Very happy to play with Henry,” Skupski said, smiling. “It’s a privilege to play with the world No 1.”Patten responded to the compliment by rolling his eyes, drawing laughter from Skupski and Smith: “It’s a privilege for me to play with the US Open champion as well. Former world No 1.”This has been a good weekend for the Davis Cup, with ties around the world attracting strong crowds and great atmospheres, including the sold-out Copper Box. This was undoubtedly a great draw for the British team – in the best tie of the weekend, the USA team were toppled 3-2 by an excellent Czech squad before 13,000 fans each day in Prague, while France fell against Canada in front of 10,000 Québecois fans led by Félix Auger-Aliassime – but this is still a good result.It is also a good reflection of the Great Britain team’s overall depth, with five British players now inside the singles top 100. They were still able to succeed in the absence of their two most successful active singles players. While Jack Draper has been sidelined for an extended period, Cameron Norrie could only passionately cheer on from the sidelines during the past week after he was forced to withdraw at the last minute because of injury.The draw for the final eight will be made on Tuesday. With Germany, Austria, South Korea, Czechia, Canada and the home nation Italy all qualified, and Spain likely to take the final spot, Britain’s next opponent will probably present a far greater challenge. “If everyone’s fit and healthy, we’re going to have some difficult choices to make as well,” Smith said. “But it’ll be tough.“You’ve seen the players that have played this weekend for the [other] nations and others will, I presume, come in, whether that’s [Jannik] Sinner or [Carlos] Alcaraz, if they make it. So it’s going to be tough, but that’s exactly why you want to be in the final eight. You want that excitement.”Explore more on these topicsDavis CupArthur FeryTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nashville clinch playoffs, Philadelphia wins after going down 0-3: MLS roundup | MLS | The Guardian
description: The Union scored four goals in nine minutes in 4-3 win, while Caden Clark helped Seattle to a late draw
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Union scored four goals in nine minutes in 4-3 win, while Caden Clark helped Seattle to a late draw
Content: Sam Surridge and Hany Mukhtar scored for Nashville, who currently lead the Shield race.Photograph: Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSam Surridge and Hany Mukhtar scored for Nashville, who currently lead the Shield race.Photograph: Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty ImagesMLSNashville clinch playoffs, Philadelphia wins after going down 0-3: MLS roundupUnion score four goals in nine minutes v Sporting KCCaden Clark helps Sounders to late drawAgenciesSun 20 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Surridge scored in the first half and Brian Schwake finished off his league-leading 12th clean sheet of the season asNashville SCclinched a playoff spot and remained unbeaten at home with a 3-0 victory over the Chicago Fire on Saturday night.Eastern Conference-leading Nashville lead the Supporters’ Shield race and are the only team in the league unbeaten at home with 12 wins in 13.Surridge staked Nashville to a 1-0 lead in the 33rd minute and it stood through half-time. Cristian Espinoza added an insurance goal in the 78th minute and Hany Mukhtar scored in the 87th to set the final margin.It was the 16th goal of the campaign for Surridge, the fourth for Espinoza and the 11th for Mukhtar as the whole frontline for Nashville found the net.Schwake, a 25-year-old first-year starter, notched one save and has surrendered only 21 goals through 26 starts.Epic Sporting KC collapse gives Philadelphia Union a 4-3 comeback victoryBruno Damiani, teenager Cavan Sullivan and Milan Iloski all scored over a five-minute span of the second half for Philadelphia, and the Union used an own goal to beatSporting Kansas City4-3 on Saturday night and extend their unbeaten streak to 11 with a fifth straight victory.Philadelphia are the fifth team inMLShistory to win a match after trailing by three goals. Orlando City pulled off the feat earlier this season in a 4-3 victory over Inter Miami.Watching Cavan Sullivan, excitement is tempered by memories of hypetrains pastRead moreSporting KC’s André Luiz scored in the fifth minute and again five minutes later to give the home side a 2-0 lead. Defender Wyatt Meyer used his head to score his first career goal in the 16th minute for a 3-0 advantage that stood through half-time.Damiani started the Union rally in the 64th minute with his career-high eighth goal in his second season. Sullivan, 16, cut it to 3-2 two minutes later with his seventh goal – using assists from Danley Jean Jacques and older brother Quinn Sullivan. Cavan Sullivan also has 12 assists this season after not contributing to a goal through his first 14 appearances after debuting in 2024.Iloski scored his career-best 13th goal in his first full season with the Union – unassisted in the 68th minute to tie it 3-3. Philadelphia got some help on an own goal by Zorhan Bassong in the 73rd minute to complete the comeback.The Union have scored 14 goals in their last three matches after posting back-to-back 5-0 victories over FC Cincinnati and San Diego FC. They haven’t lost since a 6-4 road loss to Inter Miami that left last in the Eastern Conference at the end of May.Caden Clark makes instant impact as Sounders come back to draw RapidsCaden Clark subbed on in the 83rd minute and scored in the third minute of stoppage time for the Seattle Sounders in a 3-3 draw with the Colorado Rapids on Saturday night.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCristian Roldan scored his first goal since 18 April in the 49th minute and Dejan Joveljić added a goal in the 79th for Seattle.The Sounders are winless in 13 straight but unbeaten in their last five.Morgan Whittaker scored his first two MLS goals and Donavan Phillip also scored his first career goal for Colorado.Clark, near the top of the penalty arc, skipped a shot past diving goalkeeper Nico Hansen and inside the left post for his first goal since 2024 for Montreal. Clark, a 23-year-old midfielder, was acquired on 1 September in a trade with DC United.Marco Reus the key in LA Galaxy’s win over Minnesota UnitedMarco Reus had a goal and an assist, João Klauss and Pablo Ruiz also scored a goal, and the LA Galaxy beat Minnesota United 3-2 on Saturday night.Minnesota have lost four straight and are winless in their last five.Reus played a free kick from near the left end line to the near post, where Klauss flicked a header inside the back post into the side-net in the 76th minute, then redirected a cross played into the area by Lucas Calegari into the net to give the Galaxy a 3-2 lead in the 80th.Marcus Caldeira scored in the 23rd minute and Kelvin Yeboah converted from the penalty spot to give Minnesota a 2-1 lead in the 30th minute. Yeboah has scored in three consecutive games and has six of his 14 goals this season in the past six matches.Ruiz, acquired on 3 September from Real Salt Lake in exchange for $400,000 in 2027 general allocation money, scored his first goal since 2023 to give LA a 1-0 lead in the 12th minute.Explore more on these topicsMLSSporting Kansas CityNashville SCUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: More Australians to live into their 90s as life expectancy forecast to rise over coming decades  | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Treasury’s latest intergenerational report projects life expectancy at birth will reach 89 for women and 86 for men by 2066
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: Treasury’s latest intergenerational report projects life expectancy at birth will reach 89 for women and 86 for men by 2066
Content: Australia’s population is expected to be slightly lower by the mid-2060s than forecast in the previous intergenerational report.Photograph: Lisa Maree Williams/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s population is expected to be slightly lower by the mid-2060s than forecast in the previous intergenerational report.Photograph: Lisa Maree Williams/Getty ImagesAustralia newsMore Australians to live into their 90s as life expectancy forecast to rise over coming decadesTreasury’s latest intergenerational report projects life expectancy at birth will reach 89 for women and 86 for men by 2066Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated Press andSarah Basford CanalesSun 20 Sep 2026 00.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 00.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian households will shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the latest update to forecasts of the country’s long-term future.Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, to be published in full on Monday, will project the impact of government policies 40 years into the future.An extract released on Sunday showed life expectancy at birth was forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2065/66, up from about 86 years at present.The report will also reveal that artificial intelligence (AI) will become the “defining influence” on the economy over the next four decades, as the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, warned it would come with “very substantial risks”.Life expectancy for men was predicted to rise to 86 years in the next four decades, up from 82 years.Australia’s universal healthcare system and the impact of medical research were the key drivers of rising life expectancy, Chalmers said.The report laid out the case for further investments in Medicare, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme and the recent rollout of urgent care clinics, he said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut a growing and ageing population would also be at the centre of long-term budget pressures, Chalmers told News24’s Sunday Agenda program.“There are elements of the intergenerational report which are confronting, but it’s not a pessimistic report … because Australians are genuinely better placed and better prepared for all of this accelerating change that we are seeing,” he said.Australia’s population is expected to be slightly lower by the mid-2060s than forecast in the previous intergenerational report, released in 2023.Population growth was expected to slow to 0.9% a year over the next four decades, down from 1.4% annually in the previous 40 years, according to Treasury forecasts.The nation’s population was predicted to reach 39.3 million by 2065/66, 1.8 million lower than the 2023 forecast.Much of the slowdown in population growth was tied to lower fertility rates as women continued to have fewer children.“Almost half the decline in fertility rates is actually because fewer people are having three or more kids and what that reflects is mums having fewer kids later in life,” Chalmers said.“Our job is to make it a little bit easier for people to make that choice if they want to,” he said, noting Labor’s policies to subsidise childcare, increase paid parental leave and lift mandatory superannuation contributions.Future government debt is expected to be slashed by half a trillion dollars compared to forecasts in the 2023 report, but much of the economic progress relies on emerging technologies such as AI.“Overwhelmingly, the fiscal story is a little bit better; but still, lots, lots more work to do to manage some of these pressures and risks,” Chalmers said.Previous Treasury advice suggested AI could provide significant productivity gains across the public and private sectors if the nation kept pace with the global shift towards the technology.In a press conference on Sunday, Chalmers said AI would play a central role in Australia’s future but the government would work to “minimise the very substantial risks”.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is visiting the United States this week to discuss a “global framework” for the rollout of AI, urging the “big two giants” – the US and China – to work in the interest of humanity.“We want to see cooperation. We’ve seen that in the past with new technologies, even on nuclear weapons, for example, we saw agreements and protocols put in place through the nuclear non-proliferation treaty,” Albanese told ABC’s Insiders on Sunday.“So I think we want to see progress between those two countries, but … I think middle powers such as Australia have a role to play here as well.”The US president, Donald Trump, said he would appointan AI tsarovernight and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan.Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsAustralian politicsHealthAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Reαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attack | Scams | The Guardian
description: Scam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs such as miсrosoft.com
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Scam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs such as miсrosoft.com
Content: Many scams have near-identical URLs but a closer look reveals a cyrillic letter, which offers a world of difference between legit and scam.Photograph: Kirill Ivanov/AlamyView image in fullscreenMany scams have near-identical URLs but a closer look reveals a cyrillic letter, which offers a world of difference between legit and scam.Photograph: Kirill Ivanov/AlamyScam watchScamsReαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attackScam emails are increasingly using psychological tricks, such as using near-identical URLs like miсrosoft.comHilary OsborneSun 20 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve read the email carefully and it looks legitimate. The link it asks you to click on has none of the usual red flags: there are no weird numbers or extra parts to the URL. You feel safe to proceed.But if you had looked slightly closer you may have noticed something slightly wrong with one of the characters. Just as in the headline of this piece where instead of “a” we used the Cyrillic “α”.Fraudsters can use letters from different alphabets to create URLs and email addresses that look almost identical to the real thing, but in reality send anyone who clicks on them to a spoof website or inbox. From there they can harvest personal details to use in their scams.There are other letters and symbols that are easily switched. Last year tech experts spotted fraudsters usingthe Japanese hiragana character んto look like a / in an address designed to look as though it was on Booking.com’s website.Jake Moore, global security adviser at cybersecurity company ESET, says the fraudsters “love Microsoft” as a company identity to spoof. “A fake site might use the Cyrillic “с” instead of the Latin “c” (miсrosoft v microsoft),” he says.View image in fullscreenMost phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAMoore says this type of fraud – known as a homoglyph attack – is becoming increasingly popular. A homoglyph is a character that looks very similar, or even identical, to another one.“Most phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments. Attachments can easily be scanned and caught by security software if malicious,” he says.“Therefore, criminals need to design their websites where the links look genuine and casually request people to click on them without thinking.”Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, says homoglyph attacks “are really more of a psychological trick than a technical one”, because the fraudsters are typically trying to panic you into responding quickly, rather than taking time to check things out.“The goal is to create a sense of panic so you don’t look too closely at the URL. They’re betting that when we’re in a rush, our brains see what we expect to see,” Briedis says.double quotation markIt just goes to show that the split-second decision you make when clicking a link is often the most vulnerable part of the whole security chain.”What it looks likeThe real thing. Until you look closely.You will receive an email or text message suggesting you need to click on a URL or email to sort something out.View image in fullscreenIf you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.Photograph: Sergey Tolmachev/AlamySome fonts make substitutions almost impossible to detect. In an email address given in comic sans , for example, the Cyrillic a does not look at all out of place.“We’ve spent years telling people to check the website before trusting it but the problem with this technique is that you can do exactly that and still be fooled as it can look as it should,” says Moore.If it’s a URL, Moore says typically it will lead to a site that encourages you to enter your credentials for the real site, including your username, password and even a one-time passcode.What to doIf you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.“If any text, WhatsApp or email is asking you to log in anywhere, it is vital that you independently visit the genuine website rather than trusting the link in front of you to save a few seconds,” says Moore.And apply the same thinking to email addresses. Type in the address you know to be correct, rather than clicking on a link.Keep your browser updated. It will flag up suspicious websites, and by keeping it updated it will catch the criminals’ latest workarounds.Put in place two-factor authentication, or multifactor authentication (2FA or MFA), which means you have two steps to log into a site.If you find that your details have been compromised, change your passwords immediately. Contact your bank and report the phishing attack to Report Fraud.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchCybercrimeConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can Trump and Xi cooperate to guide humanity through the AI revolution? Humanity might depend on it | Alan Finkel | The Guardian
description: The CEOs of tech firms issue stark warnings over the rate of change, with AI capability doubling every four months
Author: Alan Finkel
Headline: The CEOs of tech firms issue stark warnings over the rate of change, with AI capability doubling every four months
Content: ‘Imagine if  Trump and Xi could agree that for the sake of the human race, the US and China will collaborate on an international agreement to regulate the AI industry.’Photograph: Kenny Holston/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Imagine if  Trump and Xi could agree that for the sake of the human race, the US and China will collaborate on an international agreement to regulate the AI industry.’Photograph: Kenny Holston/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Can Trump and Xi cooperate to guide humanity through the AI revolution? Humanity might depend on itAlan FinkelThe CEOs of tech firms issue stark warnings over the rate of change, with AI capability doubling every four monthsSun 20 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.45 EDTShareRecently, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic,quit his jobover concerns that AI was on a collision course with humanity. A flurry of headlines put the spotlight on the current crisis: unregulated competition between technology companies and between the US and China is putting our global infrastructure at risk at the very least, and threatening human existence at worst.One’s mind fills with pictures of robot armies or systematic blackmail.In the spirit of never letting a good crisis go to waste, an important opportunity will come with the summit this week between the US president,Donald Trump, and China’s president, Xi Jinping.AI is everywhere. It is powerful, helping us as individuals to plan our travel, book our gym classes and order takeaway food, while at the institutional level it is boosting the efficiency of businesses and bureaucracies. In academia it is providing stunning breakthroughs in mathematics that have eluded the best theoretical mathematicians for decades. In the sense that AI is widely available and can do a lot of good, it is like medicines, electricity and road vehicles. But unlike these technologies, we have not yet worked out how to ensure that the benefits of AI outweigh the risks.I used to think AI would kill us all, until the techbro CEOs said AI will kill us all and now I’m not so sure | First Dog on the MoonRead moreIn contemplating the way forward, it is worth thinking about how much time we have, or don’t have, to get it right. Technology development used to be slow. The first use of stone tools began 3.4m years ago and barely changed for the next 2m years.Leap forward. Computer chips have been doubling their capacity every two years from 1965 to the present. That is fast, but slow compared with AI development. According to the METR research institute, generative AI capability doubled every seven months from 2020 to 2024. Since then, generative AI capability has been doubling every four months, and with the recent release of ChatGPT 6-Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, the doubling rate is most likely even faster.Just a few days after Coxon’s resignation, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei,expressed the same concerns, and called for a slowdown of AI development. He wasquickly backedby OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, and xAI’s CEO, Elon Musk.In defence of unregulated AI development, Trump dismissed their concerns, saying that statements to the effect that AI might destroy or massively harm humanity are a hoax and that calls to slow down AI development are a plot that will benefit China. He denied the need for AI guardrails, saying that all that is needed is a “strong and smart (high IQ!) president, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”So, what to do? Governments could wait it out. If they do, something serious will happen. With luck, it will be bad enough to shock governments and industry into action, but not so bad that it has catastrophic consequences. It could be a power blackout across one or more states, bank withdrawals blocked for a week, or a deliberate overload of the global internet so that information flows grind to a halt.Labor accused of throwing creatives ‘under the bus’ with proposal to ease copyright protections for AI giantsRead moreMuch better than waiting for one of these wake-up calls would be to get on the front foot. Some of the frontier AI companies are trying to do that. Anthropic’s aptly named “constitution” tries to enforce ethical behaviour of its AI models. The trouble is that it suffers from ever increasing complexity. When it was publicly announced in 2023, the Anthropic constitution was a 2,700-word document; the current version contains 23,000 words. It is inevitable that much of it will be subject to interpretation, by the AI and by the humans who train it. Indeed, Anthropicdisclosed in Julythat despite its constitution, its Claude agents broke out of a test environment and attacked three external organisations.My preferred approach to guardrails is to keep them simple, deeply fundamental and aligned to human values. Indeed, I have proposedthree laws of AIthat in the ideal world would be built into the innermost circle of code of every foundational AI model to ensure that foundational AI and its derivatives will not harm or deceive human beings, and will behave lawfully and ethically.Neither theAnthropicapproach to implementing guardrails through a constitution nor my approach to implementing guardrails through fundamental rules will have a chance of being universally effective unless governments step up and make either or both approaches a strict requirement. The prospect of the AI industry as a whole doing so is not realistic. The track record of self-regulation by industry is patchy, thus it is not a sensible option for an industry in which the operational risks could be cataclysmic.Something needs to be done, and it needs to be done very soon. We’ve been here before. Last century, we faced the prospect of mutually assured destruction from the nuclear arms race. The two nuclear superpowers – the US and the former Soviet Union – agreed on treaties to cap and ultimately reduce the number of nuclear weapons. In the case of AI, the two countries that now lead AI development must take the lead in avoiding possible threats to humanity.An ideal opportunity is the state visit this week of Xi to meet Trump. Imagine if both could agree that for the sake of the human race, the US and China will collaborate to implement an international agreement to regulate the AI industry.If AI poses even a fraction of the risk that leaders in the sector are describing, we are well past the point where the existing hands-off attitude can be justified versus the approach we take in every other sector to keep humanity safe.I look to president Trump and president Xi to step up and show the requisite leadership to ensure that AI will serve humanity rather than destroy it.Alan Finkel AC is founder and executive chair of Proudly Human. He was formerly Australia’s chief scientist, the chancellor of Monash University, president of the Australian Academy of Engineering, founder of Stile Education and founder of Axon Instruments. He was the co-founder of science magazine Cosmos and is the author of Getting to Zero (2021) and Powering Up (2023). AI had no role in drafting, writing or editing this pieceExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSam AltmanOpenAIAnthropicComputingDonald TrumpXi JinpingcommentShareReuse this content

title: In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Donald Trump addresses the 80th United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York, 23 September 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump addresses the 80th United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York, 23 September 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOpinionUnited NationsIn a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it?Steve BloomfieldAs the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lackingSun 20 Sep 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTShareIf all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of theUnited Nationsheadquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry hasaccused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out byDonald Trump’s Board of Peace. The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.All of this is happening in a world in which the very principles of the UN – multilateralism, a rules-based order and international law – are under threat.Secretary-general elections have rarely been this consequential and conversations about who should win will dominate the sidelines of the UN general assembly this week and next, as world leaders gatherfor the annual summit.The UN, and the world it speaks for, desperately needs a new leader who is both charismatic and competent. Yet the five permanent members of the security council – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – hold a veto. Anyone who wants the job will need the approval of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and, most importantly, Trump.It is not easy to argue you are best placed to save the UN when the man you need to persuade would rather it fails.Three informal straw polls have taken place so far and no frontrunner has emerged, indeed opposition to the two leading candidates rosein last Friday’s vote. For the first time in the organisation’s 80-year history serious discussions are quietly taking place about what would happen if no secretary-general is chosen at all.Ten years ago,the election of António Guterresof Portugal was widely welcomed as a shot in the arm for the UN after a decade of the low-energy leadership of theSouth Korean Ban Ki-moon. In his previous role as the UN’s refugee chief he had been an outspoken activist and had pledged to continue speaking up for the world’s most vulnerable people. Then, a month later, Trump took office as the US president.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump with António Guterres at the 80th United Nations general assembly in New York, September 2025.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersEarlier this year, he announced the US’s withdrawal from 31 UN organisations, including the bodies responsible for dealing with climate change and women’s health, while in July his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the administration’s desire to “dismantle” the international criminal court “brick by brick”. The abrupt closure of the US’s aid and development programme, USAID,led to deaths around the world.Most controversially, the establishment of Trump’s Board of Peace sparked fears that it could be used to supplant the UN itself. The UN meanwhile is in the grip of a financial crisis, with Guterres warning during the summer thatit faced “imminent financial collapse”due to unpaid dues, much of it owed by the US.And yet, despite everything, the UN is still standing – and still matters. It is only the UN, through its Framework Convention on Climate Change, that manages to focus international attention on the greatest crisis the world is facing. Despite dramatic cuts in funding, there are still 11 peacekeeping missions staffed by more than 50,000 personnel in some of the most dangerous parts of the world. The UN’s office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs remains the best hope for negotiating access to deliver aid in war zones, including Sudan.This year the general assembly passed two landmark resolutions: one recognising the transatlantic slave trade as a crime, another to adopt a new world map that correctly recognises Africa’s size.We don’t know what the candidates think of these decisions, nor do we know where they stand on the war in Ukraine or what their stance is on Israel’s actions in Gaza. Despite the election’s importance – and despite the relatively recent transparency of “vision statements” and hustings – the candidates’ campaigns have been overwhelmingly cautious.Part of the reason, of course, is that someone standing on an ambitious platform would stand no chance of getting the job.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUN experts believe there is a chance that the two current frontrunners, Guyana’s former foreign ministerCarolyn Rodrigues-Birkettand Costa Rica’s ex vice-presidentRebeca Grynspan, might become good secretary-generals. But no one is blown away by the choice on offer.For Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband, both of whom will be in New Yorkthis weekat the UN general assembly, there is a choice to be made. The UK is yet to express a preference, indeed the UK team at the UN is said to be unimpressed with all the candidates. So far, it’s understood, they have not voted in favour of anyone in the first three straw polls. The UK and France are both hoping another candidate will emerge.Whether they will be any better is an open question. The New York Postreported in Julythat Trump wanted Fifa president Gianni Infantino to get the job. There is next to no chance that would happen, but European diplomats fear a Trump-backed dark horse – possibly one without a diplomatic background – may emerge in the coming weeks. This is, after all, the man who has outsourced his nation’s diplomacy to his son-in-law and a real estate investor. So far, Trump has said nothing in public, although that may change on Tuesday when he gives his speech at the general assembly. Or a social media post spat out at two in the morning could upend the race entirely.The chances of the “Permanent Five” failing to agree on a name remain slim, but plans are already being drawn up in case the worst happens. Guterres may be asked to stay on, while another possibility is that a collection of senior UN officials is asked to serve in administrative roles until a candidate is found. Either way, it would leave the UN rudderless at a time it needs to be anything but.No one is getting this job without Trump’s say so. But once the new general secretary is in office, the US president will have less sway on their actions. They will potentially serve for 10 years, eight of which will be without Trump in the White House.But even without Trump, this will be an almost impossible job. The UN’s financial crisis is not going away. Severe cuts are coming. There will be no easy return to the 1990s and early 2000s, when the UN was at the heart of world events. A new leader will need to reinvent multilateralism in a world where it’s going out of favour.Depending on the choice they make, we could look back at this decision as the moment that the crumbling international rules-based order began to be rebuilt – or when it slid irretrievably into irrelevance.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prizeExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionHuman rightsHumanitarian responseDonald TrumpInternational lawcommentShareReuse this content

title: Star Trek is turning 60 – and the vision it promised feels more distant than ever | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the future
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the future
Content: ‘Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be bad now, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be bad now, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionStar TrekStar Trek is turning 60 – and the vision it promised feels more distant than everDave SchillingThe US’s deployment of weaponry in space marks the latest backward step from the show’s optimistic conception of the futureSun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTShareWho among us doesn’t dream of space in their youth?OK, maybe some of us. Like the ones with lives. While you were out playing hopscotch with little Jimmy and Susie, I was locked in my room mainlining episodes of Star Trek or theweird, sanitized version of Aliensthat aired on broadcast TV. Fantastical science-fiction adventure seemed to offer more than playground games and actual human connection. Spaceships over relationships.Star Trek, celebrating its 60th anniversary this month, offered a utopian vision of the future. Highly competent scientists traveling the galaxy solving moral and ethical quandaries with grace and intelligence. It was a vision of Earth that had overcome greed and selfishness to pursue a more peaceful world Kirk and Spock. Picard and Data. These were characters that were ethical, witty and heroic. Better that than little Jimmy burning ants with a magnifying glass.The Alien franchise, on the other hand, was the complete opposite. In the second film, Aliens, which coincidentally is turning 40 this year, the characters are mostly brain-dead killing-machine soldiers and venal corporate stooges. This one sounds a bit more familiar, doesn’t it? The entire known universe is controlled by a diabolical company whose only aim is profit at the expense of the average person. Both Star Trek and the Alien films offered the requisite thrills and whiz-bang action to titillate a young boy like myself back in the 1990s, but they were also diametrically opposed visions of what the world might look like when I became an adult. Would it be along the lines of alush beige carpet and colorful pajamasor asoaking wet murder machine covered in KY Jellygrinding the working class into the ground? It took a few decades, but I think I found my answer.US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in spaceRead moreThe US air force announced on Monday that it haddeployed weapons into space, thumbing its nose at the unwritten rule that space is for peace, not for war. The US rationale is,well, everyone else is doing it!Officials point to the increased militarization of space, including a 2024 Biden administration report claiming Russia wasdeveloping the capability to detonate nuclear weapons in spaceto disable or destroy orbiting satellites, which are crucial pieces of global infrastructure.The air force secretary, Troy Meink,referred to the deploymentas “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action”. He wouldn’t say what they were, what they could actually do, or even what they look like. Which is always so comforting when futuristic space guns are involved. Is it a giant laser beam? Missiles? A claw that can grab satellites out of the sky? A large hammer? A Trump-shaped robot gollum that could swallow the International Space Station with the ease and gusto of the real person chowing down on a Big Mac? My imagination, stoked by years of sci-fi television, is running rampant. At the very least, I hope it has a series of blinking lights all over it. And an off-switch.Back in the 1980s, when Star Trek was at its creative peak, the idea of weaponizing space was considered such a joke that President Reagan struggled to amass a consensus around hisStrategic Defense Initiative(derisively nicknamed “Star Wars”), which would have created a US orbiting missile deterrent. But now, Donald Trump is making fantasy space battles a key element of his rapidly deteriorating legacy. The US space force, his absurd brainchild,presented new uniformsthat look like they wereleftover from a Paul Verhoeven movie. If one wants to conquer a lifeless galaxy full of dirt, rocks and little else, one must be wearing the shiniest black boots possible. Also a hat.The space force uniforms are certainly lightyears away from the ones on Star Trek, where everyone wears bright colors that immediately make the viewer think they’ve accidentally stumbled onto a rather unique discotheque. The Star Trek creator, Gene Roddenberry, made sure that the phaser weapons depicted on the show had a non-lethal stun setting. I think if anyone proposed a non-lethal weapon for the US space force, they’d be A) fired immediately and B) called woke to their face (and on Fox News in front of millions of people).Looking back six decades at the world Star Trek was born in, there was optimism in the world, mixed in with the chaos of political assassinations, riots, a war in Vietnam, and the ever-present threat of nuclear annihilation. The idea of going to space and landing Apollo 11 on the Moon was inspiring to a world that needed more cheering up thanEd Sheeran trying to find an opening act for his tour. Star Trek posited that life on Earth might be badnow, but fear not, the good guys would win in the end. Humanity would overcome itself.Countless modern scientific achievements – cellphones, tablets, the internet, medical advancements – can be attributed to Star Trek beaming ideas of benevolent futurism into homes around the globe for 60 years. But did society actually learn anything from Star Trek? The Federation and the Klingons made peace in the film Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, but could their real-world analogues – the United States and Russia – be any further apart? Of course, if you know anything about the future-history depicted on Star Trek, you know utopia doesn’t occur until after a global nuclear holocaust, in case you want to be even more depressed today.Star Trek’s impact is immense, especially for a TV show that only lasted for three years and often deployed styrofoam rocks, wobbly models, and dodgy rubber aliens in its design. That impact is a testament to the writing, acting, and film technique that grabbed millions of people and changed their lives. But I’ve never been more pessimistic about humanity achieving the beautiful dream of Gene Roddenberry. With every fascist-looking spacesuit or space laser, I feel like we’re progressing backwards, step by step. Given the proliferation of pandemics, climate change, species extinction, and contaminated food supplies, I’m more apt to wake up expecting to have anHR Giger-inspired genetic abominationgnawing at my face. At least my years staring at my TV screen alone prepared me for what’s to come.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsStar TrekOpinionUS militaryUS televisionTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Hungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating together | Shadi Khan Saif | The Guardian
description: Mealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade stories
Author: Shadi Khan Saif
Headline: Mealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade stories
Content: ‘Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesMaking sense of itReligionHungry for connection? This is what we lose when we stop eating togetherShadi Khan SaifMealtimes offer a pause in the day for parents and children to sit together, listen to one another and trade storiesMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.46 EDTShareWhen I was growing up in a Muslim household, food was rarely just food. As the youngest child, my job was to bring out a large water jug with a matching basin pot and soap to help the family wash their hands. Mum would distribute freshly baked breads to everyone to have with the soup or curry. Dad would have me sit next to him as he presided over the gathering – asking questions, giving directions all the while passing food and utensils around. My older brother would take turns helping everyone wash their hands.There was even a small ritual around something as ordinary as a piece of bread. If it fell on the ground anywhere in the house or was even seen on the ground outside, we would pick it up, clean it, kiss it respectfully and place it somewhere clean and safe.Foodwas not to be treated carelessly.And sending a guest away without offering them a meal is unthinkable – almost a sin.As a child, I didn’t think of any of this as “spirituality”. It was simply what you did. Eating alone felt like punishment. It still does.Only later, after leaving Afghanistan and building a life in Australia, did I begin to understand what those ordinary habits carried with them: gratitude, hospitality and a sense that food was something to be celebrated – and shared.Islamis hardly alone in this.Make yourselves at home: the meaning of hospitality in a divided worldRead moreInJudaism, the Shabbat meal brings families together around food, prayer, conversation and ritual. Christianity has the shared meal at the centre of one of its most powerful religious symbols, while the Gospels repeatedly depict Jesus eating with others, including people considered outsiders.Across Hindu traditions, food is associated with gratitude, hospitality and community. In Sikhism, thetradition oflangarmakes the social meaning of eating together particularly explicit. People sit together and share a free meal regardless of wealth, status or social position. Everyone is fed. Just as importantly, everyone eats together.The traditions are different, of course. But across them runs a familiar idea: food can bring people together in ways that go well beyond satisfying hunger.During a fieldwork assignment, a group of strangers and I were thrust together for an orientation meeting over lunch.Nerves stopped everyone from taking the first bite. So our team leader smiled and said: “Buon appetito.” I replied with the Afghan equivalent: “Ishteha-e-khoob” – enjoy your meal.Halfway through eating, our team leader suddenly apologised for his habit of eating quickly. He explained that he had grown up as the youngest of nine children in a poor Italian family, where you learned early to eat before the food ran out.Others began opening up and telling their own stories about food.For some, family meals were about far more than what was on the plate. They created a pause in the day when parents and children sat together, listened to one another and traded stories. In an era before smartphones, and when many families turned the television off at dinner, the table was the centre of family life.I left that lunch thinking about how much can be contained in something as simple as sitting down to eat.These days, more often than not, I find myself eating lunch on the go – in my car, on a Teams meeting or while scrolling on my phone. Once, amid community engagement work and endless spreadsheets and trackers, I forgot that I had left my lunchbox in the car.That’s modern life, I suppose.Food is easily reduced to fuel: something we need to get through the day before moving on to the next task. We don’t always have the time to wait for others to join us. We don’t always ask whether someone has eaten.
