And yet we seem to spend an extraordinary amount of time looking at photographs of food online.Perhaps there is something slightly strange about that. We have never had so many pictures of beautifully presented meals yet so little time to sit down and enjoy our food with the people we love.Buon appetito. Ishteha-e-khoob!Explore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itIslamFoodFamilyJudaismSikhismHinduismcommentShareReuse this content

title: From Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers? | Rebecca Rideal | The Guardian
description: Another true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’, says historian and author Rebecca Rideal
Author: Rebecca Rideal
Headline: Another true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’, says historian and author Rebecca Rideal
Content: Ella Beatty as Lizzie Borden in the new Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenElla Beatty as Lizzie Borden in the new Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.Photograph: NetflixOpinionTV crime dramaFrom Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers?Rebecca RidealAnother true-crime drama about a woman accused of murder is hitting our screens, feeding into our culture’s unhelpful obsession with ‘female rage’Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.41 EDTShareOn 20 June 1893, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a packed courtroom waited with bated breath for the jury to return its verdict following a gruelling double-murder trial. Against a backdrop of intense media interest, they had heard the prosecution argue that the accused had hacked to death their own parents with a hatchet, had burned their clothing to hide evidence of blood, and had done so out of hatred. The question the jury was asked to answer was simple – was Lizzie Andrew Borden guilty of murdering her father and stepmother? Jurors took just one hour to reach a decision: not guilty.Yet, almost as soon as the trial came to an end, the mythmaking around Borden began – from fevered speculation about her motives and theinfamous nursery rhymeto the many film and TV retellings of the story. The latest incarnation, Netflix’sMonster: The Lizzie Borden Story, opens with an axe-wielding Borden committing the murders, and frames the crimes around a fictionalised queer romance between her and the family’s housemaid, Bridget Sullivan.Why, after 130 years, are we still enthralled by the Borden murders? Part of the answer, I think, speaks to a wider obsession with female killers (or alleged female killers in Borden’s case) and the way in which society ties itself in knots to try to explain, excuse or justify violent women. Statistically, globally and historically, homicide is a largely male crime – in terms of both perpetrators and victims. Female killers are rare: they representedjust 7%of convicted homicide suspects in England and Wales between 2019 and 2022. It is precisely this rarity that sees homicides with female perpetrators (or alleged perpetrators) disproportionately sensationalised, mythologised and forced into recognisable tropes – the femme fatale, the wrongfully accused, the passive victim or the monstrosity.That is not to say there isn’t some truth in each of these ideas.But very often a female perpetrator of a violent crime will also trigger or become the face of wider societal debates about crime, punishment, justice and womanhood. History is littered with examples.The execution of Marie Manning in 1849, alongside her husband, for the murder of her lover, Patrick O’Connor, was followed by tens of thousands of Londoners, includingCharles Dickens, and spawned close to 2.5m broadsheet sales. The shock of seeing a woman hanged triggered a nationwide debate about the ethics of public executions (they were abolished in Britain less than 20 years later). So notorious did Manning become that Madame Tussauds created a wax model of her, dressed in the black satin dress the killer supposedly wore at her execution.The statue remained in its chamber of horrors until 1971.View image in fullscreenCharlize Theron as the serial killer Aileen Wuornos in the 2003 film Monster.Photograph: Newmarket Films/AllstarSimilarly, the trial of the chocolate poisoner, Christiana Edmunds, forced Victorian society to confront the idea that a single middle-class woman could intentionally cause indiscriminate harm. When an attempted plea of insanity failed and she was found guilty of the murder of Sidney Barker and attempted murder of Mrs Beard, she was sentenced to death. But the home secretary stepped in, asked for her to be reassessed and granted her a reprieve. She spent the rest of her days at Broadmoor psychiatric hospital.As the historianJill Newton Ainsley attests, “Declaring her insane and therefore not responsible for her actions provided a bizarre and unprecedented crime with a relatively simple explanation.” This reluctance to acknowledge women’s agency when it comes to violent crime plays out in statistics too. Newton Ainsley has shown that between 1832 and 1901 women were twice as likely as men to be granted an acquittal on the grounds of insanity – even when charged with similar crimes.For very different reasons, the acquittal of Beatrice Pace in 1928 captured public attention. She had been accused of murdering her abusive husband by arsenic poisoning, only to become the poster girl for wronged women. Upon her acquittal, newspapers reported emotional scenes where “women clasped one another by the hands and some cried”. Hundreds of women later wrote to her expressing their well wishes for her future. A few decades later, in 1955, after shooting her abusive lover, David Blakely, five times with a revolver, there was no such sympathy for Ruth Ellis at her trial. She was found guilty of murder, but her subsequent execution shone a spotlight on theethics of capital punishment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLindsay Clancy’s case is a Rorschach test | Moira DoneganRead morePerhaps the most chilling manifestation of female violence in the 20th century comes in the person of the child killer Myra Hindley. Despite conducting the crimes alongside Ian Brady, the criminologistMark Pettigrew has notedthat the press coverage of Hindley, with the infamous mugshot, far exceeded that of Brady. Additionally, her unsuccessful parole attempts opened a wider debate about whether “life” should mean life. More recently, the case of the convicted murderer Lucy Letby has become deeply political with regard to whistleblowing, medical care and the role of expert witnesses.When it comes to this latest iteration of the Lizzie Borden story, the Netflix show appears to make a connection between Borden and 20th-century serial killer Aileen Wuornos, who received her own Hollywood treatment in a filmstarring Charlize Theron, also called Monster. This seems designed to, as the publicity materials state, tap into a “legacy of female rage” and provide an “exploration of why women kill”. From the opening episode, the show takes a highly sexualised and graphic approach to the story of the killings.Was Borden guilty? We may never know. What we do know is that there were four people in the Borden household on the morning of 4 August 1892: Andrew Borden, Abby Borden, Lizzie Borden and Bridget Sullivan. By lunchtime, Andrew and Abby were hacked to death; Abby’s body was abandoned face-down on a bedroom floor and Andrew’s lay on a blood-drenched sofa. The brutal reality is that this was a horrific crime – whether a result of “female rage” or not.Rebecca Rideal is a historian and the author of1666: Plague, War and Hellfire. She co-hosts the historical true-crime podcast seriesBuried Evidence, and writes on history, true crime and cultureDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTV crime dramaOpinionNetflixTrue crime (Podcasts)WomenDramacommentShareReuse this content

title: Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Nigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and change, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Nigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and change, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianOpinionLabourDon’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happenJohn HarrisNigel Farage’s tactics are to play up the anxiety and resentment that people feel. Labour’s job is simple: to offer hope and changeSun 20 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareDespite the energised startAndy Burnhamhas made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both theMetropolitan policeandparliament’s standards commissionermay worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and arereportedly already being spenton 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “national emergency” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’sfirst budgetis not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far beenstrangely reluctant to address. But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which areactually going down– and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words wereonce utteredby that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look –look– like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spentwilling on unrest, and where quasi-paramilitariesmenace our ports. Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshireholda referendumon leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it | Andy BurnhamRead moreAs much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quoteJuly’s bulletinfrom the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month,YouGov reportedthat 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime ministerannounced £1bn of investmentin a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only bookIn Place of Fear: in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionEconomic policyImmigration and asylumAndy BurnhamReform UKBudget 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Ms Rachel, the controversial queen of toddler TV: ‘My goal isn’t to be the most liked. It’s to help kids and speak the truth’ | Educational TV | The Guardian
description: Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics
Content: Ms Rachel: ‘All my experiences have led me to knowing that we should take care of each other.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMs Rachel: ‘All my experiences have led me to knowing that we should take care of each other.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianEducational TVInterviewMs Rachel, the controversial queen of toddler TV: ‘My goal isn’t to be the most liked. It’s to help kids and speak the truth’Sophie McBainHer catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politicsSun 20 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheYouTubestar Ms Rachel, toddler whisperer extraordinaire, spots me before I clock her, and even from a distance and without her trademark pink T-shirt and denim dungarees, she is instantly recognisable by her wave, which is accompanied by an enthusiastic bounce. I half expect her to say, “Hi, friends”, as she does at the start of many of her videos. Instead she bounds over, wearing a classic off-duty mum uniform – Sesame Street sweatshirt, grey leggings, baseball cap that reads “Mama” – and removes her oversized sunglasses. She’s very sorry, she says, rubbing her eyes, that she is so tired – but her manner remains unfailingly, characteristically peppy.It is only seven years since Rachel Accurso, who used to be a preschool music teacher, uploaded her first video to YouTube, a counting song for preschoolers calledBubble, Bubble Pop!. She and her husband, Aron Accurso, who worked as a music director on Broadway, made the video because their one-year-old son had a speech delay and there seemed to be a dearth of quality videos online that could help toddlers learn to speak.Nowadays, theMs Rachel YouTube channelhas more than 21 million followers, and since she signed with Netflix in 2025, the series has been streamed more than 69m times, becoming the highest-ranked new kids’ TV show. You can buy Ms Rachel dolls, rattles, talking toy phones, books and pyjamas. The couple are releasing their first album this month.Ms Rachel, who is 43 and has a 17-month-old daughter, Susannah, as well as her eight-year-old son, Thomas, has also amassed a huge following on Instagram (5.5 million) and TikTok (11 million), where the mums of her superfans congregate, and where she cuts a more controversial figure, having become a vocal opponent of the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, and a campaigner on other humanitarian issues, such as family immigration detention centres in the US and the war in Sudan. She champions LGBTQ rights, posts about the case for slavery reparations and free universal childcare, and is emerging as a hero of the American left. This month, when the rapper Macklemore pledged $1m to organisations supporting Palestine,Ms Rachel said she would match the donationand said every “wealthy white celebrity” should do the same. Earlier this year she was on the inauguration committee for Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s charismatic leftwing mayor. She has publicly endorsed other insurgent progressives, such as Abdul El-Sayed, who recentlywon the Democratic Senate primaryin Michigan – making her a whole lot more political than any children’s presenter needs to be.We are meeting in a park close to her in-laws’ home in Colorado, where she filmed during the pandemic, which is when Ms Rachel videos began taking off in a very big way. Her preschool fanbase are, of course, unaware of any of her politics, and they cannot get enough of her. Her videos use song and play to teach first words, early phonics and other essentials like potty training. One has been viewed over 2bn times, considerably more than the average Taylor Swift music video. Even the first clip she ever made has now been viewed 21m times. “That’s funny, because it’s not that good!” she jokes: she and Aron filmed it in their New York apartment with her phone balanced on a stack of books.View image in fullscreen‘When your child is having fun, you’re having fun.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianThere’s often something mysterious about internet fame: in a crowded field of self-taught content creators, what distinguishes the star? Accurso sometimes cannot believe the twist her family’s life has taken. “If 10 years ago someone said, ‘You’re in Rolling Stone’, we’d be like, ‘For what?’ And if they said, ‘For The Wheels on the Bus and the Caterpillar song’, we’d be like, ‘What?! How did that happen?!’” she says.But, though unpredictable, the couple’s success is hardly random. Accurso points out that they identified a niche, an untapped demand for educational content for toddlers, and that their videos were co-created with their early audience, who told them what they liked and what they wanted more of. “It almost feels like this live thing you’re creating with parents,” she says.Then there’s the fact that if you set out to identify the perfect couple to make hit toddler TV, you would struggle to improve on Rachel and Aron Accurso. Consider their professional and academic backgrounds: she has two master’s degrees – in music education and early childhood education – and early learning professionals attest to the science behind her approach. In an era of screen-time shaming, the Accursos create shows that parents don’t feel guilty about letting their young kids watch.And then there is Accurso’s personality, her wide-eyed warmth and wholesomeness. She seems to be the rare person who truly loves hanging out with kids – who is genuinelydelightedto play not only with her own, or her friends’ children, but with any five-year-old.double quotation markIt’s good to criticise governments for violating children’s rights. It’s something that everyone should be doingShe and her husband – who also just seems so freakingnice– have complementary personalities, she says. She’s always bursting with ideas; he knows how to winnow them down and organise a timeline. They call each other “instant oatmeal” and “slow-cook oatmeal” because, “I just want things fast and he takes his time,” she says. And this is “crazy”, she tells me, but once, long after they had established these nicknames, they were both making breakfast and she looked over and saw that he was stirring slow-cook porridge while she was making instant! They are ridiculously cute.So why get involved in politics? Accurso says she was advised to keep quiet on political issues, and she fielded arguments that “didn’tfeelright”, such as, “If you don’t say anything about anything controversial, you’ll help more kids, because more people will watch.” She has faced pushback from conservative parents over her support for LGBTQ rights, and for using they/them pronouns when introducing the musician Jules Hoffman, who is non-binary, but this has been eclipsed by the response to her criticism of the Israeli government.Accurso says she witnessed footage from Gaza and spoke to families there, and cannot understand why anyone who has done the same would not feel moved to do all they can to stop the violence. “It’s good to criticise governments for violating children’s rights. It’s something that everyone should be doing. Because we’re the grownups of this world and we’re meant to keep children safe. And the fact that we are not is horrific,” she says.View image in fullscreenWith her husband and creative partner, Aron Accurso, at an awards ceremony last year.Photograph: Stephanie Augello/Variety/Getty ImagesFrom a pure business perspective, the advice about staying silent may have been right. When she began speaking out about the humanitarian toll on Gaza, the backlash, which included accusations of antisemitism, took her by surprise. “I was confused and devastated that people said because you care about children who are starving, and whose food is being blocked, you don’t care about these [Jewish] kids,” she says. “I was like, oh my gosh, I have a deep love for, a deep care for, all children.” She has posted messages of sympathy for Jewish victims, and has collaborated with groups such as Parents Circle, which works with Israeli and Palestinian families who have lost loved ones, and yet the public response to her work is as messy and heated as you’d expect: the pro-Israel group StopAntisemitism nominated her for antisemite of the year in 2025, although many other Jewish organisations have rallied in her defence. She says she has grown accustomed to the maelstrom. “I had this moment when I was praying to God, like how do I handle people hating me? And I feel like I got the message that our goal in life isn’t to be the most liked or the most loved,” she tells me. “It’s that you’re meant to help kids, and stand with kids, and speak the truth about things.”Because of her outspokenness on Gaza, some Jewish parents have switched allegiance to Ms Sara, a kids’ YouTuber who even looks a lot like Ms Rachel – with the same long brunette hair and knotted headband – and who teaches Jewish culture and songs. “I think she’s wonderful!” Accurso says, when I mention her. “I’m never like, ‘Don’t watch this person – watch me’, at all.”One of her more hardline public stances is her refusal to work with people who have not publicly spoken out in defence of civilians in Gaza. “I’m going to work with people who aren’t in a privileged position, because that’s not fair to them if they could lose the ability to put food on the table. But people whoareprivileged who don’t say anything? Yeah, I’m not interested in working with them. Because I feel like maybe if we all said something, the genocide would stop,” she explains.double quotation markWe didn’t know that toddler TV could be big businessNot everyone will agree with this analysis; where some hear compassion, others will diagnose political naivety. “Why are we starving kids when there’s enough food in the world? Why are kids in Sudan starving? Why are kids in the Congo facing sexual violence? They’re kids. I don’t understand. And why do we dehumanise other people when I just feel like every person is different in beautiful ways but also so similar? How could we not want to help everyone?” she asks at one point. Sometimes she says she feels as if she’s living in a “fake, surreal world” because she does not understand how we can tolerate so much unfairness and unchecked suffering. She thinks all elected politicians should be forced to meet children like Rahaf, a three-year-old Gazan amputee she invited on the Ms Rachel show, so they understand the stakes. So is she naive, or is politics too unfeeling?“I just have a really good moral compass,” she tells me at one point. Which may be why, for all the controversy, she says she is often approached and thanked by strangers on the street, and she enjoys a lot of breathless, all-caps online support. “Ms Rachel for president,” her supporters sometimes write underneath her posts. When the Democratic candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the Maine Senate race after being accused of sexual assault, Accurso – who is from Maine – was spoken of as the dream candidate for Democrats there. “That’s hilarious,” she says. She has no interest in entering politics. But, she adds, sounding unusually tentative because “maybe everyone will be upset”, she hopes to one day become a Christian minister. One thing you need to know about Ms Rachel is that she’s the kind of person who prays every day for the people who hate her.Accurso says she was “born spiritual”. She was raised in small-town Maine by a single mum, who dropped out of university when Accurso’s elder sister was born, but later retrained as a social worker and was often juggling multiple jobs. Her mother remains her lodestar, and she named her daughter – born via surrogate in 2025 – after her. It was “rough at times”, growing up with little money, and Accurso felt rejected by her father and used to wonder why he didn’t seem to want her. That said, her mother surrounded her with “so much unconditional love”. She watched her mum shovel snow and build a treehouse and fix the plumbing by herself, and it expanded her own ambitions. It also shaped her politics. “All my experiences have led me to knowing we should take care of each other,” she says.Accurso was an anxious child, who by seven or eight was showing signs of OCD, flicking her light switch on and off to ward off trouble. She felt things deeply. Her mother has kept a note of how, at three, when she heard her neighbour was killing ants she exclaimed, “Don’t kill ants! Let them be free and feel the world!” When her mother could not take her to church because she had a new weekend job at Pizza Hut, Accurso, though only nine, went by herself. She didn’t join the children’s Sunday school but sat through the sermon for adults, praying and trying to “figure things out”.View image in fullscreen‘Space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianAs a young adult she considered joining the seminary, but while working at a school for children with disabilities she felt “led” in a new direction. She formed a close bond with a child with cerebral palsy who was nonverbal, and her supervisor told her she had a “rare talent” for connecting with kids. Galvanised, she went into teaching, and later enrolled for a master’s at New York University, where she wrote a thesis on how to use songwriting to empower children going through hardship. She joined the Unitarian church when she moved to the city – it had a preschool attached and she figured she might get work there. The first time she went, someone offered to introduce her to “the best musician in the world”, and Aron Accurso ambled over.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAron, who loved her smile, offered to walk her out, asked for her number, and made her wait a torturous three days before inviting her on a date, where she ate shrimp for the first time and thought, as they talked about music, that he might be her future husband. On their third date, she asked him if he liked Mr Rogers, the gentle, cardigan-wearing children’s TV presenter, and – what do you know? – he loves him, too. The couple married in 2016. “I feel like our souls are totally meant to be together,” she says.Rachel and Aron had always enjoyed being “silly” together, and at first their Ms Rachel videos felt like “play”, but during the pandemic, when Accurso was teaching on Zoom, and Aron was stuck at home because theatres were closed, and parents were wondering how on earth to entertain their children through long lockdown days, things started taking off. Accurso soon received offers from executives hoping to buy the company. She would sit through meetings hosted by a “bunch of men” with ideas for how to commercialise the project and, although she was suspicious of their lack of interest in the educational side of her work, it was Aron who kept reminding her that she didn’t need their expertise. “Forever, I thought I was going to be replaced as the host,” she says. “Once we had millions and millions of views I thought, oh, maybe a real TV place will get a real actor and see that this was a good concept.” For years she felt as if she was just some “35-year-old mom”, a stand-in for the real, professional Ms Rachel. “We didn’t know that toddler TV could be big business,” she says.The Accursos say their wealth is nowhere near the figures circulating online – I saw $50m – and most of their profits are put back into the company. Still, the couple must have more money than they ever imagined – enough that, on top of their recent $1m donation to Palestinian charities, the Accursos donated $1m to the World Food Programme in 2025. “My spirit doesn’t want to ever …” she says, struggling to express herself. “Well, I don’t have any fancy things, I could say that.” Oh, come off it, I say, but a bit more politely: what’s the fanciest thing you’ve bought yourself? “I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun, little fidget toys and stuff,” she replies. She has a cupboard filled with gifts in her house, so that any child who visits can pick out something for themself. That doesn’t count, I say. Have you ever bought yourself an expensive handbag? She only has one handbag, she says, because she has ADHD and has learned that if she has more than one, she loses important stuff. What about a fancy car? Nope. House? “I think space in New York is hard to come by and space is nice, but I don’t want a fancy house.”“Oh no!” Accurso suddenly exclaims, when we have been speaking for almost 90 minutes, and Aron is due to join us in the park. She is supposed to be talking about her album and she has been going off on all these tangents! Aron arrives a few minutes later, blond and very blue-eyed in a blue button-down shirt and smart linen trousers – they have taken a very different approach to dressing for this interview, she jokes with him as he approaches.The forthcoming album, I’m So Happy, is Aron’s passion project. The couple had received business advice that they should scrape their most popular songs from YouTube and get the thing out as soon as possible – but Aron wanted to devote “extra care” to the album. He ended up collaborating with 19 singers and 42 instrumentalists, and worked with Michael Starobin, who has orchestrated several Disney films. “I really believe that kids respond to it, and kids deserve that kind of rich, beautiful music,” Aron says. Among the 23 tracks are classic nursery rhymes, like The Wheels on the Bus, and songs written by the Accursos themselves, including Caterpillar, a surprisingly affecting tune Aron wrote while trying to get their son to sleep. Whenever they play the song for their children, everyone starts weeping, and I must confess that when I listened ahead of the interview I grew teary, too. “Every day you’re growing bigger, you once were a little guy, but caterpillar, caterpillar, soon you’re going to fly,” it goes. (OK, I know. But, trust me, try listening to it.)View image in fullscreen‘I like to buy toys … I think toys are fun.’Photograph: Joanna McGowan/The GuardianThe musical flourishes are a boon for parents, who will inevitably hear these songs on infinite loop – more than any human should ever have to listen to anything, I say, experiencing a sudden intrusive memory of My First Album by Peppa Pig. “When your child is having fun, you’re having fun,” Accurso replies, because that is the kind of pure-hearted person she is. But then she does mention this one annoying song that Thomas really latched on to when he was two … before requesting this detail be removed from public record because she doesn’t want to be mean.An album also has the advantage of allowing children to enjoy Ms Rachel without looking at a screen, I suggest. That’s true, Accurso says, but she does think we’re too hard on parents (and on ourselves) about screen time. “There’s a lot of judgment and shaming of parents, and I think if you understood what most parents are going through, that wouldn’t be there,” she says. She is not exactly a neutral party to the screen-time debate – toddler screen time is how she pays the bills – but she points out, quite fairly, that sometimes we all need our kids to veg out in front of the TV so that we can get stuff done. It can also be a useful tool for children with additional needs. It was a “gamechanger” for her son, who was too busy charging around to listen to Accurso as she followed after him, instructing him to “say Mama”; but when she was on a screen teaching him how to articulate his first words, he focused.So, what are her screen-time rules, I ask. “Rules?!” she exclaims, sounding confused. “Just kidding!” Although her daughter loves singing with them both, sometimes the only thing that will calm her down on planes is watching Ms Rachel on TV. That morning, Accurso let her watch Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood, a cartoon inspired by Mr Rogers, so that Susie would stop trying to do dangerous stuff while Accurso was getting Thomas ready for summer camp. Susie is “such a sweet baby, but she has a hitting problem”, Accurso says, and this morning’s episode was about feeling mad. Susie has made progress, of sorts. Now, after she has hit someone, she says, “I’m mad.”Accurso seems more relaxed – and goofier – with Aron present. At one point she slumps over the table, and he asks if she’s OK. “Just looking at a spider! Keep going!” she says. “You focus, and I’ll be the ADHD person.” Ms Rachel’s political profile must have taken a toll on the whole family. They have had security problems that they don’t want to go into. “We’re learning how to deal with that,” is all Aron says. When I ask if he ever wished for Accurso to stop talking about controversial issues, he replies that her compassion and empathy are “genuine” and are “something I fell in love with and admire about Rachel”. There was no question of stopping her, because if she didn’t stand up for her values, she wouldn’t be Rachel, he adds. “Aww, thank you, Aron,” she coos, reaching for his hand, “that is so sweet.”Accurso still suffers from anxiety and OCD, struggling with intrusive thoughts, but her health is well managed with medication and therapy. It helps that she is learning that the internet is “not real life”, and that she doesn’t need to listen to the online vitriol. This morning, she received an email warning her of some new online nastiness about her, and she decided to simply not look.Learn With Ms Rachel review – undoubtedly the TV event of the year for millions of usRead moreI noticed when I scrolled through her Instagram and trawled through the comments that I started to feel anxious myself, imagining the extraordinary pressure she is under. The pressure comes not only from the hatred but from the adulation, the weight of expectations, the requests for help. I read a message from someone who said they had designed a headstone in her likeness for their one-year-old who had died unexpectedly, and could they show her a picture?Then there is the immense responsibility that comes from having such a large platform. In January 2026, screenshots circulated showing that she had liked the comment “Free America from the Jews”, under a post she had shared that read “Free Palestine, Free Sudan, Free Congo, Free Iran”. Rachel issued a tearful apology, explaining that she had clicked “like” accidentally when she was trying to delete the remark. She shared a screenshot of the private conversation she had with a follower who drew attention to her like, which supported her version of events: “Ya I believe I deleted that earlier right when I saw it! I hate antisemitism,” she wrote.“After that I got a turtle puppet,” she says, momentarily confusing me – does she mean some kind of automatic moderation software? Before I can ask an embarrassingly stupid question, she clarifies that she literally means a turtle toy. She and Susie were playing with it, “and I was like, I need to slow down like this turtle because I can’t afford to make a mistake like that again”.She tries, as much as any supercelebrity can, to keep her focus on her family. She and Aron had always assumed they would have kids right away, but they struggled with fertility for years. Thomas, Ms Rachel’s first muse, has overcome his early speech struggles. He likes to deliver lectures to his parents that he closes with a professional, “Any questions?” Susie is currently Christmas-obsessed – Accurso recently found herself Googling short-sleeved Santa costumes, until it struck her that that isn’t a thing – and is “so cute and aggressive”. Having a toddler in the house again is, of course, providing inspiration for the show. They need to do something new about boo-boos, Accurso says, and another bathtime song and, yes, definitely, something about how it’s not OK to hit.Ms Rachel’s album,I’m So Happy, is out on 25 September.Explore more on these topicsEducational TVEarly years educationTelevisionYouTubeNetflixSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ed Sheeran says situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first show since tour plunged into turmoil | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Pop star has faced boycott calls since rapper Macklemore was removed from tour after shouting ‘free Palestine’ at concert
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pop star has faced boycott calls since rapper Macklemore was removed from tour after shouting ‘free Palestine’ at concert
Content: 3:09Ed Sheeran sorry for 'mistakes' as tour resumes – videoEd SheeranEd Sheeran says situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first show since tour plunged into turmoilPop star has faced boycott calls since rapper Macklemore was removed from tour after shouting ‘free Palestine’ at concertGuardian staff and agenciesSun 20 Sep 2026 07.16 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Sheeran has opened a solo concert in Philadelphia with comments about Gaza, saying what is happening is “catastrophic and unjustifiable”, in his first show since his tour was plunged into turmoil.“My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, of children’s lives,” Sheeran said on Saturday, adding that he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics.The singer said he had been unsure “whether this tour would be carrying on” and “whether I even wanted to be an artist at all” after criticism that had been levelled at him.‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture warRead moreOutside the stadium a small gathering of chanting protesters greeted concertgoers, waving Palestinian flags and chanting “free, free Palestine”.Sheeran’s US Loop tour has been embroiled in crisis since the rapperMacklemore was removedas opening act on Monday, after the owners of stadiums hosting coming shows objected to his shouting “free Palestine” on stage in New Jersey earlier this month.Sheeran, 35, has denied being behind the decision to removeMacklemore, instead blaming the tour promoter.Four supporting acts subsequently withdrewfrom the tour, issuing public statements citing their support for Palestinians.Sheeran’s backing band, Beoga, also announced they were stepping down, sharing a statement on Instagram that said they “fully supported” Macklemore’s message.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest outside an Ed Sheeran concert in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Joe Lamberti/Getty ImagesThe start time for the Philadelphia show was pushed back from 5.30pm local time to 8pm, according to Ticketmaster.While his previous tour was among the highest-grossing of all time, tickets for the Philadelphia show dropped to as low as $32 (£24).Some fans reported seeking refunds from ticket retailers, although this was not confirmed by Ticketmaster or the promoter Messina Touring Group.Sheeran has been accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners – led by the billionaire businessman Robert Kraft – and was targeted by boycott calls.Speaking on stage at the beginning of the concert on Saturday, he said: “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes and I’m so, so sorry for them. I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”He said the 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel were horrific and he considered what was happening inGazanow to be “catastrophic and unjustifiable”.“My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, of children’s lives,” Sheeran said.He said there were questions over whether the tour would continue after the controversy broke out. “I really didn’t know whether this tour would be carrying on,” he told fans. “I really didn’t know whether I’d be even getting on stage again, whether I even wanted to be an artist at all.“In these situations, you really find out who your friends are, and it’s been a weird week. I just feel like it happened very quickly.”Before the show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators congregated outside the stadium. Hillary Steinberg of Philadelphia said she got tickets a year ago but refunded them to attend the demonstration instead, disappointed that Sheeran had not taken a stand.“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice – even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit – is a political choice.”View image in fullscreenFans arrive at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to see Ed Sheeran.Photograph: Matthew Hatcher/AFP/Getty ImagesBrandon Ateke, a student, also accused Sheeran of “complicity” with Kraft and others in silencing Macklemore. “I decided to not attend the concert and instead attend the protest to bring light to the genocide going on in Gaza today,” the 18-year-old told Agence France-Presse.Other fans said they were sticking by the musician. Kassandra Rivera from Philadelphia said: “Everyone has their own opinion and it’s fine … I came here to have a good time and watch Ed Sheeran.”Dwayne Smith from Canada said: “We’re just here for Ed Sheeran. All politics aside, we just like the music. We are here to support him. It’s not about Palestine or Israel tonight, it’s just about the music for us.”At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the conflict in Gaza and West Bank settler violence, Sheeran has maintained an apolitical stance. “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict,” theBritish performer saidon Tuesday on Instagram. “Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them.”He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. Sheeran added that he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who relied on him to make a living.At the end of the show, a tearful Sheeran said playing the concert had given him hope. He said: “Everyone is telling me to cancel, and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned.”With Agence France-Presse, PA Media and the Associated PressExplore more on these topicsEd SheeranMacklemoreGazaIsrael-Gaza warProtestPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: I was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the Alps | Agatha Christie | The Guardian
description: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?
Content: Agatha Christie skiingPhotograph: © The Christie Archive TrustView image in fullscreenAgatha Christie skiingPhotograph: © The Christie Archive TrustAgatha ChristieI was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the AlpsHer last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime?Lucy FoleySun 20 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world ofAgatha Christiewas through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side.Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now …As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else?View image in fullscreenGeraldine McEwan (right) as Miss Marple, with Greta Scacchi.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. Perhaps because I’d started with Orient Express, a glamorous setting was a foundational part of the Christie experience for me, especially after I’d watched the 70s film with Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman and Sean Connery sweeping down the platform trailing smoke and old-school Hollywood style. Poirot gets most of the fun, far-flung locations: the French Riviera, Egypt, the Greek islands and the Dolomites, to name a few.To a younger reader, Miss Marple’s world initially felt quite small in comparison. It was only when I reread the books as an adult that I understood the genius of the character, and came to appreciate how clever and radical Christie had been in making an elderly spinster her master sleuth – occupying a space somewhere between that of a detective and a bystander. She had taken one of the “left behind” women – a figure typically both pitied and scorned by society for not having been able to find a partner after the first world war – and shown her running rings around the other characters, using her invisibility as a kind of superpower. And in creating Miss Marple, she had broken one of the oaths made by the Detection Club (of which Christie was a member) not to use “Feminine Intuition” as a means of solving the crime. So much in the Miss Marple books relies on her intuition: there are physical clues, yes, but it is her understanding of human nature, an understanding that is coded as specifically and peculiarly “female”, that really wins the day.I came to appreciate Miss Marple’s lack of ego, her sense of humour: she is always in on the joke, always understands and plays up to the image others have of her. I enjoyed her sudden and surprising touches of darkness. I also loved that, while the Poirot books can feel quite timeless, the Marple books form a fascinating portrait of social change in Britain across the decades: the evolving landscape of the English village as documented between the 1930s setting of The Murder at the Vicarage and the 1950s period of The Mirror Crack’d from Side to Side (in which a new housing estate has been built), the postwar unease about not knowing one’s neighbours in A Murder Is Announced and the swinging 60s raciness of At Bertram’s Hotel.All of which I came to appreciate anew when planning my own novel. I knew that Miss Marple herself was the key to it all, the element I had to get absolutely right. She had to be Christie’s Miss Marple in all her complexity and brilliance. The other vital factor was the perfection of Christie’s plotting: the element that had kept me up into the small hours as a preteen, trying to use all the tools provided to guess whodunnit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PRBut in other areas I knew that I had to break new ground. I didn’t want this book to be an exercise in ventriloquism – there was only one Agatha Christie, and to try to ape her exactly would be an exercise doomed to failure. It also wouldn’t be any fun, creatively. From the outset I realised that this would be a book inconversationwith the original books, and indeed with other Agatha Christie books, but one that delivers new elements, and in doing so has its own raison d’être.When I learned in my research that Death on the Nile was originally meant to be a Miss Marple novel, I found my jumping-off point: here was my way into the project. A way of including my own love of cinematic locations, and indeed what I had loved about those glamorous Poirot novels, in a new Miss Marple adventure. I would take her on holiday – high in the Swiss Alps, to the Grand Alpine Hotel, with its glorious mountain views and exclusive access to powdery slopes. I realised, too, that using multiple first-person point-of-view narrators would be a fun way of replicating something Christie does so beautifully: telling us a great deal about her characters by showing how they react to Marple, how they by turns underestimate, admire or fear her.Finally, I wanted my book to be in conversation with our own times. This wasn’t about shoe-horning in themes, but drawing out parallels between then and now. In doing so I wanted to interrogate modern society’s fear of ageing and the invisibility of old age that has hardly changed since Christie’s time. I wanted to highlight the prevalence of certain toxic male egos at the heart of culture and politics: figures who have attempted, at times, to rewrite history to further their own ends or disappear past misdeeds. All, apparently, with a total lack of consequence.Which brings me to another thing I love about Christie’s writing: the grim satisfaction of seeing the past catching up with the wicked. The meting out of just deserts. It may not be happening out there in the real world at the moment, but rest assured, it happens here.Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley is published by HarperCollins. title: Singer Becky Hill looks back: ‘Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s’ | Becky Hill | The Guardian
description: The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndrome
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndrome
Content: FlashbackBecky HillSinger Becky Hill looks back: ‘Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s’The Brit award winner on being scammed by a model agency, coming to terms with sexual assault, and wrestling with impostor syndromeHarriet GibsoneSun 20 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBecky Hill in a sleeveless lilac dress and with a comical smile in 2001 and 2026, aged seven and 32, respectivelyBecky Hill in 2001 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen. Styling: Andie Redman. Hair and makeup: Wendy Turner. Archive photograph: courtesy of Becky HillBorn in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, in 1994 and raised in Bewdley,Becky Hillis a singer and songwriter. She began making music at 14, performing in a band called Shaking Trees, before reaching the semifinals on the first series of The Voice UK. She has since had two top 10 albums and collaborated with David Guetta, Chase and Status, Joel Corry and Rudimental, and won the Brit award for best dance act in 2022 and 2023. Her latest album, Rebecca, is out on 13 November.This was taken for a kids’modellingagency,which we later discovered was a scam. Every stage of the process – getting pictures taken, sending them to the agency, getting them back – cost us more money. We’d wire over £100 and get nothing in return. Our family wasn’t rich, so Mum didn’t tell Dad what we were up to – he probably doesn’t even know about it to this day. As for my modelling ambitions, I never pursued it further. I was cute until the age of seven, then started to go on the turn.Meera Syal looks back: ‘South Asians weren’t seen as funny. We sold you fags or served you curry’Read moreI was a happy, chatty child, but my home life was quite dysfunctional. My parents were on their second marriages, I was their first baby together, and they had five children between the two of them – some lived with us, some didn’t. There was a lot of moving about – a lot of arguing, too, but I always, always felt loved. Everyone had their own taste in music: Mum listened to cassette tapes of Foreigner, Eric Clapton and the Eagles; my sister gave me her computer full of all her downloaded music; and my brother liked Eminem, Blink-182, Slipknot and drum’n’bass.I was always a mummy’s girl,and she and I would go to acting, singing and dancing classes together. She wanted me to find something I was passionate about, as I was bullied at school. I kept my singing a secret mostly, but when I was 11 there was a talent show at school and I performed JoJo’s Leave (Get Out) in front of all the parents. I’ll never forget the feeling of singing that song and realising that everyone’s jaws were on the floor. I could see other parents turning around in their chairs and asking my mum and dad: “Did you know she could do this?”On the car journey home, there was a conversation about my future. Dad asked Mum: “Do we send her to a stage school where her talent can be nurtured?” Mum knew we didn’t have the money or live in the right place. She said: “But if music is meant for her, music will find her,” which I thought was beautiful.Luckily, I found some good support in Bewdley – from my music teacher and Andy Brown, a guy who was dating a friend’s mum. He had management experience and took me under his wing – buying me a guitar and paying for singing lessons and studio time. It was a rare taste of what it was like to be nurtured without expectation.My teenage years were typically fraught – I got my braces off by the time I was 13, so at least my teeth were fixed, but I started smoking weed and was temporarily a bit of an angry kid. Discovering drum’n’bass was a real escape – when I was at a rave, I had music to focus on rather than the way I looked or felt. I remember going to [the London club] Fabric for the first time at 18, walking down the stairs and thinking, “I’m home.”double quotation markIt’s hard to be gentle on yourself in this industry – but I’ve regained the kindness that kid had in abundanceI was 17 when I entered The Voice. I was working two bar jobs and was depressed. I didn’t feel that I had much going for me, but I knew I wanted to get out of Bewdley. University wasn’t an option as I didn’t like hanging around with strangers, but The Voice ticked every box. The high pressure of the live competition each week didn’t bother me as I was so happy to be living in my own flat in London and grateful for this huge, strange experience. I didn’t win, but I came out with all the contacts I needed to start my career.Aside from the music I was making, I hated every minute of my 20s. It was a decade of establishing myself as an artist, shaking off the stigma of coming from a TV show, as well as a lot of personal turbulence. In the same year, I got dropped by my label and raped by a friend. I was 21 and remember sitting in a writing session and telling these three men I was working with about the sexual assault that had just happened – trying to externalise some of the intensity of what I was feeling. A few hours later, I was being pulled into a meeting with my management team to be told I had no label.Around this time, I also met the man who would become my husband – we broke up a few years later, then got back together again. I started having success on featured tracks, but I felt like it wasn’t my success – it was the producer’s. I was always fighting to be heard and seen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter I signed my second record andpublishing deal,I was finally able to take care of my parents. They were going through a lot of stress, and my mum’s parents had just died and she was struggling, so I said: “I’ll pay you not to work any more.” I bought them a house – which they have just paid me back for, even though I told them not to – and I’ve put some money into their pensions.My brother’s family were living in a hovel, so I bought them a house, too. I was still renting my flat at the time and wasn’t on the property ladder, but it was important to me that my family was stable before I was. My brother even works with me now. He was in the Marines from the age of 16 and got shot in the head, but is now my security guy. He comes with me everywhere.So far, I’m loving my 30s,but the landscape has changed for music, and I am probably not having the same level of success that I had in my 20s. At the start of my career, my ambition was to write songs that other people liked, whereas now I am writing songs about what I really want to say – the pressures of the job and of society. So I’m at peace if this new album isn’t as big as the others, because I’m proud of what I’ve made.I’ve been in therapy since I was 22, and have done a decade of working on my internal voice – the impostor syndrome that still creeps in and is so hard to escape when you work in music. It’s hard to be gentle on yourself when you work in an industry that is so fickle and unpredictable. Even at the start of this year, I was panicking that my job was about to end and that I was going to have to work in McDonald’s or try to get a new qualification. I’ve always thought I would like to become an electrician, actually, but I know that I’d be electrocuted within the first five minutes.Really, I can’t do anything else apart from what I’m doing now. So I am glad I am still here, and glad that I’m full of a new sense of kindness – something I lost in my 20s, and something that kid in the photo had an abundance of.Explore more on these topicsBecky HillFlashbackPop and rockDance musicDrum'n'bassFamilyPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Not I review – a mouth steals the show in Rufus Norris’s strange and deeply moving take on Beckett | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Soprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flair
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Soprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flair
Content: Lips that really move … Booth’s mouth in Not I.Photograph: University of ReadingView image in fullscreenLips that really move … Booth’s mouth in Not I.Photograph: University of ReadingTheatreReviewNot I review – a mouth steals the show in Rufus Norris’s strange and deeply moving take on BeckettMinghella theatre, ReadingSoprano Claire Booth’s mouth is isolated against a black background to capture the racing brain of a desperate woman, with added operatic flairArifa AkbarSun 20 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a long preamble to Samuel Beckett’s short play, performed in darkness by an unstoppably animated mouth. First, Luciano Berio’s experimental Sequenza III, performed by soprano Claire Booth, which becomes a musical companion piece to Beckett in retrospect for its stuttering repetitions, gasps and throat-clearings. Then a trio of short films about the Irish playwright’s relationship to Folkstone (where he got married in 1961). It is a three-part programme, part of the 2026 Beckett Biennale, culminating in the drama.None of the buildup is required. The mouth, also played by Booth, is still arresting in its speed and urgency, reaching for a truth that rests just beyond its rapid articulations, even as syntax breaks down.Under the direction of Rufus Norris, the setup is academic, the theatre part of Reading University’s campus, but the production has nothing dusty or donnish about it. It is impressively delivered by Booth, who captures the racing brain, the split interior self and the speed of desperation to replay a life that seems to be flashing before a woman’s eyes – or rather, her mouth – from her birth to this moment in a field, among the cowslips at the age of 70, which might be the moment of death. You glean, from the repetitions and verbal hiccups, that it has been hard, loveless and undermining, yet there is an insistence on speaking it aloud.View image in fullscreenClaire Booth and Rufus Norris.Photograph: University of ReadingBooth brings added musicality, singing words, adding operatic cadence. These flecks make you feel as if this woman, what’s left of her, could be a darker version of Winnie, the occasionally singing woman of Happy Days, not up to her waist or neck in earth now but reduced to just her mouth. And still speaking to herself, before the earth covers her completely, into silence.Pin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame finds fresh absurdity in ArgentinaRead moreLike many of Beckett’s characters, this mouth seems to be asserting its survival through sounds and words. She doesn’t stop talking, the play simply tunes out her voice. Her vulnerability amid the vast, pitch-black emptiness that swallows her up, startles you and wrings your heart. When the single spotlight fades to black, it almost brings tears to your eyes. A strangely, deeply moving 15 minutes.Until20 September.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSamuel BeckettreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been work to not go crazy’: Way Dynamic, the Australian folk-pop musician with fans including Elton John | Australian music | The Guardian
description: Dylan Young’s sound recalls the Beach Boys and the Beatles, both contemporary and timeless – and his latest album, Massive Shoe, is attracting international acclaim
Author: Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen
Headline: Dylan Young’s sound recalls the Beach Boys and the Beatles, both contemporary and timeless – and his latest album, Massive Shoe, is attracting international acclaim
Content: Musician Dylan Young, who performs as Way Dynamic, in Melbourne, Australia.Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMusician Dylan Young, who performs as Way Dynamic, in Melbourne, Australia.Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianGuardian Australia's headline actAustralian music‘It’s been work to not go crazy’: Way Dynamic, the Australian folk-pop musician with fans including Elton JohnDylan Young’s sound recalls the Beach Boys and the Beatles, both contemporary and timeless – and his latest album, Massive Shoe, is attracting international acclaimGiselle Au-Nhien NguyenSun 20 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 19.49 EDTShareIt’s been a huge couple of years for Way Dynamic, the Melbourne multi-instrumentalist whose real name is Dylan Young. His 2025 album Massive Shoeis about to be re-released internationallyafter Young signed with the indie giant Jagjaguwar. The likes of Elton John, Djo, Zane Lowe and Elijah Wood have sung his praises. Last year he opened for Black Country New Road, Waxahatchee and MJ Lenderman on their Australian tours. With a warm analogue crackle and subtle yet lush layers, gentle vocals and pensive lyricism, Way Dynamic’s thoughtful, sunny folk is both contemporary and timeless. It is not hard to understand his success.The astonishing voice of Grace Cummings: ‘The peace I found in music is a legitimate lifesaver’Read moreThe 30-year-old has been on the road for much of the last year, with Way Dynamic playing their first headline shows in the US and Europe, many of which sold out. When we meet at a cafe in inner-northMelbourneon a midweek morning, Young is briefly back in town before jetting off again for another European run, including summer festivals.Has all this attention and traction been gradual or has it all happened at once? “Just gradual enough that I’ve not gone crazy,” he says with a wry smile. “It is an adjustment, and it’s been work to not go crazy … all of that exciting, bigger-scope stuff feels fun and adventurous rather than nerve-wracking, if I’m just making sure I’m doing it for me and my friends.”Those human connections are at the heart of his career. Born and raised in the regional Victorian city of Ballarat, Young began learning guitar at the age of eight. Influenced by music he discovered via Rage, he started playing in bands as a teenager. In 2014 his high school band, Bel Air, won a regional competition to perform at Laneway festival. “That helped me know that I wanted to keep doing it, because of how it felt to make music with your friends,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve learned that allowing some chaos and spontaneity into the process is hugely beneficial,’ Young says. ‘It keeps the music alive and interesting.’Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianAt 18, Young moved to Melbourne and began to make connections in the local scene. Over the years he’s played in bands includingGood Morning, Snowy Band and Cool Sounds, and has been a live and session drummer for the likes of Darren Hanlon and Kankawa Nagarra.Way Dynamic’s live setup features members from many of these bands. “We all have similar approaches to our projects where it’s one person’s thing a lot of the time, and we know how to give and take,” he says. “They’re invaluable to how everything comes together and sounds …“I probably decided to start being friends with all of these people because I think they’re incredible creatively, and I’ve been very lucky to find out that they’re also the nicest people I know.”In his early 20s, through “the school of YouTube”, Young discovered the musical worlds which would shape Way Dynamic: jazz, bossa nova, “more densely arranged things”; his first album under the moniker was released in 2022. Young’s melting harmonies recall the Beach Boys and the Beatles, and his soft vocals and contemplative lyrics draw comparisons to Nick Drake, though he admits he doesn’t know much of Drake’s music.It’s the intimacy of the past, rather than any particular aural aesthetic, that Young is chasing. “It’s not necessarily the sounds of those records that have inspired me, but more what the technological limitations of that time forced music to be like,” he says.“The immediacy and reliance on playing instruments and a certain rawness was integral to that time … I try to work to take and not belabour any takes and let mistakes breathe in the music, and I think that does lend to that sound.”View image in fullscreen‘I love the Melbourne music community – I feel like it’s a really nurturing place.’Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianThese songs traverse the landscape of modern existence, contemplating life and love: what it means to settle down, how it feels to fall in love. But Young’s lyrics are also often cryptic, lending an air of mystery: “I’m starting to find how it is I like to communicate music, which is to be very specific, but also vague and broad enough at the same time that people can project what they want onto the music as well.”Good Morning: ‘I find it weird when people say that they’ve had sex to our music. That’s disgusting!’Read moreThe growth of the project has also been about relinquishing control and embracing unknowns. All three Way Dynamic albums have been co-produced with Stefan Blair of Good Morning, whose creative input Young describes as “essential”.“For the longest time, I was doing everything by myself, and I was finding that was getting me the closest to what I wanted,” he says. “From watching how [Blair] works, I’ve learned that allowing some chaos and spontaneity into the process is hugely beneficial. It keeps the music alive and interesting, not contrived.”It’s full steam ahead for Way Dynamic: Young is already at work on his next album, and will tour the US and Canada in early 2027. With many Australian musicians moving over the pond to Europe or the US once they find international success, does he see an overseas move on the cards?“It does tempt me sometimes but I’m really happy here,” he says. “I love the Melbourne music community – I feel like it’s a really nurturing place to live for that. I think I’ll be visiting overseas a lot but I think I can almost definitely see myself staying here.”Massive Shoe is re-released by Jagjaguwar on 2 October. Way Dynamic is playing shows in Australia in November, and touring the US and Canada in 2027;see here for datesWay Dynamic’s songs to live byEach month we ask our headline act to share the songs that have accompanied them through love, life, lust and death.What was the best year for music, and what five songs prove it?Maybe 1966? Or thereabouts. Some albums: Pet Sounds – Beach Boys, Blonde on Blonde – Bob Dylan, Revolver – the Beatles, Speak No Evil – Wayne Shorter, Face to Face – the Kinks.What music do you clean the house to?Phone – Preet Brar feauring Miss Pooja. It’s like a shot of adrenaline to the heart when I hear Preet.What is the last song you sang in the shower?Sabre Dance – Aram Khachaturian. I needed to be out the door in five.Which song have you listened to the most times this year?Baby Love Child – Pizzicato Five. I’m addicted. Feels like my hand being held.What is your go-to karaoke song?Prisencolinensinainciusol – Adriano Celentano. Such beautiful lyrics, always gets everyone singing along.What’s a song you can never listen to again?Dancing Queen – Abba. I think it’s genius. But it’s so melodically beautiful that it makes me cry every time I try to sing along.What classic song should be stripped of its title?We Will Rock You – Queen. The origin of stomp-clap music.What is a song you loved as a teenager?In Too Deep – Sum 41. Hooks for days. Also, relatable – I sometimes got angry at society too.What is the first song/album you bought?Jet – Get Born, at the Sanity in Bridge Mall, Ballarat. And that I did. I got born into a world full of big black boots and long brown hair. Soon enough I was rolling over DJ, and looking at what I’d done.What is the best song to have sex to?I’ll let you know when I try it.

title: ‘Resident Evil movies? I’ve never seen one’: Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchise | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans
Content: Scare in the community … Austin Abrams (left) and Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil.Photograph: Dusan MartincekView image in fullscreenScare in the community … Austin Abrams (left) and Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil.Photograph: Dusan MartincekHorror filmsInterview‘Resident Evil movies? I’ve never seen one’: Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchiseEllen E JonesRaised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fansSun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenBarbarian, Zach Cregger’s debut film as a solo writer-director, came out in 2022, it was a big success, creating a buzz among horror connoisseurs, garnering good reviews, and grossing $46m. Then his second film,Weapons, came out in 2025 and did even better. Mounting industry buzz around the project crystallised into a fierce bidding war; Jordan Peele was reportedly desperate to produce and, incensed by his failure to secure the rights, allegedly fired his managers. The rumours went viral, resulting in a wave of incredible PR that saw the film wildly outperform box office expectations and win an Academy Award (forAmy Madigan’s blunt-fringed, bonsai-pruning best supporting actress turn as instantly classic villain Aunt Gladys).Even if Cregger had not had a box-office smash that crossed over into awards contention, there would still be an atmosphere of hushed expectation around his next move.
