Both Barbarianand Weapons addressed hot-button issues – sexual assault and school shootings, respectively – while resisting easy interpretation. Both, too, started out seemingly heading in one narrative direction, before thrillingly careening off elsewhere. Thus, with just two features, Cregger had established a reputation for totally terrifying, utterly unpredictable and – most importantly – genuinely original movies.Yet the real shocker from this nascent horror auteur is still to come. For his third film, Cregger has taken inspiration from existing intellectual property – or IP, those two little letters bound to strike fear into the heart of even the most stoic cineaste. Zach Cregger has made aResident Evilmovie.View image in fullscreenMotivated cellar … Barbarian.Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy“Look, I could make a different movie now if I wanted to,” he says, when I put to him the obvious question: why? He is talking to me via video call, from a warmly furnished but ominously low-lit room, wearing a crumpled navy T-shirt, and sounding much less defensive than his words might suggest. “I understand how people could be like: ‘Why IP?’ But to me, that’s just such a secondary concern because the IP is not the point. The point is the story. The point is, it’s an original movie, even though it is Resident Evil.” He sighs. “And now I can’t wait for everyone on the internet to be like, ‘He admitted it!’”Cregger is referring to the stick he’s been getting online from more obsessive gamers ever since thefirst teaser trailer launched in April. “I feel like there’s been so many people taking what I say about this exact thing out of context and saying: ‘He just wanted to make the movie that he wanted to make, and then slap Resident Evil on it, so he could get a bigger budget.’ Which is not the case. It was conceived to be a Resident Evil story. And when you watch the movie, you’ll know that’s the case, because it’s undeniable.”But what is “a Resident Evilstory”? For those who are unfamiliar, the franchise began as a Japanese survival horror game released for PlayStation in 1996. It was then adapted into a live-action film series – Cregger’s film will be the eighth instalment – beginning in 2002, with the Paul WS Anderson-directed Resident Evil,starring model turned actor Milla Jovovich as a woman battling a zombie contagion let loose on Raccoon City by the shadowy Umbrella Corporation. The film series, like the game, has been hugely profitable – that’s why they keep making ’em – and could at one point boast (at nearly $1.2bn and counting) of being the all-time highest-grossing horror film series, until being overtaken by the Conjuring Universe and the Alien series.View image in fullscreenStrange bedfellow … Amy Madigan in Weapons.Photograph: AlamyYet from the perspective of those aforementioned cineastes – and also more casual movie lovers – Resident Evil’s reputation is distinctly mid. On reviews aggregate site Rotten Tomatoes, the highest-rated film from the franchise is 2016’s Resident Evil: The Final Chapter, which scores an ignominious 39% “splat”. So while Cregger was – and is – a big fan of the games, the films? Not so much. When I ask what the relationship is of his film to the rest of the series – a sequel? Prequel? Universe-expanding retro-reboot? – he shrugs and says, somewhat proudly: “I couldn’t really say. I’ve never seen one.”Still, as Cregger appreciates, video game adaptations are tricky for a reason: they are expected to serve the play-experienced aficionadosandthe clueless noobs. Cregger’s big idea for bridging this gap is to create a moviegoing experience that feels like a 90-minute session on the PlayStation, even for those audience members who may never have previously heard of Resident Evil. Narratively, this means following a single character, medical courier Bryan (Austin Abrams), as he attempts to deliver a cooler containing a transplant organ from hospital A in the flatlands to hospital B in the remote mountains near Raccoon City, Colorado, where – unbeknown to Bryan – a zombie outbreak is now under way. As in the game, Bryan regularly switches environment, progressing from snowy road to deserted farmhouse to sewage tunnel. In each new place, he must find the resources to survive. Shooting the film in a rural part of Czechia was, therefore, an appropriately gruelling experience for Cregger. “It was dark. It was cold. It was unrelenting,” he says. “I had pneumonia for the first half of the movie, and a horrible bacterial infection for the back half … It sucked.”View image in fullscreenFight or fright … Zach Cregger.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/Dusan MartincekIt may have sucked, but it worked. Judging by the 30-minute preview made available to press, Cregger’s film is exhilarating and immersive. He utilised the over-the-shoulder camera angles now synonymous with third-person shooters to mimic gameplay, and Bryan’s dialogue is mostly a soliloquy of disjointed profanities. “That’s how I talk to myself when I’m sitting on the couch playing Resident Evil,” says Cregger.“I mean, I basically only say ‘fuck’ and run away from things.”Is Bryan based on Cregger himself, then? “One hundred per cent,” he says. “Everything about him is me, my anxieties and my personality.” This helps explain why Bryan has a verisimilitude that isn’t always present among the plot-serving panickers and simplistic scream queens of horror. “It’s fun to have a character who is a real character and convincing in the scenario, but also behaving the way that I think most people who play Resident Evil would behave,” says Cregger. “He’s more suited to be on the couch playing Resident Evil than surviving Resident Evil,and that’s why he’s the perfect person to put into this scenario.”Cregger grew up, as video game-playing everymen tend to do, in “a typical, middle-class, suburban neighbourhood”. He was one of four boys raised by a stay-at-home mother, and a father who worked “in mortgages and foreclosures” – a job description that instantly conjures the boarded-up houses of Barbarian’s Brightmoor, Detroit setting. Cregger’s mother was always “very, very involved in the church”, and when his parents divorced, she got a job there too, meaning the brothers attended services four or five times a week. The young Cregger still found time to ride around on his bike, watch movies and play video games, of course. It was “kind of like that classic 80s American upbringing”. Which is to say, for the most part Spielbergian, but with the potential for abject Lynchian horror.As a teenager, Cregger began playing in punk bands, which gave him his first experience of “catching the big fish”, a transcendental meditation technique pioneered by David Lynch, which has become foundational to his creative process. “I remember I would write these songs and I’d be like: ‘There’s no way this is mine. This just feels like this is from somewhere else, and I’ve just been lucky enough to hook it.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe grass is always greener … Brian Sacca and Cregger in Wrecked.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThen, in college, Cregger formed his comedy troupe, The Whitest Kids U’Know (“I’ve always hated the name,” he says), which achieved success on the cable TV channels Fuse and IFC, before essentially disbanding in 2022 after the accidental death of founder member, and Cregger’s close friend, Trevor Moore. (Their final project, the film Mars, was eventually released in 2024.) It was in the midst of this bereavement that Cregger wrote the screenplays for Weapons, Resident Evil and his planned next project, a sci-fi film called The Flood, in quick succession. Of The Flood, he says: “It may be the script I’m the most proud of, because it has its own strange anatomy that just fits. I’m very excited to start.”A background in comedy – Cregger also starred in the TV shows Guys With Kids and Wrecked – is common to many of horror cinema’s most exciting new talents. To Cregger, the connection is clear: “That muscle group that you work out in comedy, where your brain is constantly trying to think, ‘What’s the surprise? How can I inject an interruption into what we’re expecting?’ That’s the same muscle group you need for a scare. So all of my time spent in comedy was going to the gym for horror as well.”And just as every good standup learns to distinguish different shades of audience laughter, so a horror film-maker hopes to elicit a whole spectrum of scares, from slight startles to full-on existential dread. “My favourite kind is anything that gets me with stillness or a bizarre image,” Cregger says, citing as an example a scene from Curry Barker’sObsession. “Her, running around, holding the flowers in front of her face? I was like, this is fucked!” And, to clarify: “That’s agoodfeeling!”Cregger is often grouped with online-adjacent horror auteurs such as Barker, Kane Parsons (the maker ofBackrooms) and Jane Schoenbrun (the writer and director ofTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma). But at 45, his inspirations bypass online “creepypasta” in favour of more enigmatic, classically rooted and traditionally cinematic influences. Barbarian, for one, was directly inspired by a self-help book, Gavin de Becker’s The Gift of Fear, published in 1997.Resident Evil at 30: how Capcom’s horror opus has survived and thrivedRead more“I have a lot of hippy ideas about creativity,” he says. “I just love the idea of being a conduit for the art, and that these objects of art exist with or without you [as an individual artist]. I understand how somebody could be like: ‘Dude, what are you talking about?’ Fine. I don’t care. I like choosing to exist in that reality where I have the ability to go into my subconscious, cast a wide net and see what I can snag. And if the universe or whatever is smiling on me, I’ll get something that will really make me happy, and that I’ll get to spend a year and a half of my life bringing it to the surface.”Back here on dry land, however, Hollywood’s current horror boom is mostly attributed to some more straightforward, bang-for-buck economics. The genre can reliably serve up sensation for a sensation-seeking generation, without relying on big budgets, big-name talent or even – sometimes – pre-existing IP. But what horror filmsdorely on – franchise fare or otherwise – is a film-maker skilled at accessing the audience’s most primal, subconscious terrors. Yes, Cregger has made a Resident Evil movie, and, more’s the surprise, it might actually be really good.Resident Evil is in cinemas now.Explore more on these topicsHorror filmsResident EvilfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dominic West backs ‘top shagger’ Byron in poetry battle with Bob Geldof | Dominic West | The Guardian
description: Actor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festival
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Actor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festival
Content: Dominic West (right) and Bob Geldof at the Big Brue festival event.Photograph: Max Milligan photosView image in fullscreenDominic West (right) and Bob Geldof at the Big Brue festival event.Photograph: Max Milligan photosDominic WestDominic West backs ‘top shagger’ Byron in poetry battle with Bob GeldofActor hails ‘proto-rock star’ as best poet, while musician argues for ‘Ireland’s Shakespeare’ WB Yeats at Somerset festivalHelena HortonSun 20 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDominic West has said Lord Byron is his favourite poet because he was a “top shagger” and said he was not concerned the rise of AI might snuff out poetry.The actor was taking part in a “poetry battle” at the Big Brue festival in Somerset, against rock starBob Geldof, who said he preferred the Irish poet WB Yeats to the excesses of Byron.West said of Byron, who was one of the great Romantic poets: “Byron was shagging everything. Byron was the proto-rock star. He was a top shagger.”He also said he was unconcerned that AI might stop humans from writing poetry, and added that today’s rappers are the new poets.“Someone described to me the last thing that AI is going to take over is standup comedy,” West said, “but it’ll definitely be poetry because no machine could ever get to someone’s soul like these guys can, and I think that’s one thing that’s safe from AI.”He added: “Poetry is still being written. Rappers are people writing amazing poetry every day.”Byron, famed for poems such as She Walks in Beauty and the unfinished epic Don Juan, went into self-enforced exile because of mounting financial debts, as well as rumours that he was sleeping with his half-sister, and accusations of homosexual behaviour which was illegal at the time.West, who is best known for his roles in The Wire and The Affair, added: “There was all sorts of reasons for his exile and being cancelled, and so I, you know, but actually he’s a towering figure.“He unfortunately towers above Yeats. I mean, Yeats is an incredible poet and a wonderful man; you wouldn’t possibly hesitate to call him a legend. You’d certainly hesitate to call him a man who enjoyed sex.”The actor then recited She Walks in Beauty, and said: “Byron wrote this one after an all-night party, as he was getting undressed, drunk, about a woman he’d just seen.”Geldof, former lead singer of the Boomtown Rats, acknowledged that his literary hero, Yeats, was not a “shagger”.He said: “He only got shagged when he was, I think, 31 by Olivia Shakespear, and he was very practical about the whole thing. But it drove a vast energy into his poetry.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYeats, the Irish poet who wrote such famed poems as The Second Coming, was one of the giants of 20th-century literature. He is known for his lyricism and his writing on Irish political struggles, including the 1916 Easter Rising, an armed rebellion by Irish Republicans against English rule.Geldof said that Yeats is the greatest poet the world has ever seen, adding: “Yeats is to us [Irish people] what Shakespeare is to the English.“He didn’t just set about writing the most beautiful lyric love poetry ever, but some of the most impassioned contemporary poetry. A lot of which you know has gone out to the world and is constantly recited in newspaper headlines.“He set up the first Irish ballet school. He set up the first Irish National Theatre. He revived the Irish language.”Explore more on these topicsDominic WestGeorge Gordon ByronPoetryBob GeldofWB YeatsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Henry Herford obituary | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Baritone with an appealing tonal quality who was an enterprising explorer of song and more than 70 roles in opera
Author: Barry Millington
Headline: Baritone with an appealing tonal quality who was an enterprising explorer of song and more than 70 roles in opera
Content: Henry Herford’s oratorio repertoire ran from Monteverdi to the present dayView image in fullscreenHenry Herford’s oratorio repertoire ran from Monteverdi to the present dayClassical musicObituaryHenry Herford obituaryBaritone with an appealing tonal quality who was an enterprising explorer of song and more than 70 roles in operaBarry MillingtonSun 20 Sep 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Scottish baritone Henry Herford, who has died aged 79, was notable for the breadth of his repertoire – offering sterling performances of often neglected works – and his warm, appealing tonal quality.He began his career in theGlyndebourneOpera Chorus (1977-78). In those years he also impressed in small solo roles, as a well-projected, spontaneous Forester in Cunning Little Vixen and the Speaker in Magic Flute. He returned to Glyndebourne in 1981 as a fiery Demetrius in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and with a powerfully delivered Boris Pasternak (a key figure who narrates the action) in Nigel Osborne’s Electrification of the Soviet Union (1987-88).He subsequently appeared atScottish Operain a variety of roles and made a couple of brief appearances at Covent Garden, as a Flemish Deputy in Don Carlos (1983 and 1985), but his most notable contribution to British operatic life lay in the more esoteric or otherwise neglected repertory he helped bring to life, consistently in charged, affecting performances.These included a well-sprung Hercules in Gluck’s Alceste with the ChelseaOperaGroup (1983), an authoritative Artaxerxes in Cesti’s underrated La Dori by Musica nel Chiostro at Christ Church, Spitalfields (1983), and Orpheus in Milhaud’s Les Malheurs d’Orphée (St John’s, Smith Square, 1984).He was also an eloquently tormented Roderick in the reconstruction by Francisco Negrin and Peter Ash of Debussy’s unfinished La Chute de la Maison Usher (Queen Elizabeth Hall, 1989), Creon in Haydn’s L’Anima del Filosofo in a concert performance with the Downshire Players of London (1989), and a dignified Duke in Stephen Storace’s Gli Equivoci (Bampton Opera, 2000). In all, he undertook more than 70 operatic roles in performances throughout Britain and Europe.View image in fullscreenHenry Herford in The Lighthouse by Peter Maxwell Davies at the Queen Elizabeth Hall, London, 1994.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHerford’s commitment to investigating less frequented corners of the song repertory was equally thoroughgoing. An impressive recorded legacy includes two volumes of songs by Charles Ives, a disc of songs by the 20th-century American composers John Corigliano, Arthur Shepherd, Ben Weber and Conrad Susa, a disc of delectable Dylan Thomas settings byPeter Dickinson, and a two-CD set featuring the most comprehensive compilation to date of the songs of Arthur Bliss (with many first recordings). The latter, released in 2000, was received by the BBC Music Magazine as “a revelatory document and a source of ever unpredictable delight”.More conventional repertory also featured in his discography, including a fervent reading of Vaughan Williams’ Five Mystical Songs with the Philharmonia Orchestra under Hilary Davan Wetton (1988), Demetrius in theRichard Hickoxrecording of A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1993), as well as Handel’s Dixit Dominus (1995) and Israel in Egypt (2000) with the King’s College Choir underStephen Cleobury.He had a large oratorio repertory extending from Monteverdi to the present day and sang with many major orchestras in Britain under such conductors as Simon Rattle,Yehudi Menuhin,Andrew Davis, John Eliot Gardiner,David Willcocks, Hickox andMichael Tilson Thomas, as well as in Europe, the Americas and Hong Kong. He appeared on three occasions at the BBC Proms, twice at the Last Night (1984 and 1985).As a recitalist he made frequent broadcasts and recordings with the Nash Ensemble, the Songmakers’ Almanac, the Endymion and Koenig ensembles, Lontano, the Lindsay Quartet and Ensemble Modern. His voice had an attractively open quality, his diction was exemplary, and he delivered his lines with infectious vigour and enthusiasm.Born in Edinburgh Henry grew up in a close-knit English family in Glasgow, the son of Jean (nee Hawkins) and Philip, a railway engineer; his mother was profoundly deaf from the age of three until her death at 104. Early musical experiences were offered by the local church choir and his elder brother, John, a fine pianist.After schooling at Glenalmond college in Perth, he went to King’s College, Cambridge, for a degree in classics and English, and then studied singing from 1971 to 1976 at the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester, where he won the Curtis gold medal.Alongside his singing career Herford held appointments at the RNCM, the Birmingham Conservatoire and the Royal College of Music in London, where he was held in high regard as a rigorous, perceptive teacher.He met his future wife, Lindsay John, when they were both in the Glydenbourne Opera Chorus; they married in 1982. With the administrative assistance of Lindsay, he later founded the Abingdon Summer School for Solo Singers, a popular seasonal destination for aspiring vocalists. Tutors beside Herford included Andrew Shore, Toby Spence, Catherine Wyn-Rogers, Joan Rodgers and James Gilchrist. The course was inaugurated in 1999 and ran until its disruption by the Covid pandemic.In 1986 the Herfords, together with their two sons, Thomas and Johnny, who were both to become successful professional singers in their own right, had moved from London, where they had initially settled, to a derelict Elizabethan farmhouse in west Oxfordshire, which they restored the building over a period of time, undertaking much of the work themselves. Their daughter, Alice, was born soon afterwards.It was a welcoming domestic environment and Herford forged strong links with the local community. For 20 years he was a churchwarden at St Denys church, Northmoor. He also compiled a history of the building and was instrumental in restoring the chancel roof. In person he was expansive, generous and vigorous, qualities that also informed his vocalism.He is survived by Lindsay and by Thomas, Johnny and Alice.Richard Henry Herford, baritone, born 24 February 1947; died 31 July 2026Explore more on these topicsClassical musicOperaScottish OperaGlyndebourneobituariesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a spin-off from Abi Morgan’s soapy, glossy, entertaining divorce drama | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Lawyers juggle private chaos with professional brilliance in this new series. Plus: Michelle Keegan’s DI tackles a murder case and a corrupt police force. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Lawyers juggle private chaos with professional brilliance in this new series. Plus: Michelle Keegan’s DI tackles a murder case and a corrupt police force. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The Split Up.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Sister PicturesView image in fullscreenThe Split Up.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Sister PicturesTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a spin-off from Abi Morgan’s soapy, glossy, entertaining divorce dramaLawyers juggle private chaos with professional brilliance in this new series. Plus: Michelle Keegan’s DI tackles a murder case and a corrupt police force. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Hannah VerdierAli CatterallandSimon WardellSun 20 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Split Up9pm, BBC OneA spin-off from Abi Morgan’s The Split, this is another glossy divorce drama with the same soapy beats – and more lawyers who have a better handle on their clients’ relationships than their own. Aria is expecting to inherit her family’s Manchester firm from her bereaved father; it’s why she’s been putting off her own wedding for 10 years. But an old flame, a high-profile case with a podcasting couple and the discovery of an affair soon change her course.Hollie RichardsonThe Great Celebrity Pottery Throwdown 20267.45pm, Channel 4Surely, there’s a high risk of comedians Lucy Beaumont, Fatiha El-Ghorri and Richard Herring “cracking” up their competition in this starry ceramics contest? Host Liza Tarbuck keeps it under control as they are tasked with making a kids’ desk set and pulling off the art of sprigging.HRWilderness With Simon Reeve9pm, BBC TwoSimon Reeve has never been afraid to get his hands dirty, and this four-part series of journeys to the most remote regions of Earth sees him plunging into more muddy, gripping adventures. He begins in Papua New Guinea trekking through the jungle in search of the elusive, outrageously cute “tree kangaroo”, the tenkile.Phil HarrisonThe Blame9pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenMichelle Keegan as DI Emma Crane in The Blame.Photograph: ITVSmashing police misogyny and solving crimes is all in a day’s work for DI Emma Crane (Michelle Keegan) in this new drama. After a teenage girl is murdered in murky circumstances, detectives search for answers, but it’s the subplot of corruption and wrongdoing that’s the one to watch.Hannah VerdierApocalypse9pm, Channel 4The latest reality spectacle loosely masquerading as a social experiment continues to be entertaining. Things get a bit Walking Dead this time as baseball bats are brandished after a dispute over stolen chickens threatens to escalate. However, one of the Westsiders is disaffected and pondering a defection.PHWilder9pm, Sky DocumentariesAn interesting companion piece to 2023’s Remembering Gene Wilder, Chris Smith’s intimate film focuses more on the actor’s anxieties, perfectionism, withdrawal from public life and search for meaning. Archive, interviews and previously lost footage flesh out the picture, while Wilder’s nephew Jordan Walker-Pearlman provides a personal lens.Ali CatterallFilm choiceWasteman (Cal McMau, 2025), NetflixView image in fullscreenDavid Jonsson and Tom Blyth in Wasteman.Photograph: Courtesy of Lionsgate UKThe brutal realities of prison life in Britain are dissected in Cal McMau’s claustrophobic, sweatily tense drama. David Jonsson, soon to be the next Black Panther, plays a very different hero here: Taylor, a drug addict incarcerated for manslaughter. He’s soon to be eligible for parole so he’s trying to keep his head down. Unfortunately, his new cellmate, Dee (a menacing Tom Blyth), will do anything to take over the jail’s drug trade from Paul (Alex Hassell, definitely not in Rivals mode) and forces the desperate Taylor to assist him.Simon WardellHow to Live on Earth (Fredi Devas, 2026), YouTubeBenedict Cumberbatch’s measured tones introduce “the world’s greatest how-to video” – Fredi Devas’s suggestion box of solutions to the climate crisis. The documentary sweeps across the globe from China to Chad, Brazil to Singapore, with chapters focusing on ways to protect and respect nature, create sustainable agriculture, even put a monetary value on biodiversity. It’s all tentatively optimistic despite the devastation on display, and the praiseworthy activists and scientists profiled offer at least some hope for the future.SWNirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (Matthew Johnson, 2026), 6.45am, 6.15pm, Sky Cinema PremiereThis mockumentary is a sequel to a 2007 Canadian web series and 2017 Vice TV sitcom you probably haven’t heard of. But don’t let that get in the way of enjoying a gloriously silly Back to the Future rip-off. Endearingly inept Toronto musicians Matt Johnson and Jay McCarrol (playing themselves) decide to skydive from the CN Tower to promote a gig they haven’t even secured. But an inadvertent trip in a time-travelling RV throws their plan into comic chaos.SWLive sportPremier League Football: Bournemouth v Liverpool, 1pm, Sky Sports Main EventFulham v Man Utd is at 4pm.Cycling: World Road Championships, 2.45pm, BBC TwoCoverage of the women’s individual time-trial from Montreal.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Turn of the Screw review – Henry James’s classic ghost story with added jump scares | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own cleverness
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own cleverness
Content: Startling moments … Amy Tara in Turn of the Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStartling moments … Amy Tara in Turn of the Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewThe Turn of the Screw review – Henry James’s classic ghost story with added jump scaresArcola theatre, LondonThis slick production of Morgan Lloyd Malcolm’s adaptation is hampered by its own clevernessArifa AkbarSun 20 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is Henry James’s canonical ghost story with modern-day jump scares. And, more audaciously, a new framing device by writer-adapter, Morgan Lloyd Malcolm, which explains itself in a final, added, twist.The jump scares do their work, Hattie North’s jagged sound design enacting its shocks, and the production is slick and stylised – but not all the elements pay off.It is the same story, of a governess (Amy Tara) who, wooed by a roguish gentleman (Jim Fish) becomes a tutor to two young charges in a tenure that culminates in tragedy.Lloyd Malcolm’s framing device features an unnamed (imaginary or real?) man interrogating the governess’ version of events: that her two seemingly angelic charges are possessed. His accusatory questioning suggests the age-old contention that the woman is an unreliable narrator and unhinged fantasist but his interruptions are too numerous, hampering the buildup of dread and tension. The chopped up nature of the story (you hear what is coming, travelling back and forth in time sequences) has the same effect.The production sets itself up with great promise. The two children, Flora (Kathleen McAuley Irvine) and Miles (Toby Beynon), appear suddenly out of darkness on Matthew Cassar’s elegantly gothic set of screens. So does housekeeper, Mrs Grose (Katy Slater, not the friend and confidante she is in the novella), as well as the apparitions of dead manservant Quint and former governess Miss Jessel (played by the children).Directed by Nicky Allpress, the action is stylised, with minimal props used. Flora’s eerie doll raises the hairs and the screens are used inventively. But you don’t always know what is going on, which becomes most apparent in the lake scene in which the governess finds herself under water. There are whistles, screams and characters who suddenly appear and disappear. It’s creepy, but too much too soon, leading to inevitable repetition.View image in fullscreenInventive screens … Tara, Toby Beynon and Kathleen McAuley in Turn Of The Screw.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe children look like grownups, in costume, and this draws them closer to the adults (Quint for Miles, and Miss Jessel for Flora) who the governess believes have taken possession of them. It gives them an added edge of sinister knowingness that comes close to menace at times: Flora’s glassy-eyed smiles and Miles’s joshing as he queasily puts his head under the governess’s skirts. But his innocence is particularly eclipsed by Beynon’s physicality: he looks like Quint from the off, so it is harder to believe in him as the 10-year-old.There are some startling visual moments: the screens do a fine job of bringing on characters as if out of nowhere. The final twist, looping back to the beginning, half explains the puzzle of the governess’s interrogation (Who is the man? What does he want to prove? Which timeframe is she in?) and the idea of women having to eternally defend their version of events. But the production is hampered by its own cleverness, the elliptic storytelling a distraction from the clarity and intrigue of this story’s psychological questions around fear, sexual desire and moral corruption.AtArcola theatre, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreHenry JamesArcola theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time review – a fun and inventive sensory assault | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Alex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Alex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging
Content: Puzzled by human interactions … Alex Keenan with Joe McFadden in The Curious Incident of the Dog in The Night-Time.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenPuzzled by human interactions … Alex Keenan with Joe McFadden in The Curious Incident of the Dog in The Night-Time.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewThe Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time review – a fun and inventive sensory assaultBirmingham RepAlex Keenan perfectly captures protagonist Chris’s bewilderment and cheeriness in Ned Bennett’s ambitious new stagingMark FisherSun 20 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most alarming moment in Mark Haddon’s young adult novel is when Christopher Boone, a 15-year-old on the autism spectrum, flees his Swindon home for London. After a perilous train journey, he arrives at Paddington station and is overwhelmed. The book’s text becomes a barrage of fonts and type sizes to express the information overload: announcements, shop signs and adverts all shouting for his attention.That sense of cacophony, a sensory assault of products, people and places, characterises Ned Bennett’s ambitious new staging of theSimon Stephens adaptationfor Birmingham Rep and Melting Pot. Eleanor Bull’s bare stage, an outsize studio in white, alternates between clean geometric lines, such as the row of pastel-coloured houses that form a picture-book street, and more detailed high-definition projections.Hayley Egan’s excellent video design lays out everyday objects – wrench, tampon, wooden spoon – for careful study as if in a Dorling Kindersley illustrated hardback. It makes the familiar seem strange and demanding. The busy percussive score by Giles Thomas only offers more to process, while a multitasking ensemble drift in and out, surreal and playful, police officers one minute, tumblers the next. There is much to take in, much to make sense of.View image in fullscreen‘A clever theatrical representation of Haddon’s literary idea’ … Alex Keenan’s Chris is greeted by giant yellow balls at Paddington station.Photograph: Johan PerssonAt the vulnerable centre, a gender-swapped Chris (Alex Keenan) gets to Paddington and is plunged into a storm of bouncing balls – all yellow, her hated colour, all bearing advertising slogans and all trying to knock her off course. It is a clever theatrical representation of Haddon’s literary idea: Chris v an unfathomable world. To make it on to a tube train, she has to master a skipping rope, as if navigating the city were like making it through an adventure playground.Elbows high, head tilted, Keenan captures Chris’s combination of bewilderment and cheeriness. She is puzzled by human interactions, certain in her love of maths and science. In a high-energy professional debut, she charms with her enthusiasm enough to carry us through the distressing times when Chris turns inwards or lashes out as facts and emotions become too much to process.Fun and inventive, Bennett’s staging has the dreamlike quality of something created before our eyes. Sex, death and infidelity are handled with matter-of-fact sensitivity as we cheer Chris for triumphing in the face of adversity.Touringuntil 28 May.Explore more on these topicsTheatreMark HaddonBirmingham RepreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Taryn Simon on her most ambitious exhibition yet: ‘It’s built almost like a novel’ | Taryn Simon | The Guardian
description: The multidisciplinary artist delves into pockets of history, including within her family, for the largest ever debut of new work staged at the Guggenheim
Author: Quinn Moreland
Headline: The multidisciplinary artist delves into pockets of history, including within her family, for the largest ever debut of new work staged at the Guggenheim
Content: Taryn Simon, One little room on fire, 2026 (detail)Photograph: Taryn SimonView image in fullscreenTaryn Simon, One little room on fire, 2026 (detail)Photograph: Taryn SimonTaryn SimonTaryn Simon on her most ambitious exhibition yet: ‘It’s built almost like a novel’The multidisciplinary artist delves into pockets of history, including within her family, for the largest ever debut of new work staged at the GuggenheimQuinn MorelandSun 20 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaryn Simon is seated in a conference room at the Guggenheim, looking dazed. Her new show, Father Country I Do Love You, opens in under three weeks. It’s a big deal, the first monographic exhibition by a photography-based artist in the iconic spiral rotunda, and the largest debut of new work ever staged at the museum. There’s still a lot of work to be done.‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favouritesRead moreDownstairs, the lobby is being transformed into the Bangkok living room of Jim Thompson, a silk businessman-slash-spy who disappeared in 1967. Simon’s father, a US government worker, was living in Thailand at the time and figured that the Chinese got him, if not a tiger. When Simon was nine, the father and daughter recreated Thompson’s famous wood-panelled den back in Long Island. “And then I built it here with fake teak,” she says, voice wilting. “It’s driving me nuts. I’ve spent so much time trying to make non-teak look like teak.”Attention to detail is a defining quality of Simon’s practice, which spans photo, video, performance, sculpture and bookmaking. An academic’s artist, she applies journalistic rigor and archival methodology to art photography, turning research, preparation and curiosity into artistic mediums of their own. Developed over 10 years, Father Country is based on Simon’s extended correspondence with a retired federal agent. She follows the ripples of this middleman figure, identifying witnesses – tangential or immediate, innocent or otherwise – to acts of espionage, conspiracy and violence. “I thought his life was unbelievable,” she says, “but anybody’s is when you dig into it, right?”View image in fullscreenInstallation view, Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love YouPhotograph: David HealdFather Country may be Simon’s most ambitious work yet, which is saying something. She has spent 25 years using a symbiosis of image and text to examine systems of information, organization and power from borders to botany to genealogy. Her breakthrough,The Innocentsfrom the early 2000s, depicted exonerees at the site of their alleged crimes, exploring photography’s role in wrongful convictions.Simon has spent five days cataloguing seizedcontrabandat John F Kennedy international airport (“It was an exercise in sleeplessness”); imported more than 4,000 specimens to recreatefloral centerpiecesfrom the signings of international treaties; and traced and documented thebloodlines, including those of the first female airplane hijacker, the body double of Saddam Hussein’s son, and a lab rabbit. She spent years writing letters and making phone calls to gain access to sites and objects typically unseen by American eyes, froma federal biothreat research facilityto a braille edition of Playboy.What kind of person would have the idea, let alone the patience, to go to such lengths?View image in fullscreenTaryn SimonPhotograph: Eli Baden-LasarSimon, 51, has requested that our interview not be recorded. When asked, the New York City-based artist explains that she prefers to talk “normally” and gestures at an invisible recorder between us, an unsavory intruder. She was eager, if not anxious, to introduce her latest work and narrated long chunks of text while sipping an iced tea. She was quick to giggle or performatively groan over her tendency to make things harder on herself. (“I wish,” she says, at the idea of slapping a print on the wall with Scotch tape à laWolfgang Tillmans.)Simon has worn a uniform style of dress since her 20s, favoring a knee-length suspender skirt for functionality. Amish by way of Comme des Garçons, an apron pocket is perfect for holding film, cameras and what have yous during a shoot. Pants are not a part of her wardrobe, unless, “I have to go someplace with ticks,” she says. “If I want to take a picture in the woods somewhere, I’m gonna put on some pants.” She designed these garments herself and once made them, too, but has since employed a seamstress. She’s wearing a lacy camisole instead of her typical billowy blouse, but her long, dark hair, now streaked with silver, is parted to the side per usual.She reveals a recent alteration to today’s black outfit, multicolor godets inspired by a stewardess uniform: “I just thought: ‘That’s so good I need to have it.’”During the decade spent making Father Country, Simon experimented with interactive installations, among them a performance piece involving professionalmourners, anin-gallery cold plungeand a votingmachine. Concurrently, she was going down rabbit holes from the agent’s stories. “I would find this marginal thing on the periphery, and follow it,” Simon says. “I spend a lot of time trying to get to that special spot, and really picking it apart.”View image in fullscreenTaryn Simon, Earth two, 2026Photograph: Taryn Simon“The project is built almost like a novel,” Simon explains, “each chapter is color-coded and begins with a first-person narrative text in the voice of the agent, written by me, based on text messages and visits.” Some connective tissue between image and text is linear: the agent and his colleagues were tasked with finding the bullet that killed deputy White House counsel Vince Foster in 1993. Instead, Simon says:“They ended up with tons of civil war objects,” which she catalogues like an encyclopedia of evidence.Other translations are more sinuous, as if Simon is entering a story through a side door. For instance, the agent was once tasked with babysitting two kids at a hotel and took them to the pool. Turns out, their mother was part of a sting operation that led to the arrest of a DC mayor. Thirtysomething years later, Simon tracked down the woman, Rasheeda Moore, and photographed alookbookfor her sister’s fashion brand at the hotel pool.If Simon onceconsciously erased herselffrom the work, she now pulls the curtain back a bit. An occasional snippet of text will reference her in the third-person like an intelligence dossier. This Taryn Simon figure develops confiscated film, collaborates via post with the DC sniper and is threatened“during a photoshoot at a warehouse in Fort Meade where excess Department of Defense property is stored”.View image in fullscreenTaryn Simon, You have to backfill it, 2026 (video still)Photograph: Taryn SimonSeveral moments in Father Country are weird by Simon’s standards, especially one in which she takes portraits of various individuals and collages them together into patterns and shapes. “I challenged myself to be a little more all over the place, let go a little bit, and let the voice be fractured and faulty and fun and wrong,” she says. “That was scary, but it was very important to me to try.” As for why, Simon suggests that the reality of life is messy, that incredible grief must coexist alongside the mundanities of daily life. “I let the things that don’t feel like they should be together.”Father Country concludes with a chapter about memory loss. On election day 2020, the agent experienced transient global amnesia, a temporary episode in which new memories cannot be formed. That same year, Simon’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, and this project is dedicated to him. “I never got his full story,” Simon writes. “He left out as much as he told.” In a final video, recordings of her father’s distressed babbling play atop images of Kodachrome slides from his travels. “He would give me these slideshows of all these countries and talk about them,” she says. “That was really how I traveled and understood the world.” Father Country ended up far from where it began, she says: “The world kept unfolding alongside me.” The final image in the catalogue is of Simon as a child at Jim Thompson’s house, hands perched on a staircase made of real teak.Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love You is in show at the Guggenheim in New York until 14 March 2027Explore more on these topicsTaryn SimonArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie | Adventure travel | The Guardian
description: Beautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbers
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Beautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbers
Content: Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa ‘has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order’.Photograph: David Forster/AlamyView image in fullscreenCabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa ‘has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order’.Photograph: David Forster/AlamyAdventure travel10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomieBeautifully situated refuges with superlative views offering sanctuary to intrepid hikers and climbersKevin RushbySun 20 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCabaña Verónica, SpainA good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity.€15,reservarefugios.comI skied up to the highest mountain hut in the Swedish Arctic. My reward? A whiteout …Read moreLåktatjåkko, SwedenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Wolfgang Kaehler/AlamyAn absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions.When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such asFridtjof Nansen(there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather.From 515 Swedishkronor(£40),laktatjakko.seGaustatoppen, NorwayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Robert Harding/AlamyLike many other huts belonging to the wonderfulNorwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-schoolfunicular railwayone kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province,Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway.From 1,550 Norwegiankroner(£122),dnt.noChata pod Rysmi, SlovakiaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vladimir Cuvala/AlamyThe Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October.€65,chatapodrysmi.kst.skKredaricaon Triglav, SloveniaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mikadun/ShutterstockThis is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential).€30 half-board,triglavskidom.siLe Refuge deCiottuludi Mori, CorsicaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Florian Neukirchen/AlamyOne of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker.€15,le-gr20.frBreiðuvik, IcelandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gestur Gislason/AlamyThe east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations,Brieðvikis part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association.11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70),ferdaf.isScotland’s mountain bothiesView image in fullscreenElphin Bothy in Sutherland.Photograph: Tom Richardson Scotland/AlamyThe UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them.mountainbothies.org.ukRifugio Nuvolau, ItalyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kevin Rushby/The GuardianThe Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from theBaron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory.€51 B&B,rifugionuvolau.itRifugio Lagazuoi, ItalyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Frank Bienewald/AlamyMany huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido.From €85 with breakfast,rifugiolagazuoi.comExplore more on these topicsAdventure travelEurope holidaysHotelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect apfelschmarrn – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: This fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our resident perfektionistin flips through a selection of the best recipes
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect apfelschmarrn.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect apfelschmarrn.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.How to cook the perfect ...FoodHow to make the perfect apfelschmarrn – recipeThis fruity central European pancake dish can be served as part of a main course or as a dessert. Our residentperfektionistinflips through a selection of the best recipesFelicity CloakeSun 20 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchmarrn, orschmarren,Anja Dunkwrites, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation,pancake, a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and abatter pudding. Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports inher book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings, it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, includingkaiserschmarren(studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.View image in fullscreenAlfons Schuhbeck’sapfelschmarrnuses twice as much flour as other recipes. All thumbnail images by Felicity Cloake.The batterAll the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important.Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipein The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who senthis recipe to the New York Times in 1980in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes fromDunkand theDiscover SüdTirol website, which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft andHinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book, for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.The flavouringsAs Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargenkirschwasser, all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.View image in fullscreenErnest R Schulz’s apfelschmarrn employs similar quantities of milk and flour.The fruitBoth Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).View image in fullscreenAnja Dunk’s apfelschmarrn is ‘filling, simple and comforting’.The methodTraditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.View image in fullscreenDiscover SudTirol’s apfelschmarrn is more egg-heavy than most.The toppingA cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). We also like Dunk’s crunchy flaked almonds, but both are entirely optional. As with the nutmeg, chopped hazelnuts, pecans or walnuts would make a fine substitute for those not concerned with authenticity, and even those who are should know that this can be served with any sort of fruit compote, and is particularly good with plums.Perfect apfelschmarrnPrep10 minCook15 minServes2-4, depending on appetite40g butter90g flour½ tsp salt3 eggs75ml milk75ml cream(single, whipping or double), or 50ml extra milkFinely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemon(optional)1 tbsp caster sugar1 dessert apple25g raisins, or currants or sultanas (optional)1 tbsp icing sugar½ tsp ground cinnamon(optional)Flaked almonds, to finish (optional)Melt the butter in a medium ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat, leave to brown to a pale golden colour, then take off the heat – reheating will continue the browning process. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.View image in fullscreenPut the flour and salt in a large bowl. Separate the eggs, then put the whites in a large glass or metal bowl and the yolks in a smaller bowl.Beat the milk and cream, if using, into the egg yolks, then whisk into the flour to make a smooth batter. Stir in the lemon zest.Beat the egg whites until foamy, then add the caster sugar and whisk to soft, creamy peaks that hold their shape but flop over at the top. Fold a little of the egg-white mix into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest.View image in fullscreenCut the apple into thin wedges, and remove and discard the core. Pour two tablespoons of the melted butter into a bowl, put the pan back on a medium heat and, once sizzling, pour in the batter. Arrange the apple slices and raisins, if using, on top, then leave to cook to a rich golden brown underneath. Carefully flip over the pancake (don’t worry if it breaks), then put in the hot oven for five minutes.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenMeanwhile, mix the icing sugar with the cinnamon, if using. Use two forks to break the pancake into bite-size pieces. Tip out on to a plate or work surface and put the pan back on a medium-high heat with the reserved melted butter. Add the almonds, if using, and lightly toast, then top with the pieces of pancake and sprinkle with most of the sugar. Toss over the heat to coat, then divide between plates. Sprinkle with the remaining sugar and serve hot.View image in fullscreenSchmarren, schmarrn – however you spell it, please share your wisdom on this homely Germanic mountain favourite. Or do you prefer to enjoy it in the sophisticated coffee houses of Vienna? Sweet or savoury? Fruity or plain? Baked or fried? All tips appreciated!Explore more on these topicsFoodHow to cook the perfect ...BakingCakeDessertMain courseFruitGerman food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Kid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant review | Turkish food and drink | The Guardian
description: Our main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Our main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean
Content: Kid, London W1: ‘A rhapsody of browns.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKid, London W1: ‘A rhapsody of browns.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsTurkish food and drinkReviewKid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant reviewOur main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely cleanGrace DentSun 20 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this month, a kind-of Turkishocakbaşıopened on a corner in London’s Soho. The brains behindKidare chef Sertaç Dirik and restaurateur David Carter, and I say “kind-of” because, yes, while it has a Turkish-influenced menu –sucukwith grilled peach,pide,börek, hummus,içli köftewith aged beef – and the whiff of live fire, nothing either of them does is ever remotely straightforward, hence the buzz around their new place.Carter foundedSmokestaka decade ago in Shoreditch, a wild, Americana-tinged barbecue joint where, somehow, he made brisket in buns and peach cobbler old fashioneds London’s hottest ticket. Five years later, he openedManteca, also in Shoreditch, a reimagining of the Italian trattoria for the 2020s, followed byOma, his Greek-influenced Michelin-starred venture in Borough, and its little sister Agora, and all of them remain dependable places where you get serious bang for your buck. All of those influences – American smoke, Italian flair and Greek boldness – are present and correct at Kid. Dirik’s story, meanwhile, has about it elements of TV’sThe Bear: a Copenhagen-trained chef cajoled home to bolster the family business and going on to create the hugely lovedMangal 2in Dalston. What Dirik and Carter have in common, aside from reputation, is a love of setting fire to stuff, in a culinary sense rather than in aProdigy’s Twisted Firestartersense. Kid’s Galata mackerel is testament to this: it’s almost completely blackened and has an incredible hit of smoke in its flesh.View image in fullscreenKid’s menu is familiarly Turkish but with clever tweaks, as in the likes ofsucukwith grilled peach puree.Kid’s website says it’s on Frith Street, but the entrance is actually on Bateman Street, thanks to an aggressively discreet front door that will have you wandering around the glass-fronted corner like some confused visitor at Sea Life, pressing their nose against the tank looking for jellyfish and turtles. Here, however, there are diners beyond that glass, and you may cry when you see them inside sipping theirgemlikmartinis (black olive, black pepper, white vermouth, frozen gin). Warning: do not accidentally wander into Regulation, a boutique emporium of a very different persuasion just 10 metres away and where a very different type of lubrication is on offer. And of stuffing, for that matter. I shall leave the parallels there.Kid, as its name suggests, favours the use of kid goat, which will either delight or unsettle the British diner, because as a nation we still quibble about goat meat but for some reason raise no such objection to lamb. They have much in common taste-wise, and Kid’s signature dish – a £65 kid with fig leaf and freekeh for two – comes in an earthenware pot looking very much like a plump lamb shank just waiting for all that flesh to be pulled through the cooked grains beneath. The dish arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean, as did the pickles alongside: fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance.View image in fullscreen‘Undoubtedly the star of this show’: Kid’s Galata mackerel.The room is a rhapsody of browns, with an industrial feel and wilfully uncosy, a design movement that I’m calling “sumptuous sackcloth and ashes”, and there’s a long counter that focuses on a central grill. We visited on day four, and the place was already packed with Smokestak cultists, Mangal 2 zealots and assorted food writers, all of them gazing at the fire and tearing at blistered, kaymak-slicked grilled pide, as well as seededramazanpide as fluffy as a Turkish morning after too many rakis.We began with courgette flowers, which at £7 each will make some people reach for the smelling salts. But these are not those flaccid petals draped over unseasoned ricotta with which Brits habitually offend the French. Here, the batter is intensely crisp, the goat’s cheese insides rich, with atom honey to cut through: it’s a crunchy, sticky, oozing delight. A round of bluefin tunaezme, a fine, fresh tartare in the Turkish style, comes on what can only be described as a poppadom-like cracker – fried, decadent and completely naughty.View image in fullscreenKid’s mastic ice-cream topped with mint oil ‘tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment’.The mackerel, however, is when you understand the point of all this live-fire hoopla. A huge butterflied fish with blackened skin comes crisp from the grill, its flesh all soft and meaty, and stuffed with a carrot-based slaw cooked in what tastes like rich, deep shellfish liquor. It’s the undoubted star of this show.We end with mountain tea rice pudding infused withsideritis, a wild Anatolian herb that’s warm and vaguely honeyed, and finished with a crunchy, brulee top; it’s also one of the finest desserts I’ve eaten all year. Don’t skimp on the mint oil-topped mastic ice-cream, either: it tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment.A very long lunch closed with shots of Turkish coffee that even Carter admitted tastes “slightly muddy”.
